# The plain tone. Cliff's notes: what happens, in order, no jokes.
#
# Format, tab-separated:   BOOK CH:FIRST-LAST<TAB>summary
#
# Sister file to summaries.txt (dry) and summaries-cheeky.txt (cheeky). All
# three are validated against the same day splits by ./build-summaries.py, and
# the page lets a reader flip between them. A day present in one file and not
# another renders whichever exists, labelled.
#
# This is the only tone with no attitude at all. Someone who missed a day and
# wants to know what they missed reads this one. State the events, the people
# and the outcome, in the order the passage gives them. No wry framing, no
# asides, no editorial. Being dull is allowed. Being wrong is not.
GEN 1:1-31	God creates the heavens and the earth, which begin formless and dark. Over six days he makes light and separates it from darkness; the sky; dry land and seas; vegetation; the sun, moon and stars; sea creatures and birds; land animals; and finally humans, male and female, in his own image, giving them authority over the other creatures. Plants are given to both humans and animals for food. At the end of the sixth day God reviews everything he has made and calls it very good.
GEN 2:1-25	God finishes his work on the seventh day, rests, and makes that day holy. The account then returns to the making of humanity. God forms a man from the dust and breathes life into him, and plants a garden in Eden, from which four rivers divide. The man is put there to tend it and told he may eat from any tree except the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, on pain of death. God judges it not good for the man to be alone and brings the animals to him to name, but no suitable partner is found. God puts the man to sleep, takes a rib, and forms a woman. The two are naked and unashamed.
GEN 3:1-24	The serpent tells the woman that eating from the forbidden tree will not kill her but make her like God, knowing good and evil. She eats and gives some to her husband. They realise they are naked and sew fig leaves together. God finds them hiding; the man blames the woman, the woman blames the serpent. God curses the serpent, tells the woman she will bear children in pain and be ruled by her husband, and curses the ground for the man's sake. He clothes them both in animal skins and drives them out of Eden, placing cherubim and a flaming sword to guard the way to the tree of life.
1CH 1:1-54	The book opens with nine generations listed as bare names, Adam to Noah, then the descendants of Japheth, Ham and Shem. Nimrod gets one line as a mighty man. The line narrows through Eber, whose son Peleg is named for the earth being divided, to Abraham. Then come Ishmael's twelve sons, the sons of Keturah, Isaac, and Esau's descendants with the clans of Seir. It closes with eight kings who reigned in Edom before Israel had any king, and eleven Edomite chiefs.
1CH 2:1-55	The twelve sons of Israel are listed, then Judah's line in detail. Er is killed by Yahweh for wickedness, Tamar bears Perez and Zerah, and Achar is named the troubler of Israel. Perez's line runs through Nahshon and Boaz to Jesse, whose sons are given with David seventh. Zeruiah's sons Abishai, Joab and Asahel follow. Hezron fathers a son at sixty; Sheshan, having no sons, marries his daughter to his Egyptian servant Jarha. Caleb's families close the chapter with the scribes of Jabez.
1CH 3:1-24	David's six sons born in Hebron are listed with their mothers, followed by the four sons of Bathshua including Solomon, and nine more born in Jerusalem, with Tamar named as their sister. He reigned seven and a half years in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem. The kings of Judah follow in order from Solomon to Josiah, then Josiah's four sons, Jeconiah the captive, Shealtiel and Zerubbabel. The list keeps going for six more generations past the exile, ending with Anani.
1CH 4:1-43	More families of Judah, including the potters and linen workers who lived with the king for his work. Jabez, named for the sorrow of his birth, prays for blessing and enlarged borders and God grants it. Simeon's line follows: Shimei has sixteen sons and six daughters, but the tribe as a whole did not multiply like Judah. Their towns are listed as theirs until David's reign. In Hezekiah's day they seize good pasture at Gedor, and five hundred men take Mount Seir from the surviving Amalekites.
1CH 5:1-26	Reuben was the firstborn, but his birthright went to Joseph's sons after he defiled his father's couch, while the ruling prince came from Judah. The Reubenites, Gadites and half-tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan are listed with their territories. Their forty-four thousand seven hundred sixty fighting men beat the Hagrites and take fifty thousand camels, two hundred fifty thousand sheep, two thousand donkeys and a hundred thousand captives. Later they worship the local gods, and God stirs up two Assyrian kings to deport them.
1CH 6:1-48	Levi's three sons head the chapter, then the high-priestly line from Aaron through Zadok down to Jehozadak, who went into captivity when Nebuchadnezzar carried Judah away. The families of Gershom, Kohath and Merari follow, including Samuel and his two sons. Then come the men David put over the music of Yahweh's house once the ark had a resting place: Heman the singer, Asaph on his right, Ethan on his left, each traced back generation by generation to Levi.
1CH 6:49-81	Aaron and his sons are the ones who offer on the altars and make atonement, as Moses commanded. His line is given again, Eleazar to Ahimaaz. Then the Levites' dwelling places: Hebron and twelve other towns to Aaron's sons, with the surrounding fields given to Caleb instead. Kohath's remaining families get ten cities, Gershom thirteen, Merari twelve, all assigned by lot from the other tribes. The rest of the chapter names each town with its pasture lands, cities of refuge included.
1CH 7:1-40	Issachar, Benjamin and Naphtali are listed with their fighting strength, Naphtali in a single verse. Manasseh's line includes Zelophehad, who had daughters. Ephraim's sons Ezer and Elead are killed by men of Gath while raiding livestock; Ephraim mourns for days, then fathers Beriah, named for the trouble in his house. His daughter Sheerah builds Upper and Lower Beth Horon and Uzzen Sheerah. The line runs on to Nun and Joshua. Asher closes with twenty-six thousand men fit for war.
1CH 8:1-40	Benjamin's descendants are given again, at greater length. Shaharaim fathers children in Moab after sending away his wives. Elpaal's sons build Ono and Lod, and Beriah and Shema drive out the inhabitants of Gath. Long strings of names follow, heads of households who lived in Jerusalem. The chapter ends with Saul's family: Ner fathered Kish, Kish fathered Saul, and Saul fathered Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab and Eshbaal, with Jonathan's line traced nine generations further to Azel and his six sons.
1CH 9:1-20	All Israel had been recorded by genealogy, and Judah went to Babylon for disobedience. The first to resettle their own towns were Israelites, priests, Levites and temple servants. Those living in Jerusalem are counted by family: six hundred ninety of Zerah's line, nine hundred fifty-six Benjaminites, and a thousand seven hundred sixty priests described as very able men for the service of God's house. Levites and gatekeepers follow, Shallum chief among them, with Phinehas named as their ruler in the past.
1CH 9:21-44	Two hundred twelve gatekeepers were appointed, ordained by David and Samuel the seer, posted on all four sides and relieved every seven days by their brothers from the villages. Four chief gatekeepers held the storerooms and treasuries and opened the house every morning. Others counted the vessels in and out, handled the flour, wine, oil and spices, baked in pans, or prepared the showbread each Sabbath. The singers lived in the rooms and were excused all other duty. The chapter closes by repeating Saul's genealogy.
1KI 1:1-27	David is old and cannot keep warm, so his servants find Abishag the Shunammite to attend him, though he does not know her intimately. Adonijah, Absalom's younger brother, declares himself king, acquires chariots, horsemen and fifty runners, and holds a sacrificial feast at the stone of Zoheleth with Joab and Abiathar backing him. He invites his brothers and the men of Judah, but not Nathan, Benaiah, the mighty men or Solomon. Nathan warns Bathsheba that her life and Solomon's are at stake and coaches her to remind David of his oath that Solomon would reign. She does so, adding that otherwise she and Solomon will be treated as criminals. Nathan enters and asks whether the king has really named Adonijah, since he was not invited.
1KI 1:28-53	David swears again that Solomon will reign, and Bathsheba blesses him. He orders Zadok, Nathan and Benaiah to set Solomon on the king's own mule, take him down to Gihon, anoint him, sound the trumpet and proclaim him king. Benaiah answers amen and prays Solomon's throne be greater than David's. It is done, and the people come up piping and rejoicing so that the earth shakes. Adonijah's guests hear the noise as they finish eating, and Jonathan son of Abiathar arrives with the full report: Solomon anointed, seated on the throne, and blessed by the king's servants. The guests scatter in fear, and Adonijah takes hold of the horns of the altar and asks for an oath that he will not be killed. Solomon says that if he proves worthy not a hair will fall, and sends him home.
1KI 2:1-23	Dying, David charges Solomon to be strong and keep the law of Moses so the promise of a man on the throne holds. He then leaves instructions: Joab, who killed Abner and Amasa, must not go to the grave in peace; the sons of Barzillai are to eat at the king's table; and Shimei, whom David swore not to kill himself, is not to be held guiltless. David dies after forty years, seven in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem, and Solomon's kingdom is established. Adonijah then asks Bathsheba to request Abishag as his wife. She takes it to Solomon, who is enthroned beside her, and he explodes: she may as well ask the kingdom for him, along with Abiathar and Joab, and he swears Adonijah has spoken against his own life.
1KI 2:24-46	Solomon has Benaiah kill Adonijah that day. Abiathar is spared for carrying the ark before David but banished to his fields at Anathoth, which fulfils the word spoken against the house of Eli. Joab flees to the Tent and takes hold of the altar, refusing to come out, so Solomon orders Benaiah to strike him there, citing the blood of Abner and Amasa, and he is buried at his own house in the wilderness. Benaiah is given the army and Zadok the priesthood. Shimei is confined to Jerusalem on pain of death if he crosses the Kidron; three years later he goes to Gath to recover two runaway slaves, and on his return Solomon has him killed for breaking the oath. The kingdom is established in Solomon's hand.
1KI 3:1-28	Solomon allies with Pharaoh and marries his daughter. The people still sacrifice at high places because no temple exists, and Solomon does the same, offering a thousand burnt offerings at Gibeon. There God appears in a dream and invites him to ask for anything. Solomon, calling himself a little child who does not know how to go out or come in, asks for an understanding heart to judge. God is pleased that he asked for neither long life, riches nor victory, grants unmatched wisdom, and adds riches and honour. Two prostitutes then bring a dispute over a living and a dead baby. Solomon calls for a sword and orders the child divided; the real mother begs him to give it away instead, and he awards her the child. All Israel hears and fears the king.
1KI 4:1-34	Solomon's officials are listed: Azariah the priest, two scribes, Jehoshaphat as recorder, Benaiah over the army, Zadok and Abiathar as priests, Zabud as the king's friend, and Adoniram over forced labour. Twelve district officers each supply the court for one month of the year. Israel and Judah are as numerous as sand, eating, drinking and merry, and Solomon rules from the Euphrates to Egypt with tribute and peace on every side. Daily provisions run to thirty cors of fine flour, ten fatted cattle, a hundred sheep and game besides, with forty thousand stalls of chariot horses. God gives him wisdom like the sand of the seashore; he speaks three thousand proverbs and a thousand and five songs, and describes trees, animals, birds and fish. Foreign kings send men to hear him.
1KI 5:1-18	Hiram of Tyre, who had always loved David, sends greetings to Solomon, who replies that his father could not build the temple because of constant war, but that he now has rest and intends to build. He asks for cedar to be cut in Lebanon, offering wages and Israelite labour, and admitting nobody cuts timber like the Sidonians. Hiram is delighted, blesses Yahweh for giving David a wise son, and agrees to float cedar and cypress by sea as rafts in exchange for food. Solomon sends him twenty thousand cors of wheat and twenty cors of pure oil yearly, and the two make a treaty. Solomon raises thirty thousand men working Lebanon in monthly shifts under Adoniram, with seventy thousand carriers, eighty thousand stonecutters and three thousand three hundred overseers.
1KI 6:1-18	In the four hundred and eightieth year after the exodus and the fourth year of his reign, in the month Ziv, Solomon begins the temple. It is sixty cubits long, twenty wide and thirty high, with a porch twenty by ten, latticed windows, and three storeys of side rooms around the walls, five, six and seven cubits wide, resting on offsets so no beams pierce the walls. The stone is dressed at the quarry, so no hammer, axe or iron tool is heard at the site. Yahweh tells Solomon that if he keeps the commandments the promise made to David will stand and he will dwell among Israel. The interior is lined with cedar from floor to ceiling on a cypress floor, carved with buds and open flowers, with no stone visible.
1KI 6:19-38	The inner sanctuary is prepared for the ark, twenty cubits each way, overlaid with pure gold, with gold chains drawn across in front of it and the whole house and its altar overlaid with gold. Two cherubim of olive wood, ten cubits high, stand inside with wings outstretched so that one wing touches each wall and the inner wings meet in the middle. All the walls are carved with cherubim, palm trees and open flowers, inside and out, and the floor is gold. The doors of the sanctuary are olive wood, the temple doors have folding cypress leaves, all carved and gilded. The inner court is three courses of cut stone and one of cedar beams. Founded in the fourth year in Ziv and finished in the eleventh year in Bul, it took seven years.
1KI 7:1-26	Solomon spends thirteen years on his own buildings. The House of the Forest of Lebanon is a hundred cubits by fifty by thirty on four rows of cedar pillars; there is a porch of pillars, a porch of judgment where he holds court, his own residence, and a house for Pharaoh's daughter, all of costly cut stone and cedar. He then brings Hiram of Tyre, son of a widow of Naphtali and a bronze worker, filled with skill. Hiram casts two bronze pillars eighteen cubits high with five-cubit capitals of network, chainwork, lilies and two hundred pomegranates each, set at the porch and named Jachin and Boaz. He also casts the round bronze sea, ten cubits across, standing on twelve oxen and holding two thousand baths.
1KI 7:27-51	Hiram makes ten bronze stands, four cubits by four by three, panelled with lions, oxen, cherubim and palm trees, each on four bronze wheels made like chariot wheels, all cast to one measure and one pattern. On each stand sits a bronze basin holding forty baths; five stands are placed on each side of the house, with the sea to the south-east. He finishes all his bronze work: pillars, capitals, networks, four hundred pomegranates, ten stands, ten basins, the sea and its twelve oxen, cast in the clay ground of the Jordan plain between Succoth and Zarethan. So much bronze is used that Solomon leaves it unweighed. The gold work follows: the altar, the showbread table, ten lampstands, lamps, tongs, cups, snuffers, spoons, fire pans and even the door hinges.
1KI 8:1-24	Solomon assembles the elders and tribal heads at the feast in the seventh month to bring the ark up from Zion. The priests carry the ark, the Tent of Meeting and the holy vessels, with countless sacrifices, and set the ark in the inner sanctuary under the wings of the cherubim; the carrying poles can be seen from the holy place. The ark holds nothing but the two stone tablets from Horeb. When the priests come out, a cloud fills the house so they cannot minister, because Yahweh's glory fills it. Solomon says Yahweh had spoken of dwelling in thick darkness, and that he has built him a house forever. He blesses the assembly, recalling that David wanted to build but was told his son would.
1KI 8:25-44	Solomon asks that the promise of a man on David's throne be kept, then admits that heaven itself cannot contain God, much less this house, and asks only that God's eyes be open toward the place where his name is, hearing from heaven and forgiving. He then works through cases: a man swearing an oath at the altar, defeat by enemies, drought, famine, plague, blight, locust and siege, asking each time that God hear, forgive, and give each man according to his heart. He also asks for the foreigner who comes from a far country because of God's name, so that all peoples may know it, and for Israel praying toward the city when sent out to battle.
1KI 8:45-66	Solomon's last petitions cover captivity: since no one is without sin, if they are carried off and repent in the land of their captors, praying toward this land and this house, he asks God to hear, forgive, and move their captors to compassion, since they are his inheritance brought out of the iron furnace of Egypt. He rises from kneeling with hands spread out and blesses the assembly aloud, saying not one word of God's promise through Moses has failed, and urging them to keep their hearts perfect with Yahweh. The peace offerings come to twenty-two thousand cattle and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep, since the bronze altar was too small for the whole offering. The feast lasts seven days and seven more, and on the eighth day he sends the people home glad.
1KI 9:1-28	Yahweh appears to Solomon a second time, saying he has heard his prayer, but warning that if Solomon or his children turn to other gods, Israel will be cut off, the house cast away, and the nation become a proverb, with passers-by asking why. Hiram, who supplied timber and gold, is given twenty cities in Galilee, is unimpressed, calls them the land of Cabul, and sends a hundred and twenty talents of gold. The forced levy built the temple, the palace, Millo, Jerusalem's wall, Hazor, Megiddo, Gezer and the storage and chariot cities. Solomon conscripts the surviving Canaanite peoples as bondservants but not Israelites, with five hundred and fifty overseers. He builds a fleet at Ezion Geber, and Hiram's sailors bring four hundred and twenty talents of gold from Ophir.
1KI 10:1-29	The queen of Sheba comes to test Solomon with hard questions, bringing camels loaded with spices, gold and jewels. He answers everything, and when she has seen his wisdom, his house, his table and his officials, there is no spirit left in her. She says the report she heard was not half of it, and gives a hundred and twenty talents of gold. Hiram's fleet brings almug wood and jewels from Ophir, used for pillars and instruments. Solomon's annual gold income is six hundred and sixty-six talents; he makes gold shields, an ivory throne with six steps and twelve lions, and gold drinking vessels, silver being reckoned worthless. Ships bring gold, ivory, apes and peacocks every three years. He keeps fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen, trading horses out of Egypt.
1KI 11:1-23	Solomon loves many foreign women from the nations Yahweh had warned about, seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, and in his old age they turn his heart to other gods: Ashtoreth of Sidon, Milcom of Ammon, and high places for Chemosh and Molech. Yahweh, angry because he had appeared to Solomon twice and commanded him otherwise, says he will tear the kingdom away and give it to a servant, though not in Solomon's lifetime and not entirely, leaving one tribe for David's sake. Adversaries are raised up: Hadad the Edomite, who as a child escaped Joab's slaughter of every male in Edom and grew up favoured in Pharaoh's house, and who asks leave to go home once David and Joab are dead; and Rezon son of Eliada.
1KI 11:24-43	Rezon gathers a troop, takes Damascus and reigns over Syria, hostile to Israel all Solomon's days. Jeroboam son of Nebat, an industrious Ephraimite whom Solomon had put in charge of the forced labour of the house of Joseph, also rebels. The prophet Ahijah the Shilonite meets him alone in a field, tears his own new garment into twelve pieces, and tells him to take ten: Yahweh will tear the kingdom from Solomon and give him ten tribes, leaving one so David may have a lamp in Jerusalem, because of the worship of Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom. If Jeroboam keeps the commandments he will be given a sure house like David's. Solomon tries to kill him, and he flees to Shishak of Egypt until Solomon dies. Solomon reigns forty years and Rehoboam succeeds him.
1KI 12:1-17	Rehoboam goes to Shechem to be made king, and Jeroboam is called back from Egypt. The assembly asks him to lighten the hard service and heavy yoke his father laid on them, and they will serve him. He sends them away for three days. The elders who served Solomon advise him to be a servant to the people and answer them kindly. He rejects that and asks the young men he grew up with, who tell him to say his little finger is thicker than his father's waist, that he will add to the yoke, and that where his father used whips he will use scorpions. On the third day he answers roughly in those words, because this was brought about by Yahweh to fulfil Ahijah's word. Israel replies that they have no share in David, and goes home.
1KI 12:18-33	Rehoboam sends Adoram, his officer over forced labour, and Israel stones him to death, while the king flees to Jerusalem by chariot. Israel makes Jeroboam king, and only Judah follows David's house. Rehoboam musters a hundred and eighty thousand men from Judah and Benjamin, but Shemaiah the man of God tells them not to fight their brothers because this is from Yahweh, and they go home. Jeroboam fortifies Shechem and Penuel, then reasons that if the people sacrifice in Jerusalem they will return to Rehoboam and kill him. So he makes two golden calves, sets one in Bethel and one in Dan, and calls them the gods who brought Israel out of Egypt. He builds high places, appoints priests who are not Levites, and invents a feast in the eighth month.
1KI 13:1-17	A man of God comes from Judah to Bethel while Jeroboam is burning incense, and cries out against the altar that a son named Josiah will be born to David's house who will sacrifice its priests on it. The sign is that the altar will split and its ashes pour out. Jeroboam points at him and orders his arrest, and his hand withers; the altar splits as promised. At the king's request the man of God prays and the hand is restored. Invited home for a reward, he refuses, saying he was commanded to eat no bread, drink no water and not return by the way he came. An old prophet in Bethel hears of it, rides after him, finds him under an oak and invites him to eat; he refuses again.
1KI 13:18-34	The old prophet claims an angel told him to bring the man of God home to eat, which is a lie, and the man of God goes back with him and eats and drinks. At the table Yahweh's word comes to the old prophet, who announces that because his guest disobeyed, his body will not reach his fathers' tomb. On the road a lion kills him and stands beside the body with the donkey, eating neither. Travellers report it, and the old prophet fetches the body, buries it in his own grave, mourns him as a brother, and tells his sons to lay his bones beside the man of God's. Jeroboam does not turn from his way, consecrating as priests of the high places anyone who wanted the office, which became the sin that destroyed his house.
1KI 14:1-14	When Jeroboam's son Abijah falls ill, Jeroboam tells his wife to disguise herself, take bread, cakes and honey, and ask the prophet Ahijah at Shiloh what will happen to the boy. Ahijah is blind with age, but Yahweh tells him she is coming and what to say. He recognises her step and calls her in by name. The message is that God raised Jeroboam up and tore the kingdom from David's house for him, yet he has been nothing like David, making molten images and casting God behind his back; therefore his whole house will be swept away like dung, with dogs and birds eating the dead. Her son will die as she reaches the city, mourned by all Israel because some good was found in him.
1KI 14:15-31	Yahweh will shake Israel like a reed, uproot it from the land and scatter it beyond the River because of its Asherah poles and Jeroboam's sins. Jeroboam's wife reaches Tirzah, and the child dies as she crosses the threshold; all Israel mourns and buries him. Jeroboam reigns twenty-two years and Nadab succeeds him. In Judah, Rehoboam reigns seventeen years from the age of forty-one, his mother Naamah an Ammonite. Judah does evil, building high places, pillars and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every green tree, with cult prostitutes in the land, following the practices of the nations. In Rehoboam's fifth year Shishak of Egypt takes the treasures of the temple and palace, including Solomon's gold shields, which Rehoboam replaces with bronze ones carried by the guard. There was war with Jeroboam continually, and Abijam succeeds him.
1KI 15:1-19	Abijam reigns three years in Judah, walking in his father's sins, though for David's sake he is given a lamp in Jerusalem, since David did right all his life except in the matter of Uriah. Asa succeeds him and reigns forty-one years, doing right like David: he removes the cult prostitutes and the idols his fathers made, deposes his mother Maacah as queen for making an Asherah image, and burns it at the Kidron, though the high places remain. He brings dedicated silver, gold and vessels into the temple. War with Baasha of Israel lasts all their days, and when Baasha fortifies Ramah to blockade Judah, Asa sends the remaining temple and palace treasure to Ben Hadad of Syria, asking him to break his treaty with Baasha.
1KI 15:20-34	Ben Hadad agrees, striking Ijon, Dan, Abel Beth Maacah, all Chinneroth and Naphtali, so Baasha abandons Ramah and stays in Tirzah. Asa then conscripts all Judah, with nobody exempt, to carry off Ramah's stone and timber and build Geba and Mizpah with it. In old age he is diseased in his feet, and Jehoshaphat succeeds him. In Israel, Nadab son of Jeroboam reigns two years and does evil in his father's way, until Baasha son of Ahijah, of Issachar, kills him at the siege of Gibbethon and takes the throne. Baasha then destroys every last member of Jeroboam's house, as Ahijah the Shilonite had said would happen because of Jeroboam's sins. War with Asa continues all their days, and Baasha reigns twenty-four years in Tirzah, walking in Jeroboam's way himself.
1KI 16:1-17	Yahweh's word comes through Jehu son of Hanani against Baasha: raised out of the dust and made prince, he walked in Jeroboam's way, so his house will be swept away like Jeroboam's, with dogs and birds eating his dead. Baasha dies and Elah his son reigns two years in Tirzah. Zimri, captain of half his chariots, conspires and kills him while he is getting drunk in Arza's house, then wipes out the whole house of Baasha, relatives and friends alike, fulfilling Jehu's word against Baasha and Elah. Zimri reigns seven days. The army, camped against Gibbethon, hears of the conspiracy and makes Omri, its commander, king that same day; Omri marches from Gibbethon and besieges Tirzah.
1KI 16:18-34	Seeing the city taken, Zimri burns the palace down over himself and dies. Israel then splits between Tibni and Omri, and Omri's supporters prevail. Omri reigns twelve years, six of them in Tirzah, then buys the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver, builds a city there and names it after him. He does evil, worse than any before him. Ahab his son reigns twenty-two years in Samaria and does worse still: he marries Jezebel daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, serves Baal, builds him a temple and altar in Samaria, and makes an Asherah, provoking Yahweh more than all the kings before him. In his time Hiel of Bethel rebuilds Jericho, losing his firstborn Abiram and his youngest Segub, as Joshua had said.
1KI 17:1-24	Elijah the Tishbite tells Ahab there will be no dew or rain except by his word, then is sent to hide by the brook Cherith, where ravens bring him bread and meat until the brook dries up. He is sent to Zarephath in Sidon, where a widow says she has only a handful of meal and a little oil and is preparing a last meal for herself and her son. Elijah tells her to bake for him first, promising the meal and oil will not run out until rain comes, and they eat for many days. Later her son sickens and stops breathing, and she accuses Elijah of coming to kill him. Elijah carries him upstairs, stretches himself on him three times and prays, and the child revives. She says she now knows he is a man of God.
1KI 18:1-24	In the third year Yahweh sends Elijah to show himself to Ahab, promising rain. Ahab and Obadiah, his household officer who had hidden a hundred prophets in caves when Jezebel was killing them, split the land to look for grass. Elijah meets Obadiah, who is afraid to announce him because Ahab has searched every kingdom for him and would kill the messenger if Elijah vanished. Elijah swears he will appear that day. Ahab greets him as the troubler of Israel; Elijah replies that Ahab's house are the troublers, for following the Baals, and calls for all Israel and four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal at Carmel. He asks how long they will waver, gets silence, and proposes two bulls and no fire: the god who answers by fire is God.
1KI 18:25-46	Baal's prophets go first, calling from morning to noon and leaping around the altar with no answer. Elijah suggests their god may be thinking, away, travelling, or asleep. They cut themselves with knives until the blood runs and prophesy until evening, with no voice and no answer. Elijah repairs Yahweh's altar with twelve stones, digs a trench, lays the wood and the bull, and has twelve jars of water poured over it. At the evening offering he prays that the people may know Yahweh is God, and fire falls and consumes the offering, the wood, the stones, the dust and the water. The people fall on their faces, and Elijah has the prophets of Baal killed at the Kishon. At a cloud like a hand the sky blackens, and Elijah runs ahead of Ahab's chariot to Jezreel.
1MA 1:1-29	Alexander the Macedonian beats Darius, conquers to the ends of the earth, divides his kingdom among his officers and dies after twelve years. His successors crown themselves and multiply evils. Antiochus Epiphanes takes the throne in the 137th year. Men from Israel persuade others to make a covenant with the Gentiles; the king licenses it, and they build a gymnasium in Jerusalem and undo their circumcision. Antiochus defeats Ptolemy in Egypt, then turns on Jerusalem, stripping the golden altar, lampstand, table and vessels and scaling the gold off the temple front. Israel mourns. Two years later he sends a chief tribute collector with a large force.
1MA 1:30-64	The collector speaks peaceably, then attacks the city, kills many, burns and plunders it, and fortifies the city of David as a citadel manned by renegades. Jerusalem empties, her feasts turned to mourning. Antiochus decrees his whole kingdom be one people with one law: no burnt offerings, Sabbaths profaned, swine's flesh sacrificed, sons left uncircumcised, all on pain of death. On the fifteenth of Chislev, the 145th year, an abomination of desolation is built on the altar. Copies of the law are torn up and burned. Women who had their children circumcised are put to death with their babies. Many choose death over eating unclean food.
1MA 2:1-34	Mattathias, a priest of the sons of Joarib, leaves Jerusalem for Modin with five sons: John Gaddis, Simon Thassi, Judas Maccabaeus, Eleazar Avaran and Jonathan Apphus. Seeing the desecration, he tears his clothes and mourns. The king's officers come to Modin and offer him silver, gold and the rank of the king's Friend if he sacrifices first. He refuses for himself and his house. When a Jew steps up to the altar to sacrifice, Mattathias kills him and the officer, pulls down the altar, and calls everyone zealous for the law to follow him into the mountains. Others flee to the wilderness, where troops corner them on the Sabbath.
1MA 2:35-70	The refugees will not fight or even block the entrances, and about a thousand die with their wives, children and cattle. Mattathias and his friends decide they will fight if attacked on the Sabbath rather than be wiped out. Hasidaeans join them; they tear down altars, circumcise uncircumcised children by force, and rescue the law. Dying, Mattathias tells his sons to be zealous and recites the examples of Abraham, Joseph, Phinehas, Joshua, Caleb, David, Elijah, the three in the flame and Daniel. He names Simon as counselor and Judas as commander, blesses them, and dies in the 146th year, buried at Modin.
1MA 3:1-31	Judas Maccabaeus succeeds his father, described as a lion roaring for prey. He kills Apollonius in battle and keeps his sword for the rest of his life. Seron of Syria comes looking to make a name, and Judas meets him at the pass of Bethhoron with a small company who have not eaten; Judas tells them strength comes from heaven, not numbers, and routs Seron, leaving about eight hundred dead. Antiochus, furious, musters his forces and pays them a year in advance, then finds his treasury short because of the trouble he has caused, and heads for Persia to collect tribute.
1MA 3:32-60	Antiochus leaves Lysias in charge from the Euphrates to Egypt, with half the army, the elephants and the king's son, and orders to destroy Israel and settle strangers on the land. Lysias sends Ptolemy, Nicanor and Gorgias with forty thousand foot and seven thousand horse to Emmaus. Slave dealers arrive with silver and fetters to buy Jewish captives. Judas gathers the people at Mizpeh, where they fast, wear sackcloth and ashes, spread open the book of the law, bring out priests' garments, first fruits and tithes, and pray. He appoints captains of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens, and sends home the newly betrothed, the builders, the planters and the fearful as the law allows.
1MA 4:1-33	Gorgias takes five thousand foot and a thousand horse to fall on Judas by night, guided by men from the citadel. Judas slips past him and attacks the camp at Emmaus instead, so Gorgias finds nobody. At dawn Judas appears in the plain with three thousand poorly armed men, reminds them of the Red Sea, and routs the enemy, killing about three thousand in the pursuit. He forbids looting because Gorgias is still in the hills; Gorgias sees the smoke of the burning camp and flees. Only then do they take the spoils. The next year Lysias returns with sixty thousand foot and five thousand horse to Bethsura, and Judas meets him with ten thousand and prays.
1MA 4:34-61	About five thousand of Lysias's men fall, and Lysias withdraws to Antioch to hire more. Judas goes up to Mount Zion and finds the sanctuary desolate, the gates burned and shrubs growing in the courts. Blameless priests cleanse the place, carry the defiled stones away, and pull down the profaned altar, storing its stones until a prophet can say what to do with them. They build a new altar of whole stones, make new vessels, and on the twenty-fifth of Chislev in the 148th year, the same day it was profaned, rededicate it with songs, harps, lutes and cymbals. The eight-day feast is made annual. They fortify Mount Zion and Bethsura.
1MA 5:1-23	The surrounding nations, angry that the altar has been rebuilt, begin killing the Jews living among them. Judas defeats the children of Esau at Akrabattine, destroys the sons of Baean in their towers, and beats Timotheus and the Ammonites, taking Jazer. Letters arrive from Jews besieged in the stronghold of Dathema in Gilead, and while they are still being read, messengers from Galilee turn up with their clothes torn. Judas sends Simon with three thousand men to Galilee and takes eight thousand to Gilead with Jonathan, leaving Joseph and Azarias to hold Judea with orders not to fight. Simon drives the enemy to the gate of Ptolemais and brings the Galilean Jews home.
1MA 5:24-44	Judas and Jonathan cross the Jordan and march three days into the wilderness, where friendly Nabathaeans tell them Jews are shut up in Bosora, Bosor, Alema, Casphor, Maked and Carnaim, and are to be destroyed the next day. Judas takes Bosora, marches through the night, and arrives at the stronghold as it is being stormed. He attacks from behind in three companies with trumpets, and about eight thousand of Timotheus's men fall. More cities are taken. Timotheus regroups at Raphon with hired Arabians, planning to attack only if Judas hesitates at the brook. Judas crosses first; the enemy flee to the temple at Carnaim, which is burned.
1MA 5:45-68	Judas gathers every Jew in Gilead, with wives, children and goods, to bring back to Judah. Ephron sits across the only road and shuts its gates against his offer of peaceful passage, so he storms it, kills the males and razes it. They cross the Jordan and reach Mount Zion without losing a man, and offer burnt offerings. Meanwhile Joseph and Azarias, wanting a name of their own, disobey orders and attack Jamnia; Gorgias routs them and about two thousand Israelites fall, because they were not of the family through whom deliverance came. Judas then strikes Hebron and Azotus, burns the idols, and returns to Judah.
1SA 1:1-28	Elkanah of Ramathaim Zophim has two wives: Peninnah, who has children, and Hannah, who has none. Each year he sacrifices at Shiloh, where Eli's sons Hophni and Phinehas are priests, and each year Peninnah provokes Hannah until she weeps and will not eat. Elkanah asks whether he is not better to her than ten sons. At the temple Hannah prays silently, vowing that if she is given a son she will give him to Yahweh and no razor will touch his head. Eli, seeing only her lips move, accuses her of being drunk; she explains, and he blesses her. She conceives and bears Samuel, whose name she ties to having asked for him. Once he is weaned she brings him to Shiloh with bulls, meal and wine, and gives him to Yahweh for life.
1SA 2:1-20	Hannah prays a song: her heart exults, God weighs actions, the bows of the mighty break while the stumbling are armed, the full hire themselves out for bread while the hungry are filled, the barren bears seven. Yahweh kills and makes alive, brings low and lifts up, raises the poor from the dust to sit with princes, and will give strength to his king. Elkanah goes home and the boy serves before Eli. Eli's sons, meanwhile, are wicked men who do not know Yahweh: their servants take meat with a three-pronged fork before the fat is burned and demand it raw, by force if refused. Samuel ministers in a linen ephod, and his mother brings him a new robe each year. Eli blesses Elkanah and Hannah.
1SA 2:21-36	Hannah bears three more sons and two daughters, and Samuel grows up before Yahweh. Eli, very old, hears that his sons sleep with the women serving at the door of the Tent of Meeting, and rebukes them: a man who sins against Yahweh has nobody to intercede for him. They do not listen, because Yahweh intends to kill them. A man of God asks Eli why he honours his sons above God and grows fat on Israel's offerings. The promise that his father's house would serve forever is revoked: no old man will be left in it, his descendants will die young, and Hophni and Phinehas will both die on one day as the sign. God will raise a faithful priest instead, and Eli's survivors will beg him for a post and a loaf of bread.
1SA 3:1-21	Samuel serves Eli at a time when Yahweh's word is rare and visions few. Eli's eyes are failing. One night, with the lamp still burning and Samuel lying near the ark, Yahweh calls him; three times he runs to Eli, who finally understands and tells him to answer that his servant is listening. Yahweh says he will do something in Israel that will make both ears of every hearer tingle, and will carry out everything he said against Eli's house, whose guilt no sacrifice will ever remove, because Eli knew what his sons were doing and did not restrain them. Samuel is afraid to repeat it, but Eli demands it and accepts it. Samuel grows, none of his words fall to the ground, and all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knows he is a prophet.
1SA 4:1-22	Israel fights the Philistines at Ebenezer and loses about four thousand men, so the elders send to Shiloh for the ark of the covenant, which arrives with Hophni and Phinehas. Israel's shout makes the ground ring, and the Philistines, recognising the ark and remembering the plagues on Egypt, tell each other to fight like men. Israel is routed: thirty thousand foot soldiers fall, the ark is captured, and both of Eli's sons are killed. A Benjamite runs to Shiloh with torn clothes and dirt on his head. Eli, ninety-eight and blind, is sitting by the road; when he hears the ark is taken he falls backward off his seat, breaks his neck and dies, having judged Israel forty years. Phinehas' wife goes into labour, names the child Ichabod, and dies saying the glory has departed from Israel.
1SA 5:1-12	The Philistines take the ark from Ebenezer to Ashdod and set it beside Dagon in his temple. The next morning Dagon has fallen face down before the ark; they set him up again, and the following morning he has fallen again with his head and both hands broken off on the threshold, which is why nobody there steps on it. Yahweh's hand grows heavy on Ashdod and its territory, striking the people with tumors, so they call the Philistine lords together and the ark is sent to Gath, where the same thing happens. Sent on to Ekron, it is met with the cry that it has come to kill them. The lords agree to send it back to its own place; those who did not die were struck with tumors, and the city's outcry went up to heaven.
1SA 6:1-21	After seven months the Philistines ask their priests how to return the ark, and are told not to send it empty but with a guilt offering: five golden tumors and five golden mice, one for each lord, and a warning not to harden their hearts as Pharaoh did. They put the ark on a new cart drawn by two milk cows that have never been yoked, shut the calves up at home, and let it go as a test. The cows go straight to Beth Shemesh, lowing, without turning aside. The people are reaping wheat and rejoice; the cart stops at a great stone in Joshua's field, the cows are offered up, and the Levites set the ark down. Fifty thousand and seventy men are struck for looking into it, so the town sends for Kiriath Jearim.
1SA 7:1-17	Kiriath Jearim brings the ark to Abinadab's house on the hill and consecrates his son Eleazar to keep it, where it stays twenty years while Israel laments after Yahweh. Samuel tells them to put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth and serve Yahweh only. They do, and gather at Mizpah, where they pour out water, fast and confess, and Samuel judges them. When the Philistines march up, Israel begs Samuel to keep crying out for them. As he offers a suckling lamb, Yahweh thunders and throws the Philistines into confusion, and Israel pursues them past Beth Kar. Samuel sets up a stone called Ebenezer. The captured cities from Ekron to Gath are restored, and Samuel judges Israel on a circuit of Bethel, Gilgal, Mizpah and Ramah for life.
1SA 8:1-22	Samuel, now old, makes his sons Joel and Abijah judges at Beersheba, but they take bribes, chase dishonest gain and pervert justice. The elders come to Ramah and ask for a king to judge them like all the nations. Samuel is displeased and prays; Yahweh tells him to listen, since it is not Samuel they have rejected but God himself, as they have done since Egypt, but to warn them plainly what a king will be. Samuel lists it: he will take their sons for his chariots and armies, their daughters as cooks and perfumers, the best of their fields, vineyards and olive groves, a tenth of their grain, vineyards and flocks, their servants and donkeys, and they will be his servants and cry out unanswered. The people refuse to listen, and Yahweh tells Samuel to make them a king.
1SA 9:1-13	Kish, a Benjamite of standing, has a son named Saul, an impressive young man taller than anyone in Israel from the shoulders up. When Kish's donkeys go missing, Saul and a servant search Ephraim, Shalishah, Shaalim and Benjamin without finding them. In the land of Zuph Saul wants to turn back before his father starts worrying about them instead, but the servant says there is a man of God in the city whose words always come true. Saul objects that they have no gift; the servant has a quarter shekel of silver. The narrator notes that a prophet used to be called a seer. Girls drawing water tell them the seer has come to the city for a sacrifice at the high place and can be caught before he goes up.
1SA 9:14-27	Samuel comes out to meet them, having been told the day before that a man from Benjamin would arrive to be anointed prince over Israel and would save the people from the Philistines. Saul, not recognising him, asks where the seer's house is. Samuel says he is the seer, invites Saul to eat with him, promises to tell him everything in the morning, says the donkeys are found, and hints that everything desirable in Israel belongs to him. Saul protests that he is from the smallest tribe and the least family in it. Samuel seats him at the head of thirty guests and has the cook bring out a thigh reserved for him. They talk on the roof, and at dawn Samuel sends the servant ahead so that Saul can hear God's message alone.
1SA 10:1-27	Samuel pours oil on Saul's head, kisses him, and gives him three signs: two men at Rachel's tomb reporting the donkeys found, three men at the oak of Tabor giving him two loaves, and a band of prophets at the hill of God where the Spirit will come on him and turn him into another man. He is to go to Gilgal and wait seven days. All of it happens, and those who know him ask whether Saul is also among the prophets, which becomes a proverb. Asked by his uncle, Saul mentions the donkeys and not the kingdom. At Mizpah Samuel rebukes Israel for rejecting God, then casts lots: Benjamin, the Matrites, Saul, who is found hiding in the baggage. The people shout for the king, though some despise him.
1SA 11:1-15	Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh Gilead and offers terms only if every right eye is gouged out, to disgrace all Israel. The elders ask for seven days to seek help. When the messengers reach Gibeah the people weep, and Saul, coming in behind his oxen, asks why. The Spirit comes on him and his anger burns: he cuts a yoke of oxen in pieces and sends them through Israel, warning that anyone who does not follow him and Samuel will get the same. Three hundred thousand come, with thirty thousand from Judah. He promises rescue by the heat of the next day, attacks in three companies at the morning watch, and scatters the Ammonites. When the people want the earlier doubters executed, Saul refuses. At Gilgal the kingdom is renewed and Saul made king.
1SA 12:1-25	Samuel tells Israel he has given them the king they asked for, and challenges anyone to name an ox, a donkey or a bribe he ever took; they clear him, and he calls Yahweh and the anointed king as witnesses. He then reviews the history: Egypt, the forgetting, Sisera and the Philistines and Moab, the deliverers Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah and Samuel, and finally their demand for a king when Nahash came, though Yahweh was already king. If they fear Yahweh, both they and the king will be his; if not, his hand will be against them. To prove the point he calls for thunder and rain in wheat harvest, and gets it. The frightened people ask him to pray for them, and he promises not to stop, while warning that continued evil will consume them and their king.
1SA 13:1-23	Saul, king at thirty, keeps three thousand men, two thousand with him and a thousand with Jonathan, who attacks the Philistine garrison at Geba. The Philistines muster thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen and troops beyond counting at Michmash, and Israel hides in caves, thickets, rocks, tombs and pits, some crossing the Jordan. Saul waits the seven days Samuel set, and as his men scatter he offers the burnt offering himself. Samuel arrives immediately after and tells him he has acted foolishly: his kingdom will not continue, and Yahweh has sought a man after his own heart. Saul is left with about six hundred men at Geba while Philistine raiders go out in three companies. There is no blacksmith in Israel, so only Saul and Jonathan have a sword or spear.
1SA 14:1-26	Without telling his father, Jonathan and his armour bearer cross toward the Philistine garrison between the crags Bozez and Seneh, saying Yahweh can save by many or by few. They agree on a sign: if the Philistines tell them to come up, that is the signal. The garrison mocks them and invites them up, so Jonathan climbs on hands and feet and the two kill about twenty men in a small space. Panic spreads through the camp and the earth quakes. Saul's watchmen see the enemy melting away, a roll call shows Jonathan missing, and Saul calls for the ark then breaks off as the tumult grows. The Philistines strike each other, defectors and hidden Israelites join the pursuit, and Saul binds the people by oath to eat nothing until evening.
1SA 14:27-52	Jonathan, who never heard the oath, dips his staff in honeycomb and his eyes brighten; told of it, he says his father has troubled the land and that a fed army would have won a greater victory. The Philistines are beaten from Michmash to Aijalon, and the starving people slaughter plunder on the ground and eat it with the blood, so Saul has a great stone rolled up for proper slaughtering and builds his first altar. He proposes a night pursuit, but God does not answer, so he casts lots to find the sin, swearing that even Jonathan will die. The lot falls on Jonathan, who admits the honey; Saul insists on the sentence and the people refuse and rescue him. Saul fights Moab, Ammon, Edom, Zobah, the Philistines and Amalek, and recruits every strong man he sees.
1SA 15:1-35	Samuel sends Saul to destroy Amalek completely for what it did to Israel after Egypt. Saul musters two hundred and ten thousand men, warns the Kenites to leave, and strikes Amalek from Havilah toward Shur, but keeps Agag alive along with the best livestock, destroying only what was worthless. Yahweh tells Samuel he regrets making Saul king. Saul claims to have obeyed; Samuel asks what the bleating is. Saul blames the people and says the animals were for sacrifice. Samuel answers that obedience is better than sacrifice and that Yahweh has rejected him as king. Saul admits he feared the people, grabs Samuel's robe and tears it, and is told the kingdom is torn from him. Samuel kills Agag at Gilgal and never sees Saul again.
1SA 16:1-23	Yahweh tells Samuel to stop mourning and to take oil to Jesse of Bethlehem, one of whose sons is the new king. Fearing Saul, Samuel goes with a heifer and calls it a sacrifice. The elders meet him trembling. He assumes Eliab is the one, and is told that people look at appearance while Yahweh looks at the heart. Seven sons pass and none is chosen; the youngest is out with the sheep, and Samuel refuses to sit down until he comes. David is brought in and anointed among his brothers, and the Spirit comes on him from that day. The Spirit leaves Saul and an evil spirit from Yahweh troubles him, so his servants find a harpist. David is recommended and sent for, becomes Saul's armour bearer, and his playing relieves the king.
1SA 17:1-31	The Philistines camp between Socoh and Azekah, Israel in the valley of Elah. Goliath of Gath, six cubits and a span tall, in bronze helmet and a coat of mail weighing five thousand shekels, with a spear like a weaver's beam, offers single combat to decide the war and defies Israel morning and evening for forty days. Saul and all Israel are terrified. David, youngest of Jesse's eight sons, is sent with grain, loaves and cheeses for his three eldest brothers and their captain. He hears the challenge and asks what the man who kills the Philistine will get, and who this man is to defy the armies of the living God. Eliab accuses him of pride. His words reach Saul, who sends for him.
1SA 17:32-58	David tells Saul not to lose heart and offers to fight. Saul objects that he is only a boy, so David recounts killing a lion and a bear that took lambs from his flock. Saul dresses him in armour, which David takes off because he has not tested it, and takes his staff, five smooth stones and his sling. Goliath despises him, asks whether he is a dog to be met with sticks, and curses him by his gods. David answers that he comes in the name of Yahweh of Armies, who does not save with sword and spear. He slings a stone into his forehead, then takes Goliath's sword and cuts off his head. The Philistines flee to Ekron. Saul asks Abner whose son the boy is, and David says he is Jesse's.
1SA 18:1-30	Jonathan binds himself to David in a covenant and gives him his robe, sword, bow and sash. Saul keeps David at court and sets him over the men of war, and he does well. But the women sing that Saul killed thousands and David ten thousands, and Saul, angry, wonders what is left for David but the kingdom, and watches him from then on. Twice he throws his spear at David while David plays the harp, and twice David escapes. Saul, afraid because Yahweh is with David, makes him captain over a thousand. He offers Merab, then marries her elsewhere, then offers Michal, who loves David, for a dowry of a hundred Philistine foreskins, hoping the Philistines will kill him. David brings two hundred. Saul gives him Michal and becomes his permanent enemy.
1SA 19:1-24	Saul tells Jonathan and his servants to kill David. Jonathan warns David to hide, then argues his case: David has not sinned, he risked his life against the Philistine, and killing him would be innocent blood. Saul swears David will not die, and David returns to court and fights the Philistines again. Then the evil spirit comes and Saul throws his spear while David plays, striking the wall, and David flees that night. Saul posts men to kill him in the morning, but Michal lets him down through a window and puts a household idol in the bed, saying he is sick. David reaches Samuel at Ramah and they stay at Naioth. Three sets of messengers sent to seize him prophesy instead, and so does Saul, who strips and lies naked a day and a night.
1SA 20:1-20	David comes to Jonathan asking what he has done to deserve being hunted. Jonathan insists his father tells him everything, but David swears there is only a step between him and death. They agree on a test: David will miss the new moon meal and hide in the field, and Jonathan will say he asked leave to attend the family sacrifice at Bethlehem. If Saul takes it well, David is safe; if he is angry, the intent is settled. In the field Jonathan swears to tell him either way, and asks in return that David keep faith with his house forever. He arranges a signal: he will shoot three arrows near the stone Ezel.
1SA 20:21-42	Jonathan explains the code: if he tells the boy the arrows are on this side, David is safe; if beyond, he must go. At the new moon feast David's seat is empty and Saul says nothing, assuming ritual uncleanness. On the second day he asks where the son of Jesse is, and Jonathan gives the Bethlehem story. Saul's anger breaks out; he insults Jonathan and his mother, tells him he will never be established while David lives, and orders David brought to be killed. Jonathan asks what David has done, and Saul throws his spear at him. Jonathan leaves the table in anger and eats nothing. In the morning he shoots an arrow beyond the boy and calls out the words, sends the boy away with his weapons, and he and David weep together and part.
1SA 21:1-15	David comes alone to Ahimelech the priest at Nob, who meets him trembling and asks why he has no men. David says the king has sent him on secret business and asks for bread. The only bread is the holy showbread, which Ahimelech gives once David assures him his men have kept from women. Doeg the Edomite, Saul's chief herdsman, is there that day. David also asks for a weapon, and is given the sword of Goliath, kept wrapped behind the ephod; he says there is none like it. He then flees to Achish king of Gath, whose servants recognise him as the David of the song. Afraid, David feigns madness, scribbling on the gate doors and letting spittle run into his beard, and Achish asks why a madman has been brought to him.
1SA 22:1-23	David escapes to the cave of Adullam, where his family joins him and about four hundred men in distress, debt or discontent gather to him as their captain. He settles his parents with the king of Moab, and the prophet Gad tells him to leave the stronghold for Judah, so he goes to the forest of Hereth. Saul, spear in hand under a tamarisk at Gibeah, accuses his Benjamites of conspiring with his son. Doeg reports that Ahimelech gave David bread, an oracle and Goliath's sword. Ahimelech protests David's loyalty and his own ignorance, and Saul condemns him and his whole family. The guards refuse to kill priests, so Doeg does it: eighty-five men in linen ephods, then all of Nob, people and livestock. Only Abiathar escapes to David, who takes responsibility and shelters him.
1SA 23:1-29	Hearing the Philistines are raiding Keilah, David asks Yahweh twice, because his men are afraid, and is told to go; he defeats them and saves the town. Abiathar arrives with the ephod. Saul, told David is shut inside a walled town, musters an army, so David asks through the ephod whether Saul will come and whether Keilah will hand him over, and the answer to both is yes. He and his six hundred leave, and Saul gives up on Keilah. David stays in the strongholds of the wilderness of Ziph. Jonathan comes to him in the woods, strengthens him, says David will be king with himself second, and they make a covenant. The Ziphites offer to betray him, and Saul is closing in around a mountain when a Philistine raid calls him away. David moves to En Gedi.
1SA 24:1-22	Told David is at En Gedi, Saul takes three thousand chosen men to the rocks of the wild goats, and goes into a cave to relieve himself, not knowing David and his men are at the back of it. His men urge him to act, and David cuts off the edge of Saul's robe instead, then regrets even that, refusing to raise his hand against Yahweh's anointed. When Saul leaves, David calls after him, bows, and shows the piece of robe as proof that he could have killed him but did not, asking why the king of Israel is chasing a dead dog or a flea and leaving judgment to Yahweh. Saul weeps, calls David more righteous than himself, admits David will be king, and asks him to spare his descendants. David swears it, and they part.
1SA 25:1-23	Samuel dies and all Israel mourns and buries him at Ramah, and David goes down to the wilderness of Paran. Nabal, a rich man of Maon shearing three thousand sheep at Carmel, is surly and harsh, while his wife Abigail is intelligent and beautiful. David sends ten men with a courteous greeting, noting that his men protected Nabal's shepherds and asking for whatever he can spare. Nabal asks who David is, calls him a runaway servant, and refuses to give his bread and meat to strangers. David straps on his sword and takes four hundred men. A servant warns Abigail, who loads donkeys with bread, wine, dressed sheep, grain, raisins and figs and rides out without telling her husband, meeting David as he swears to leave Nabal nothing alive.
1SA 25:24-44	Abigail takes the blame herself, points out that Nabal's name means folly, and argues that Yahweh has kept David from bloodguilt and private revenge, and that when he is prince over Israel he will be glad to have no needless blood behind him. She asks only to be remembered. David blesses her discretion, admits she has saved him from killing every male in the house, accepts the gift and sends her home. Nabal is drunk at a great feast, so she waits until morning; when she tells him, his heart dies within him and he becomes like stone, and ten days later Yahweh strikes him dead. David sends for Abigail and she becomes his wife, as does Ahinoam of Jezreel. Saul has given Michal to Palti son of Laish.
1SA 26:1-25	The Ziphites betray David's position again and Saul comes to the wilderness of Ziph with three thousand men. David's spies confirm it, and he and Abishai walk into the camp at night, where Saul lies asleep among the wagons with his spear stuck in the ground at his head and a deep sleep from Yahweh on everyone. Abishai asks to pin him with one stroke; David refuses to touch Yahweh's anointed and takes the spear and the water jar instead. From a hilltop he calls out to Abner, mocking him for failing to guard the king and pointing to the missing spear. Saul recognises his voice; David asks what he has done and calls himself a hunted flea. Saul admits he has played the fool and promises no more harm, and they part.
1SA 27:1-12	Concluding that Saul will kill him eventually, David crosses into Philistine territory with his six hundred men, their households and his two wives, Ahinoam and Abigail, and settles with Achish king of Gath. Saul stops searching for him. David asks for a country town rather than the royal city, and Achish gives him Ziklag, which has belonged to the kings of Judah ever since. He stays in Philistine country a year and four months. During that time he raids the Geshurites, Girzites and Amalekites toward Shur and Egypt, leaving no survivors and taking sheep, cattle, donkeys, camels and clothing. Asked where he has been raiding, he names the south of Judah, the Jerahmeelites and the Kenites, and leaves nobody alive to contradict him. Achish believes Israel now detests him and counts him a servant for life.
1SA 28:1-25	The Philistines muster for war and Achish tells David he and his men will march with him. Samuel is dead, and Saul has expelled the mediums and wizards. Facing the Philistine camp at Shunem, Saul is terrified and gets no answer from Yahweh by dreams, Urim or prophets, so he asks for a medium and is told of one at Endor. Disguised, he goes by night and asks her to bring up Samuel, swearing she will not be punished. When Samuel appears she recognises Saul and cries out. Samuel tells Saul that Yahweh has become his adversary, that the kingdom is David's because he spared Amalek, and that tomorrow he and his sons will be with him. Saul collapses, and the woman feeds him a calf and bread before he leaves.
1SA 29:1-11	The Philistines gather at Aphek while Israel camps by the spring at Jezreel, and David and his men march in the rear with Achish. The Philistine commanders object to the Hebrews being there. Achish defends David as a man he has found no fault in for years, but they insist he be sent back, arguing that he could turn on them mid-battle and that the cheapest way for him to make peace with Saul would be their own heads, and they quote the song about Saul's thousands and David's ten thousands. Achish tells David he has been upright as an angel of God but that the lords will not have him, and asks him to go in peace. David protests, then rises early and returns to Philistine territory.
1SA 30:1-15	David and his men reach Ziklag on the third day and find it burned, with every wife, son and daughter carried off by an Amalekite raid, though nobody was killed. They weep until they have no strength left. David's own wives are among the captives, and the men talk of stoning him. He has Abiathar bring the ephod and asks whether he should pursue; the answer is that he will overtake them and recover everything. Six hundred set out, and two hundred are too exhausted to cross the brook Besor. In the field they find an Egyptian, a slave abandoned by his Amalekite master when he fell ill, and revive him with bread, water, figs and raisins. He offers to lead them to the raiders if his life is spared.
1SA 30:16-31	The Egyptian brings them to the Amalekites, spread out across the ground eating, drinking and dancing over their plunder. David attacks from twilight until the following evening; only four hundred young men on camels escape. He recovers everything, including his two wives, with nothing missing, and claims the captured flocks and herds as his own plunder. When they return to the two hundred left at the brook Besor, some of David's men want to give them nothing but their families, and David refuses: the share of the man who stays with the baggage is the same as the share of the man who fights. He makes it a lasting statute for Israel. He then sends portions of the plunder to the elders of Judah in Bethel, Jattir, Aroer, Hebron and other places where he and his men had stayed.
1SA 31:1-13	Israel is defeated on Mount Gilboa and the Philistines kill Saul's sons Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchishua. Hard pressed by the archers, Saul asks his armour bearer to run him through so the Philistines cannot abuse him; the man is too afraid, so Saul falls on his own sword, and the armour bearer does the same. Saul, his three sons, his armour bearer and all his men die that day. Israelites across the valley abandon their towns, and the Philistines occupy them. The next day the Philistines cut off Saul's head, take his armour to the temple of Ashtaroth and fasten his body to the wall of Beth Shan. The men of Jabesh Gilead march all night, take down the bodies, burn them and fast seven days.
2SA 1:1-27	Two days after David returns to Ziklag, a man arrives from the battle with torn clothes and dirt on his head and reports that Israel has fled and that Saul and Jonathan are dead. Asked how he knows, he says he found Saul leaning on his spear, that Saul asked him to finish him, and that he did so and took the crown and bracelet. David and his men tear their clothes, mourn and fast until evening. On learning the man is an Amalekite, David asks why he was not afraid to kill Yahweh's anointed, and has him executed. He then sings a lament, taught to Judah as the song of the bow: do not tell it in Gath, let no dew fall on Gilboa, Saul and Jonathan were swifter than eagles, and Jonathan's love surpassed the love of women.
2SA 2:1-32	David asks Yahweh where to go, is sent to Hebron, and is anointed king over Judah, reigning there seven and a half years. He thanks the men of Jabesh Gilead for burying Saul. Abner meanwhile makes Saul's son Ishbosheth king at Mahanaim over Gilead, Ephraim, Benjamin and the rest. At the pool of Gibeon Abner and Joab set twelve men from each side to fight; all twenty-four kill each other, and a full battle follows in which Abner is beaten. Asahel, Joab's swift brother, chases Abner, who twice tells him to turn aside and then kills him with the butt of his spear. Abner appeals to Joab to stop the slaughter between brothers, and Joab blows the trumpet. David loses twenty men, Abner three hundred and sixty. Asahel is buried at Bethlehem.
2SA 3:1-21	The war between the houses drags on, David growing stronger and Saul's house weaker. Six sons are born to David in Hebron, including Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah. Ishbosheth accuses Abner of sleeping with Saul's concubine Rizpah, and Abner, furious at being reproached over a woman when he has kept the kingdom out of David's hands, swears to transfer the kingdom to David from Dan to Beersheba. Ishbosheth is too afraid to answer. Abner opens negotiations with David, who agrees on one condition: Michal must be returned first. She is taken from Paltiel, who follows her weeping as far as Bahurim. Abner canvasses the elders of Israel and Benjamin, then comes to Hebron, is given a feast, and is sent away in peace.
2SA 3:22-39	Joab returns from a raid, learns Abner has come and gone in peace, and tells David he has been deceived and spied on. Without David's knowledge he brings Abner back from the well of Sirah, takes him aside in the gateway, and kills him for the blood of his brother Asahel; Abishai shares the act. David declares himself guiltless and curses Joab's house, then orders sackcloth and public mourning, walks behind the bier, weeps at the grave and laments that Abner died as a fool dies, unbound and unfettered. He swears to eat nothing until sundown, which convinces all Israel that the king had no part in the killing. He calls Abner a prince and a great man, and admits the sons of Zeruiah are too hard for him.
2SA 4:1-12	With Abner dead, Ishbosheth loses his nerve and Israel is troubled. Two of his raiding captains, Rechab and Baanah, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, are introduced, along with a note that Jonathan left a son, Mephibosheth, lamed at five when his nurse fled with him. The two brothers enter Ishbosheth's house at midday while he is resting, kill him on his bed, behead him, and travel all night to bring the head to David at Hebron, claiming Yahweh has avenged him. David reminds them that he executed the man who reported Saul's death, and asks how much more he should require the blood of men who murdered an innocent man in his own bed. He has them killed and their bodies hung by the pool at Hebron, and buries the head in Abner's grave.
2SA 5:1-25	All the tribes come to Hebron, call David their own flesh, and anoint him king over Israel. He is thirty, and will reign forty years: seven and a half in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem. He attacks the Jebusites, who taunt that the blind and lame will keep him out, and takes the stronghold of Zion, which becomes David's city; he builds from the Millo inward. Hiram of Tyre sends cedar, carpenters and masons to build him a house. He takes more wives and concubines and has more children in Jerusalem, including Solomon and Nathan. The Philistines come up twice into the valley of Rephaim. The first time Yahweh tells him to go up and he wins at Baal Perazim; the second time he is told to circle behind and wait for the sound of marching in the mulberry trees.
2SA 6:1-23	David gathers thirty thousand chosen men to bring the ark up on a new cart driven by Uzzah and Ahio, with music and dancing. At the threshing floor of Nacon the oxen stumble, Uzzah takes hold of the ark, and God strikes him dead. David, angry and afraid, names the place Perez Uzzah and leaves the ark at the house of Obed-Edom for three months, where it brings blessing. Hearing this, David brings it up with sacrifices every six paces, dancing with all his might in a linen ephod. Michal watches from a window and despises him. After the offerings he blesses the people and gives everyone bread, dates and raisins. Michal mocks him for exposing himself before servants; David answers that he danced before Yahweh, who chose him over her father. She has no child ever after.
2SA 7:1-29	Settled in a cedar house and at rest from his enemies, David tells Nathan it is wrong that the ark still lives in curtains. Nathan approves, then that night receives Yahweh's word: God never asked any tribe for a house of cedar, and has moved in a tent since Egypt. Instead he reminds David he was taken from following the sheep, promises him a great name, a settled place for Israel, and a house of his own line. After David's death his offspring will build the temple, and that throne will stand forever; God will discipline him if he sins, but will not withdraw his kindness as he did from Saul. David sits before Yahweh and prays, asking who he is to be brought this far, and asking that the promise to his house be confirmed forever.
2SA 8:1-18	David subdues the Philistines, then defeats Moab, measuring the captives by line and putting two lines to death and sparing one, and the Moabites bring tribute. He strikes Hadadezer of Zobah, taking seventeen hundred horsemen and twenty thousand foot soldiers and hamstringing the chariot horses except for a hundred chariots. When Damascus comes to help, he kills twenty-two thousand Syrians and garrisons the country. He takes Hadadezer's gold shields and quantities of bronze. Toi of Hamath sends his son Joram with silver, gold and bronze vessels, which David dedicates to Yahweh along with plunder from Syria, Moab, Ammon, Philistia and Amalek. He kills eighteen thousand in the Valley of Salt and garrisons Edom. He reigns with justice, with Joab over the army, Jehoshaphat as recorder, Zadok and Ahimelech as priests, Seraiah as scribe and Benaiah over the guard.
2SA 9:1-13	David asks whether anyone is left of Saul's house whom he can treat kindly for Jonathan's sake. Saul's servant Ziba is summoned and reports that Jonathan has a surviving son who is lame in both feet, living at Lo Debar in the house of Machir son of Ammiel. David sends for him. Mephibosheth comes and bows, and David tells him not to be afraid: he will restore all of Saul's land to him and he will eat at the king's table continually. Mephibosheth calls himself a dead dog. David gives everything of Saul's household to him and orders Ziba, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants, to farm the land and bring in the harvest for him. Mephibosheth lives in Jerusalem, eating at the table like one of the king's sons, and has a young son named Mica.
2SA 10:1-19	When the Ammonite king dies, David sends envoys to comfort his son Hanun, whose advisers persuade him they are spies. Hanun shaves off half of each man's beard, cuts their garments off at the buttocks, and sends them away, so David has them wait at Jericho until their beards grow. The Ammonites then hire twenty thousand Syrian foot soldiers from Beth Rehob and Zobah, a thousand men from Maacah and twelve thousand from Tob. Joab, caught between two forces, takes the picked men against the Syrians and gives the rest to Abishai against the Ammonites. The Syrians flee, then the Ammonites. Hadadezer brings out the Syrians from beyond the River under Shobach, and David crosses the Jordan to Helam and kills seven hundred charioteers and forty thousand horsemen, including Shobach. Hadadezer's vassals make peace.
2SA 11:1-27	In the season when kings go to war, David sends Joab to besiege Rabbah and stays in Jerusalem. From his roof he sees Bathsheba, wife of Uriah the Hittite, bathing, sends for her and lies with her, and she conceives. David recalls Uriah from the front and tells him to go home, but Uriah refuses to sleep in his own house while the army camps in the field, even after David makes him drunk. So David sends him back carrying a letter telling Joab to put him at the front of the fighting and withdraw from him. Uriah is killed at the wall. David sends word that the sword devours one as well as another. After Bathsheba's mourning he takes her as his wife and she bears a son. Yahweh is displeased.
2SA 12:1-16	Nathan tells David a story about a rich man with many flocks who took a poor man's one beloved ewe lamb to feed a traveller. David's anger burns and he declares the man deserves death and fourfold restitution. Nathan answers that he is the man: God anointed him, saved him from Saul and gave him everything, yet he struck down Uriah and took his wife. Therefore the sword will never leave his house, evil will rise from his own family, and his wives will be taken in public because he acted in secret. David says he has sinned, and Nathan tells him Yahweh has put away his sin, but the child will die. The child falls ill, and David fasts and lies all night on the ground.
2SA 12:17-31	David refuses to be raised from the ground or to eat, and on the seventh day the child dies. His servants are afraid to tell him, but he sees them whispering and asks. On hearing it he washes, changes his clothes, worships in Yahweh's house, and eats. Asked why he mourned while the child lived and stopped when it died, he says that while it lived he hoped God might be gracious, and now he cannot bring the child back but will go to him. He comforts Bathsheba, and she bears Solomon, whom Nathan names Jedidiah. Joab, having taken the water city of Rabbah, calls David to finish the siege so it is not named after himself. David takes it and the king's gold crown, and puts the people to forced labour with saws, picks, axes and brick kilns.
2SA 13:1-18	Amnon, David's son, becomes obsessed with his half-sister Tamar and makes himself ill over her. His cousin Jonadab advises him to feign sickness and ask David to send Tamar to make food for him. David does so. Tamar bakes cakes in his sight, and when she brings them into the room Amnon has everyone sent out and takes hold of her. She refuses, tells him such a thing is not done in Israel, and urges him to ask the king for her instead. He overpowers and rapes her. Then his love turns to hatred and he orders her out; she tells him sending her away is a greater wrong than the first. He has a servant put her out and bolt the door.
2SA 13:19-39	Tamar puts ashes on her head, tears her robe and goes away crying aloud. Absalom tells her to stay quiet and she remains desolate in his house. David is very angry but does nothing, and Absalom says nothing to Amnon while hating him. Two years later Absalom holds a sheep shearing at Baal Hazor and invites the king's sons; David declines to come himself but is pressed into letting Amnon and the others go. Absalom's servants kill Amnon when the wine has made him merry, and the rest of the king's sons flee on their mules. David is told all his sons are dead and lies on the ground until Jonadab explains that only Amnon is dead, and that Absalom had intended this since Tamar. Absalom flees to Talmai king of Geshur for three years while David mourns daily.
2SA 14:1-17	Joab, seeing the king's heart turned toward Absalom, brings a wise woman from Tekoa, dresses her as a long-time mourner, and puts words in her mouth. She comes to David with a case: a widow whose two sons fought, one killing the other, and now the family demands the survivor's life, leaving her husband no heir. David promises to act, then swears no hair of her son will fall. She then presses further: why has the king devised the same thing against the people of God by not bringing home his own banished one? We all die like water spilled on the ground, yet God devises means so the banished are not cast off.
2SA 14:18-33	David asks whether Joab's hand is in this, and the woman admits it. David tells Joab to bring Absalom back, and Joab fetches him from Geshur, but Absalom is sent to his own house and may not see the king's face. Absalom is the most admired man in Israel for his looks, without a blemish, and cuts his heavy hair once a year, weighing two hundred shekels; he has three sons and a daughter named Tamar. After two years without seeing the king he summons Joab twice, and when Joab will not come he has Joab's barley field set on fire. Joab comes, and Absalom sends him to ask why he was brought back at all. David calls him in and kisses him.
