2SA 15:1-19	Absalom acquires a chariot, horses and fifty runners, then stands by the gate intercepting anyone coming to the king for judgment, telling each that his case is good but nobody has been appointed to hear it, wishing aloud that he were judge, and embracing whoever bows to him. So he steals the hearts of Israel. He then asks leave to pay a vow at Hebron, and David lets him go. He sends agents through all the tribes to proclaim him king at the trumpet, takes two hundred unwitting guests, and summons David's counsellor Ahithophel. Told that Israel's heart is with Absalom, David orders immediate flight to spare the city, leaving ten concubines behind. His household and six hundred Gittites go with him, and he tells Ittai the Gittite to turn back.
2SA 15:20-37	Ittai swears to be wherever the king is, in death or life, and crosses over with his men. The country weeps as the people cross the Kidron toward the wilderness. Zadok and the Levites bring the ark, and David sends it back, saying that if he finds favour God will bring him back to see it, and if not, let God do as he sees fit; the priests are to stay in the city with their sons Ahimaaz and Jonathan as messengers while David waits at the fords. David climbs the Mount of Olives weeping, barefoot and with his head covered, and on hearing Ahithophel has joined the conspiracy prays that his counsel be turned to foolishness. Hushai the Archite meets him, and David sends him back to feign loyalty to Absalom and undermine Ahithophel.
2SA 16:1-23	Past the summit, Ziba meets David with donkeys, bread, raisins, fruit and wine, and says Mephibosheth stayed in Jerusalem expecting the kingdom back; David grants Ziba everything of Mephibosheth's. At Bahurim, Shimei son of Gera, of Saul's family, curses David as a man of blood, throws stones and dust, and says the kingdom has been handed to Absalom. Abishai asks to take his head, and David refuses: if his own son seeks his life, why not a Benjamite, and perhaps Yahweh will repay good for the cursing. The party arrives weary. Absalom enters Jerusalem with Ahithophel, and Hushai greets him with long live the king, explaining that he serves whoever Israel chooses. Ahithophel advises Absalom to sleep with his father's concubines publicly, which he does on the roof, and his counsel was regarded like an oracle of God.
2SA 17:1-29	Ahithophel advises taking twelve thousand men to strike David that night while he is exhausted, killing only the king. Absalom likes it but calls Hushai, who argues that David is a seasoned warrior hidden somewhere and any early losses would panic the army, and urges instead that all Israel be gathered and Absalom lead them himself. Absalom prefers Hushai, because Yahweh had ordained to defeat Ahithophel's counsel. Hushai sends word through the priests; Jonathan and Ahimaaz are spotted, but a woman at Bahurim hides them in a well under grain. They reach David, who crosses the Jordan by dawn. Ahithophel, seeing his advice ignored, goes home, sets his house in order and hangs himself. David comes to Mahanaim, where Shobi, Machir and Barzillai bring food and bedding. Absalom crosses the Jordan and makes Amasa his commander.
2SA 18:1-17	David organises his men in three divisions under Joab, Abishai and Ittai, and is talked out of going himself because he is worth ten thousand of them. He orders all three commanders, in the army's hearing, to deal gently with Absalom. The battle is fought in the forest of Ephraim, twenty thousand fall, and the forest kills more than the sword. Absalom, riding his mule, is caught by the head in the branches of a great oak. A man who sees it refuses Joab's offer of ten pieces of silver, citing the king's order. Joab goes himself and drives three darts through Absalom's heart, then blows the trumpet to stop the pursuit, and they throw the body into a pit under a heap of stones.
2SA 18:18-33	Absalom had raised a pillar in the king's valley for himself, having no son to keep his name. Ahimaaz asks to carry the news, and Joab refuses because the king's son is dead, sending a Cushite instead; Ahimaaz insists and outruns him. David sits between the gates while the watchman reports first one runner, then another. Ahimaaz arrives with news of victory, and when the king asks whether Absalom is well says only that he saw a great tumult. The Cushite then reports that Yahweh has avenged the king, and when asked about Absalom answers that the king's enemies should all be as that young man is. David goes up to the room over the gate and weeps, crying out for his son Absalom and wishing he had died in his place.
2SA 19:1-22	The victory turns to mourning because the king is grieving, and the troops slip into the city like men ashamed of fleeing. Joab confronts David: he has shamed the men who saved his life and his family, and if he does not go out and speak to them, nobody will stay with him. David sits in the gate and the people come. Across the tribes there is argument about bringing the king back, and David works on Judah through the priests, promising Amasa command of the army in Joab's place. Shimei hurries down with a thousand Benjamites and Ziba, falls before the king and confesses. Abishai wants him executed, and David refuses to put anyone to death that day.
2SA 19:23-43	David swears Shimei will not die. Mephibosheth comes down unwashed and untrimmed since the king left, and says Ziba deceived him and slandered him because he is lame, adding that he has no claim beyond the seat at the king's table. David divides the land between them, and Mephibosheth says Ziba may take it all now the king is home. Barzillai the Gileadite, who supplied David at Mahanaim, escorts him over the Jordan but declines to come to Jerusalem: at eighty he can no longer taste food or hear singers, and asks to die by his parents' grave, sending Chimham in his place. David kisses him and blesses him. Then Israel complains that Judah stole the king away, Judah answers that he is their close relative, and Israel claims ten parts in him. Judah's words are the fiercer.
2SA 20:1-26	Sheba son of Bichri blows a trumpet and declares Israel has no share in David, and all Israel follows him while Judah stays with the king. Back in Jerusalem David puts the ten concubines in custody, provided for but shut up in widowhood for life. Amasa is told to muster Judah in three days and is late, so David sends Abishai after Sheba. At the great stone in Gibeon Joab greets Amasa, takes his beard as if to kiss him, and kills him with the sword that had fallen from its sheath, then goes on with the pursuit while a man drags the body out of the road. Sheba is besieged in Abel of Beth Maacah, and a wise woman negotiates with Joab: the city throws Sheba's head over the wall and Joab withdraws. The officers of state are listed.
2SA 21:1-22	A three-year famine is attributed to Saul's killing of the Gibeonites, whom Israel had sworn to spare. The Gibeonites refuse silver and ask instead for seven of Saul's sons to be handed over and hanged at Gibeah. David spares Mephibosheth because of his oath to Jonathan, and gives up two sons of Rizpah and five sons of Michal, who are killed at the start of barley harvest. Rizpah spreads sackcloth on the rock and guards the bodies from birds and animals until the rains come. Hearing of it, David gathers the bones of Saul and Jonathan from Jabesh Gilead and buries them with the others in Kish's tomb, after which God answers prayer for the land. Four battles with Philistine giants follow: Abishai saves an exhausted David from Ishbibenob, and three more giants are killed.
2SA 22:1-51	David's song of deliverance, sung when Yahweh had rescued him from all his enemies and from Saul. It opens by piling up names: rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, horn of salvation, high tower. Death's waves and Sheol's cords had closed around him, and his cry reached God's temple, at which the earth shook, smoke came from his nostrils, and he rode a cherub through thick darkness, scattering his enemies with arrows and lightning until the sea floor lay bare. He drew David out of deep water because he delighted in him. The middle claims clean hands and a kept covenant, and says God shows himself merciful to the merciful and shrewd to the crooked. The rest is a soldier's thanks: trained hands, a bow of bronze, feet that do not slip, and kindness promised to his offspring forever.
2SA 23:1-39	David's last words: the Spirit spoke through him, and a ruler who governs justly and in the fear of God is like morning light after rain, while the ungodly are thorns nobody can gather by hand. Then the roll of his mighty men. Josheb Basshebeth killed eight hundred at once. Eleazar fought until his hand froze to his sword. Shammah held a lentil field alone. Three of the thirty broke through the Philistine lines to fetch water from the well at Bethlehem, and David poured it out rather than drink what men had risked their lives for. Abishai killed three hundred with his spear. Benaiah killed two Moabites, a lion in a pit in the snow, and an Egyptian with the man's own spear. The thirty are then listed by name, thirty-seven in all, ending with Uriah the Hittite.
2SA 24:1-25	Yahweh's anger moves David to number Israel and Judah. Joab objects and is overruled, and the census takes nine months and twenty days, returning eight hundred thousand fighting men in Israel and five hundred thousand in Judah. David's conscience strikes him and he confesses his folly. Through the prophet Gad he is offered three punishments: seven years of famine, three months of flight before his enemies, or three days of plague. He chooses to fall into Yahweh's hand, and seventy thousand die. When the angel reaches Jerusalem, Yahweh tells him to stop, at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. David asks that the hand fall on him and not the sheep, and Gad tells him to build an altar there. Araunah offers the site and oxen free, but David insists on paying fifty shekels, and the plague is stopped.
ACT 1:1-26	Luke addresses Theophilus again, recalling that Jesus appeared alive over forty days speaking of the kingdom, and told them to wait in Jerusalem for the promised Spirit. Asked whether he is restoring the kingdom to Israel, he says the times are not theirs to know, but they will receive power and be witnesses from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth. He is taken up in a cloud, and two men in white ask why they are staring at the sky. The eleven return to the upper room, named, and pray with the women, Mary and his brothers. Peter stands among about a hundred and twenty, cites the psalms about Judas, whose field became known as Akeldama, and says a witness of the resurrection must replace him. Two are put forward, and the lot falls on Matthias.
ACT 2:1-24	At Pentecost, all together in one place, a sound like a rushing wind fills the house, tongues like fire rest on each of them, and they are filled with the Spirit and speak in other languages. Devout Jews from every nation are bewildered to hear their own language, and Luke lists them, from Parthians and Medes to Cretans and Arabians. Some ask what it means; others say they are drunk on new wine. Peter stands with the eleven and points out it is only the third hour, then quotes Joel on the Spirit poured out on all flesh, signs in the sky, and everyone who calls on the Lord's name being saved. He says Jesus of Nazareth was handed over and crucified, and that God raised him because death could not hold him.
ACT 2:25-47	Peter argues from a psalm of David about not being left in Hades: David died and his tomb is still there, so he spoke as a prophet about the Christ's resurrection, to which they are witnesses. Exalted at God's right hand, Jesus has poured out what they see and hear; David himself did not ascend. He concludes that God has made Lord and Christ the Jesus they crucified. Cut to the heart, the crowd asks what to do, and Peter tells them to repent and be baptized for forgiveness and the gift of the Spirit, promised to them, their children and those far off. About three thousand are baptized that day. They devote themselves to teaching, fellowship, breaking bread and prayer, hold everything in common, sell property to meet needs, and are added to daily.
ACT 3:1-26	Going up to the temple at the ninth hour, Peter and John pass a man lame from birth who is carried daily to the Beautiful Gate to beg. Peter tells him to look at them, says he has no silver or gold but gives what he has, and in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth tells him to get up and walk. Taken by the right hand, he stands, and goes into the temple walking, leaping and praising God. As the crowd gathers in Solomon's porch, Peter asks why they stare, says it was not his own power, and tells them the God of their fathers glorified Jesus, whom they denied before Pilate, asking for a murderer instead. He calls them to repent, citing Moses and the prophets and the promise to Abraham.
ACT 4:1-37	While they are speaking, the priests, the temple captain and the Sadducees arrest Peter and John for teaching resurrection, and hold them overnight; the number of believers reaches about five thousand. Before Annas, Caiaphas and the council, asked by what power they acted, Peter says it was the name of Jesus of Nazareth, whom they crucified and God raised, and that there is no other name by which people must be saved. The council marvels at unlearned men, cannot deny the healing with the man standing there, and settles on threats. Peter and John reply that they cannot stop speaking of what they saw. Released, the group prays, citing a psalm about kings and rulers, and asks for boldness; the place shakes. They hold everything in common, and Barnabas sells a field and lays the money at the apostles' feet.
ACT 5:1-21	Ananias, with his wife Sapphira's knowledge, sells property and keeps back part of the price while presenting the rest. Peter asks why Satan filled his heart to lie to the Holy Spirit, and says he lied to God rather than to men. Ananias falls down dead and is carried out and buried. Three hours later Sapphira arrives, is asked whether the sale price was as stated, says yes, and is told the burial party is at the door; she falls dead and is buried beside him. Great fear comes on everyone. Signs and wonders follow, the sick are laid in the streets hoping for Peter's shadow, and crowds come from nearby towns. The high priest and the Sadducees, jealous, jail the apostles, and an angel opens the doors at night.
ACT 5:22-42	The officers find the prison locked and guarded but empty, and report it; the authorities are perplexed until someone says the men are teaching in the temple. They are fetched without force, for fear of stoning by the people. The high priest points out the order not to teach in this name, and Peter answers that they must obey God rather than men, that God raised the Jesus they killed on a tree and exalted him to give repentance and forgiveness, with the Spirit as witness. The council wants them dead until Gamaliel, a respected Pharisee, cites Theudas and Judas of Galilee, whose followers came to nothing, and says that if this is from God they cannot stop it. They beat the apostles and release them, and the apostles leave rejoicing and go on teaching daily.
ACT 6:1-15	As the numbers grow, the Hellenists complain that their widows are being neglected in the daily distribution. The twelve say it is not right for them to leave the word to serve tables, and ask for seven men full of the Spirit and wisdom to take it on. The assembly chooses Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch, who are prayed over and have hands laid on them. The word spreads, and many priests become obedient to the faith. Stephen works wonders, and members of several synagogues dispute with him without being able to withstand his wisdom, so they get men to claim he blasphemed Moses and God. Accused by false witnesses of speaking against the temple and the law, he stands with a face like an angel's.
ACT 7:1-31	Asked whether the charges are true, Stephen answers with a history. God appeared to Abraham and sent him to a land he was given no foothold in, promising it to offspring he did not yet have, and foretelling four hundred years of slavery. Isaac, Jacob and the twelve patriarchs follow; the brothers sell Joseph into Egypt, where he becomes governor, and famine brings the family down, seventy-five in all. As the promise neared, a new king mistreated them and forced them to expose their babies. Moses is born, raised by Pharaoh's daughter, and educated in Egyptian wisdom. At forty he kills an Egyptian defending an Israelite, expecting to be understood as a deliverer, and is not; the next day he flees to Midian. Forty years later a bush burns.
ACT 7:32-60	The voice names itself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and sends Moses back to Egypt. Stephen argues that Israel rejected the deliverer God sent and made a calf, and that the Most High does not live in houses made by hands. He calls them stiff-necked killers of the prophets and the Righteous One. When he says he sees the Son of Man standing at God's right hand, they drive him out and stone him, laying their coats at the feet of Saul. He asks that the sin not be held against them, and dies.
ACT 8:1-40	With Saul consenting to Stephen's death, persecution scatters the church through Judea and Samaria, apostles excepted, and Saul drags men and women to prison. Those scattered preach, and Philip goes to a Samaritan city, where crowds listen, spirits come out, the lame are healed, and there is great joy. Simon, a sorcerer whom the city called the great power of God, believes and is baptized. Peter and John lay hands on the Samaritans, who receive the Spirit; Simon offers money for the ability and is told his silver can perish with him. An angel then sends Philip to the Gaza road, where an Ethiopian official reading Isaiah asks who the passage is about; Philip explains, baptizes him, and is taken away, and the eunuch goes on rejoicing.
ECC 1:1-18	The Preacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem, opens with vanity of vanities and asks what a man gains from all his labour. Generations come and go while the earth remains; the sun rises and hurries back to where it rises, the wind circles, the rivers all run to a sea that is never full. The eye is never satisfied with seeing and the ear never filled with hearing. Nothing is new under the sun, and nobody will be remembered. He reports that he applied his heart to search out everything done under the sky and found it all a chasing after wind, that the crooked cannot be straightened, and that in much wisdom there is much grief.
ECC 2:1-26	The Preacher runs an experiment on himself. He tries mirth and wine, then large projects: houses, vineyards, gardens, parks, orchards, pools, servants, herds, silver and gold, singers and every kind of instrument. He withholds nothing his eyes desire and becomes greater than anyone before him in Jerusalem, then looks at all of it and calls it a chasing after wind with no profit. Wisdom does exceed folly as light exceeds darkness, but the same event happens to both the wise man and the fool, and neither is remembered. He comes to hate his labour because he must leave it to a successor who may be a fool. His conclusion is modest: eat, drink and find enjoyment in your work, which is from God's hand.
ECC 3:1-22	The poem of times opens the chapter: a time to be born and to die, to plant and to uproot, to kill and to heal, to weep and to laugh, to keep silence and to speak, to love and to hate, for war and for peace. He says God has made everything beautiful in its time and set eternity in human hearts, yet nobody can grasp the whole work from beginning to end. So rejoice, do good, eat and drink, since that is God's gift. Then he notes that wickedness sits in the place of justice, and that the same thing happens to people as to animals, since both have one breath, both come from dust and both return to it, and nobody knows which way the spirit goes.
ECC 4:1-16	The Preacher looks at oppression and sees the tears of people with no comforter while power sits with their oppressors, and concludes that the dead are better off than the living, and the unborn better than both. Achievement turns out to be driven by envy of a neighbour. Better one handful with quiet than two with labour. He describes a man with no son or brother working endlessly and asking who he is doing it for. Then the case for company: two are better than one, one can lift the other after a fall, two keep warm, two can withstand an attacker, and a threefold cord is not quickly broken. Finally a poor wise youth is better than an old king who can no longer take advice.
ECC 5:1-20	Advice on worship: guard your steps at God's house, listen rather than offer the sacrifice of fools, keep your words few since God is in heaven and you are on earth, and pay a vow rather than make one you will not keep. On oppression, do not be amazed when justice is taken away in a district, because every official has another official above him. Then money: whoever loves silver is never satisfied with it, more goods only mean more mouths, and the labourer sleeps sweetly while the rich man's abundance keeps him awake. A man leaves as naked as he came. What is good is to eat, drink and enjoy your work, and the ability to enjoy wealth is itself God's gift.
ECC 6:1-12	The Preacher names a heavy evil: a man given riches, wealth and honour who lacks nothing he desires, and then is given no power to enjoy any of it, so a stranger eats it instead. He pushes it further. A man with a hundred children and many years whose soul is never filled with good, and who is not even buried, is worse off than a stillborn child, which at least has rest. Even two thousand years without enjoyment ends in the same place. All a man's labour goes to his mouth and the appetite is still not filled. Better the sight of the eyes than the wandering of desire. Nobody knows what is good for a life spent like a shadow.
ECC 7:1-29	A run of sayings preferring the sober to the pleasant: a good name beats fine perfume, the day of death beats the day of birth, the house of mourning beats the house of feasting, and a fool's laughter is thorns crackling under a pot. Do not ask why the former days were better, since that is not a wise question. In prosperity be joyful and in adversity consider, because God has set the two side by side. He has watched righteous men perish and wicked men live long, and advises against being either excessively righteous or wicked. There is no righteous man who never sins. Do not listen to everything said about you, since you have cursed others too. God made man upright, and people went looking for schemes.
ECC 8:1-17	Advice on serving a king: keep his command, do not be hasty to leave his presence, and remember his word is supreme and nobody can ask what he is doing. There is a time and procedure for everything, though a man does not know what is coming. No one controls the spirit or the day of death, and there is no discharge in war. Because sentence against evil is not carried out quickly, people set their hearts on doing it. He admits the outward evidence runs both ways, with righteous men treated as if wicked and wicked men as if righteous. So he commends eating, drinking and being joyful, and concludes that no one can find out the work of God, however hard a wise man labours at it.
ECC 9:1-18	One event comes to everyone, righteous and wicked, clean and unclean, whoever sacrifices and whoever does not. A living dog is better than a dead lion, since the living at least know they will die while the dead know nothing and are forgotten. So eat your bread with joy, drink your wine with a merry heart, wear white, keep oil on your head, live joyfully with the wife you love, and do whatever your hand finds with all your strength, since there is no work or knowledge in Sheol. The race is not to the swift nor the battle to the strong: time and chance happen to all. A poor wise man once saved a besieged city and nobody remembered him.
ECC 10:1-20	Dead flies spoil the perfumer's oil, and a little folly outweighs wisdom and honour. A fool announces himself to everyone as he walks along. Gentleness lays great offences to rest, even when a ruler is angry. He has seen folly seated in dignity, servants on horses and princes walking on foot. A run of occupational hazards follows: digging a pit, breaking a wall, quarrying stone, splitting wood, and a snake that bites before it is charmed. A blunt axe means more effort, since skill brings success. Woe to a land whose king is a child. Slothfulness makes the roof sink and the house leak. Do not curse the king even in your thoughts, since a bird may carry your voice.
ECC 11:1-10	Cast your bread on the waters and you will find it after many days; give a portion to seven and even to eight, since you do not know what evil is coming. Anyone who watches the wind will not sow and anyone who studies the clouds will not reap. You do not know how the wind travels or how bones grow in the womb, so sow in the morning and do not withhold your hand in the evening, because you do not know which will prosper. Light is sweet and seeing the sun is pleasant. Rejoice through all your years, but remember the days of darkness will be many. He tells the young man to enjoy his youth and to know that God will bring him into judgment.
ECC 12:1-14	Remember your Creator while you are young, before the days when there is no pleasure left. Then the extended picture of old age: the keepers of the house tremble, the strong men bow, the grinders stop because they are few, those who look out of the windows go dark, doors shut in the street, a man wakes at a bird's voice, the almond tree blossoms and a grasshopper is a burden. The silver cord is severed, the golden bowl broken, the pitcher broken at the spring, and the dust returns to the earth while the spirit returns to God. Vanity of vanities. The epilogue notes the Preacher's care with his proverbs, warns that making many books never ends, and concludes: fear God and keep his commandments.
EXO 1:1-22	Jacob's seventy descendants have become a nation, and a new Egyptian king who never knew Joseph decides they are a security risk. He puts them to forced labour building the storage cities Pithom and Raamses, but the harder they are worked the more they multiply. He orders the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah to kill every newborn boy. They refuse, telling Pharaoh the Hebrew women give birth before they arrive, and God gives them households of their own. Pharaoh then orders all his people to throw every Hebrew boy into the Nile.
EXO 2:1-25	A Levite couple hide their newborn son three months, then set him in a tarred papyrus basket among the reeds. Pharaoh's daughter finds him, and his sister arranges for his own mother to nurse him for wages. She names him Moses. Grown, he kills an Egyptian beating a Hebrew and hides the body; the next day a Hebrew throws it in his face, and Moses flees to Midian. He defends the priest's seven daughters at a well, marries Zipporah, and fathers Gershom. The king of Egypt dies, and God hears Israel's groaning and remembers his covenant.
EXO 3:1-22	Keeping Jethro's flock at Horeb, Moses sees a bush burning without being consumed. God calls him by name, tells him to remove his sandals, and identifies himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. He has seen the affliction in Egypt and is sending Moses to bring the people out to a land flowing with milk and honey. Moses asks who he is to go, and what name to give. God answers I AM WHO I AM, and Yahweh. He warns Pharaoh will refuse until struck with wonders, and promises the people will leave with Egyptian silver, gold and clothing.
EXO 4:1-31	Moses objects that no one will believe him, so God gives him three signs: a rod that becomes a snake, a hand that turns leprous and back, and river water that becomes blood on dry land. Moses pleads that he is slow of speech, then simply asks God to send someone else. God's anger burns, and he appoints Aaron as spokesman. Moses takes leave of Jethro and returns to Egypt with his family and the rod. At a lodging place God moves to kill him, and Zipporah circumcises their son with a flint. Aaron meets him, and the elders and people believe and worship.
EXO 5:1-23	Moses and Aaron deliver Yahweh's demand to let the people go and hold a feast in the wilderness. Pharaoh says he does not know Yahweh and refuses. He accuses the people of idleness and orders that straw no longer be supplied for brickmaking while the daily quota stays the same. The people scatter to gather stubble, and the Israelite officers are beaten for falling short. They appeal to Pharaoh, who repeats the order, then turn on Moses and Aaron for making them a stench in his eyes. Moses complains to God that nothing has been rescued.
EXO 6:1-30	God answers that Pharaoh will not merely release Israel but drive them out. He declares his name Yahweh, unknown by that name to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and repeats the covenant promise of land with a chain of I will statements. The people are too crushed by their bondage to listen. Moses protests that he has uncircumcised lips. A genealogy follows, listing Reuben, Simeon and then the Levites in detail down through Kohath and Amram to Aaron and Moses, Aaron's four sons, Korah's sons, and Eleazar's son Phinehas. Moses repeats his objection.
ISA 1:1-31	Isaiah's vision concerning Judah and Jerusalem opens with Yahweh calling heaven and earth to witness that his children have rebelled. The ox knows its owner, but Israel does not. The country is desolate, Zion left like a hut in a melon field. God says he is sick of their sacrifices, incense, new moons and festivals, because their hands are full of blood; he tells them to wash, seek justice and defend the widow and orphan. Though their sins are scarlet, they can be white as snow. The faithful city has become a prostitute, her silver turned to dross, her princes taking bribes. God will smelt her clean, restore her judges, and burn the rest like tinder.
ISA 2:1-22	Isaiah sees the mountain of Yahweh's house raised above the hills in the last days, with all nations streaming to it to be taught, beating swords into plowshares and giving up war. He then turns on the present: the land is full of silver, horses and idols people made with their own fingers. A day of Yahweh is coming against everything high and proud, cedars of Lebanon, oaks of Bashan, towers, walls and ships of Tarshish. People will hide in caves and rock holes and throw their silver and gold idols to the moles and bats. Stop trusting man, whose breath is in his nostrils.
ISA 3:1-26	Yahweh strips Jerusalem and Judah of every support: bread, water, soldier, judge, prophet, elder, craftsman and enchanter. Boys will rule, neighbours will oppress each other, and a man will be drafted as ruler just because he owns a coat, then refuse. God brings the elders to trial for eating up the vineyard and grinding the faces of the poor. Then the women of Zion, walking with outstretched necks and jingling anklets, lose an itemised inventory of finery: headbands, earrings, veils, perfume bottles, signet rings, nose rings, mirrors, shawls. Rottenness instead of spices, rope instead of a belt, baldness instead of styled hair. Her men fall by the sword and the city sits on the ground.
ISA 4:1-6	Seven women take hold of one man, offering to feed and clothe themselves if only they can carry his name and lose their disgrace. Then the tone turns: in that day Yahweh's branch will be beautiful, and whoever is left in Zion and written among the living will be called holy, once the Lord has washed away the filth of Zion's daughters by a spirit of justice and burning. Over Mount Zion he creates cloud and smoke by day and flaming fire by night, a canopy over all the glory, a shelter for shade from heat and refuge from storm and rain.
ISA 5:1-30	Isaiah sings a love song about his friend's vineyard: he cleared it, planted the best vines, built a tower and cut a winepress, and it produced wild grapes. So he will pull down its hedge and wall, stop pruning it and order the clouds to withhold rain. The vineyard is Israel; he looked for justice and got bloodshed. Six woes follow, against those who buy up house after house and field after field, drunks who start at dawn, people who drag sin behind them like a cart, those who call evil good and good evil, the self-satisfied wise, and judges who acquit for a bribe. He whistles for a distant nation that never tires, arrows sharp, hooves like flint, roaring like lions.
ISA 6:1-13	In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah sees the Lord on a high throne, his robe filling the temple, with six-winged seraphim above calling holy, holy, holy to each other until the thresholds shake and the house fills with smoke. Isaiah says he is undone, a man of unclean lips among a people of unclean lips. A seraph takes a live coal from the altar with tongs, touches his mouth, and declares his guilt gone. God asks whom to send, Isaiah volunteers, and is told to preach to a people who will hear without understanding. He asks how long, and is told: until the cities are empty and the land waste, with only a stump left.
ISA 7:1-25	Syria and Israel march on Jerusalem and Ahaz's heart shakes like trees in wind. Isaiah meets him with his son Shearjashub at the upper pool conduit and tells him to keep calm, because these two kings are only smoking stubs of torches and their plan will not stand. Offered any sign he likes, in the depths or the heights, Ahaz piously refuses to ask. So God gives one anyway: a young woman will bear a son called Immanuel, and before the child can tell right from wrong the two kings' lands will be abandoned. Then Assyria comes, whistled up like flies and bees, and shaves the land bare with a hired razor until vineyards are briers.
ISA 8:1-22	Isaiah is told to write Maher Shalal Hash Baz on a large tablet before witnesses, and when the prophetess bears a son he gives him that name: before the boy can say father or mother, Assyria will carry off the wealth of Damascus and Samaria. Because the people rejected the gently flowing waters of Shiloah, the River will flood over them up to the neck, wings outspread across the land. Plots against Judah will collapse, because God is with us. Isaiah is warned not to cry conspiracy with everyone else; God will be a sanctuary to some and a trap to others. Consulting mediums who chirp and mutter is no substitute for consulting God, and those who try find only distress and thick darkness.
ISA 9:1-21	The gloom lifts for Zebulun and Naphtali: people walking in darkness see a great light and rejoice like harvesters dividing plunder, the oppressor's yoke broken as at Midian and the bloodied battle gear burned as fuel. A child is born, a son given, called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace, and his government on David's throne will never stop growing. Then judgment resumes on the north: Samaria boasts it will rebuild in cut stone and cedar, so Syrians and Philistines devour Israel from both sides. Leaders and lying prophets are cut off as head and tail in one day. Wickedness burns like brush fire, and Manasseh and Ephraim eat each other. His hand is still stretched out.
ISA 10:1-34	Woe to legislators who write oppressive laws to make widows their plunder, and no wealth they hide will help them on the day of reckoning. Assyria is the rod of God's anger, but Assyria does not know it: the king boasts of conquering Calno, Carchemish, Hamath, Arpad, Samaria and gathering the earth like eggs from an abandoned nest. So God asks whether an axe brags against the man swinging it, and promises to burn Assyria's forest down to a remnant a child could count. Judah is told not to fear the Assyrian rod, since the anger is nearly spent. The invader's march is named town by town, Aiath, Migron, Michmash, Geba, Ramah, Nob, and there the tall trees are lopped and Lebanon falls.
ISA 11:1-16	A shoot comes out of the stump of Jesse, resting on him the spirit of wisdom, counsel, might and knowledge. He will not judge by what his eyes see but will judge the poor with righteousness and kill the wicked with the breath of his lips. Then the animals change: wolf with lamb, leopard with young goat, lion eating straw, a nursing child playing at a cobra's hole, with a little child leading them. Yahweh will recover the remnant a second time from Assyria, Egypt, Cush, Elam and the islands, ending Ephraim's envy of Judah, and split the River into seven streams so people cross in sandals.
ISA 12:1-6	A short song of thanks for the day of rescue. The speaker thanks Yahweh because his anger has turned away and he now comforts, declares God his salvation and refuses to be afraid, and calls Yahweh his strength and song. Water will be drawn with joy from the wells of salvation. The second half turns outward: give thanks, call on his name, tell the nations what he has done, sing, and shout aloud, because the Holy One of Israel is great in the middle of Zion.
ISA 13:1-22	The burden of Babylon. A banner goes up, Yahweh musters an army from a far country, and the day of Yahweh arrives as destruction: hands go limp, hearts melt, faces turn to flame, and labour pains seize everyone. The stars, sun and moon give no light. God says he will punish arrogance and make people rarer than the gold of Ophir, shaking heaven and earth out of place. The account of the sack is brutal: the found are run through, infants killed before their parents' eyes, houses looted and wives raped. The Medes are stirred up, unbribable by silver or gold. Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, becomes Sodom, never inhabited again, left to jackals, ostriches and wild goats.
ISA 15:1-9	The burden of Moab. In a single night Ar and Kir are laid waste. Moab goes up to the high places to weep, heads shaved and beards cut, wailing over Nebo and Medeba, in sackcloth in the streets and on the rooftops. Heshbon and Elealeh cry out as far as Jahaz, and even the armed men are shaking. The prophet's own heart cries out for Moab as its nobles flee to Zoar by the ascent of Luhith. The waters of Nimrim dry up, the grass withers, refugees carry their savings across the brook of the willows, and the waters of Dimon run with blood, with a lion waiting for whoever escapes.
ISA 16:1-14	Moab is told to send lambs as tribute to Zion and its daughters are pictured as birds shaken out of a nest at the fords of Arnon. Judah is asked to give shade like night at noon, hide the outcasts and not betray the fugitive, with a throne established in loving kindness in the tent of David. But Moab's pride and boasting are nothing, so Moab wails for Moab and mourns the raisin cakes of Kir Hareseth. The vine of Sibmah is broken down; the prophet waters Heshbon with his own tears, and the battle shout has fallen on the summer fruit. No one treads the winepresses. Moab's prayers on the high place will not prevail, and within three years, counted like a hired worker's contract, its glory will be brought into contempt.
ISA 17:1-14	The burden of Damascus, which stops being a city and becomes a ruined heap, its cities left to undisturbed flocks. Ephraim's fortress and Syria's kingdom both end. Jacob's glory grows thin, like a field after the harvester, with only gleanings left, two or three olives at the top of the tree. In that day people will look to their Maker instead of to the altars, Asherah poles and incense altars their own fingers made. Their strong cities will be deserted, because they forgot the God of their salvation and planted exotic seedlings that flower fast and yield nothing but grief. Nations roar like the sea, but he rebukes them and they blow away like chaff and whirling dust: terror at evening, gone before morning.
ISA 18:1-7	An oracle to the land of rustling wings beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, which sends ambassadors by sea in papyrus boats to a tall and smooth people, awesome from the beginning, whose land the rivers divide. The world is told to watch for the banner on the mountains and listen for the trumpet. Yahweh says he will stay still and watch from his dwelling, like clear heat in sunshine or a cloud of dew at harvest. Then, before the harvest, while the flower is turning into a ripening grape, he cuts off the shoots and spreading branches and leaves them to birds of prey and animals, who summer and winter on them. Afterwards that same people brings a gift to Mount Zion.
ISA 19:1-25	The burden of Egypt. Yahweh rides in on a swift cloud, the idols tremble, and Egypt turns on itself, city against city and kingdom against kingdom, until its counsel fails and it consults charmers and wizards. It is handed to a cruel lord. The Nile dries up, so fishermen mourn and the flax workers and weavers are ruined. The princes of Zoan and Memphis are called fools whose advice has gone stupid, staggering like a drunk in his own vomit because Yahweh mixed a spirit of perverseness into them. Then the oracle turns: five Egyptian cities will speak the language of Canaan, an altar and a pillar to Yahweh will stand in Egypt, God will strike and heal them, and a highway will run from Egypt to Assyria, with Israel a third alongside them as a blessing.
ISA 20:1-6	In the year Sargon of Assyria sent his commander Tartan to take Ashdod, Yahweh tells Isaiah to take off his sackcloth and his sandals, and Isaiah goes naked and barefoot for three years as a sign concerning Egypt and Ethiopia. The point is explained: the king of Assyria will lead Egyptian captives and Ethiopian exiles away, young and old, naked and barefoot with buttocks uncovered. Those who had been counting on Ethiopia and Egypt will be dismayed, and the coastland people will ask how they themselves can possibly escape.
ISA 35:1-10	The desert is glad and blossoms like a rose, given Lebanon's glory and the excellence of Carmel and Sharon, and it will see the glory of Yahweh. Weak hands are to be strengthened, feeble knees made firm, and the fearful told to be strong because God is coming with retribution and rescue. Then the blind see, the deaf hear, the lame leap like a deer and the mute sing, while water breaks out in the wilderness, burning sand becomes a pool and reeds grow where the jackals used to lie. A road runs through it called The Holy Way, closed to the unclean and to wicked fools, with no lion or predator on it, only the redeemed. Yahweh's ransomed come back to Zion singing, with everlasting joy on their heads, and sorrow and sighing run away.
ISA 39:1-8	Merodach Baladan of Babylon sends letters and a gift because he has heard Hezekiah was ill and recovered. Hezekiah is delighted and gives them a full tour: the treasury, the silver and gold, the spices and precious oil, the armoury, everything, with nothing in his house or his realm held back. Isaiah comes and asks what the men said and where they came from, then what they saw. Hezekiah answers that they came from Babylon and saw everything. Isaiah tells him that everything in his house, including what his ancestors stored, will be carried to Babylon with nothing left, and that his own sons will be made eunuchs in the Babylonian palace. Hezekiah replies that the word of Yahweh is good, adding that there will at least be peace in his own days.
ISA 14:1-32	Yahweh will restore Jacob, and captives will rule their captors. Israel takes up a taunt song over the king of Babylon: the oppressor has stopped, the earth is quiet, even the cedars are relieved no lumberjack is coming. Sheol stirs and dead kings rise from their thrones to ask whether he is weak like them, his pomp bedded on maggots. He is named morning star, son of the dawn, who meant to set his throne above the stars, and is thrown out unburied like a trampled corpse. Yahweh swears to cut off Babylon's name and leave it to porcupines, to break Assyria, and warns Philistia not to celebrate a broken rod.
ISA 21:1-17	The burden of the wilderness of the sea. A grievous vision comes like a whirlwind, Elam and Media are called to attack, and the prophet's body reacts with labour pains, deafness, blindness and a fluttering heart, his longed-for evening turned to trembling. A banquet is laid, and the princes are told to oil the shield. A watchman is posted, sees horsemen in pairs and troops of camels, and reports that Babylon has fallen with her gods smashed. Then Dumah, where a voice from Seir keeps asking about the night and is told morning comes, and also night. Then Arabia, where Tema feeds fugitives, and Kedar's glory ends within a year.
ISA 22:1-25	The burden of the valley of vision, addressed to a city up on its rooftops. Its dead did not die in battle and its rulers were caught fleeing, so the prophet asks to be left alone to weep. Elam and Kir bring quiver and shield. The city's response is engineering without repentance: they inspect the breaches, gather the pool water, tear down houses for the wall and build a reservoir, never looking to the one who planned it. Called to sackcloth, they feast instead, saying tomorrow we die. Then Shebna, caught carving himself a rock tomb, is thrown like a ball into a wide country, and Eliakim gets his robe and the key of David's house, until that nail gives way.
ISA 23:1-18	The burden of Tyre. The ships of Tarshish are told to howl because their harbour is gone, the news reaching them from Kittim. Sidon is shamed, the sea itself says it never bore children, and Egypt is in anguish at the report. Tyre, the ancient joyous city whose merchants were princes and who handed out crowns, has been planned against by Yahweh himself, to stain the pride of all glory. Sidon's daughter is told to flee to Kittim and will find no rest there either. Tyre will be forgotten seventy years, then take up her trade again like a prostitute singing to be remembered, and her earnings end up holy to Yahweh, spent on food and lasting clothing.
ISA 24:1-23	Yahweh empties the earth and scatters its people, and the levelling is universal: priest like people, servant like master, buyer like seller, creditor like debtor. The land is polluted because its inhabitants broke the everlasting covenant, so the curse eats it and few are left. Wine mourns, tambourines and harps stop, drink turns bitter, the confused city is shut up. What remains is like gleanings after vintage, though voices from the islands still shout for Yahweh's majesty. Fear, the pit and the snare wait for everyone: escape the noise and you fall in the pit, climb out and the snare takes you. The earth staggers like a drunk and will not rise. Then sun and moon are shamed because Yahweh reigns on Zion.
ISA 25:1-12	A song of praise. God is exalted for doing what he planned long ago: making a fortified city a heap and a foreigners' palace no city at all, never rebuilt, so that strong nations fear him. He has been a stronghold to the poor and needy, shade from heat and shelter from storm, and he silences the song of the ruthless the way a cloud's shade kills heat. On this mountain he makes all peoples a feast of rich meat and refined wine, destroys the veil spread over all nations, swallows death forever and wipes tears off every face. People will say, this is our God, we waited for him. Then Moab is trampled like straw in a dung pit, its high walls laid in the dust.
ISA 26:1-21	A song for Judah: we have a strong city, its walls are salvation, so open the gates for the faithful nation. Whoever's mind is steadfast is kept in perfect peace, because Yahweh is an everlasting rock. He has flattened the lofty city, and the feet treading it down are the feet of the poor. Judgments in the earth teach righteousness, while favour shown to the wicked teaches him nothing. Israel's record is honest: they were in labour and gave birth only to wind. Then the promise that the dead will live and those in the dust should wake and sing. The people are told to go into their rooms and shut the doors until the indignation passes, because the earth will stop covering its slain.
ISA 27:1-13	In that day Yahweh punishes leviathan the fleeing serpent and leviathan the twisted serpent, and kills the dragon in the sea. Then a kinder vineyard song: Yahweh keeps it, waters it every moment, guards it day and night, and says there is no wrath in him, though he would burn briers unless they take hold of his strength and make peace. Jacob will take root and fill the world with fruit. His guilt is forgiven when he grinds his altar stones to chalk and leaves no Asherah pole standing. The fortified city sits deserted with a calf grazing it. Then Yahweh threshes from the Euphrates to the brook of Egypt, and a great trumpet brings the outcasts back from Assyria and Egypt to worship at Jerusalem.
ISA 28:1-29	Woe to the drunkards of Ephraim and their fading flower of a crown, picked and eaten like the first ripe fig, while Yahweh becomes the real crown for the remnant. Priest and prophet reel with wine, err in their visions, and every table is covered in vomit. They mock Isaiah's teaching as baby talk, precept on precept, line on line, so that is exactly what God's word becomes to them. Jerusalem's rulers boast of a covenant with death and a refuge of lies. God answers with a tried cornerstone in Zion, justice as the measuring line, righteousness as the plumb line, and hail sweeping the lie away. The bed is too short and the blanket too narrow. It closes on farming: dill and cumin are beaten with a stick, not crushed under a cart wheel.
ISA 30:1-18	Woe to rebellious children who make an alliance without consulting God, going down to Egypt to shelter in Pharaoh's shadow. Their envoys reach Zoan and Hanes, and their caravans haul treasure on donkeys and camels through country full of lions and flying serpents to a people who cannot help. Egypt's help is empty, so God nicknames her Rahab Who Sits Still. Isaiah is told to write it on a tablet against a people who tell the prophets to prophesy pleasant lies. Their guilt is a bulge in a high wall that collapses in an instant and shatters too thoroughly to leave a shard worth carrying coals in. Offered strength in quietness and confidence, they chose horses, so their pursuers will be faster. Even so Yahweh waits, so as to be gracious.
ISA 31:1-9	Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, counting horses, chariots and horsemen while refusing to look to the Holy One of Israel. God is wise too, and will not take back his words. The argument is blunt: Egyptians are men and not God, their horses flesh and not spirit, so when God stretches out his hand the helper and the helped fall together. Yahweh will fight on Mount Zion like a lion growling over prey that shouting shepherds cannot scare off, and will shield Jerusalem like birds hovering. Israel is told to return and throw away the silver and gold idols their own hands made. Assyria will fall by a sword belonging to no man, its young men put to forced labour and its princes panicking at a banner.
ISA 32:1-20	A king will reign in righteousness with princes ruling justly, and a man will be shelter from wind and storm, streams in dry ground, the shade of a big rock in a weary land. Eyes will not be dim, the rash will understand, stammerers will speak clearly, and fools will no longer be called noble, since a fool empties the soul of the hungry while a scoundrel plots against the humble with lies. Then Isaiah turns on the women at ease: the vintage will fail, so strip, put on sackcloth and beat your breasts for the pleasant fields. Thorns take the houses of joy, the palace is abandoned, and the watchtower becomes donkey pasture, until the Spirit is poured out from on high and the wilderness becomes farmland where justice lives.
ISA 33:1-24	Woe to the destroyer who has never been destroyed and the betrayer nobody has betrayed: when he finishes, it will be done to him. A prayer for grace and morning strength follows, and at God's thunder the nations scatter and their plunder is stripped like a field stripped by locusts. The highways are empty, the covenant broken, the envoys of peace weeping, Lebanon and Carmel withered. God says now he will rise: you will conceive chaff and give birth to stubble, and your own breath will burn you. Sinners in Zion ask who can live with everlasting burning, and the answer is whoever walks righteously, refuses a bribe, and shuts his eyes to evil. Zion becomes a tent whose stakes are never pulled, and the lame carry off the plunder.
ISA 34:1-17	The nations are called in to listen. Yahweh is enraged with all of them, their slain thrown out to stink and the mountains melting with their blood, the sky rolled up like a scroll and its armies falling like leaves off a vine. The sword, drunk in heaven, comes down on Edom as a sacrifice at Bozrah, greasy with fat and blood, until the land is drunk with blood. It is a day of vengeance for Zion's cause. Edom's streams become pitch and its dust sulphur, burning forever and never crossed again. Pelican, porcupine, owl and raven take possession, measured out with a line of confusion and a plumb line of emptiness. Thorns fill the palaces, jackals and ostriches the courts, the arrow snake nests, and all of them are recorded in Yahweh's book, none missing her mate.
ISA 29:1-24	Woe to Ariel, the city where David camped. God besieges it until it whispers out of the dust like a medium, then the besieging crowd becomes blowing chaff in an instant, visited with thunder, earthquake and fire. The nations fighting Zion will be like a hungry man who dreams he is eating and wakes still hungry. The people stagger without wine, because God has poured out a spirit of deep sleep: the vision is a sealed book handed to a literate man, who cannot read it because it is sealed, then to an illiterate man, who cannot read at all. Their worship is lips without heart. Soon the deaf hear the book and the blind see.
ISA 30:19-33	The promise turns to Zion: no more weeping, an answer as soon as they cry out. They will still get the bread of adversity, but their teachers will no longer be hidden, and a voice behind them will say this is the way, walk in it. They will strip the plating off their idols and throw them out as filth. Rain, rich harvests and winnowed feed for the working animals follow, with streams on every hill when the towers fall, and the moon shining like the sun. Then his name arrives in thick smoke, breath like a river up to the neck, while every blow of the rod on Assyria falls in time with tambourines and harps.
ISA 36:1-22	Sennacherib takes all the fortified cities of Judah and sends Rabshakeh to Jerusalem with a large army. Eliakim, Shebna and Joah get a speech: Egypt is a bruised reed that pierces the hand leaning on it, and the Yahweh they trust is the God whose high places Hezekiah demolished. He offers two thousand horses if Judah can find riders, and claims Yahweh sent him. Asked to speak Aramaic, he shouts in Hebrew that the men on the wall will eat their own dung, and lists the gods of Hamath and Samaria that saved nobody. The officials stay silent as ordered and report back with their clothes torn.
ISA 37:1-21	Hezekiah tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and goes into the temple, sending Eliakim, Shebna and the senior priests to Isaiah with the message that the children have come to the birth and there is no strength to deliver. Isaiah answers that God will put a spirit in the Assyrian king, who will hear news, go home and fall by the sword there. Rabshakeh returns to find his king fighting Libnah, and news arrives that Tirhakah of Ethiopia is coming. So Sennacherib sends a letter listing Gozan, Haran, Hamath and Sepharvaim as places whose gods failed. Hezekiah spreads the letter out before Yahweh and prays.
ISA 37:22-38	The answer to Sennacherib is a taunt. The virgin daughter of Zion has shaken her head at him, and Yahweh asks whom he thinks he has been shouting at. His boasts are quoted back: with my chariots I climbed Lebanon, cut its cedars, and will dry up the rivers of Egypt with my feet. But God planned this long ago, and the peoples he flattened were grass on a housetop. He will put a hook in his nose and turn him back the way he came. Judah gets two years of volunteer crops. Then Yahweh's angel strikes a hundred and eighty five thousand men, dead by morning, and Sennacherib is killed by his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer while worshipping.
ISA 38:1-22	Hezekiah falls sick and Isaiah tells him to set his house in order because he will die. Hezekiah turns his face to the wall, prays that he has walked in truth, and weeps bitterly. God sends Isaiah back with fifteen added years, and the sign is the shadow on Ahaz's sundial going back ten steps. The rest is Hezekiah's own written prayer: entering the gates of Sheol in mid-life, his life rolled up like a weaver's cloth and cut from the loom, his bones broken as by a lion, moaning like a dove. He concludes that Sheol cannot praise anyone and the living do. Isaiah had prescribed a cake of figs as a poultice for the boil.
ISA 40:1-31	The tone changes to comfort: tell Jerusalem her warfare is over and she has received double for her sins. A voice calls for a highway through the wilderness, valleys raised and mountains flattened, so all flesh sees God's glory. Another says all flesh is grass, but God's word stands forever. The messenger shouts, behold your God, who comes as a mighty one and also carries lambs in his arms. Then the questions: who measured the sea in his palm, weighed the mountains in scales? The nations are a drop in a bucket, and idols are cast by a workman. He calls every star by name with none missing, and those who wait for him rise on wings like eagles.
ISA 41:1-29	God calls the islands to court. He asks who raised up the conqueror from the east who tramples kings like dust, and answers himself: I, Yahweh, the first and the last. The frightened nations encourage each other, and the picture of their solidarity is craftsmen cheering over an idol, the soldering pronounced good, the thing nailed down so it will not fall over. Israel, by contrast, is his chosen servant, told not to fear because he holds their right hand. He calls Jacob a worm and then makes it a threshing sledge with teeth. He plants cedar, myrtle and cypress in the desert. Then he challenges the idols to predict anything, and finds only wind and confusion.
ISA 42:1-25	Behold my servant, upheld and chosen, with the Spirit on him, who will bring justice to the nations without shouting in the street, will not break a bruised reed or snuff out a smouldering wick, and will not give up until justice is set in the earth. He is called as a covenant for the people and a light to the nations, to open blind eyes and bring prisoners out of the dungeon. A new song is called for from the sea and the islands. God says he has been silent a long time and will now cry out like a woman in labour, leading the blind by unknown paths. Then the reproach turns inward: who is as blind as my own servant? The one who handed this plundered people over was Yahweh himself.
ISA 43:1-28	Do not be afraid, says the one who created Jacob and called him by name: through water he will be with them, through fire they will not be burned. Egypt, Ethiopia and Seba are given as ransom in their place. Offspring will be brought from east and west. The blind with eyes and the deaf with ears are the witnesses in a trial where the nations cannot produce a prediction. There is no savior besides him, and nobody can take anything out of his hand. Stop remembering the old things, he says, because he is making a road in the wilderness and rivers in the desert, honoured by jackals and ostriches. Yet Israel brought no offerings and burdened him with sins, which he blots out for his own sake.
ISA 44:1-28	God tells Jacob, whom he formed in the womb, not to fear: he will pour water on dry ground and his Spirit on their offspring, who will spring up like willows by watercourses. He is the first and the last, with no other God and no other Rock. Then a long dismantling of idol-making. The blacksmith works the coals and goes hungry and faint; the carpenter measures with a line and compasses and shapes a figure like a man. He plants a tree, then burns half to bake bread and roast meat, saying aha, I am warm, and makes a god of the leftovers, asking it to save him. He feeds on ashes. God has blotted out Israel's sins like a cloud and names Cyrus as his shepherd.
ISA 45:1-25	Yahweh addresses Cyrus as his anointed, whose right hand he holds, going ahead of him to break the bronze doors and give him treasures of darkness. All of it is for Jacob's sake, and Cyrus is called by name although he does not know God. God declares he forms light and creates darkness, makes peace and creates calamity. Then the potter argument: woe to the clay pot that argues with its maker. Cyrus will build the city and free the exiles without payment. Egypt, Ethiopia and the Sabeans come over in chains and admit God is with Israel, a God who hides himself. He calls the ends of the earth to look to him and be saved, swearing that every knee will bow.
ISA 46:1-13	Bel bows down and Nebo stoops, their idols loaded onto pack animals as heavy freight, unable to save themselves and going into captivity with everyone else. The contrast is direct: Israel has been carried by God from the womb, and he will keep carrying them to grey hair. People pour out gold, hire a goldsmith to make a god, hoist it on their shoulders, set it where it cannot move, and cry to something that cannot answer. God tells the transgressors to remember the old things: he declares the end from the beginning and does whatever he pleases. He is calling a bird of prey from the east, and his salvation will not wait.
ISA 47:1-15	Babylon, addressed as a pampered virgin daughter, is told to come down and sit in the dust with no throne, take up the millstones and grind flour, and lift her skirt to wade the rivers, exposed and shamed. She will no longer be called mistress of kingdoms. God handed his people over and she showed no mercy, putting a heavy yoke on the aged while telling herself she would be a princess forever. She says I am, and there is no one besides me, and I will never be a widow, so widowhood and childlessness arrive in a single day. Let the astrologers and monthly forecasters save her: they are stubble, and every trading partner wanders off.
ISA 48:1-22	God addresses people who swear by his name but not in truth. He announced things in advance precisely because he knew they were obstinate, iron-necked and brass-browed, and would otherwise credit their idols. Now he tells new hidden things so they cannot claim to have known already. They were treacherous from the womb, and he defers his anger for the sake of his own name: he refined them, but not as silver, choosing them in the furnace of affliction. The one he loves will do as he pleases to Babylon. Then a regret: if only they had listened, their peace would have been like a river. They are told to leave Babylon singing. There is no peace for the wicked.
ISA 49:1-26	The servant addresses the islands: called from the womb, his mouth made a sharp sword, himself a polished arrow kept in the quiver. He complains he has laboured in vain, and is told that raising up Jacob is too small a job, so he will also be a light to the nations. Though despised, kings will stand when they see him. The returning people will not hunger or thirst. Zion says she has been forgotten, and the answer is a nursing mother who cannot forget her child, and hands with Zion engraved on the palms. The ruined land will be too small for the children arriving, and the mother who thought herself childless will ask where they came from. Kings will bow and lick the dust.
ISA 50:1-11	God asks where the certificate of divorce is, or which creditor he sold them to: nobody bought them, they were sold for their own sins. He asks whether his arm is too short to rescue, then notes that at his rebuke the sea dries up and the sky is dressed in sackcloth. The servant then speaks: God has given him the tongue of a learner so he can sustain the weary with words, and wakens his ear morning by morning. He gave his back to those who beat him and his cheeks to those who tore out his hair, and did not hide his face from spitting, having set his face like flint. Those who light their own torches will walk in that light and lie down in sorrow.
ISA 51:1-23	Those who seek righteousness are told to look at the rock they were cut from, at Abraham and Sarah, who were one before being made many. Zion's wilderness becomes like Eden. Though the heavens vanish like smoke and the earth wears out like a garment, that salvation lasts forever, so insults from men who will be eaten by moths are not worth fearing. Then a summons to God's own arm: wake up as in the days when you cut Rahab to pieces and dried the sea into a road. Then Jerusalem, having drunk the cup of staggering to the bottom, her children fainting in the streets like antelope in a net, has the cup taken from her and given to those who walked over her back.
ISA 52:1-15	Wake up, Zion, put on your best clothes, shake off the dust, sit up and untie your neck. You were sold for nothing and will be redeemed without money. Israel went down to Egypt and Assyria oppressed them for no reason, and now God's name is blasphemed all day, so he will act. The feet of the messenger who says your God reigns are called beautiful on the mountains. The watchmen sing as Yahweh returns to Zion, and the ruins break into song. Those carrying the temple vessels are told to leave and purify themselves, and this time they will not go out in haste, because God goes ahead of them and behind. The servant will be exalted, though his appearance was marred beyond any man's.
ISA 53:1-12	Who has believed the message? The servant grew up like a shoot from dry ground, with no beauty to attract anyone, despised and rejected, a man of suffering acquainted with disease. He carried the sickness that was theirs while onlookers assumed God had struck him. He was pierced for their transgressions and crushed for their iniquities, and by his wounds they are healed, since all of them strayed like sheep. Oppressed and afflicted, he stayed silent, like a lamb led to slaughter. His grave was made with the wicked and with a rich man, though he had done no violence. Yet made an offering for sin, he will see offspring, see light and be satisfied, justify many, and be counted with transgressors.
ISA 54:1-17	The barren woman who never gave birth is told to sing, because the desolate will have more children than the married wife, so she should enlarge her tent and drive the stakes in harder. The shame of her youth and widowhood will be forgotten, because her Maker is her husband. God says he forsook her for a small moment but gathers her with great mercies, swearing it as he swore about the waters of Noah, and says the mountains may leave but his loving kindness will not. The storm-tossed city gets rebuilt in colour, foundations of sapphire, gates of sparkling jewels. He created the blacksmith as well as the destroyer, so no weapon made against her will succeed.
ISA 55:1-13	An open invitation: everyone thirsty should come to the water, and whoever has no money should buy wine and milk without price. Why spend money on what is not bread and labour on what does not satisfy? Listen and your soul will live, under an everlasting covenant, the sure mercies of David. Seek Yahweh while he can be found; let the wicked abandon his way and be freely pardoned. God's thoughts are as high above theirs as the heavens are above the earth. His word works like rain and snow, which do not go back up but give bread to the eater. They will go out with joy while the mountains sing and the trees clap their hands.
ISA 56:1-12	Keep justice and do right, because salvation is near, and blessed is the one who keeps the Sabbath. Then two groups are addressed directly. The foreigner who has joined himself to Yahweh should not say he will be separated out, and the eunuch should not call himself a dry tree: eunuchs who keep the covenant get a name better than sons and daughters, and foreigners will be brought to the holy mountain, because his house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples. Then the tone drops: the animals of the field are invited to eat, because the watchmen are blind, mute dogs that cannot bark, dozing and greedy, each chasing his own profit and planning more wine tomorrow.
ISA 57:1-21	The righteous die and nobody notices, and no one considers that they are being spared the coming evil. Then the accusation, addressed to children of a sorceress: they mock and stick out their tongues, inflame themselves under every green tree, and kill children in the valleys under the rock clefts. Their inheritance is the smooth stones of the wadi, which they pour drink offerings to. They set their bed on a high mountain, put their memorial behind the door, went to the king with oil and perfume, and never once said it is useless. Then the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity says he lives both in the high holy place and with the contrite, and creates the words peace, peace. But the wicked are a churning sea that throws up mud.
ISA 58:1-14	Shout like a trumpet and tell them their sins, says God, of a people who complain that they have fasted and he has not noticed. The reply: on your fast day you pursue your own pleasure and drive your workers, fasting for strife and hitting people with your fist. Is bowing the head like a reed the fast he chose? The fast he chose is to undo the yoke, let the oppressed go free, share bread with the hungry, house the homeless poor, clothe the naked and not hide from your own family. Then light breaks out like morning and God answers with here I am. You become a watered garden and are called Repairer of the Breach. Keep the Sabbath as a delight.
ISA 59:1-21	God's hand is not too short to save and his ear is not deaf; their sins separated them, hands defiled with blood and lips speaking lies. They hatch adders' eggs and weave spiders' webs: eating the eggs kills you, crushing one produces a viper, and the webs will never make clothing. Their feet run to shed innocent blood. So justice is far off: they look for light and get darkness, grope along the wall like the blind, stumble at noon, roar like bears and moan like doves. Truth has fallen in the street. God saw there was no justice and was astonished there was no intercessor, so his own arm brought salvation: breastplate, helmet, garments of vengeance and zeal as a cloak. A Redeemer will come to Zion.
ISA 60:1-22	Zion is told to get up and shine, because her light has come while thick darkness covers the peoples, and nations and kings will come to her brightness. Her daughters are carried in arms, and camels from Midian, Ephah and Sheba arrive with gold and frankincense while Kedar's flocks are accepted on the altar. Foreigners rebuild her walls, her gates stay open day and night, and Lebanon's timber beautifies the sanctuary. The children of her oppressors bow at her feet. Gold replaces brass, silver replaces iron, peace becomes her governor; her walls are named Salvation and her gates Praise. Sun and moon are no longer needed because Yahweh is her everlasting light, and mourning ends.
ISA 61:1-11	The Spirit of the Lord is on the speaker, anointed to bring good news to the humble, bind up the broken hearted, proclaim liberty to captives, announce the year of Yahweh's favour and the day of vengeance, and comfort mourners with a garland instead of ashes, oil of joy instead of mourning and a garment of praise instead of heaviness, so they can be called trees of righteousness. They will rebuild ruins derelict for generations while foreigners tend their fields, and they will be called Yahweh's priests. Instead of shame they get double. The speaker rejoices, clothed in salvation and righteousness like a bridegroom and a bride, and says God will make righteousness spring up before all nations like a garden.
ISA 62:1-12	For Zion's sake the speaker will not keep quiet until her righteousness shines like the dawn and her salvation burns like a lamp. She will get a new name spoken by Yahweh's own mouth, becoming a crown in his hand. She will not be called Forsaken or her land Desolate, but Hephzibah and Beulah; as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so God rejoices over her. Watchmen are posted who never keep silent, and those who call on Yahweh are to give him no rest until Jerusalem is a praise in the earth. God swears that enemies will not eat her grain: the harvesters will drink it in the sanctuary courts. Clear the highway, pick out the stones, raise a banner.
ISA 63:1-19	Someone comes from Edom in stained clothing, marching in strength, and identifies himself as mighty to save. Asked why his clothes are red, he says he trod the winepress alone with nobody helping, trampling the peoples until their lifeblood stained his clothes, because no one upheld him and his own arm brought salvation. The speaker then recounts God's kindnesses: he called them his people, was afflicted in their affliction, and carried them all the days of old. But they grieved his holy Spirit, so he became their enemy. Then a plea: look down from heaven, where is your zeal, you are our Father though Abraham does not know us, our enemies have trampled your sanctuary.
ISA 64:1-12	The prayer continues with a wish that God would tear the heavens open and come down so the mountains shake, and make his name known to his adversaries. No eye has seen any God besides him who acts for the one who waits. Then the confession: you were angry and we sinned, so can we be saved? All of them are unclean, their righteousness like a filthy garment, fading like leaves and carried off by their own sins. Nobody calls on his name, because he has hidden his face. But he is their Father, they are the clay and he the potter. Zion is a wasteland and the beautiful house where their fathers praised him is burned. Will you keep silent?
ISA 65:1-25	God says he was found by people who were not looking and said see me to a nation that did not bear his name, while spreading his hands out all day to a rebellious people who sacrifice in gardens, burn incense on bricks, sit among graves, eat pig's meat, and tell others to keep away because they are holier. They are smoke in his nose. But as one keeps a cluster because there is wine in it, he will not destroy them all. Those who set a table for Fortune get the sword. His servants will eat and sing while these go hungry and wail. He creates new heavens and a new earth with no weeping, houses they live in, and wolf and lamb feeding together.
ISA 66:1-24	Heaven is his throne and the earth his footstool, so what house could anyone build him: the man he looks at is poor and contrite and trembles at his word. Sacrifice offered by the self-willed is equated with murder and pig's blood. Then a birth image: she gave birth before the labour pains, a nation born in one day. Jerusalem's lovers nurse at her comforting breasts while peace flows to her like a river, and God says he will comfort them as a mother comforts her child. Then he comes with fire and whirlwind chariots, judging all flesh. Survivors are sent to Tarshish, Lud, Tubal and distant islands, and the scattered come home on camels. The last verse is grim: corpses whose worm does not die.
JDG 1:1-18	With Joshua dead, Israel asks Yahweh who should attack the Canaanites first, and Judah is chosen. Judah and Simeon strike ten thousand men at Bezek and capture Adoni-Bezek, cutting off his thumbs and big toes; he says he did the same to seventy kings. Judah burns Jerusalem, takes Hebron and Debir, where Othniel wins Caleb's daughter Achsah, who asks her father for springs of water. Judah also takes Gaza, Ashkelon and Ekron.
JDG 1:19-36	Yahweh is with Judah in the hill country, but the valley is not taken because its people have iron chariots. Caleb receives Hebron and drives out the three sons of Anak. Benjamin leaves the Jebusites in Jerusalem. The house of Joseph takes Bethel after a man shows them the way in and is spared, and he founds another city named Luz. Manasseh, Ephraim, Zebulun, Asher, Naphtali and Dan all fail to clear their territories; the remaining Canaanites are put to forced labour.
JDG 2:1-23	Yahweh's angel comes to Bochim and says that because Israel made covenants with the inhabitants instead of tearing down their altars, those nations will stay as a snare. The people weep and sacrifice. Joshua dies at a hundred and ten, and once his generation is gone a new one arises that does not know Yahweh. They serve the Baals and Ashtaroth, are handed over to raiders, are rescued by judges, and relapse worse each time a judge dies. Yahweh leaves the remaining nations in place as a test.
JDG 3:1-31	The nations left behind serve to test Israel and to teach war to those who had never fought. Israel intermarries and serves their gods, so Yahweh sells them to Cushan Rishathaim of Mesopotamia for eight years until Othniel delivers them and the land rests forty years. Next they serve Eglon of Moab eighteen years. Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite, hides a two-edged sword on his right thigh, asks for a private word, and kills the very fat king; his servants assume he is relieving himself. Israel takes the Jordan fords and kills ten thousand Moabites. Shamgar later kills six hundred Philistines with an ox goad.
JDG 4:1-24	Israel does evil again and is oppressed twenty years by Jabin of Hazor, whose commander Sisera has nine hundred iron chariots. Deborah, a prophetess judging under her palm tree, summons Barak to take ten thousand men to Mount Tabor. Barak will only go if she comes, so she says the honour will go to a woman. Yahweh routs Sisera's army and Sisera flees on foot to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite. She gives him milk, covers him, and while he sleeps drives a tent peg through his temple. Barak arrives to find him dead.
JDG 5:1-31	Deborah and Barak sing a victory song. It recalls Yahweh marching from Seir with the earth shaking, the abandoned highways before Deborah arose as a mother in Israel, and the tribes who came: Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir, Zebulun, Issachar and Naphtali. Reuben stayed among the sheepfolds, Dan by the ships, Asher at the coast, and Meroz is cursed for not helping. The stars fought from heaven and the Kishon swept the enemy away. Jael is blessed above women for the tent peg, while Sisera's mother waits at the window wondering why his chariot is late.
JDG 6:1-21	Midian oppresses Israel seven years, coming up like locusts with countless camels and stripping the harvest, until Israel hides in caves and cries out. A prophet reminds them what Yahweh did in Egypt and that they did not listen. Yahweh's angel sits under the oak at Ophrah where Gideon is threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it, and greets him as a mighty man of valour. Gideon objects that his clan is the poorest and he is the least in it, then asks for a sign and prepares a goat and unleavened cakes.
JDG 6:22-40	Fire consumes the offering and the angel vanishes; Gideon, alarmed at having seen the angel face to face, is told he will not die and builds an altar called Yahweh is Peace. That night he pulls down his father's Baal altar and the Asherah beside it, using ten servants and working after dark out of fear. When the town demands his death, Joash answers that a real god can defend his own altar, and nicknames him Jerub-Baal. Midian and its allies camp in Jezreel, Gideon musters four tribes, and twice tests God with a fleece, wet then dry.
