JDG 7:1-12	Gideon camps at the spring of Harod with Midian to the north. Yahweh says the army is too large, or Israel will claim it saved itself, so everyone afraid is sent home and twenty-two thousand leave, with ten thousand remaining. Still too many: at the water, the three hundred who lap like dogs are kept and the rest, who kneel, are dismissed. That night Yahweh tells Gideon to go down to the camp, and to take his servant Purah if he is afraid. They go, and find the Midianites, Amalekites and easterners lying in the valley like locusts, camels beyond counting.
JDG 7:13-25	Gideon overhears a man describe a dream of a barley loaf rolling into the camp and flattening a tent, which his friend reads as the sword of Gideon. Gideon worships, returns, and splits his three hundred into three companies with trumpets and torches hidden in empty pitchers. At the middle watch they blow, smash the pitchers, and shout for Yahweh and for Gideon. The Midianite army turns its swords on itself and flees. Naphtali, Asher and Manasseh pursue, and Ephraim seizes the waters as far as the Jordan, capturing the princes Oreb and Zeeb and bringing their heads to Gideon.
JDG 8:1-17	Ephraim complains at not being called to the fight, and Gideon flatters them into calm by pointing out they took Oreb and Zeeb. Exhausted but still pursuing, he crosses the Jordan and asks Succoth for bread; its princes refuse until the Midianite kings are actually caught, and Penuel answers the same way. Gideon promises retaliation to both. He surprises the fifteen thousand survivors at Karkor and captures Zebah and Zalmunna. On his return he identifies Succoth's seventy-seven elders and punishes them with desert thorns and briers, then breaks down the tower of Penuel and kills the men of the city.
JDG 8:18-35	Gideon asks Zebah and Zalmunna about the men they killed at Tabor and learns they were his own brothers. He orders his firstborn Jether to kill them; the boy is too afraid, so Gideon does it himself and takes the crescents from their camels. Israel asks him to rule as a dynasty and he refuses, saying Yahweh will rule, then asks for the gold earrings of the plunder: seventeen hundred shekels. He makes an ephod of it at Ophrah and Israel prostitutes itself to it. The land rests forty years. Gideon fathers seventy sons, plus Abimelech by a Shechemite concubine, and dies old. Israel immediately turns to Baal Berith.
JDG 9:1-28	Abimelech persuades his mother's relatives at Shechem that one ruler beats seventy, and with seventy pieces of silver from the temple of Baal Berith hires men and kills his seventy brothers on one stone; only Jotham escapes by hiding. Shechem crowns Abimelech. From Mount Gerizim, Jotham tells a fable of trees inviting olive, fig and vine to be king, all refusing, until the bramble accepts and threatens fire, then applies it to Shechem's treatment of Gideon's house. Jotham flees to Beer. After three years God sends an evil spirit between Abimelech and Shechem; ambushes begin, and Gaal son of Ebed arrives and openly mocks Abimelech.
JDG 9:29-57	Zebul, the city's ruler, secretly warns Abimelech to ambush by night. Gaal sees men coming down the mountains and Zebul tells him it is only shadows, then taunts him into fighting; Gaal is routed and later expelled from Shechem. Abimelech ambushes the people in the field, takes the city, kills its people, and sows it with salt. The thousand men and women in the tower of Shechem are burned alive with branches Abimelech cuts himself. At Thebez a woman drops an upper millstone from the tower and cracks his skull; he has his armour bearer run him through so nobody says a woman killed him. God had repaid Abimelech and Shechem, and Jotham's curse landed.
JDG 10:1-18	Tola of Issachar judges Israel twenty-three years, then Jair the Gileadite twenty-two, whose thirty sons ride thirty donkey colts and hold thirty towns called Havvoth Jair. Israel then serves the gods of Syria, Sidon, Moab, Ammon and the Philistines, and is oppressed eighteen years by the Philistines and Ammonites, who also cross the Jordan against Judah, Benjamin and Ephraim. When Israel cries out, Yahweh lists every past rescue and refuses to save again, telling them to call on the gods they chose. They put away the foreign gods and serve him, and he is grieved by their misery. Ammon camps in Gilead, Israel at Mizpah, and Gilead's princes ask who will lead.
JDG 11:1-20	Jephthah of Gilead is a capable fighter and the son of a prostitute, driven out by his half-brothers so he would inherit nothing, and living in Tob with a band of outlaws. When Ammon attacks, Gilead's elders come to hire him; he asks why they want him now, and they agree before Yahweh that he will be their head. He then sends messengers to the king of Ammon asking why he has come. The king claims Israel took his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok. Jephthah replies with a history: Israel asked Edom and Moab for passage and was refused, went around both, and then asked Sihon of Heshbon, who attacked instead.
JDG 11:21-40	Jephthah finishes his case: Yahweh gave Sihon's land to Israel, Ammon should keep what Chemosh gives it, Balak never fought Israel over it, and three hundred years passed without a claim. The king ignores him. The Spirit comes on Jephthah and he vows that if Ammon is delivered to him he will offer as a burnt offering whatever comes out of his door to meet him. He defeats twenty cities from Aroer to Abelcheramim. Returning home, the one who comes out to meet him with tambourines is his daughter, his only child. He tears his clothes and says he cannot take back what he said. She accepts it and asks for two months in the mountains with her companions to mourn her virginity. She returns, and he does as he vowed. Israel's daughters commemorate her four days a year.
JDG 12:1-15	Ephraim confronts Jephthah for fighting Ammon without them and threatens to burn his house down. He answers that he did call and they did not come. Gilead fights Ephraim and wins, then holds the Jordan fords; anyone denying he is an Ephraimite is made to say Shibboleth, and those who say Sibboleth are killed. Forty-two thousand Ephraimites fall. Jephthah judges six years and dies. Ibzan of Bethlehem judges seven years, with thirty sons and thirty daughters married out and thirty brought in. Elon the Zebulunite judges ten years. Abdon the Pirathonite judges eight, with forty sons and thirty grandsons on seventy donkey colts.
JDG 13:1-25	Israel does evil again and is under the Philistines forty years. Yahweh's angel appears to the barren wife of Manoah of Zorah, a Danite, and tells her she will bear a son who must be a Nazirite from the womb, with no razor on his head, and that she must avoid wine and unclean food. He will begin to save Israel from the Philistines. She tells Manoah, who asks for the visitor to return. The angel comes again and repeats the instructions. Manoah offers food, is told to sacrifice to Yahweh instead, asks the visitor's name and is told it is beyond understanding. The angel rises in the altar flame; Manoah fears they will die, but his wife reasons otherwise. She bears Samson, and Yahweh's Spirit begins to move him at Mahaneh Dan.
JDG 14:1-20	Samson sees a Philistine woman at Timnah and tells his parents to get her for him; they object, but this is Yahweh seeking an occasion against the Philistines. On the way a young lion attacks and he tears it apart bare-handed, telling nobody. Returning later, he finds bees and honey in the carcass and eats it, again saying nothing. At the wedding feast he sets thirty companions a riddle about food from the eater and sweetness from the strong, wagering thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes. Unable to solve it, they threaten his wife, who weeps until he tells her; she tells them. Samson accuses them of plowing with his heifer, kills thirty men at Ashkelon to pay the wager, and goes home angry. His wife is given to his friend.
JDG 15:1-20	At wheat harvest Samson returns with a young goat and is refused entry to his wife, whose father has given her to Samson's companion and offers the younger sister instead. Samson catches three hundred foxes, ties them tail to tail with torches, and burns the Philistine grain and olive groves. The Philistines learn who did it and burn his wife and her father. He strikes them hip and thigh and hides in the cave at Etam's rock. Three thousand men of Judah come to bind him, and he agrees on condition they will not kill him. At Lehi the Spirit comes on him, the ropes fall apart, and he kills a thousand men with a fresh donkey's jawbone. Dying of thirst, he calls on Yahweh, who splits open a spring at En Hakkore. He judges Israel twenty years.
JDG 16:1-16	In Gaza Samson visits a prostitute, and the Gazites wait at the gate to kill him at dawn. At midnight he pulls up the gate doors, posts and bar and carries them to a hill facing Hebron. Later he loves Delilah in the valley of Sorek, and the Philistine lords offer her eleven hundred pieces of silver each to learn the secret of his strength. He says seven undried cords will hold him; she binds him, calls out, and he snaps them. He then says new ropes, which break like thread, then weaving his seven locks into the loom, and he pulls the pin away. She accuses him of mocking her and of not loving her, and presses him daily until he is troubled to death.
JDG 16:17-31	Samson tells Delilah he has been a Nazirite from birth and that shaving his head would take his strength. She summons the Philistine lords with their money, has his seven locks shaved while he sleeps on her knees, and calls out. He wakes expecting to break free, not knowing Yahweh has left him. The Philistines blind him, bind him in bronze at Gaza and set him grinding at the mill, while his hair grows back. At a feast to Dagon they bring him out to entertain them, with three thousand on the roof. He asks the boy leading him to place him at the two central pillars, prays for strength to avenge his eyes, and brings the house down on everyone in it, killing more in his death than in his life.
JDG 17:1-13	Micah of the hill country of Ephraim admits to his mother that he stole her eleven hundred pieces of silver, which she had cursed. She blesses him, and when he returns it she dedicates it to Yahweh, giving two hundred pieces to a silversmith to make a carved image and a molten image for Micah's house. Micah keeps a shrine with an ephod and teraphim and consecrates one of his sons as priest. There was no king in Israel, and everyone did what was right in his own eyes. A young Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, looking for somewhere to live, arrives at Micah's house and is hired as priest for ten pieces of silver a year, clothing and food. Micah concludes Yahweh will now treat him well, since he has a Levite.
JDG 18:1-15	With no king in Israel, the tribe of Dan is still looking for territory, so it sends five fighting men from Zorah and Eshtaol to scout the land. They lodge at Micah's house, recognise the young Levite's voice, and ask what he is doing there; he explains he was hired as priest, and when asked for an oracle tells them their journey is before Yahweh. They go on to Laish and find people living quietly and securely, far from the Sidonians and dealing with nobody. They report the land is very good and its people unsuspecting, and six hundred armed Danites set out, camping at Kiriath Jearim, which is called Mahaneh Dan. Passing Micah's house, the five scouts mention the ephod, teraphim and images inside.
JDG 18:16-31	While six hundred armed men stand at the gate, the five scouts go in and take the carved image, the ephod, the teraphim and the molten image. The priest objects and is told to be quiet and come along: better to be priest to a whole tribe than to one man. He is glad, and goes with them. Micah's neighbours catch up; he says they have taken his gods and his priest and asks what is left to him, and the Danites tell him to be quiet or lose his household. He sees they are stronger and goes home. Dan attacks Laish, a quiet and unsuspecting people with nobody to help them, kills them and burns the city, then rebuilds it as Dan. Jonathan son of Gershom son of Moses and his sons served as their priests until the captivity.
JDG 19:1-16	With no king in Israel, a Levite from the far hill country of Ephraim takes a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah. She leaves him for her father's house for four months, and he travels with a servant and two donkeys to bring her back. Her father welcomes him and keeps him three days, then presses him to stay a fourth and a fifth. On the fifth day the Levite refuses another night and leaves late with his concubine and servant. Passing Jebus, which is Jerusalem, the servant suggests lodging there, but the Levite will not stay in a foreign city and pushes on to Gibeah of Benjamin. They sit in the open street because nobody takes them in, until an old man from Ephraim comes in from the fields.
JDG 19:17-30	The old man asks where they are going, learns they have been left in the street, and takes them in. While they are eating, men of the city surround the house and demand the Levite be brought out to them. The old man refuses and offers his own virgin daughter and the concubine instead. They will not listen, so the Levite puts his concubine out to them, and they rape and abuse her all night, letting her go at dawn. She reaches the door and collapses with her hands on the threshold. In the morning her master tells her to get up and there is no answer. He puts her on the donkey, goes home, cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them through all Israel. Everyone who sees says nothing like this has happened since Egypt.
JDG 20:1-25	All Israel assembles at Mizpah, from Dan to Beersheba, four hundred thousand armed men, and asks how the crime happened. The Levite says the men of Gibeah surrounded the house meaning to kill him, raped his concubine, and she is dead, and that he cut her up and sent her through Israel. The assembly resolves to act against Gibeah and demands Benjamin hand the guilty men over. Benjamin refuses and musters twenty-six thousand swordsmen plus seven hundred chosen men of Gibeah, including seven hundred left-handed slingers who can hit a hair. God tells Israel that Judah goes first. Benjamin kills twenty-two thousand Israelites on the first day; Israel weeps, is told to go up again, and loses eighteen thousand more on the second.
JDG 20:26-48	Israel fasts and weeps at Bethel, where the ark is and Phinehas is serving, and asks again; Yahweh says go up and promises Benjamin tomorrow. Israel sets ambushes around Gibeah and on the third day feigns the same battle, drawing Benjamin onto the highways after about thirty Israelites fall. The ambush breaks out from Maareh Geba, ten thousand chosen men engage, and Yahweh strikes Benjamin. The ambush party takes Gibeah and burns it, and the pillar of smoke is the agreed signal. Seeing the city gone, Benjamin breaks for the wilderness: eighteen thousand fall, five thousand on the roads, two thousand at Gidom, twenty-five thousand in all. Six hundred reach the rock of Rimmon and stay four months. Israel then destroys the Benjamite towns, people and livestock, by sword and fire.
JDG 21:1-25	Israel had sworn at Mizpah to give no daughter to Benjamin, and now weeps at Bethel that a tribe is being cut off. They ask who failed to come to the assembly, since that carried a death oath, and find nobody came from Jabesh Gilead. Twelve thousand men are sent to destroy its inhabitants, sparing four hundred young virgins, who are given to the six hundred Benjamites at Rimmon, and it is not enough. So the elders point to the yearly feast at Shiloh and tell the remaining Benjamites to hide in the vineyards and seize wives from the girls who come out to dance, since the daughters were neither given nor taken in battle. Benjamin does it and settles. There was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
JER 1:1-19	Jeremiah, a priest's son from Anathoth, is called in Josiah's thirteenth year. God says he knew and set him apart before the womb and appointed him prophet to the nations. Jeremiah objects that he is only a child; God touches his mouth, puts his words in it, and sets him over nations to uproot and to plant. Two visions follow: an almond branch, because God watches over his word, and a cauldron tipping from the north, because invaders will come from there. He is made an iron pillar against kings and priests, who will fight him and lose.
JER 2:1-19	God tells Jeremiah to proclaim in Jerusalem that he remembers the kindness of her youth, how she followed him through unsown wilderness as the first fruits of his harvest. Then the question: what fault did your fathers find in me that they went after worthless things? Nobody asked where Yahweh was who brought them out of Egypt. He gave them a plentiful land and they defiled it, with priests not asking after him and prophets prophesying by Baal. He tells them to check Kittim and Kedar for any nation that swapped its gods, because his people traded their glory for nothing. Two evils: they abandoned the spring of living water and dug themselves cracked cisterns that hold none. Their own wickedness will correct them, and going to Egypt or Assyria for a drink will gain them nothing.
JER 2:20-37	God recalls breaking their yoke, only to be told they would not serve; they bowed on every high hill and under every green tree. He planted a noble vine and it went degenerate, and no lye or soap hides the stain. They are likened to a fast dromedary and a wild donkey in heat, calling wood their father and stone their mother, with as many gods as they have towns. A bride does not forget her jewellery, but they forgot him beyond counting. Egypt will shame them as Assyria did.
JER 3:1-25	The law bars a divorced wife who remarries from returning, yet God tells Israel, who has had many lovers, to come back. Backsliding Israel went up every high mountain and was given a certificate of divorce; her sister Judah watched, did the same, and returned only in pretence, so Israel is called the more righteous. The northern tribes are told to return, since God will not stay angry forever: he promises shepherds after his own heart, a Jerusalem called Yahweh's Throne, and an ark nobody remembers. The people close with a confession that the hills are useless.
JER 4:1-31	If Israel puts away her abominations the nations will bless themselves in Yahweh, and Judah is told to break up fallow ground and circumcise their hearts. Then the alarm: blow the trumpet and get into the fortified cities, because a destroyer of nations is coming from the north with chariots like a whirlwind and horses faster than eagles. Jeremiah's anguish is physical. He sees the earth waste and void, the heavens dark, no people and no birds, though God says he will not make a full end. Zion decks herself for lovers who want her dead.
JER 5:1-31	God tells Jeremiah to search Jerusalem for one person who does justice, and he will pardon the city. Jeremiah tries the poor, then the great men, and finds both have broken the yoke, so lion, wolf and leopard wait for them. They deny that sword or famine will come and call the prophets wind, so God makes his words fire and the people wood. A distant nation whose language they do not know will eat their harvest and flocks. Prophets prophesy falsely, priests rule by their own authority, and the people love it that way.
JER 6:1-30	Flee Jerusalem and blow the trumpet, because evil looks out from the north. Enemy shepherds camp around Zion and debate attacking at noon or by night, and God orders siege mounds against a city that produces wickedness the way a well produces water. From least to greatest everyone is greedy; prophets and priests patch the wound saying peace, peace, when there is no peace, without the ability to blush. Told to ask for the old paths, they refused to walk in them. Jeremiah, set as a tester of metals, reports rejected silver.
JER 7:1-19	Standing in the temple gate, Jeremiah tells worshippers to amend their ways and not to trust the lying words Yahweh's temple, Yahweh's temple, Yahweh's temple. If they truly do justice, stop oppressing the foreigner, the orphan and the widow, and stop following other gods, they can stay in the land. Instead they steal, murder and swear falsely, then shelter in his house as though it were a den of robbers. He points them to Shiloh, where his name lived first, and forbids Jeremiah to pray for them. Whole families bake cakes for the queen of the sky.
JER 7:20-34	God's wrath will pour out on man, animal, tree and crop. What he commanded at the exodus was obedience, not sacrifice, and since Egypt he has sent prophets and been ignored; Jeremiah is told they will not listen to him either, and to call them the nation that would not hear. They built the high places of Topheth in the valley of the son of Hinnom and burned their sons and daughters there, which he never commanded and which never entered his mind. So it will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter, and every wedding voice in Judah silenced.
JER 8:1-22	The bones of Judah's kings, priests and prophets will be dug up and spread before the sun, moon and stars they worshipped, left unburied like dung, and the survivors will prefer death to life. God asks why a people that falls will not get up, each rushing on like a horse into battle. Stork, turtledove, swallow and crane keep their seasons; his people do not know his law. Prophet and priest patch the wound saying peace, peace, when there is no peace. Jeremiah's heart faints: the harvest is past, and he asks whether there is no balm in Gilead.
JER 9:1-26	Jeremiah wishes his head were water and his eyes a spring of tears, and wishes he could leave for a lodge in the wilderness, because they all bend their tongues like bows for falsehood and no one, not even a brother, can be trusted. God will melt and test them, feed them wormwood and gall, scatter them, and make Jerusalem a heap for jackals. Professional mourning women are summoned to teach their daughters wailing, since death has climbed in through the windows. Then the rule: boast of nothing but knowing the God who does loving kindness and justice.
JER 10:1-25	Do not learn the way of the nations or fear signs in the sky. Their customs are empty: a tree is cut, a workman shapes it, they plate it with silver and nail it down so it cannot fall over. Such gods must be carried, cannot speak, and can do neither harm nor good. Yahweh, by contrast, made the earth by his power and brings the wind out of his storehouses, and every goldsmith is disappointed by his own breathless image. Then the siege: gather your goods. Jeremiah admits a man cannot direct his own steps.
JER 11:1-23	Jeremiah proclaims the covenant terms: cursed is the man who will not obey the words God commanded when he brought their fathers out of the iron furnace of Egypt. Their fathers walked in the stubbornness of their hearts, and now a conspiracy has been found in Judah, which has as many gods as it has cities. Israel was a green olive tree, and God has set fire to it. Jeremiah then learns of a plot against himself: the men of his own town, Anathoth, tell him to stop prophesying or die.
JER 12:1-17	Jeremiah concedes God is righteous but argues the case anyway: why do the wicked prosper? God planted them, and he is near their mouths and far from their hearts. The reply is not an answer: if running with footmen tires you, how will you race horses? Even Jeremiah's own family have betrayed him. Then God's grief, at having handed the beloved of his soul to her enemies because his heritage roared at him like a lion. Neighbouring nations will be uprooted too, then restored if they swear by Yahweh's name.
JER 13:1-27	Jeremiah buys a linen belt, wears it unwashed, hides it in a rock cleft by the Euphrates, and digs it up ruined: so God will ruin the pride of Judah, which he made cling to him as a belt clings to a waist. A saying about filling wine bottles becomes God filling kings, priests and prophets with drunkenness and smashing them together. The king and queen mother are told to sit down, their crowns fallen. Can an Ethiopian change his skin, or a leopard his spots? Then neither can people trained in evil.
JER 14:1-22	The word concerning the drought. Judah mourns, jars come back from the cisterns empty, and the doe abandons her fawn. The people admit their rebellions but ask why God acts like a stranger passing the night. He answers that they loved to wander, refuses Jeremiah's prayers, and promises sword, famine and plague. The prophets promising assured peace were never sent and will die by the sword they denied. Jeremiah's eyes are to run with tears night and day. The chapter ends pleading: no idol makes rain, so we wait for you.
JER 15:1-21	God says that even Moses and Samuel standing before him would not change his mind, and appoints four destroyers, sword, dogs, birds and animals, because of what Manasseh did in Jerusalem. He says plainly that he is weary of showing compassion. The woman who bore seven sons gives up her spirit, her sun setting while it is still day. Jeremiah then curses his own birth as a man of strife cursed by everyone, and asks whether God will be a brook that runs dry. The promise back is conditional.
JER 16:1-21	Jeremiah is forbidden to marry or have children here, since children born in this place die unlamented and unburied. He is barred from houses of mourning, because God has withdrawn his peace, and barred from feasts, because the voices of bridegroom and bride will be silenced. Asked what they did wrong, he is to say their fathers forsook God and they did worse. Then a reversal: God will send fishermen and hunters to bring them back, and the nations will admit their fathers inherited only lies.
JER 17:1-27	Judah's sin is engraved with an iron pen and a diamond point on their hearts and their altars' horns. Cursed is the man who trusts in flesh, a desert bush in a salt land; blessed is the one who trusts Yahweh, a tree by water whose leaf stays green in drought. The heart is deceitful above all things, and wealth got wrongly is a partridge sitting on eggs she did not lay. Then a Sabbath oracle at the gates: keep it holy, or fire devours Jerusalem's palaces.
JER 18:1-23	Sent down to the potter's house, Jeremiah watches a vessel go wrong on the wheel and the potter make it into something else. God asks whether he cannot do the same with Israel, and states the principle both ways: he relents when a threatened nation turns, and withdraws good from a nation that does evil. Judah answers that amending is useless, they will follow their own plans. His people have left the ancient paths. When they plot to strike him with the tongue, Jeremiah prays in detail against them.
JER 19:1-15	Carrying a potter's earthen bottle, Jeremiah takes elders and priests to the valley of the son of Hinnom and announces disaster that will make ears tingle, because they filled the place with innocent blood and built high places of Baal to burn their sons, which God never commanded and which never entered his mind. It will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter, and in the siege they will eat the flesh of their own children. He smashes the bottle: God will break this people the same way, beyond mending.
JER 20:1-18	Pashhur son of Immer, chief officer in the temple, has Jeremiah beaten and locked in the stocks at the upper gate of Benjamin. Released, Jeremiah renames him Magormissabib and tells him he will die in Babylon with the friends he prophesied lies to. Then Jeremiah turns on God: you persuaded me and prevailed, and I am a laughing stock all day. Keeping silent only makes the word a fire shut up in his bones. He affirms that Yahweh is with him, breaks into praise, then curses the day he was born.
JER 21:1-14	Zedekiah sends Pashhur and Zephaniah the priest to ask Jeremiah for a wonder that makes Nebuchadnezzar withdraw. The answer is the opposite: God will turn their own weapons back into the city, fight against them himself, and hand Zedekiah and the survivors over without mercy. The people are offered the way of life and the way of death: stay and get sword, famine and plague, surrender to the Chaldeans and live. The house of David is told to do justice in the morning or watch its forest burn.
JER 22:1-30	Jeremiah takes terms to the royal palace: do justice, protect the foreigner, orphan and widow, and kings will keep riding through these gates; refuse, and God swears the house will be desolate. Weep not for the dead but for Shallum, exiled and never to see his country again. Woe to the king who panels a spacious house in red cedar on unpaid labour, when his father did justice for the poor, which was what knowing God meant. Jehoiakim gets a donkey's burial. Coniah is recorded as childless, with no descendant ever ruling in Judah.
JER 23:1-18	Woe to the shepherds who scatter the flock and never visit them: God will visit their evil on them, gather the remnant himself, and appoint shepherds who actually feed the sheep. He will raise for David a righteous Branch called Yahweh Our Righteousness. Then, concerning the prophets, Jeremiah's bones shake like a drunk man's, because prophet and priest alike are profane and their wickedness is found in God's own house. Samaria's prophets prophesied by Baal; Jerusalem's are worse. Do not listen: they speak visions out of their own hearts.
JER 23:19-40	A whirling storm of wrath is already out and will not return until it has done what God intended. He did not send these prophets, yet they ran; had they stood in his council they would have turned people from evil. He has heard them announcing I had a dream, I had a dream, which teaches his people to forget his name. Let the dreamer tell his dream and the one with the word speak it faithfully: what is straw to wheat? His word is fire, and a hammer that shatters rock.
JER 24:1-10	After Jeconiah, the craftsmen and the smiths are carried off to Babylon, God shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs before the temple, one of first-ripe figs and one too bad to eat. The interpretation reverses the obvious expectation. The good figs are the exiles already in Chaldea: God will set his eyes on them for good, bring them back and give them a heart to know him. The bad figs are Zedekiah, his princes and the remnant left behind, who will be tossed among the kingdoms and consumed by sword, famine and plague.
JER 25:1-18	In Jehoiakim's fourth year, Nebuchadnezzar's first, Jeremiah reckons up twenty three years of speaking to a people who would not listen, to him or to any prophet before him. So God will bring the families of the north and Nebuchadnezzar, called his servant, against the land, taking away the voice of bridegroom and bride, and these nations will serve Babylon seventy years, after which Babylon itself is punished. Then God hands Jeremiah a cup of the wine of wrath to make the nations drink until they go insane. He starts with Jerusalem.
JER 25:19-38	The cup goes round: Pharaoh, Uz, the Philistine cities, Edom, Moab and Ammon, Tyre and Sidon, the desert kingdoms, Elam and the Medes, all the kings of the north, and every kingdom on earth, with the king of Sheshach drinking last. They are told to drink, be drunk, vomit and not get up, and refusing the cup changes nothing, since judgment has begun at the city that bears God's name. Yahweh roars like a man treading grapes and has a controversy with the nations. The slain will lie unburied like dung.
JER 26:1-24	Early in Jehoiakim's reign, Jeremiah stands in the temple court and warns that if Judah will not walk in the law, this house will become like Shiloh. The priests, prophets and people seize him and say he must die. Tried before the princes, he answers that God sent him and that killing him puts innocent blood on the city; the princes and people rule that he does not deserve death. Elders recall Micah of Moresheth, whom Hezekiah spared, and Uriah, whom Jehoiakim killed. Ahikam son of Shaphan protects him.
JER 27:1-22	Wearing bonds and bars on his neck, Jeremiah sends word by visiting envoys to the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon: God gives the earth to whomever he pleases, and has given these lands to Nebuchadnezzar, his servant. Any nation refusing the yoke gets sword, famine and plague, so their diviners should be ignored. He tells Zedekiah the same, and warns the priests not to believe prophets promising the temple vessels back soon. The pillars and the bronze sea will go to Babylon and stay until God brings them back.
JER 28:1-17	In Zedekiah's fourth year, Hananiah son of Azzur announces in the temple that God has broken Babylon's yoke and that within two years the vessels, Jeconiah and all the captives will be home. Jeremiah says he hopes so, then points out that a prophet promising peace is only proved genuine when it happens. Hananiah breaks the wooden bar off Jeremiah's neck; Jeremiah walks away, then returns with word that bars of wood are now bars of iron. He tells Hananiah he was never sent and will die this year. He dies.
JER 29:1-17	Jeremiah writes to the exiles in Babylon, sending the letter by Elasah and Gemariah. The instructions are practical: build houses, plant gardens, marry, have children, and seek the peace of the city you were carried into, since your peace depends on its peace. Their prophets, diviners and dreams were never sent. After seventy years God will visit them and bring them back, because his thoughts toward them are of peace, to give them hope and a future. Meanwhile the king and people still in Jerusalem get sword, famine and plague, and become rotten figs.
JER 29:18-32	Those left in Jerusalem will be pursued with sword, famine and plague and tossed among the kingdoms, because they would not listen to the prophets God sent. Two named liars, Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, will be killed in front of the exiles and become a curse formula. Shemaiah the Nehelamite, who wrote to Zephaniah the priest asking why Jeremiah had not been put in the stocks for telling the exiles to settle down, hears that he and his offspring will be punished.
JER 30:1-24	Jeremiah is told to write all these words in a book, because God will reverse the captivity of Israel and Judah. First the terror: men clutching their waists like women in labour, faces gone pale, the day of Jacob's trouble, out of which he will be saved. Then the diagnosis: your hurt is incurable, no one pleads your cause, your lovers have forgotten you, and it was God who wounded you because your sins increased. But those who devoured Israel will be devoured, and the city they called an outcast will be rebuilt.
JER 31:1-20	The survivors of the sword found favour in the wilderness, and God says he has loved them with an everlasting love. The virgin of Israel will be rebuilt, dancing with tambourines and planting vineyards on the mountains of Samaria, until watchmen on the hills of Ephraim call people up to Zion. He will bring them from the ends of the earth, the blind, the lame and pregnant women among them, on a road where they will not stumble. Then Rachel is heard weeping in Ramah for children who are no more.
JER 31:21-40	Set up road signs and turn back along the road you came by, backsliding daughter, because God has created a new thing: a woman will encompass a man. Judah will again bless the habitation of righteousness, with farmers and shepherds living there together. Jeremiah notes he woke at this point and his sleep had been sweet. Nobody will repeat the proverb about sour grapes, since each will die for his own sin. Then the new covenant: the law written on their hearts, everyone knowing him, their sin remembered no more.
JER 32:1-23	In Zedekiah's tenth year, with Babylon besieging Jerusalem, Jeremiah is shut in the court of the guard for prophesying that the city will fall. God tells him his cousin Hanamel will come offering him the field at Anathoth, and when Hanamel arrives Jeremiah knows the word is genuine. He buys the field for seventeen shekels, seals the deed before witnesses, and hands both copies to Baruch son of Neriah to store in a jar, because fields will be bought in this land again. He prays to the God for whom nothing is too hard.
JER 32:24-44	Jeremiah finishes his prayer by pointing at the siege ramps: the city is already handed over, and yet you told me to buy a field. God answers with Jeremiah's own words as a question, is there anything too hard for me, then confirms the worst, that the Chaldeans will burn a city that has provoked him since it was built, passing its children through fire to Molech. Then the turn: he will gather them from every country, give them one heart, and make an everlasting covenant. Fields will be bought again throughout Benjamin and Judah.
JER 33:1-26	Still shut in the court of the guard, Jeremiah gets a second word: call to me and I will answer and show you great and difficult things you do not know. The houses torn down for siege defences will fill with the dead, and yet God will bring the city health and cure, reverse the captivity, and make it a name of joy the nations tremble at. Where they call it waste, the voices of bridegroom and bride will be heard again. A righteous Branch will grow for David, who will never lack an heir.
JER 34:1-22	While Nebuchadnezzar's army fights Jerusalem, Jeremiah tells Zedekiah the city will burn and he will speak to the king of Babylon mouth to mouth, though he will die in peace. Lachish and Azekah are the only fortified cities left. Then a covenant to free every Hebrew slave, which everyone kept and promptly reversed. God notes that the law required release after six years, and proclaims a liberty of his own: liberty to the sword, plague and famine. The Babylonian army, which had withdrawn, will come back and burn the city.
JER 35:1-19	Jeremiah brings the Rechabites into a room of the temple, sets out bowls and cups, and tells them to drink. They refuse: their ancestor Jonadab son of Rechab commanded them never to drink wine, never to build houses or plant vineyards but to live in tents, and they have kept all of it. The point is the comparison. Jonadab is still obeyed generations on, while God has sent prophet after prophet to Judah and been ignored. The Rechabites are promised they will never lack a man to stand before him.
JER 36:1-15	In Jehoiakim's fourth year Jeremiah is told to write everything he has been given since Josiah's day on a scroll, in the hope that Judah will hear and turn. Baruch son of Neriah writes it from dictation. Jeremiah, restricted and unable to enter the temple himself, sends Baruch to read it there on a fast day. In the fifth year a fast is proclaimed and Baruch reads it in Gemariah's room. Micaiah son of Gemariah reports to the princes in the palace, who send for Baruch and have him read it again.
JER 36:16-32	The princes hear it, take fright, and tell Baruch to hide with Jeremiah and let nobody know where. They report to the king, who sends Jehudi to fetch the scroll and read it aloud. Sitting in the winter house with a fire in the brazier, he cuts it up with a penknife every three or four columns and burns it, piece by piece. Nobody tears their clothes, and Elnathan, Delaiah and Gemariah plead in vain. He orders both men arrested, but God hides them. Jeremiah dictates it again to Baruch, with many similar words added.
JER 37:1-21	Zedekiah sends Jehucal and Zephaniah the priest to ask Jeremiah to pray for the city. Egypt's army draws the Chaldeans off, but the word is that Pharaoh will go home and the siege will return and burn Jerusalem. Leaving for Benjamin to see to his property, Jeremiah is arrested at the gate as a defector, beaten, and shut in Jonathan the scribe's prison. Brought out secretly, he tells Zedekiah he will be handed to Babylon, and begs not to go back there. He is moved to the court of the guard.
JER 38:1-14	Four officials hear Jeremiah telling the people that whoever stays in the city dies and whoever surrenders to the Chaldeans lives, and ask the king to have him killed. Zedekiah says he cannot stop them, so they lower Jeremiah by ropes into Malchijah's dungeon, which holds no water but mire, and he sinks into the mud. Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, a palace eunuch, tells the king he will starve there and is sent with thirty men. He fetches rags to pad Jeremiah's armpits under the ropes, and they haul him up.
JER 38:15-28	Jeremiah warns Zedekiah that answering will get him killed and that the advice will be ignored anyway, so the king swears secretly not to hand him over. The terms are simple: surrender and the city stands, refuse and it burns. Zedekiah admits his real fear is being mocked by the Judeans who have already defected. If he refuses, the palace women will be led out and his wives and children taken. Told to keep it secret, Jeremiah tells the princes only that he begged not to be returned to Jonathan's house.
JER 39:1-18	In Zedekiah's eleventh year, on the ninth day of the fourth month, the wall is breached and the Babylonian officers take their seats in the middle gate. Zedekiah flees by night through the king's garden, is overtaken in the plains of Jericho, and is brought to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah, who kills his sons in front of him, then blinds him and takes him in fetters to Babylon. The city is burned and the people deported. Nebuchadnezzar orders Jeremiah protected, and Ebedmelech is told he will be spared because he trusted God.
JER 40:1-16	Nebuzaradan finds Jeremiah in chains among the captives at Ramah, takes them off, and offers him a choice: Babylon, or anywhere he likes. He recommends Gedaliah son of Ahikam, whom Babylon has made governor, gives him food and lets him go. Jeremiah joins Gedaliah at Mizpah, where the captains left in the countryside are told that serving the Chaldeans is safe. Scattered Jews return from Moab, Ammon and Edom to a large harvest. Johanan warns that Baalis of Ammon has sent Ishmael to kill Gedaliah, who will not believe it.
JER 41:1-18	In the seventh month Ishmael son of Nethaniah comes to Mizpah with ten men, eats with Gedaliah, then kills him along with the Jews and Chaldean soldiers there. The next day eighty pilgrims arrive from Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria with offerings; Ishmael goes out weeping to meet them and kills them in the city, throwing the bodies into Asa's cistern. Ten survive by revealing hidden food stores. He takes the rest of Mizpah captive and heads for Ammon, but Johanan son of Kareah catches him at Gibeon and the captives change sides.
JER 42:1-22	Johanan son of Kareah, Jezaniah and all the captains ask Jeremiah to pray and show them the way to go, swearing to obey whatever comes. After ten days the answer arrives: stay in the land and God will build and plant them, and they need not fear the king of Babylon. Go to Egypt instead and the sword they fear will overtake them there, with famine close behind and none escaping. Jeremiah tells them plainly that they have dealt deceitfully with themselves, and will die in the place they want to go.
JER 43:1-13	Azariah son of Hoshaiah, Johanan son of Kareah and all the proud men accuse Jeremiah of lying, and blame Baruch for turning him against them. They take the whole remnant, including Jeremiah and Baruch, into Egypt as far as Tahpanhes. There God tells Jeremiah to hide large stones in the brickwork at the entry of Pharaoh's house and announce that Nebuchadnezzar will set his throne on them. He will strike Egypt, burn the houses of its gods, wrap himself in the land the way a shepherd puts on his coat, and leave in peace.
JER 44:1-16	The word comes to the Jews living at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis and in Pathros. They have seen Judah left desolate, and the cause was burning incense to gods they did not know. So why, God asks, do it again in Egypt, cutting off man, woman and nursing child and leaving no remnant? He sets his face against them: the remnant in Egypt will be consumed by sword and famine, from least to greatest, and only a few will see Judah again. The people answer that they will not listen.
JER 44:17-30	The people say they will keep every vow, burning incense to the queen of the sky as their fathers and kings did in Judah, because back then they had plenty of food and famine only came after they stopped. The women add that their husbands knew about the cakes. Jeremiah answers that God remembered that incense, which is exactly why the land became a desolation. He tells them to go ahead, and swears that no man of Judah in Egypt will say As the Lord Yahweh lives again.
JER 45:1-5	A short word to Baruch son of Neriah, dated to the fourth year of Jehoiakim, when he wrote Jeremiah's words in a book. God quotes Baruch's own complaint back to him: woe is me, sorrow has been added to my pain, I am worn out with groaning and find no rest. The answer offers no comfort about the situation, only perspective. What God built he is breaking down, and what he planted he is plucking up, and this across the whole land. So Baruch should not seek great things for himself, because disaster is coming on all flesh. The single promise is personal and small: wherever he goes, he will escape with his life.
JER 46:1-28	The oracles against the nations begin with Egypt, and with Pharaoh Necoh's army beaten at Carchemish by the Euphrates. Shields are readied and spears polished, and then the question: why do I see them turning back, terror on every side? Egypt rises like the Nile in flood, but the day belongs to Yahweh. Go up to Gilead for balm, virgin daughter of Egypt: there is no healing. Then Nebuchadnezzar invades Egypt itself, and the beautiful heifer meets destruction from the north, her hired soldiers running like stall-fed calves. Jacob is told not to fear.
JER 47:1-7	A word concerning the Philistines, given before Pharaoh struck Gaza. Waters rise out of the north into an overflowing stream that covers the land and everyone in it. At the sound of stamping hooves and rumbling wheels, fathers do not turn back for their children, their hands too feeble. Every remaining helper from Tyre and Sidon is cut off, Gaza is shaved bald and Ashkelon brought to nothing. The sword of Yahweh is asked how long until it goes back in its scabbard, and cannot rest, having been given a command.
JER 48:1-26	The oracle against Moab names town after town: Nebo laid waste, Kiriathaim taken, Heshbon plotting to end Moab as a nation, weeping up the ascent of Luhith. Flee and save your lives, because your treasures will not help and Chemosh himself goes into captivity. Moab has sat undisturbed like wine settled on its lees, never poured from vessel to vessel, so his taste is unchanged; now men will pour him off and smash the jars. He will be ashamed of Chemosh as Israel was of Bethel, and will wallow in his own vomit.
JER 48:27-47	God asks whether Moab did not make a derision of Israel, shaking his head whenever he spoke of him. Now Moab is told to leave the cities and live in the rocks like a dove nesting over a chasm, since his boasting has accomplished nothing. Then God says he will wail for Moab himself, weeping more than Jazer wept for the vine of Sibmah, because the wine presses are silent and the shouting is no shouting. The terror, the pit and the snare wait, yet Moab's captivity will one day be reversed.
JER 49:1-19	Concerning Ammon: God asks why Malcam possesses Gad if Israel has heirs, and promises war on Rabbah until it is a desolate heap, with Malcam going into captivity beside his priests. Concerning Edom: is wisdom gone from Teman? Grape gatherers leave gleanings and thieves stop when they have enough, but Esau is stripped bare, his hiding places uncovered. Those who never deserved the cup are drinking it, so Edom will drink too, and Bozrah becomes a curse. Edom nested as high as an eagle and will be brought down like Sodom.
JER 49:20-39	Edom will be dragged off like the little ones of the flock, the earth trembling at the noise, an eagle spreading its wings over Bozrah. Concerning Damascus: Hamath and Arpad melt at the news, the city of praise is asked how it is not forsaken, and fire devours the palaces of Ben Hadad. Concerning Kedar and Hazor, struck by Nebuchadnezzar: tents, flocks and camels carried off, a people living at ease with neither gates nor bars scattered to the winds. Concerning Elam: God breaks its bow and brings the four winds against it.
JER 50:1-23	The word concerning Babylon, announced openly with a standard raised: Babylon is taken, Bel disappointed, her idols shamed, because a nation from the north will empty her land. Israel and Judah will come back together weeping. God calls his people lost sheep whose shepherds led them astray, and whose devourers claimed innocence on the grounds that the sheep had sinned. So flee out of Babylon like goats ahead of the flock. Babylon's king will be punished as Assyria's was, Judah's sins searched for and not found, and the hammer of the whole earth lies broken.
JER 50:24-46	God says he laid a snare and Babylon walked into it without noticing. He has opened his armoury and brought out the weapons of his indignation, and the attackers are told to come from the farthest border, open her storehouses and leave nothing; those who escape are to announce in Zion the vengeance taken for his temple. Israel's captors refuse to release them, but their Redeemer is strong and will plead their cause. A sword is announced against her princes, soldiers, horses and treasures, and a drought against her waters.
JHN 1:1-28	John begins before the beginning: the Word was with God and was God, and everything was made through him. In him was life, the light that the darkness has not overcome. A man named John is sent to testify to the light, not to be it. The world made through him did not recognise him, but those who received him were given the right to become God's children. The Word became flesh and lived among them, full of grace and truth. Questioned by priests and Levites, John denies being the Christ, Elijah or the prophet, and calls himself the voice in the wilderness from Isaiah. Asked why he baptizes, he says one stands among them whom they do not know.
JHN 1:29-51	Seeing Jesus the next day, John calls him the Lamb of God who takes away the world's sin, and says he was told to watch for the Spirit descending and remaining, which he saw. The following day he says it again to two of his disciples, who follow Jesus; asked what they want, they ask where he is staying, and he says come and see. One is Andrew, who fetches his brother Simon, saying they have found the Messiah, and Jesus renames him Cephas. The next day Philip is called, and finds Nathanael, who asks whether anything good comes out of Nazareth. Jesus says he saw him under the fig tree; Nathanael calls him Son of God and King of Israel, and is told he will see angels ascending on the Son of Man.
JHN 2:1-25	At a wedding in Cana the wine runs out, and Jesus's mother tells him; he says his hour has not come, and she tells the servants to do whatever he says. Six stone purification jars are filled with water, and what is drawn out is wine, which the master of the feast praises the bridegroom for saving until last. John calls this the first of the signs. Jesus then goes up to Jerusalem for Passover, makes a whip of cords, drives the sheep and oxen out of the temple, pours out the money changers' coins and overturns their tables, and tells the dove sellers not to make his Father's house a marketplace. Asked for a sign, he says destroy this temple and he will raise it in three days, meaning his body.
JHN 3:1-36	Nicodemus, a Pharisee and ruler, comes at night and concedes that Jesus must be from God. Jesus tells him no one sees the kingdom without being born anew, of water and spirit; Nicodemus asks how an old man can be born again, and is told the Spirit is like wind. Jesus speaks of the Son of Man lifted up as Moses lifted the serpent, of God loving the world and giving his only Son, and of judgment as light coming into a world that preferred darkness. Afterwards Jesus baptizes in Judea while John baptizes at Enon. Told that everyone is going to Jesus, John says the friend of the bridegroom is glad to hear his voice, that he himself must decrease, and that the one from heaven is above all.
JHN 4:1-27	Jesus leaves Judea for Galilee and goes through Samaria, stopping at Jacob's well at midday while his disciples buy food. He asks a Samaritan woman for a drink, and she points out that Jews have no dealings with Samaritans. He speaks of living water that becomes a spring welling up to eternal life; she asks for it, since the well is deep. Told to fetch her husband, she says she has none, and he says she has had five and the present man is not her husband. She calls him a prophet and asks which mountain to worship on; he answers that the hour is coming for worship in spirit and truth, and tells her plainly that he is the Messiah. The disciples return and are surprised he is talking to a woman.
JHN 4:28-54	The woman leaves her water pot and tells the town about a man who told her everything she did, asking whether he could be the Christ, and they come out to him. Meanwhile the disciples urge him to eat, and he says his food is to do the will of the one who sent him, then tells them to look at fields already white for harvest. Many Samaritans believe because of her testimony, and after he stays two days many more believe from hearing him themselves, calling him the Savior of the world. At Cana a nobleman begs him to come down to Capernaum for his dying son; Jesus tells him the boy lives, and the man learns the fever broke at that hour. John counts this the second sign.
JHN 5:1-22	At a feast in Jerusalem, by the pool of Bethesda with its five porches, crowds of the sick wait for the water to be stirred. A man has been ill thirty-eight years and has no one to put him in. Jesus asks whether he wants to be made well, then tells him to take up his mat and walk; it is the Sabbath, and he is told carrying the mat is unlawful. He does not know who healed him until Jesus finds him in the temple. They then persecute Jesus, who says his Father is still working, so he is working too, which they take as making himself equal with God. He answers that the Son does only what he sees the Father doing, and that all judgment is given to the Son.
JHN 5:23-47	Whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him. Anyone who hears and believes has eternal life and has passed out of death; the hour is coming when the dead in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, to a resurrection of life or of judgment. He says he can do nothing of himself and judges as he hears. On evidence, his own testimony would not count, so he lists others: John, a burning lamp they enjoyed for a while; the works the Father gave him; and the Father himself. They search the scriptures for life but will not come to him, and take glory from one another rather than from God. Their accuser will be Moses, who wrote about him.
JHN 6:1-34	Across the sea of Galilee a great crowd follows him, and near Passover he asks Philip where bread can be bought, to test him. Philip prices it at two hundred denarii, and Andrew mentions a boy with five barley loaves and two fish. Jesus seats about five thousand men on the grass, distributes bread and fish as much as they want, and has twelve baskets of scraps gathered so nothing is lost. When they try to make him king by force, he withdraws alone. That evening the disciples cross toward Capernaum, see him walking on the sea, and are afraid until he speaks. The crowd follows, and he tells them they came because they ate, and that the true bread from heaven comes from his Father.
JHN 6:35-71	Jesus says he is the bread of life, that whoever comes to him will not be turned away, and that he will raise up all the Father gives him. The crowd objects that they know his parents. Their fathers ate manna and died; this bread gives life, and the bread he will give is his flesh. When they argue about how he can give his flesh to eat, he sharpens it: unless they eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood they have no life. He says this in the synagogue at Capernaum, and many disciples call it a hard saying and stop following him. Asked whether they too will leave, Peter answers that there is nowhere else to go. Jesus notes that one of the twelve is a devil, meaning Judas.
JHN 7:1-26	Jesus stays in Galilee because Judea wants him dead. His brothers, who do not believe in him, tell him to go to the Feast of Booths and show himself openly; he says his time has not come and that the world hates him for testifying its works are evil. After they leave he goes up privately. The crowds are divided between calling him a good man and saying he misleads people. Halfway through the feast he teaches in the temple, and they wonder how an uneducated man knows so much. He says the teaching is his sender's, asks why they want to kill him when none of them keeps the law, and points out that they circumcise on the Sabbath.
JHN 7:27-53	They object that they know where he comes from, whereas the Christ's origin will be unknown; Jesus answers that they know neither him nor the one who sent him. Attempts to seize him fail because his hour has not come. On the last and greatest day of the feast he calls the thirsty to come and drink, promising rivers of living water, which John explains means the Spirit not yet given. The crowd divides over whether the Christ can come from Galilee rather than Bethlehem. The officers sent to arrest him return empty-handed saying no one ever spoke like him, and Nicodemus, asking whether the law condemns a man unheard, is told to check whether any prophet came from Galilee.
JHN 8:1-29	Teaching in the temple early, Jesus is brought a woman caught in adultery, with a question about stoning designed to trap him. He stoops and writes on the ground, then says the one without sin should throw first; the accusers leave one by one from the oldest. He tells her he does not condemn her and to sin no more. He then says he is the light of the world. The Pharisees object that self-testimony is invalid, and he answers that the Father testifies with him, which makes two witnesses. Asked where his Father is, he says they know neither. Nobody arrests him, since his hour has not come. He says they will seek him and die in their sins, since he is from above and they are from below.
JHN 8:30-59	To those who believed him he says that remaining in his word makes them disciples, and the truth will free them. They reply that as Abraham's offspring they have never been in bondage, and he answers that everyone who sins is sin's slave. He grants their descent from Abraham but says Abraham did not try to kill men who told the truth, and tells them their father is the devil, a murderer and the father of lies. They call him a Samaritan with a demon. He says whoever keeps his word will never see death, which they take as proof, since Abraham died. He answers that Abraham rejoiced to see his day, and when they ask how, being under fifty, he saw Abraham, he says that before Abraham was, I AM. They pick up stones.
JHN 9:1-41	Asked whose sin caused a man's blindness from birth, Jesus says neither his nor his parents', makes mud with saliva, anoints his eyes and sends him to wash in the pool of Siloam, and he comes back seeing. The neighbours argue about whether it is really him, and take him to the Pharisees, since it happened on a Sabbath. They are divided; he calls Jesus a prophet. His parents, afraid of expulsion from the synagogue, refer them back to their son. Questioned again, he says he knows only that he was blind and now sees, then asks whether they want to be disciples too, and is thrown out. Jesus finds him and he believes. Jesus says claiming to see is what leaves the Pharisees' sin in place.
JHN 10:1-42	Jesus describes a sheepfold: the shepherd comes in by the door and the sheep know his voice, while strangers are fled from. When they do not understand, he says he is the door, and then the good shepherd who lays down his life, unlike a hired hand who runs from the wolf. He has other sheep not of this fold, and there will be one flock. Opinion divides between demon possession and the fact that demons do not open blind eyes. At the Feast of the Dedication they ask him to say plainly whether he is the Christ, and he says his works testify, that his sheep cannot be snatched from his hand, and that he and the Father are one. They take up stones, and he answers from a psalm before escaping beyond the Jordan.
JHN 11:1-31	Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Mary and Martha, falls sick, and his sisters send word. Jesus says the illness is for God's glory and stays two days where he is. He then proposes going back to Judea, which alarms the disciples, since people there tried to stone him. He says Lazarus has fallen asleep, and when they take that as recovery, tells them plainly that he is dead. Thomas says they may as well go and die with him. Arriving, Jesus finds Lazarus four days in the tomb. Martha meets him and says he could have prevented it; he tells her her brother will rise, and that he is the resurrection and the life, and she says she believes he is the Christ.
JHN 11:32-57	Mary falls at his feet and says the same thing her sister said. Seeing her and the mourners weeping, Jesus is troubled and weeps, which some read as affection and others as a reason to ask why he did not prevent the death. At the tomb he orders the stone taken away; Martha objects that four days means a stench. He thanks the Father aloud for the sake of the crowd, then calls Lazarus out, and the dead man comes out bound in wrappings. Many believe, and some report it to the Pharisees. The council worries that Rome will act, and Caiaphas says it is better for one man to die for the people, which John calls a prophecy. From then on they plan his death.
JHN 12:1-25	Six days before Passover Jesus is at Bethany, where Lazarus is at the table. Mary anoints his feet with a pound of costly nard and wipes them with her hair. Judas asks why it was not sold for three hundred denarii for the poor, which John says was because he stole from the money box; Jesus says she has kept it for his burial. Crowds come to see Lazarus too, and the chief priests plan to kill him as well. The next day palm branches and shouts of Hosanna greet Jesus riding a young donkey, which the disciples only later connect to prophecy. Some Greeks ask Philip to see Jesus, and he answers that his hour has come and that a grain of wheat must die to bear fruit.
JHN 12:26-50	Serving him means following him. Jesus says his soul is troubled but that this is why he came, and asks the Father to glorify his name; a voice answers from the sky, which the crowd takes for thunder or an angel. He says the voice was for their sake, that the prince of this world is cast out, and that being lifted up will draw all people, meaning the kind of death he would die. Asked how the Christ can be lifted up if he remains forever, he tells them to walk while they have the light, and then hides. John explains their unbelief from Isaiah, and notes that many rulers believed but would not say so, preferring human praise. Jesus says his word will judge those who reject it.
JHN 13:1-38	Before Passover, knowing his hour has come and that Judas has already been prompted to betray him, Jesus gets up from supper, ties a towel round his waist and washes the disciples' feet. Peter objects, is told he will have no part otherwise, then asks to be washed all over. Dressed again, Jesus says that since the Lord and Teacher has washed their feet they should wash one another's. He quotes the psalm about a man eating bread with him lifting his heel against him, then says one of them will betray him. At Peter's prompting the disciple leaning on him asks who, and Jesus gives the dipped bread to Judas, telling him to be quick; Judas goes out, and it is night. Then the new commandment to love one another, and the warning about Peter's three denials.
JHN 14:1-31	Jesus tells them not to be troubled: his Father's house has many rooms, and he goes to prepare a place and will come back. Thomas says they do not know the way, and he answers that he is the way, the truth and the life, and no one comes to the Father except through him. Philip asks to be shown the Father, and is told that seeing him is seeing the Father. Believers will do greater works, and whatever is asked in his name he will do. He promises another Counselor, the Spirit of truth, who will teach them everything and remind them of what he said. Asked by Judas, not Iscariot, why only they will see him, he says anyone who keeps his word will be made a home with. He leaves them peace, not as the world gives.
JHN 15:1-27	Jesus calls himself the true vine and the Father the farmer, who removes fruitless branches and prunes fruitful ones. They are the branches and can do nothing apart from him; a branch that does not remain withers and is burned. If they remain and his words remain in them, they can ask what they want. He tells them to remain in his love by keeping his commandments, and gives the commandment to love one another as he loved them, since no love is greater than laying down your life for your friends. He calls them friends rather than servants, because he has told them everything, and reminds them he chose them. Then the warning: the world hated him first, and will persecute them for his name. The Spirit will testify, and so will they.
JHN 16:1-33	Jesus warns them so they will not stumble: they will be put out of synagogues, and people will think killing them is service to God. He says it is to their advantage that he goes, since otherwise the Counselor will not come, who will convict the world about sin, righteousness and judgment, and guide them into all truth. He says that in a little while they will not see him, then will see him again, which they discuss without understanding. He compares their sorrow to a woman in labour whose anguish is forgotten in joy. In that day they will ask the Father directly in his name, and he will speak plainly instead of in figures. When they say they now believe, he says they will all be scattered, but that he has overcome the world.
JHN 17:1-26	Looking up, Jesus prays that the hour has come and asks the Father to glorify the Son, defining eternal life as knowing the only true God and the one he sent. He says he finished the work given him and asks for the glory he had before the world existed. He prays for those given to him out of the world, not for the world; he asks that they be kept in the Father's name and be one, noting that none was lost except the son of destruction. He does not ask that they be taken out of the world but kept from the evil one, and asks that they be sanctified in the truth, since he is sending them as he was sent. He prays also for those who will believe through them, that all may be one.
JHN 18:1-21	Jesus crosses the Kidron into a garden Judas knows. Judas arrives with soldiers and officers carrying lanterns, torches and weapons. Jesus asks whom they want, and when he says I am he they fall back to the ground; he asks again and tells them to let the others go. Peter cuts off the right ear of the high priest's servant, named Malchus, and is told to sheathe the sword, since he must drink the cup the Father has given. They bind him and take him to Annas, father-in-law of Caiaphas. Peter follows with another disciple known to the high priest, and denies being a disciple to the woman keeping the door, then warms himself at the fire. Asked about his teaching, Jesus says he taught openly.
JHN 18:22-40	An officer slaps him for how he answered, and he asks what evil he has spoken. Annas sends him bound to Caiaphas. At the fire Peter denies him twice more, the second time to a relative of the man whose ear he cut off, and the rooster crows. They bring him to the Praetorium but stay outside to avoid defilement before the Passover. Pilate asks for the charge and is told only that he is an evildoer; told to judge him himself, they answer that they cannot put anyone to death. Pilate asks whether he is king of the Jews, and Jesus says his kingdom is not of this world, and that he came to testify to the truth. Pilate asks what truth is, finds no case, and offers to release him by custom; they call for Barabbas, a robber.
JHN 19:1-22	Pilate has him flogged, and the soldiers crown him with thorns, dress him in purple, hail him as king and slap him. Pilate brings him out saying he finds no case and presents him with the words behold the man; the chief priests shout for crucifixion and say their law condemns him for making himself the Son of God, which frightens Pilate more. Asked where he is from, Jesus says nothing, then tells Pilate his power is given from above. Pilate tries to release him until they say that would make him no friend of Caesar. He sits at the Pavement, presents their king, and hears that they have no king but Caesar. Jesus carries his cross to Golgotha, crucified between two others.
JHN 19:23-42	The soldiers divide his clothes four ways and cast lots for the seamless coat rather than tear it, which John ties to scripture. His mother, her sister, Mary the wife of Clopas and Mary Magdalene stand by the cross, and he gives his mother and the disciple he loved to each other. Knowing everything is finished, he says he is thirsty, is given vinegar on a sponge, says it is finished, and gives up his spirit. Because of the Sabbath the legs of the other two are broken, but he is already dead, so a soldier pierces his side and blood and water come out. Joseph of Arimathaea, a secret disciple, asks for the body, and Nicodemus brings a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes; they lay him in a new tomb in a garden.
JHN 20:1-31	Mary Magdalene finds the stone gone before dawn and tells Peter and the disciple Jesus loved that the body has been taken. They run, the other disciple arrives first but waits, Peter goes in and sees the linen and the head cloth rolled up separately, and the other believes. Mary stays weeping, sees two angels, then Jesus, whom she takes for the gardener until he says her name; he tells her not to hold him and to go and tell his brothers. That evening, behind locked doors, he stands among them, shows his hands and side, sends them as the Father sent him, and breathes the Spirit on them. Thomas, absent, demands to touch the wounds, and eight days later is invited to, and answers my Lord and my God.
JHN 21:1-25	At the sea of Tiberias, Peter goes fishing with six others and they catch nothing all night. At daybreak a man on the beach tells them to cast on the right side, and the net fills; the disciple Jesus loved recognises him, and Peter wraps his coat round himself and jumps in. On shore there is a charcoal fire with fish and bread, and Peter drags in a net holding a hundred and fifty-three fish without tearing. After breakfast Jesus asks Peter three times whether he loves him, telling him each time to feed or tend the sheep, and Peter is grieved by the third. He is told how he will die, and to follow. Asked about the other disciple, Jesus says it is not Peter's concern.
JOB 1:1-22	Job of Uz is blameless, rich in seven thousand sheep and ten children, and offers burnt offerings in case his sons have sinned at their feasts. In the divine council Satan asks whether Job fears God for nothing, since God has hedged him about. God permits him to strike everything but Job himself. Four messengers arrive back to back: Sabeans take the oxen, fire burns the sheep, Chaldeans take the camels, a wind kills all ten children. Job tears his robe, worships, and says Yahweh gave and has taken away.
JOB 2:1-13	The council meets again. Satan argues that skin is given for skin and a man will surrender everything for his own life, so God permits an attack on Job's body but not his life. Job is struck with sores from sole to head and sits in the ashes scraping himself with a piece of broken pottery. His wife tells him to renounce God and die; he answers that they should accept evil from God as well as good. Three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, come and sit with him seven days in silence.
JOB 3:1-26	Job breaks the silence by cursing the day he was born. He wants that day blotted from the calendar, seized by darkness, cursed by those who rouse Leviathan. He asks why he did not die at birth, since in the grave kings and prisoners and slaves all lie at rest together and the wicked stop troubling anyone. He asks why light is given to people who long for death and dig for it like treasure. He ends saying the thing he feared has come, and he has no quiet, no rest, only trouble.
JOB 4:1-21	Eliphaz answers first, gently. He points out that Job has strengthened others in trouble and now collapses when trouble reaches him. His argument is that the innocent never perish: those who plough iniquity reap it, and lions with all their roaring still starve. Then he reports a night vision, a spirit passing before his face that made his hair stand up, and a voice asking whether a mortal can be more just than God. If God charges even his angels with error, people who live in houses of clay have no case at all.
JOB 5:1-27	Eliphaz continues. Resentment kills the fool, and man is born to trouble as sparks fly upward. He recommends taking the case to God, who lifts the low, frustrates the crafty and catches the wise in their own cleverness. Then the pivot: the man God corrects is happy, because God wounds and binds up the same wound. He promises deliverance from six troubles and seven, from famine, war and slander, peace with the animals and the stones of the field, and a grave reached in full age like harvested grain. He closes saying they have researched this and it is so.
JOB 6:1-30	Job wishes his grief could be weighed against the sand of the seas, which would explain why his words are rash. God's arrows are in him and his spirit is drinking the poison. He asks whether a donkey brays over good grass, or whether the white of an egg has any taste, and asks God to finish the job and crush him while he still has not denied God's words. His friends, he says, are like a wadi: full of ice in winter, gone by summer, so the caravans that counted on them arrive and find nothing. He asks them to show him where he actually erred.
JOB 7:1-21	Job compares life to forced labour, a hired hand watching for the shadow of evening and the wages that follow. His nights are appointed misery, his flesh is covered in worms and crusted dust, his days run out faster than a weaver's shuttle. He refuses to keep quiet, asking whether he is the sea or a sea monster that God needs a guard on him, and complaining that even sleep brings terrifying dreams. He turns the psalm about God's attention to humanity into a complaint: stop watching me, look away long enough for me to swallow, and pardon me before I am gone.
JOB 8:1-22	Bildad answers, less gently. He asks how long Job will blow words about like wind, and states flatly that God does not pervert justice, which means Job's children died for their own sin. His advice is to make supplication and be pure, and then the small beginning will end great. He appeals to earlier generations, since we know nothing and our days are a shadow, then gives his image: papyrus cannot grow without mire, and the godless man's confidence is a spider's web that will not hold his weight. God will not cast away a blameless man, so Job's mouth will be filled with laughter yet.
JOB 9:1-35	Job agrees that no man can win a case against God, who moves mountains without their noticing, shakes the earth, commands the sun not to rise, made the Bear, Orion and the Pleiades, and passes by unseen. Since God is both stronger and the one who would summon the court, Job says even a righteous man's own mouth would condemn him. He concludes that God destroys the blameless and the wicked alike. His days run faster than a runner, than ships, than a swooping eagle. Washing in snow and lye would not help; there is no umpire to lay a hand on them both.
JOB 10:1-22	Job says he will give his complaint free rein. He asks God why he contends with him: does God have eyes of flesh, or years as short as a man's, that he needs to hunt out sin? He reminds God that these hands shaped him like clay, poured him out like milk and curdled him like cheese, clothed him with skin and knit him with bones, then set about destroying the work. Guilty or innocent, he cannot lift his head. He asks why he was brought out of the womb at all, and asks God to leave him alone for a little comfort before he goes to the land of darkness.
JOB 11:1-20	Zophar answers, offended by the volume of talk. He wishes God would speak up and show Job the secrets of wisdom, and states that God is exacting less than Job's sin deserves. God's mystery is higher than heaven, deeper than Sheol, longer than the earth and broader than the sea, and an empty-headed man will become wise about the day a man is born as a wild donkey's colt. His terms are the usual ones: set your heart right, put away iniquity, and misery will pass like water gone by, life will be brighter than noon, and you will sleep unafraid. The wicked, by contrast, have nowhere to run.
JOB 12:1-25	Job opens sarcastically, granting that wisdom will die with them, then says he knows all of it too and is nobody's inferior. He notes that the blameless man is now a joke to his neighbours while robbers' tents prosper. Ask the animals, the birds, the earth and the fish, he says, and they will tell you Yahweh's hand did this. Then he gives his own catalogue of God's power, aimed at the powerful: God tears down what cannot be rebuilt, strips counsellors, makes judges fools, leads priests away, silences trusted men, pours contempt on princes, builds nations and destroys them, and leaves chiefs groping in the dark and staggering like drunks.
JOB 13:1-28	Job says he has seen and heard all of it and would rather take his case to the Almighty than to them. He calls them forgers of lies and worthless physicians whose best move would be complete silence, and asks whether they really intend to show partiality to God and lie on his behalf, since he will examine them too. Their memorable sayings are proverbs of ashes. He resolves to speak even if God kills him, asks only that God withdraw his hand and lift the terror so the two can question each other, and asks to be told what his sins actually are. Why harass a driven leaf, a man already rotting like a moth-eaten garment?
JOB 14:1-22	Job describes human life as short and full of trouble, growing like a flower and cut down, fleeing like a shadow, its months already counted. He contrasts man with a tree: a felled tree sprouts again at the scent of water, but a man lies down and does not rise until the heavens are no more. He wishes God would hide him in Sheol until the wrath passed and then set a time to remember him, and asks whether a man who dies can live again. As it is, his steps are counted and his sin sealed in a bag. Water wears away stone and so God wears away hope; a man leaves without knowing whether his sons rise or fall.
JOB 15:1-35	Eliphaz returns, sharper. He accuses Job of filling himself with the east wind, of undermining reverence, and of being condemned by his own mouth rather than by anyone else. He asks whether Job was born before the hills or sat in on God's private council, and points out that their side has grey-haired men older than Job's father. His doctrine: no one born of woman is clean, God does not even trust his holy ones, and the heavens are not clean in his sight.
