Then a long portrait of the wicked man, hearing terrors, wandering for bread, fat and stiff-necked, living in ruined houses, his branch withered, shedding unripe grapes and blossom, his tents consumed by fire.
JOB 16:1-22	Job calls all three of them miserable comforters and says he could easily make their speeches if their positions were swapped, but he would use his mouth to strengthen instead. Speaking does not ease his grief and silence does not either. He describes God as an attacker: tearing him in wrath, gnashing teeth, taking him by the neck and dashing him to pieces, setting him up as a target with archers around him, splitting his kidneys, running at him like a giant. He has sewn sackcloth to his skin and his face is red with weeping, though his hands hold no violence. He asks the earth not to cover his blood and insists his witness is in heaven.
JOB 17:1-16	Job says his spirit is used up, his days are out and the grave is ready. He asks for a pledge, someone to strike hands and stand as his collateral, since nobody else will. He has been made a byword and people spit in his face; his eyes are dim and his limbs are a shadow. He grants that the upright will be appalled and the clean-handed will grow stronger, then tells his friends to try again, since there is not a wise man among them. They keep calling night day and saying light is near while it is dark. If he makes Sheol his house and calls the worm his mother and sister, where is his hope, and who will see it?
JOB 18:1-21	Bildad objects to being treated as an animal and asks how long Job will hunt for words. Then he delivers his own portrait of the wicked man's end, built almost entirely out of traps: his lamp goes out, his own counsel throws him down, his feet carry him into a net, a snare takes him by the heel, a noose waits hidden in the ground. Terrors chase him from every side, the firstborn of death eats his limbs, he is dragged from his tent to the king of terrors, and sulphur is scattered where he lived. His roots dry up, his branch is cut, his name vanishes from the street, and he leaves no son or grandson behind.
JOB 19:1-29	Job says they have reproached him ten times and asks how long they will crush him with words. He describes God as having walled up his path, stripped his glory, taken his crown, uprooted his hope like a tree, and set troops to build a siege ramp against his tent. Then he lists the social damage: brothers gone, relatives departed, servants treating him as a stranger, his breath offensive to his wife, small children despising him, and his bones sticking to his skin. He asks his friends for pity and asks why they hunt him as God does. He wishes his words were engraved in rock with an iron pen, and declares that his Redeemer lives and that after his skin is destroyed he will see God himself.
JOB 20:1-29	Zophar answers, admitting he is in a hurry and stung by the rebuke. His thesis is that the triumph of the wicked is brief. Such a man may reach to the clouds and still perish like his own dung, vanishing like a dream nobody can find again. The imagery is digestive: wickedness is sweet in his mouth and he keeps it under his tongue, but in his belly it turns to cobra venom, and the riches he swallowed he vomits up because God empties his stomach. He will never see the streams of honey and butter. Rain of wrath falls while he eats, a bronze arrow comes out through his liver, unfanned fire eats his tent, and heaven and earth testify against him.
JOB 21:1-34	Job asks them to listen and then mock afterwards, and points out that his complaint was never addressed to men. His question is why the wicked live long and grow powerful: their children are established, their houses are safe, their bulls always breed, their cows never miscarry, their children dance to tambourine and harp, and they go down to Sheol in an instant after a comfortable life, having told God to leave them alone. How often, he asks, does the lamp of the wicked actually go out? He rejects the idea that punishing a man's children counts, since a dead man does not care. One dies at ease with full milk pails and another in bitterness, and the same worms cover both.
JOB 22:1-30	Eliphaz asks whether a man's righteousness benefits God at all, and then, for the first time, brings specific charges: Job took pledges for nothing, stripped the naked, withheld water from the weary and bread from the hungry, sent widows away empty and broke the arms of the fatherless. That, he says, is why snares surround him. He accuses Job of thinking God cannot see through the thick clouds, and warns him against the old way of wicked men swept away before their time. Then the offer: come to terms with God, receive his instruction, put away unrighteousness, lay your gold in the dust, and God himself will be your treasure, your prayers heard and light on your paths.
JOB 23:1-17	Job admits his complaint is rebellious and wishes he knew where to find God, so he could come to his seat, lay out his case in order and fill his mouth with arguments. He believes God would not overpower him but would listen, and an upright man could reason with him. But God cannot be found east, west, north or south. Still, God knows the way Job takes, and when tried he will come out like gold, since his foot has held to God's steps and he has treasured God's words more than his food. What frightens him is that God acts alone and does whatever he wants, and has already appointed Job's portion. His heart is faint and the thick darkness is still in front of his face.
JOB 24:1-25	Job asks why God does not set fixed times for judgment. He catalogues what goes unpunished: men move boundary markers, steal flocks, drive off the orphan's donkey and take the widow's ox as a pledge. The poor scavenge like wild donkeys in the desert, glean the vineyards of the wicked, sleep naked in the cold, and hug rocks for shelter from mountain rain. They carry sheaves while hungry and tread wine presses while thirsty. Then the night workers: the murderer who rises at dawn, the adulterer waiting for twilight with his face disguised, the burglars digging through houses in the dark, for whom morning is like thick darkness. God, he says, keeps the mighty secure, and then they die like everyone else.
JOB 25:1-6	Bildad's last speech, and the shortest in the book. Dominion and fear belong to God, who makes peace in the heights and whose armies cannot be counted. Given that, he asks how any man can be just with God, or anyone born of woman be clean. Even the moon has no brightness in God's sight and the stars are not pure, so a human being, twice called a worm, has no standing at all. He offers no application to Job's situation and does not speak again.
JOB 26:1-14	Job replies sarcastically, thanking them for the help given to the powerless and the wisdom supplied to a man with none, and asking whose spirit exactly was speaking. Then he outdoes Bildad at his own hymn: the dead tremble, Sheol is naked before God and Abaddon uncovered, God stretches out the north over empty space and hangs the earth on nothing, binds water in clouds that do not burst, draws the boundary between light and darkness. The pillars of heaven shake at his rebuke; he stirs the sea, strikes through Rahab and pierces the swift serpent. All of that, Job says, is only the outskirts of his ways, a whisper, and nobody can understand the thunder.
JOB 27:1-23	Job swears by the God who has taken away his right that he will not speak falsely, will not concede that his friends are correct, and will hold his integrity until he dies. Then he takes over their material: this is the portion of the wicked. If such a man's children multiply it is for the sword, his survivors are buried without their widows mourning, and the silver he heaps up like dust is worn and divided by the innocent instead. He builds his house like a moth or a watchman's flimsy shelter. He lies down rich, opens his eyes and is gone, carried off by an east wind in the night while onlookers clap and hiss him out of his place.
JOB 28:1-28	A poem about mining and wisdom. Men sink shafts far from anywhere, dangling and swinging on ropes, breaking into flinty rock, overturning mountains by the roots, damming underground streams and bringing hidden things to light, in places no falcon has seen and no lion has walked. But wisdom is not found that way. The deep says it is not here, the sea says it is not with me, and it cannot be bought with gold of Ophir, onyx, sapphire, coral, crystal, rubies or topaz. Destruction and Death have only heard a rumour of it. God alone knows its place, having measured the waters and set the rules for wind, rain and lightning. To man he says the fear of the Lord is wisdom and turning from evil is understanding.
JOB 29:1-25	Job remembers his former life. God's lamp shone on his head, his children were around him, his steps were washed with butter and rock poured out oil for him. When he came to the city gate young men hid, old men stood, princes stopped talking and nobles fell silent. He earned it, he says, by rescuing the poor and the fatherless, making the widow's heart sing, wearing justice like a robe and a crown, being eyes to the blind and feet to the lame, taking cases of strangers and breaking the jaws of the unrighteous. He expected to die at home after days as numberless as sand. Men waited for his counsel like rain, and he sat as chief, like a king among his troops.
JOB 30:1-31	Now, Job says, he is mocked by younger men whose fathers he would not have trusted with his sheep dogs, outcasts driven from society who live in rocky holes and eat salt herbs and broom roots. He has become their song and their byword, and they spit in his face without hesitation. A rabble crowds his right hand and pours through the breach in his ruin. His bones are pierced at night, the pain never rests, and God has thrown him into the mire so that he is dust and ashes. He cries out and gets no answer, only a stare. He wept for the troubled once; now he looks for good and gets evil, is brother to jackals and companion to ostriches, his skin blackening and peeling, his harp turned to mourning.
JOB 31:1-40	Job's final speech is a long oath of innocence, each charge answered with a curse on himself if it is true. He made a covenant with his eyes not to look at a young woman. If he walked in falsehood, let him be weighed in an honest balance. If he committed adultery, let his wife grind for another. If he dismissed the complaint of a servant, he asks what he will say when God rises, since the same God made them both in the womb. He denies withholding food or clothing from the poor, trusting gold, kissing his hand to the sun or moon, gloating over an enemy's ruin, turning away travellers, or hiding sin like Adam. He signs his name and demands the indictment, saying he would wear it as a crown. The words of Job are ended.
JOB 32:1-22	The three friends stop answering, since Job is righteous in his own eyes. A younger man named Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram, is angry, both at Job for justifying himself rather than God and at the three for condemning Job without finding any answer. He explains that he held back out of respect for their age, having assumed that years teach wisdom, but the spirit in man and the breath of the Almighty give understanding, so it is not the great or the aged who are necessarily wise. He notes that none of the three convinced Job. He says he is full of words, like new wineskins ready to burst, and promises to use no flattering titles.
JOB 33:1-33	Elihu addresses Job directly, insisting he is clay like him and will not frighten him. He quotes Job's claim to be clean and treated as an enemy with his feet in the stocks, and answers that God is greater than man and owes no account. God speaks twice over, in dreams and night visions, to turn a man from his purpose and keep his soul from the pit; and he chastens with pain in bed until food is repulsive and the bones stick out. Then, if an interpreting angel, one in a thousand, shows a man what is right, God says he has found a ransom and delivers him: his flesh becomes fresher than a child's and he sings his confession publicly. God does this twice and three times. Elihu tells Job to be quiet and learn wisdom.
JOB 34:1-37	Elihu addresses the wise men present, quoting Job's claim to be righteous while God has denied him his right, and objecting that Job also said it profits a man nothing to delight in God. His argument is that God cannot commit injustice, since nobody appointed him over the earth and if he withdrew his breath all flesh would perish. God shows no partiality to princes over the poor, since all are the work of his hands; he sees every step, needs no further investigation, and overturns mighty men in the night because they ignored his ways and made the poor cry out. He asks whether Job has ever simply said he was guilty and would not offend again, and concludes that Job speaks without knowledge and adds rebellion to his sin.
JOB 35:1-16	Elihu takes up Job's question about what profit there is in righteousness. He tells Job to look at the skies, which are higher than he is, and argues that sin does nothing to God and righteousness gives God nothing: wickedness hurts other people and righteousness benefits them. When the oppressed cry out under the arm of the mighty, nobody asks where God their Maker is, the one who gives songs in the night and teaches people more than the animals and birds. God does not answer an empty cry, and still less does he answer a man who claims not to see him while his case waits before him. Because God has not visited in anger, Elihu says, Job talks emptily and multiplies words without knowledge.
JOB 36:1-33	Elihu asks for a little more patience, since he still has something to say on God's behalf, and claims one perfect in knowledge is present. God is mighty and despises no one; he gives the afflicted their right and sets the righteous with kings. When people are bound in fetters he shows them what they did and opens their ears; if they listen they prosper, and if not they die without knowledge. He delivers the afflicted by means of their affliction. Elihu warns Job not to be swayed by wealth or a bribe and not to long for the night. Then he turns to weather: God draws up water that falls as rain, spreads clouds nobody understands, and covers his hands with lightning, commanding it to strike the mark.
JOB 37:1-24	Elihu's own heart trembles at the storm. God's voice thunders under the whole sky, sending lightning to the ends of the earth and doing great things nobody can comprehend. He tells snow to fall and sends heavy rain, which seals up men's hands from work and drives animals into their dens. Ice comes by the breath of God and the wide waters freeze. Clouds are loaded with moisture and steered wherever he commands, whether for correction or kindness. Then he presses Job with questions: do you know how the lightning is made to shine, can you spread out the sky like a cast metal mirror? Out of the north comes golden splendour. God cannot be reached and will not oppress, and pays no regard to those who are wise in their own hearts.
JOB 38:1-41	Yahweh answers Job out of the whirlwind, asking who darkens counsel with words without knowledge and telling him to brace himself for questioning. Where was Job when the earth's foundations were laid and the morning stars sang together? Who shut the sea behind doors and told its proud waves to come no further? The questions run through the dawn, the springs of the sea, the gates of death, the dwelling of light, the treasuries of snow and hail kept for the day of battle, the channels cut for floodwater, rain on wilderness where no one lives. Does the rain have a father, and out of whose womb came the ice? Can Job bind the Pleiades, loosen Orion, guide the Bear, or hunt prey for lions and feed the raven's crying young?
JOB 39:1-30	God's questioning turns to animals. Does Job know when mountain goats give birth or count the months a doe carries? Who set the wild donkey free in the salt land, where it scorns the noise of the city and hears no driver shouting? Will the wild ox work a furrow or bring in the grain? The ostrich waves her wings proudly but leaves her eggs in the dust and forgets a foot may crush them, because God withheld wisdom from her, and yet she outruns horse and rider. The horse gets the longest treatment: a quivering mane, a snort that is glorious, leaping like a locust, mocking fear, snorting Aha at the trumpet and smelling the battle from far off. Finally the hawk and the eagle, nesting on the cliff point, spying prey from a distance.
JOB 40:1-24	God asks whether the one who argues will contend with the Almighty, and Job answers briefly: he is of small account, he lays his hand on his mouth, he has spoken twice and will go no further. God resumes anyway, telling him to brace himself again and asking whether Job means to condemn God in order to justify himself. If Job has an arm like God's and a voice like his thunder, let him put on majesty, pour out his anger, look at every proud man and bring him low, and then God will admit Job's own hand can save him. Then he introduces behemoth, made alongside Job, grass-eating, with brass tubes for bones and iron bars for limbs, lying under the lotus trees unbothered while the river rises to his mouth.
JOB 41:1-34	God describes Leviathan at length. Can Job hook him, rope his nose, pierce his jaw, keep him as a pet for the girls, or sell him among merchants? Anyone who lays a hand on him does not try twice. His scales are sealed so tightly no air passes between them, his sneezing flashes light, his eyes are like the eyelids of morning, torches come from his mouth and smoke from his nostrils, and his breath kindles coals. His heart is hard as a lower millstone. Sword, spear, arrow, sling stone and club are straw and chaff to him. He boils the deep like a pot and leaves a shining white wake. Nothing on earth is his equal, and he is king over all the sons of pride.
JOB 42:1-17	Job answers that God can do anything, that he spoke of things too wonderful for him, and that where he had only heard of God he now sees him; so he repents in dust and ashes. God tells Eliphaz his anger is kindled against him and his two friends, because they did not speak rightly about him as Job did, and orders seven bulls and seven rams offered while Job prays for them. They obey and are accepted. When Job prays for his friends, God restores him double. Relatives return to eat with him, each giving money and a gold ring. He ends with fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, seven sons and three daughters, Jemimah, Keziah and Keren Happuch, who inherit alongside their brothers. Job lives a hundred and forty years.
LUK 1:1-35	Luke opens with a dedication to Theophilus, explaining that he has traced everything carefully so his reader can be certain of what he was taught. In the days of Herod, the priest Zacharias and his wife Elizabeth are childless and old. While Zacharias burns incense in the temple, Gabriel tells him Elizabeth will bear a son named John, who will drink no wine, be filled with the Spirit, and go before the Lord in the spirit of Elijah. Zacharias asks how he can be sure and is struck silent until it happens. He comes out unable to speak, and Elizabeth conceives. In the sixth month Gabriel is sent to Mary in Nazareth, promising her a son named Jesus who will reign forever. She asks how, being a virgin.
LUK 1:36-80	Gabriel points to Elizabeth's pregnancy as proof that nothing God says is impossible, and Mary consents. She travels to the hill country, and at her greeting Elizabeth's baby leaps and Elizabeth blesses her. Mary sings of God scattering the proud, pulling princes off thrones, lifting the lowly, filling the hungry and sending the rich away empty. She stays three months. Elizabeth gives birth, and at the circumcision insists the boy is called John; the relatives object, Zacharias writes the name on a tablet, and his speech returns. The neighbourhood is afraid and the story spreads. Zacharias prophesies about a horn of salvation in David's house and about his son going before the Lord to prepare his ways. John grows up in the desert.
LUK 2:1-25	A decree from Caesar Augustus for a census, the first under Quirinius, sends Joseph from Nazareth to Bethlehem with Mary, who is pregnant. She gives birth there, wraps the child and lays him in a feeding trough because there is no room in the inn. Shepherds keeping watch at night are terrified by an angel who announces a Savior born in David's city, with a baby in a trough as the sign, and then a great company of the heavenly army praising God. The shepherds go, find the child as described, and tell everyone; Mary keeps it all and ponders it. On the eighth day he is circumcised and named Jesus. The family goes to Jerusalem to present him and offer two birds, where a devout man named Simeon is waiting.
LUK 2:26-52	Simeon, promised he would not die before seeing the Lord's Christ, takes the child in his arms and says he can now be released in peace, having seen a light for the nations and the glory of Israel. He tells Mary the child is set for the falling and rising of many, and that a sword will pierce her own soul. Anna, a prophetess widowed some eighty-four years who never leaves the temple, gives thanks and speaks of him. The family returns to Nazareth. At twelve, Jesus stays behind after Passover, and after three days his parents find him among the teachers in the temple, asking questions. Told his mother was anxious, he asks why they were looking, since he had to be in his Father's house. He goes home with them and grows.
LUK 3:1-38	Luke dates John's ministry precisely, by Tiberius, Pilate, the Herods, Lysanias and the high priests. John preaches a baptism of repentance around the Jordan, quoting Isaiah on valleys filled and mountains levelled. He calls the crowds a brood of vipers and, when asked what to do, gives specific answers: share a spare coat and food, collect no more tax than appointed, extort nobody and be content with your wages. Asked whether he is the Christ, he points to one mightier who will baptize with the Spirit and fire. Herod, rebuked over Herodias, imprisons him. Jesus is baptized among all the people and, while praying, sees the sky open and the Spirit descend, with a voice naming him Son. Luke then traces his line back through David and Abraham to Adam and to God.
LUK 4:1-23	Full of the Spirit, Jesus is led into the wilderness for forty days without food and tempted three times. The devil offers bread from a stone, then all the kingdoms of the world for an act of worship, claiming they were delivered to him, then a leap from the temple pinnacle with scripture quoted about angels. Jesus answers each from scripture, and the devil leaves until another time. He returns to Galilee, teaching in synagogues and widely praised. At Nazareth he reads Isaiah about good news to the poor, release for captives and sight for the blind, sits down, and says the scripture is fulfilled today. The crowd marvels and asks whether he is not Joseph's son, and he anticipates their demand for a sign.
LUK 4:24-44	Jesus says no prophet is accepted at home, and reminds them that Elijah was sent to a widow in Sidon and Elisha cleansed only Naaman the Syrian. The synagogue turns on him, drives him out of town and takes him to the brow of the hill to throw him off, but he walks through the middle of them and leaves. At Capernaum his teaching astonishes people by its authority. A man with an unclean spirit shouts that he knows who he is, the Holy One of God, and the demon is ordered out without harming him. Word spreads. He heals Simon's mother-in-law of a fever, and at sunset lays hands on everyone brought to him, silencing the demons who name him. At daybreak he withdraws, and tells the crowds who find him that he must preach in other cities too.
LUK 5:1-39	Pressed by the crowd at the lake, Jesus teaches from Simon's boat, then tells him to put out into deep water. Simon, who has caught nothing all night, obeys and nets a catch that breaks the nets and nearly sinks two boats. He falls at Jesus's knees calling himself a sinful man, and is told he will catch people; he, James and John leave everything. A man full of leprosy is cleansed by touch and sent to the priest, and Jesus withdraws to pray. With Pharisees and teachers of the law watching, a paralyzed man is lowered through the roof tiles; Jesus forgives his sins, is accused of blasphemy, and heals him as proof. He calls Levi, who holds a feast, and answers complaints about fasting with a bridegroom and new wineskins.
LUK 6:1-26	Disciples pick and rub grain on a Sabbath, and Jesus answers with David eating the show bread, saying the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath. On another Sabbath, watched by scribes and Pharisees, he calls a man with a withered right hand into the middle, asks whether the Sabbath is for doing good or harm, and restores the hand; they are enraged and begin discussing what to do about him. He spends a whole night praying on a mountain and in the morning chooses twelve apostles, ending with Judas Iscariot. On a level place he heals a large crowd, then blesses the poor, the hungry, the weeping and the hated, and pronounces matching woes on the rich, the full, the laughing and the well spoken of.
LUK 6:27-49	The teaching continues: love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, offer the other cheek, give to everyone who asks and do not demand your goods back. Treat others as you want to be treated, since even sinners love those who love them; lend expecting nothing. Be merciful as the Father is merciful. Do not judge or condemn, and give, since the measure you use is measured back, pressed down and running over. A blind guide leads the blind into a pit. Deal with the beam in your own eye before the speck in your brother's. Each tree is known by its fruit, and the mouth speaks out of the heart. Calling him Lord without obeying is a house without a foundation.
LUK 7:1-24	In Capernaum a centurion whose servant is dying sends Jewish elders to ask for help, and they commend him for building the synagogue. As Jesus approaches, the centurion sends friends to say he is not worthy to have him under his roof and that a word will do, since he understands orders. Jesus says he has found no such faith in Israel, and the servant is found well. At the gate of Nain he meets the funeral of a widow's only son, tells her not to cry, touches the coffin and raises him, and the crowd says a great prophet has arisen. John sends two disciples to ask whether he is the one; Jesus heals many and sends back a list of what they have seen.
LUK 7:25-50	Jesus asks what they went out to see: not fine clothing, which belongs in palaces, but a prophet and more, the promised messenger, than whom none born of women is greater, though the least in the kingdom is greater still. The people and tax collectors, baptized by John, agree God is just; the Pharisees and lawyers, who refused baptism, do not. He compares the generation to children who will not dance or weep. At a Pharisee's table a woman known as a sinner wets his feet with tears, wipes them with her hair and anoints them. Simon objects silently, and Jesus tells him about two debtors forgiven fifty and five hundred, points out Simon offered no water, kiss or oil, and tells the woman her faith has saved her.
LUK 8:1-27	Jesus travels the towns preaching with the twelve and with women he had healed, including Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna, who fund the group from their own means. He tells a crowd about seed falling on the road, on rock, among thorns and on good ground, then explains it: the seed is the word, and the soils are those from whom it is taken, those with no root, those choked by cares and riches, and those who bear fruit. A lamp is not lit to be hidden. Told his mother and brothers are outside, he says his family are those who hear the word and do it. Crossing the lake he sleeps, a storm nearly swamps the boat, and he stills it. Ashore, a naked man from the tombs meets him.
LUK 8:28-56	The man begs not to be tormented, and gives his name as Legion. The demons ask not to be sent to the abyss but into a herd of pigs, which then drowns in the lake. The townspeople find the man clothed and sane, are frightened, and ask Jesus to leave; he sends the man home to tell what God has done. Back across the lake, Jairus, a synagogue ruler, begs him to come for his dying twelve-year-old daughter. On the way a woman ill twelve years, who has spent everything on physicians, touches his cloak and is healed; Jesus insists someone touched him and she confesses publicly. Word comes that the girl is dead. He takes Peter, John, James and the parents inside, calls the girl, and she rises and is given food.
LUK 9:1-31	The twelve are given authority over demons and disease and sent out with nothing, told to shake the dust off where they are not received. Herod, hearing the reports, is perplexed by talk that John has risen. When the apostles return he withdraws to Bethsaida, and the crowds follow. He tells the twelve to feed them, and from five loaves and two fish about five thousand men eat in groups of fifty, with twelve baskets left. Praying with them, he asks who the crowds say he is, then who they say he is; Peter answers, the Christ of God. He predicts his death and rising, and calls for a cross to be taken up. Eight days later, on a mountain, Moses and Elijah speak of his departure at Jerusalem.
LUK 9:32-62	Peter and the others, heavy with sleep, wake to see the glory, and Peter proposes three tents without knowing what he is saying. A cloud covers them, a voice says to listen to the Son, and Jesus is left alone. Next day a father asks for his only son, whom the disciples could not help, and Jesus rebukes the spirit and gives the boy back. While everyone marvels he says the Son of Man will be handed over, which they fear to ask about. They argue about who is greatest, and he sets a child beside him. John reports stopping an outsider casting out demons, and is told not to. Refused by a Samaritan village, he rebukes James and John for offering to call down fire. Three would-be followers are answered, ending with no looking back from the plow.
LUK 10:1-21	Jesus appoints seventy others and sends them out in pairs ahead of him, saying the harvest is large and the workers few, and that they go as lambs among wolves. They carry no purse, bag or sandals, greet no one on the road, say peace to each house they enter, stay put rather than moving around, eat what they are given, heal the sick and announce that the kingdom has come near. Where they are refused they are to wipe off the dust and say the same thing. Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum are warned. The seventy return delighted that even demons obey them, and he says he saw Satan fall like lightning, gives them authority over serpents and scorpions, and tells them to rejoice instead that their names are written in heaven.
LUK 10:22-42	Jesus says all things have been given to him and that only the Son knows the Father, then tells the disciples how much prophets and kings wanted to see what they see. A lawyer asks what he must do to inherit eternal life, answers his own question from the law, love of God and neighbour, then asks who counts as a neighbour. Jesus describes a man robbed and left half dead on the Jericho road, a priest and a Levite who pass by, and a Samaritan who binds his wounds, carries him to an inn and pays the host. Asked who was the neighbour, the lawyer says the one who showed mercy, and is told to do the same. At a village Martha complains that Mary is sitting listening while she serves, and is told Mary chose the better part.
LUK 11:1-28	Asked to teach them to pray as John taught his disciples, Jesus gives a short prayer for the kingdom, daily bread, forgiveness and rescue from temptation. He follows it with a man banging on a friend's door at midnight for bread, who gets it not out of friendship but persistence, then tells them to keep asking, since no father gives a stone for bread or a scorpion for an egg. After he casts out a mute demon, some credit Beelzebul and others want a sign; he answers that a divided kingdom falls and that if he acts by God's finger the kingdom has arrived. An evicted spirit returns with seven worse. A woman blesses his mother; he blesses those who keep the word.
LUK 11:29-54	Jesus calls it an evil generation seeking a sign, and offers only Jonah, adding that the queen of the south and the men of Nineveh will condemn it. A lamp goes on a stand, and the eye is the lamp of the body, so check that the light in you is not darkness. Invited to dine with a Pharisee, he is criticised for not washing, and answers with cups clean outside and full of extortion within. The woes follow: tithing mint and rue while bypassing justice and God's love, loving the best seats and public greetings, being hidden graves people walk over unknowing. A lawyer objects that this insults them too, and gets his own set: loading burdens they will not carry, building tombs for prophets their fathers killed, and taking away the key of knowledge.
LUK 12:1-30	With thousands crowding in, Jesus warns the disciples against the yeast of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy, since nothing hidden stays hidden. They are not to fear those who can only kill the body: five sparrows sell for two coins and none is forgotten. Confessing him brings his confession before the angels, and blasphemy against the Spirit is unforgiven. Before rulers they need not prepare, since the Spirit will teach them. Asked to settle an inheritance dispute, he refuses and warns against greed, telling of a rich man whose harvest outgrows his barns and who plans bigger ones, and dies that night. He tells the disciples not to be anxious: ravens have no barns and God feeds them, lilies outdress Solomon.
LUK 12:31-59	Seek the kingdom and the rest follows; the little flock is to be given it. He tells them to sell what they have and give it away, since treasure in heaven does not rot and the heart follows the treasure. Lamps are to stay lit for a master returning from a wedding, who will serve the servants he finds awake. Asked by Peter whether this is for them or everyone, he describes a steward found feeding the household or found beating it and drunk, and adds that much given means much required. He says he came to throw fire on the earth, has a baptism still ahead, and brings division rather than peace, splitting families. The crowd can read the weather but not the times, and should settle with an adversary before reaching the judge.
LUK 13:1-35	Told about Galileans killed by Pilate, Jesus asks whether they were worse sinners, says no, and warns of the same end without repentance, adding the eighteen crushed by the tower in Siloam. He tells of a fig tree given one more year before being cut down. On a Sabbath he calls over a woman bent double for eighteen years and straightens her; the synagogue ruler objects, and Jesus points out that they all water their animals on the Sabbath. The kingdom is like a mustard seed grown into a tree and like yeast in three measures of flour. Asked whether few are saved, he speaks of a narrow door that gets shut. Warned that Herod wants to kill him, he calls him a fox, and laments over Jerusalem as a hen refused by her chicks.
LUK 14:1-35	At a Pharisee ruler's house on a Sabbath, watched closely, Jesus asks whether healing is lawful, gets silence, heals a man with dropsy, and asks who would not pull a son or an ox out of a well. Noticing guests taking the best seats, he advises taking the lowest. He tells the host to invite the poor, maimed, lame and blind, who cannot repay. When a guest praises the kingdom's feast, he tells of a man whose invited guests all make excuses about a field, oxen and a wife, so the servant fills the house from the streets and highways. To the crowds he says a disciple must put him before family and life, carry a cross, count the cost like a builder or a king going to war, and renounce everything.
LUK 15:1-32	With tax collectors and sinners crowding around and the Pharisees complaining that he eats with them, Jesus tells three stories. A shepherd leaves ninety-nine sheep to find one, carries it home and calls the neighbours to celebrate. A woman lights a lamp and sweeps the house for one lost coin, then gathers her friends. Then a younger son takes his share, wastes it abroad, ends up feeding pigs in a famine, and rehearses a speech about being made a hired servant. His father sees him far off, runs, and calls for a robe, a ring, shoes and the fattened calf. The elder brother refuses to come in, listing his years of service and the goat he never got. His father says all he has is his, and that his brother was dead and is alive.
LUK 16:1-31	A manager accused of wasting his employer's property, about to be dismissed, cuts the bills of his master's debtors so they will take him in, and is commended for shrewdness; Jesus observes that the children of this world are shrewder than the children of light, and that nobody serves God and money. The Pharisees, who love money, scoff, and he tells them what is exalted among men is detestable to God, and speaks about divorce. Then a rich man in purple and a beggar named Lazarus at his gate both die: Lazarus is carried to Abraham, the rich man is in torment and asks for water, then for a warning to his five brothers. Abraham answers that they have Moses and the prophets, and would not be persuaded by a resurrection either.
LUK 17:1-37	Jesus warns that anyone who makes a little one stumble would be better off drowned with a millstone, and tells them to forgive a repentant brother seven times a day. Asked for more faith, he says mustard-seed faith could uproot a sycamore, then compares them to servants who expect no thanks for doing their duty. Passing between Samaria and Galilee, ten lepers call out and are sent to the priests; all are cleansed, one comes back to give thanks, and he is a Samaritan. Asked when the kingdom comes, he says it comes without observation and is within them. As in the days of Noah and of Lot, ordinary life will be going on: nobody should turn back, and they should remember Lot's wife. Two in a bed, two grinding, one taken.
LUK 18:1-43	To teach persistence in prayer, Jesus tells of a widow who wears down a judge who fears neither God nor man. To the self-satisfied he contrasts a Pharisee listing his fasts and tithes with a tax collector who asks only for mercy, and says the second went home justified. Babies are brought and the disciples object; he says the kingdom belongs to such as these. A ruler asks about eternal life, has kept the commandments, and is told to sell everything, which saddens him because he is rich. Taking the twelve aside, he says everything written about the Son of Man will be completed, mocking, flogging, death and rising, and they understand none of it. Near Jericho a blind beggar shouts over those hushing him and is given his sight.
LUK 19:1-23	In Jericho, Zacchaeus, a rich chief tax collector too short to see over the crowd, runs ahead and climbs a sycamore. Jesus looks up, calls him by name and says he must stay at his house, which the crowd resents. Zacchaeus promises half his goods to the poor and fourfold restitution for anything he has extorted, and Jesus says salvation has come to the house. Because they are near Jerusalem and expect the kingdom immediately, he tells of a nobleman who goes abroad to receive a kingdom, leaving ten servants a mina each, while his citizens say they do not want him. He returns and calls for accounts: one has made ten, one five, and one produces the coin in a handkerchief.
LUK 19:24-48	The unused mina is taken and given to the servant with ten, and the citizens who rejected him are killed in front of him. Jesus goes on up to Jerusalem, sending two disciples to fetch a colt no one has ridden. They spread cloaks on it and on the road, and at the descent of the Mount of Olives the disciples praise God and call him the King who comes in the Lord's name. Told to rebuke them, he says the stones would cry out instead. Seeing the city he weeps over it, describing a siege, its children thrown down and not one stone left, because it did not know the time of its visitation. In the temple he drives out the traders, and teaches daily while the chief priests look for a way to destroy him.
LUK 20:1-47	Asked in the temple by what authority he acts, Jesus asks whether John's baptism came from heaven or men; unable to answer either way, they plead ignorance and he declines to tell them. He then tells of a vineyard whose tenants beat three servants and kill the owner's son, and says the owner will destroy them and give the vineyard to others; the crowd protests, and he quotes the rejected stone made cornerstone. Spies pretending to be sincere ask about paying tax to Caesar, and he asks whose image is on the coin. Sadducees pose a woman married to seven brothers, and he answers that the resurrected do not marry and cites Moses at the bush. He asks how David can call the Christ his Lord, and warns the people about scribes who love long robes and devour widows' houses.
LUK 21:1-38	Watching the rich put gifts into the treasury, Jesus notes a poor widow's two small coins as more than all of them, since she gave everything she had to live on. When people admire the temple's stonework he says not one stone will be left on another. Asked when, he warns of impostors and says wars are not the end. Before all that, they will be arrested and tried, and should not prepare a defence, since he will give them words; families will hand them over and some will be killed, yet not a hair will perish. When armies surround Jerusalem, Judea should flee, and he speaks plainly of the distress for pregnant and nursing women. Then signs in sun, moon and stars, and the Son of Man in a cloud. A budding fig tree means summer.
LUK 22:1-36	As Passover approaches, the chief priests look for a way to kill him, Satan enters Judas, and Judas agrees a price. Peter and John are sent to follow a man carrying a pitcher of water and prepare the meal in an upper room. At the table Jesus says he has longed to eat this Passover before he suffers, gives a cup, then bread as his body given for them, and a cup as the new covenant in his blood, then says his betrayer's hand is on the table. They ask who, then argue about which of them is greatest, and he says the greatest must serve. He tells Simon that Satan asked to sift them and that Peter will deny him three times. Then he tells them to buy a sword.
LUK 22:37-71	Told two swords are available, Jesus says that is enough. On the Mount of Olives he kneels a stone's throw off and asks for the cup to be taken away, adding that God's will be done; an angel strengthens him, and in agony his sweat is like drops of blood. He finds the disciples asleep from grief. Judas arrives leading a crowd and comes to kiss him, and Jesus names it. Someone cuts off the high priest's servant's right ear, and Jesus heals it, then asks why they came with swords. In the courtyard Peter denies him three times, the rooster crows, Jesus turns and looks at him, and he goes out and weeps. Blindfolded and beaten, he is asked to prophesy. At daybreak the council asks whether he is the Christ.
LUK 23:1-28	Before Pilate they accuse him of subverting the nation, forbidding taxes and claiming to be a king. Pilate finds no case, and on hearing Galilee mentioned sends him to Herod, who hopes for a miracle, gets no answers, mocks him and sends him back in fine clothing; Luke notes that Herod and Pilate became friends that day. Pilate says neither he nor Herod found anything worthy of death and offers to chastise and release him. They call instead for Barabbas, imprisoned for insurrection and murder, and shout for crucifixion until their voices prevail. On the way out Simon of Cyrene is made to carry the cross, and Jesus tells the mourning women to weep for themselves and their children.
LUK 23:29-56	Jesus says days are coming when the childless will be called blessed and people will ask the hills to cover them. At the place called the Skull he is crucified between two criminals, and asks the Father to forgive them, since they do not know what they are doing. Rulers and soldiers mock him, and an inscription in Greek, Latin and Hebrew names him king of the Jews. One criminal insults him; the other says Jesus has done nothing wrong, and is promised Paradise that day. Darkness covers the land, the temple veil tears, and he commits his spirit to the Father and dies. The centurion calls him a righteous man, and Joseph of Arimathaea, who had not consented, lays him in an unused tomb before the Sabbath.
LUK 24:1-26	At dawn the women bring their spices, find the stone rolled away and no body, and are met by two men in dazzling clothes who ask why they seek the living among the dead and remind them what he said in Galilee. They report to the eleven; Luke names Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Mary the mother of James. The apostles think it nonsense, though Peter runs to the tomb, sees the linen lying alone, and goes home wondering. That same day two of them walk to Emmaus, and Jesus joins them unrecognised. Cleopas explains about the prophet who was crucified, their hope that he would redeem Israel, and the women's report. Jesus calls them slow to believe the prophets.
LUK 24:27-53	Starting from Moses and the prophets, he explains the scriptures about himself. At Emmaus they press him to stay, and when he breaks the bread their eyes are opened, he vanishes, and they say their hearts were burning on the road. They return to Jerusalem and find the eleven saying the Lord has appeared to Simon. Jesus stands among them, and they take him for a spirit until he shows his hands and feet and eats broiled fish in front of them. He tells them everything written in the law, prophets and psalms had to be fulfilled, and says repentance and forgiveness will be preached to all nations beginning at Jerusalem, with them as witnesses, but they must wait for power. At Bethany he blesses them and is carried up.
MAT 1:1-25	Matthew opens with a genealogy from Abraham through David to Joseph, arranged as three sets of fourteen generations and naming Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and the wife of Uriah along the way. Mary is found pregnant by the Holy Spirit before she and Joseph live together. Joseph, unwilling to disgrace her, plans a quiet divorce, until an angel tells him in a dream to take her as his wife and to name the child Jesus.
MAT 2:1-23	Wise men from the east arrive in Jerusalem asking where the king of the Jews has been born. Herod is troubled, learns from the chief priests that the prophets name Bethlehem, and sends the visitors on with instructions to report back. They find the child, give gold, frankincense and myrrh, and are warned in a dream to go home another way. An angel sends Joseph to Egypt. Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem two years old and under. After Herod dies the family returns and settles in Nazareth.
MAT 3:1-17	John the Baptizer preaches repentance in the wilderness of Judea, dressed in camel hair and eating locusts and wild honey, and crowds come from Jerusalem and the whole Jordan region to be baptized. He calls the arriving Pharisees and Sadducees a brood of vipers, warns that descent from Abraham counts for nothing, and says one is coming who will baptize with the Holy Spirit. Jesus comes to be baptized; John objects and then agrees. The heavens open, the Spirit descends as a dove, and a voice names him God's beloved Son.
MAT 4:1-25	Led into the wilderness and fasting forty days, Jesus is tempted three times: bread from stones, a leap from the temple, and all the kingdoms of the world in exchange for worship. He answers each with scripture, the devil leaves, and angels attend him. Hearing John has been arrested, he moves to Capernaum and begins preaching repentance. He calls Peter and Andrew, then James and John, from their nets. He teaches and heals across Galilee, and crowds follow from Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea and beyond the Jordan.
MAT 5:1-24	Jesus goes up a mountain and begins to teach. He pronounces blessing on the poor in spirit, the mourners, the gentle, the hungry for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers and the persecuted. His hearers are salt and light, meant to be seen. He insists he has not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it, and that not one pen stroke of it will pass away. Then he raises the standard: anger toward a brother carries the weight of murder, and a gift at the altar waits until the quarrel is settled.
MAT 5:25-48	The teaching continues. Settle with your accuser before court. A lustful look is already adultery, and an offending eye or hand is better lost than kept. Divorce is restricted, and oaths are dropped altogether in favour of a plain yes or no. Retaliation is replaced by the turned cheek, the surrendered cloak and the second mile. Enemies are to be loved and persecutors prayed for, since God sends sun and rain on everyone alike, and loving only your friends is nothing special.
MAT 6:1-34	Charity, prayer and fasting are all to be done unseen, because a performance already has its reward. Jesus gives the disciples a short prayer, then warns that unforgiving people are not forgiven. Treasure stored on earth rots or is stolen, and the heart follows the treasure. No one can serve both God and money. He tells them not to be anxious about food or clothing: birds do not sow, lilies outdress Solomon, and worry adds nothing to a lifespan. Seek God's kingdom first, and let tomorrow do its own worrying.
MAT 7:1-29	Judging invites judgment by the same measure, and the speck in a brother's eye should wait until the beam in your own is gone. Do not throw pearls to pigs. Ask, seek and knock, since a father who is asked for bread does not hand over a stone. Do to others what you want done to you. The gate to life is narrow. False prophets are known by their fruit, and saying "Lord, Lord" is not enough. The sermon ends with two houses, one on rock and one on sand, and crowds astonished that he teaches with authority.
MAT 8:1-34	Coming down the mountain Jesus cleanses a leper by touch and sends him to the priest. A centurion asks for his servant to be healed at a distance and is praised for a faith greater than any in Israel. Peter's mother-in-law is healed of a fever, and many possessed and sick are brought at evening. Two would-be followers are warned that the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head and that the dead can bury their own. He stills a storm at sea, then meets two demoniacs among the tombs and sends their demons into a herd of pigs, which drown. The town asks him to leave.
MAT 9:1-38	A paralyzed man is brought on a bed; Jesus forgives his sins, and when scribes call it blasphemy he heals the man as proof. He calls Matthew from the tax office and eats with tax collectors and sinners, telling the Pharisees he wants mercy rather than sacrifice. Asked about fasting, he answers with a bridegroom, a patch and old wineskins. On the way to raise a ruler's dead daughter, a woman bleeding twelve years is healed by touching his clothes. He then heals two blind men and a mute demoniac, and says the harvest is plentiful and the workers few.
MAT 10:1-42	Jesus gives the twelve authority over unclean spirits and disease, and Matthew lists their names, ending with Judas Iscariot. They are sent only to Israel, to preach and heal, carrying no money, bag, spare coat or staff, and to shake the dust off their feet at any town that will not receive them. He warns of councils, floggings, trials before governors and kings, and betrayal within families, and tells them the Spirit will supply their words. They are not to fear those who can kill only the body: sparrows are not forgotten and their hairs are counted. He says he brings a sword rather than peace, that loyalty to him outranks family, and that whoever receives them receives him, down to a cup of cold water.
MAT 11:1-30	From prison John sends to ask whether Jesus is the one, and is answered with a list of what is happening: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, the poor hear good news. Jesus then praises John to the crowd as more than a prophet, the promised messenger, and Elijah for those willing to hear it. He compares the generation to children who will not dance or mourn, noting that John was called demon-possessed for fasting and he is called a glutton for eating. He denounces Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum, saying Tyre, Sidon and Sodom would have repented. He thanks the Father for revealing these things to infants rather than the wise, and invites the weary to take his yoke, which is easy.
MAT 12:1-28	Hungry disciples pick grain on the Sabbath, and Jesus answers the Pharisees with David eating the show bread and with priests who work in the temple on the Sabbath, calling himself Lord of the Sabbath. In the synagogue he is asked whether healing on the Sabbath is lawful, replies that any of them would lift a sheep out of a pit, and restores a man's withered hand. The Pharisees begin plotting to destroy him. He withdraws, heals the crowds, and tells them not to make him known, which Matthew ties to Isaiah's servant who will not break a bruised reed. When he heals a blind and mute demoniac the Pharisees credit Beelzebul, and he asks how a divided kingdom stands.
MAT 12:29-50	Jesus adds that plundering a strong man's house requires binding him first, and warns that while every other sin can be forgiven, blasphemy against the Holy Spirit cannot. A tree is known by its fruit, the mouth speaks out of the heart, and every idle word will be accounted for. Asked for a sign, he offers only the sign of Jonah: three days in the belly of the whale, three days in the heart of the earth. Nineveh and the queen of the south will condemn this generation. He describes an evicted spirit returning with seven worse to a swept and empty house. Told his mother and brothers are outside, he points to his disciples and says whoever does his Father's will is his family.
MAT 13:1-30	Sitting in a boat off the beach, Jesus tells the crowd about a farmer whose seed falls on the roadside, on rocky ground, among thorns and on good soil, yielding a hundred, sixty or thirty times. Asked why he teaches in parables, he says the mysteries are given to the disciples and not to the crowd, and quotes Isaiah on people who hear without understanding. He then explains the parable: the roadside is the word snatched away, the rocky ground is joy without root, the thorns are cares and riches, the good soil hears and understands. A second parable follows: an enemy sows weeds among the wheat at night, and the owner refuses to pull them, ordering both left until harvest.
MAT 13:31-58	More comparisons follow: a mustard seed that grows into a tree birds nest in, and yeast a woman hides in three measures of meal, Matthew noting Jesus taught the crowds in nothing but parables. Indoors, he explains the weeds: the sower is the Son of Man, the field the world, the weeds the children of the evil one, the harvest the end of the age, the reapers angels. He adds treasure hidden in a field and a single costly pearl, both bought by selling everything, and a dragnet sorted on the beach. Returning to his own town he is dismissed as the carpenter's son, whose mother and brothers and sisters they all know, and he does few works there because of their unbelief.
MAT 14:1-36	Herod hears about Jesus and assumes John the Baptizer has risen. Matthew explains: John had told Herod his marriage to Herodias was unlawful and was imprisoned for it, and at Herod's birthday Herodias's daughter danced, was promised anything under oath, and asked for John's head on a platter. Herod, unwilling to break the oath in front of his guests, had John beheaded, and John's disciples buried him and told Jesus. Jesus withdraws by boat, is followed on foot, heals the sick, and feeds about five thousand men besides women and children from five loaves and two fish, with twelve baskets left. That night he walks out to the boat on the water. Peter asks to come, walks, sees the wind, sinks, and is pulled up. Ashore at Gennesaret, the sick are healed by touching his clothes.
MAT 15:1-39	Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem complain that the disciples eat without washing their hands. Jesus answers that their tradition voids God's command, since a gift declared devoted to God excuses a man from supporting his parents, and quotes Isaiah on lip service. He tells the crowd that what comes out of the mouth defiles, not what goes in, and lists what comes out of the heart. In the region of Tyre and Sidon a Canaanite woman begs for her possessed daughter; he says nothing, then that he was sent to Israel, then speaks of children's bread and dogs. She answers that dogs eat the crumbs, and he praises her faith and heals the girl. He then feeds four thousand men from seven loaves and a few fish, with seven baskets left.
MAT 16:1-28	Pharisees and Sadducees ask for a sign from heaven. Jesus says they can read the sky for weather but not the signs of the times, and offers only the sign of Jonah. He warns the disciples about the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees; they think he means bread, and he reminds them of the five loaves and the seven. At Caesarea Philippi he asks who people say he is, then who they say he is. Peter answers that he is the Christ, the Son of the living God, and is told he is Peter, the rock, with the keys of the kingdom. Jesus then says he must suffer, be killed and rise. Peter objects and is called a stumbling block. Followers are told to take up their cross.
MAT 17:1-27	Six days later Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain, where his face shines like the sun and his clothes turn white, and Moses and Elijah appear talking with him. Peter offers to build three tents. A bright cloud covers them and a voice names Jesus as his beloved Son and says to listen to him; the disciples fall on their faces. Coming down, they are told to say nothing until the resurrection, and that Elijah has already come in John. A man whose epileptic son the disciples could not cure brings him to Jesus, who cures the boy and tells them mustard-seed faith moves mountains. He again predicts his death and resurrection. At Capernaum he sends Peter to find the temple tax in a fish's mouth.
MAT 18:1-35	Asked who is greatest, Jesus stands a child among them and says the kingdom belongs to those who become like children. Anyone who makes one of these little ones stumble would be better off drowned with a millstone, and a hand, foot or eye that causes stumbling is better lost. He tells of a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine to find one stray. For a brother who sins, the procedure is private correction, then two or three witnesses, then the assembly. Where two or three gather in his name he is present. Peter asks whether seven times is enough forgiveness and is told seventy times seven, followed by a king who cancels a debt of ten thousand talents and a servant who then jails a man over a hundred denarii.
MAT 19:1-30	Leaving Galilee for Judea beyond the Jordan, Jesus is tested on whether divorce is lawful for any reason. He answers from creation, that the two become one flesh, and says Moses permitted divorce because of hard hearts, allowing it only for sexual immorality. The disciples conclude marriage is inadvisable, and he speaks of eunuchs, including those who make themselves so for the kingdom. Children are brought and the disciples try to stop them; he says the kingdom belongs to such as these. A man asks what he must do for eternal life, is given commandments, says he has kept them, and is told to sell everything and follow. He leaves sad, being wealthy. Jesus says a camel passes through a needle's eye more easily than a rich man enters, and promises twelve thrones to those who followed.
MAT 20:1-34	A landowner hires laborers at dawn for a denarius, hires more at the third, sixth, ninth and eleventh hours, and pays everyone the same, starting with the last. The dawn workers complain and are told they got what they agreed to. Going up to Jerusalem, Jesus tells the twelve he will be condemned, mocked, flogged and crucified, and raised on the third day. The mother of James and John asks for the two seats beside him; he says the cup is theirs but the seats are not his to give, and the other ten are indignant. Greatness among them means service, since the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom. Leaving Jericho he restores the sight of two blind men the crowd tried to silence.
MAT 21:1-23	Near Jerusalem, two disciples are sent to fetch a donkey and colt, which Matthew ties to the prophecy of a king coming humble on a colt. Cloaks and branches go down on the road, the crowds shout Hosanna to the son of David, and the city asks who he is. In the temple he drives out the buyers and sellers and overturns the money changers' tables, calling the place a den of robbers instead of a house of prayer. He heals the blind and lame there, and answers the chief priests' complaint about the children with a psalm. Next morning he curses a fruitless fig tree, which withers, and speaks of faith moving mountains. Back in the temple the chief priests demand to know by what authority he acts.
MAT 21:24-46	Jesus offers to answer if they will first say whether John's baptism came from heaven or from men. Cornered either way, they say they do not know, so he declines to tell them. He then asks about two sons: one refuses to work and goes, the other agrees and does not, and says tax collectors and prostitutes who believed John are entering the kingdom ahead of them. Next, a landowner leases a vineyard, and the tenants beat, kill and stone the servants sent for the fruit, then kill his son to take the inheritance. Asked what the owner will do, they pronounce their own verdict. He quotes the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone. They realise the parables are about them, and fear the crowd too much to arrest him.
MAT 22:1-46	A king's wedding invitations are refused, some guests killing the servants sent to call them, so the king destroys them and fills the hall from the highways; a guest without wedding clothes is thrown out. The Pharisees send disciples with the Herodians to ask whether it is lawful to pay taxes to Caesar; Jesus asks whose image is on the coin. Sadducees, who deny resurrection, pose a woman married in turn to seven brothers, and are told that people do not marry in the resurrection and that God is God of the living. A lawyer asks for the greatest commandment and gets two, love of God and of neighbour. Jesus then asks how David can call the Christ his Lord, and nobody dares question him again.
MAT 23:1-39	Jesus tells the crowds and disciples to do what the scribes and Pharisees say but not what they do, since they load burdens on others and carry none, widen their phylacteries and fringes, and want the best seats and the title Rabbi. His followers are to take no such titles, since greatness means service. Then come the woes: shutting the kingdom, making converts worse, splitting hairs over which oaths bind, tithing mint and dill while neglecting justice, mercy and faith, straining out gnats and swallowing camels, cleaning the outside of the cup, looking like whitewashed tombs full of bones, and honouring the prophets their ancestors killed. He tells them the blood from Abel to Zachariah comes on this generation, then laments over Jerusalem as a hen whose chicks would not come, and says her house is left desolate.
MAT 24:1-27	Shown the temple buildings, Jesus says not one stone will be left on another. On the Mount of Olives the disciples ask when, and what the sign of his coming will be. He warns first of deception: many will come claiming to be the Christ. Wars, famines, plagues and earthquakes are only the beginning of birth pains. His followers will be handed over, killed and hated by all nations, many will fall away and betray each other, and love will grow cold, but whoever endures will be saved, and the good news will reach all nations first. When the abomination spoken of by Daniel stands in the holy place, Judea should run for the mountains without stopping.
MAT 24:28-51	The coming will be as unmistakable as vultures over a carcass and lightning across the sky. After that distress the sun and moon go dark, the stars fall, the Son of Man appears on the clouds, and angels gather the chosen from the four winds. A fig tree in leaf means summer is near, and this generation will not pass before it happens, though heaven and earth pass and his words do not. No one knows the day, not even the angels. It will be like the days of Noah, people eating and marrying until the flood came: two in a field, two at a mill, one taken and one left. A servant left in charge is either found feeding the household or found beating it, and is dealt with accordingly.
MAT 25:1-25	Ten virgins take lamps to meet a bridegroom; five bring extra oil and five do not. He is delayed, they all sleep, and at midnight the cry goes up. The five without oil ask to borrow, are told to go and buy, and while they are gone the door is shut and they are told he does not know them. The lesson is to watch, since the day and hour are unknown. A man going abroad then entrusts five, two and one talents to three servants according to ability. The first two trade and double their share, and each is praised. The third says he knew his master was a hard man, so he buried the money and has brought it back untouched.
MAT 25:26-46	The master calls the third servant wicked and lazy: on his own account of things he should at least have banked the money for interest. The talent goes to the servant with ten, since more is given to those who have, and the unprofitable servant is thrown out. Jesus then describes the Son of Man coming in glory, seated, with all nations gathered and separated as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. Those on the right inherit the kingdom because they fed, watered, welcomed, clothed and visited him; they ask when, and are told that whatever was done for the least of his brothers was done for him. Those on the left are sent away for the same list left undone, and ask the same question. The two groups go to eternal punishment and eternal life.
MAT 26:1-39	Jesus tells the disciples that in two days he will be handed over to be crucified, while the chief priests agree at Caiaphas's house to take him by stealth but not during the feast. At Bethany a woman pours expensive ointment on his head; the disciples call it waste, and Jesus says she has prepared him for burial. Judas is paid thirty pieces of silver. At the Passover meal Jesus says one of them will betray him, and answers Judas directly. He gives them bread as his body and the cup as his blood of the new covenant. He says they will all fall away and that Peter will deny him three times before the rooster crows. In Gethsemane he asks that the cup pass from him.
MAT 26:40-75	Three times Jesus prays, and three times he returns to find Peter, James and John asleep. Judas arrives with an armed crowd and identifies him with a kiss. One of those with Jesus cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant and is told to put the sword away, since Jesus could ask for twelve legions of angels. He asks why they came with swords for a man who taught daily in the temple, and all the disciples flee. Before Caiaphas the search for testimony fails until two witnesses report his words about the temple. Asked under oath whether he is the Christ, he answers that they will see the Son of Man at the right hand of Power. He is condemned, spat on and beaten. Outside, Peter denies him three times and weeps bitterly.
MAT 27:1-32	At morning the chief priests hand Jesus over to Pilate. Judas brings back the thirty pieces of silver, says he has betrayed innocent blood, is told it is his own problem, throws the money into the sanctuary and hangs himself; the priests buy the potter's field with it. Before Pilate, Jesus answers the question about being king of the Jews and then says nothing to the accusations. Pilate offers the crowd a choice between Barabbas and Jesus, and his wife sends word about a dream. Urged by the priests, the crowd asks for Barabbas and calls for crucifixion. Pilate washes his hands and hands Jesus over after flogging. The soldiers robe him, crown him with thorns, mock and strike him, then compel Simon of Cyrene to carry the cross.
MAT 27:33-66	At Golgotha he refuses the wine mixed with gall. He is crucified between two robbers, his clothes divided by lot, with a written charge above his head. Passers-by, the chief priests and the robbers all mock him for not saving himself. Darkness covers the land from the sixth hour to the ninth, when he cries out asking why God has forsaken him; some think he is calling Elijah, and he cries out again and dies. The temple veil tears from top to bottom, the earth quakes and tombs open. The centurion says he was truly the Son of God. Women who followed from Galilee watch from a distance. Joseph of Arimathaea lays the body in his own new tomb. The next day the priests seal the tomb and post a guard.
MAT 28:1-20	At dawn on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene and the other Mary come to the tomb. An earthquake accompanies an angel who rolls the stone away and sits on it, and the guards go rigid with fear. The angel tells the women Jesus has risen as he said and sends them to tell the disciples to go to Galilee. On the way Jesus meets them, and they take hold of his feet. Meanwhile the guards report to the chief priests, who pay them to say the disciples stole the body while they slept. The eleven go to the mountain in Galilee, where they worship him though some doubt. He tells them all authority has been given to him, sends them to make disciples of all nations, and promises to be with them always.
PRO 1:1-33	The book opens by stating its purpose: to teach wisdom, discernment, justice and equity, to give prudence to the simple and discretion to the young, and to let the wise increase in learning and understand proverbs and riddles. The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge. A father tells his son to listen to both parents and to refuse sinners who invite him to ambush the innocent and share one common purse, since their trap catches themselves. Then Wisdom is personified, shouting in the streets and at the city gates, asking how long the simple will love simplicity, and warning that having called and been ignored she will laugh when disaster arrives and not answer when they finally call.
PRO 2:1-22	The instruction is conditional: if you receive these words, store up the commandments, turn your ear to wisdom and search for her like silver and hidden treasure, then you will understand the fear of Yahweh and find the knowledge of God. Yahweh gives wisdom and is a shield to those who walk in integrity. Once wisdom enters the heart, discretion and understanding stand guard, delivering you from men who abandon the straight paths to walk in darkness and take pleasure in doing evil, and from the strange woman who flatters, has forsaken the friend of her youth, and whose house leads down to the dead. The upright will remain in the land and the treacherous will be rooted out.
PRO 3:1-35	The father promises length of days and peace to the son who keeps his teaching, and tells him to bind kindness and truth around his neck and write them on his heart. The famous instruction follows: trust Yahweh with all your heart, do not lean on your own understanding, acknowledge him in all your ways and he will make your paths straight. Honour Yahweh with the firstfruits and the barns will fill. Discipline is a father's love, not rejection. Wisdom is worth more than silver, gold or rubies, holds long life in one hand and riches in the other, and is a tree of life; Yahweh founded the earth by her. The chapter closes with neighbour rules: pay what is owed today, plot nothing, and do not envy violent men.
PRO 4:1-27	The father passes on what his own father taught him, tender and an only child: keep my words and live, get wisdom, get understanding, and buy it with everything you own if that is the price. Wisdom exalts those who esteem her and puts a garland of grace on the head. He urges his son to hold onto instruction as his life, and to avoid the path of the wicked entirely, not merely walk carefully on it, since such men cannot sleep unless they have made someone fall and eat the bread of wickedness. The righteous path is like dawn brightening toward full day; the wicked stumble in the dark over things they cannot see. Guard your heart, keep your eyes straight ahead, and turn neither right nor left.
PRO 5:1-23	A warning about adultery. The adulteress speaks lips that drip honey and a mouth smoother than oil, but the end is bitter as wormwood and sharp as a two-edged sword, and her steps go straight down to Sheol. Keep away from her door, or your honour goes to others, strangers feast on your wealth, and you will groan at the end of your life admitting you hated instruction and ignored every teacher. The positive advice uses water: drink from your own cistern, keep your springs to yourself rather than running them into the streets, rejoice in the wife of your youth, a loving doe. Yahweh watches every path, and a man's own sins bind him like cords.
PRO 6:1-35	Three warnings and a list. First, if you have guaranteed a stranger's debt, get out of it urgently, without sleeping, like a bird escaping a snare. Second, the sluggard is sent to study the ant, who has no overseer and still stores food in summer, while a little sleep and a little folding of the hands brings poverty like an armed robber. Third, the worthless man who winks, signals with his feet and sows discord will be broken suddenly. Then the list: six things Yahweh hates, seven that are an abomination, ending with sowing discord among brothers. The chapter closes on adultery, since a man cannot carry fire in his lap unburned, and a jealous husband will accept no ransom or gift.
PRO 7:1-27	The father tells his son to keep the commandments as the apple of his eye and to call wisdom his sister, then illustrates the alternative with a story he claims to have watched through his own window lattice. A young man without understanding walks past a corner at twilight. A woman dressed as a prostitute meets him, loud and never at home, and delivers a full pitch: her peace offerings are paid, she came out specially to find him, her couch is spread with Egyptian tapestry and perfumed with myrrh, aloes and cinnamon, and her husband is away on a journey with a bag of money and will not be back until the full moon. He follows like an ox to slaughter. Her house is the road down to death.
PRO 8:1-36	Wisdom speaks for herself, standing at the crossroads and the city gates. She insists her words are true and plain, worth more than silver, gold or rubies, and that she hates pride and a perverse mouth; kings reign and princes decree justice by her, and she brings riches, honour and enduring wealth to those who love her. Then the famous passage on her age: Yahweh possessed her at the beginning of his work, before the depths, the springs, the mountains or the dust of the world. She was there when the heavens were established and the sea was given its boundary, as the craftsman at his side, a daily delight, rejoicing in the world and in humanity. Whoever finds her finds life.
PRO 9:1-18	Two invitations, one at each end. Wisdom builds her house with seven carved pillars, slaughters her meat, mixes her wine, sets the table and sends her maids out to call the simple in to eat and live. In the middle sits a short block of sayings: correcting a mocker earns you abuse, correcting a wise man earns his love, the fear of Yahweh is the beginning of wisdom, and whoever mocks bears it alone. Then the mirror image: the foolish woman, loud and knowing nothing, sits at her own door in the high places and uses the same words to call passers by in, adding that stolen water is sweet. Her guests, unknown to them, are already in the depths of Sheol.
PRO 10:1-32	Solomon's collection of individual proverbs begins, most of them a single contrast between the righteous and the wicked. The themes are work and speech. Diligent hands bring wealth while a lazy hand brings poverty, and gathering in summer beats sleeping through harvest. The mouth of the righteous is a spring of life and a tongue like choice silver, while too many words guarantee sin and restraint is wise; hidden hatred makes lying lips, and slander makes a fool. Love covers all wrongs where hatred stirs up strife. Yahweh's blessing brings wealth without trouble attached. The sluggard is vinegar to the teeth and smoke in the eyes of whoever sent him. When the whirlwind passes the wicked are gone.
PRO 11:1-31	The chapter opens on commercial honesty, since a false balance is an abomination and accurate weights are Yahweh's delight, and returns repeatedly to how a community fares under each kind of person: the city rejoices when the righteous do well and is overthrown by the mouth of the wicked, and a nation without wise guidance falls while many counsellors bring victory. Gossip betrays a confidence and a trustworthy spirit keeps a secret. Generosity is treated as arithmetic that works backwards: the one who scatters increases, the one who waters is watered, and hoarding grain earns a public curse. Riches are no help on the day of wrath, and trusting them makes a man fall. A beautiful woman without discretion is a gold ring in a pig's snout.
PRO 12:1-28	More paired sayings, weighted toward speech, work and temperament. Loving correction is knowledge and hating reproof is stupidity, stated bluntly. A worthy wife is her husband's crown and a disgraceful one is rot in his bones. A righteous man looks after his animal. Tilling your land brings bread while chasing fantasies does not, and a lazy hunter does not even cook what he caught. On temper: a fool shows his annoyance the same day, while overlooking an insult is prudent. Rash speech pierces like a sword and the wise tongue heals. Anxiety weighs the heart down and a kind word lifts it. Better to be unknown with a servant than self-important and short of bread.
PRO 13:1-25	The subjects are the mouth, money and discipline. Guarding your mouth guards your life, while opening your lips wide brings ruin. Some pretend to be rich with nothing and some pretend to be poor while wealthy. Money gained dishonestly dwindles and money gathered by hand grows. Pride breeds quarrels. The best known line arrives here: hope deferred makes the heart sick, and fulfilled longing is a tree of life. Walking with wise men makes you wise and keeping company with fools brings harm. A good man leaves an inheritance to his grandchildren. The poor have abundance in their fields until injustice sweeps it away. Sparing the rod is called hatred of your son, and disciplining him is called love.
PRO 14:1-35	A wise woman builds her house and a foolish one pulls it down with her own hands. Several sayings admit complication rather than stating a rule: the heart knows its own bitterness and will not share it with a stranger, laughter can hide sorrow and mirth can end in heaviness, and there is a way that seems right to a man which ends in death.
