The simple believe everything while the prudent consider. Where there are no oxen the stall is clean, but the harvest comes by the ox's strength. Poverty loses you even your neighbour while wealth attracts friends. Envy rots the bones. Oppressing the poor shows contempt for their Maker, and righteousness exalts a nation while sin disgraces a people.
PRO 15:1-33	The chapter is mostly about how things are said. It opens with the gentle answer that turns away wrath against the harsh word that stirs anger, and returns to the theme repeatedly: a gentle tongue is a tree of life, the righteous weigh their answers while the wicked gush, and a word at the right time is a genuine pleasure. Yahweh's eyes are everywhere and even Sheol and Abaddon lie open before him. Two comparisons carry the values: better a little with the fear of Yahweh than great treasure with trouble, and better a dinner of herbs where there is love than a fattened calf with hatred. A cheerful heart is a continual feast, and humility comes before honour.
PRO 16:1-33	A cluster of sayings about human planning and divine direction: a man's heart plans his course but Yahweh directs his steps, and all a man's ways look clean to himself while Yahweh weighs the motives. A block on kings follows, since their wrath is a messenger of death and their favour is like a spring rain cloud, and the throne is established by righteousness. Familiar lines arrive together: pride goes before destruction and a haughty spirit before a fall; there is a way that seems right to a man which ends in death; pleasant words are a honeycomb. Grey hair is a crown of glory. Ruling your own spirit beats capturing a city, and the lot is cast but the decision is Yahweh's.
PRO 17:1-28	It opens with a dry morsel eaten in quiet beating a feast full of strife. Yahweh tests hearts as a furnace tests gold. Mocking the poor insults their Maker, and being glad at calamity will be punished. Covering an offence promotes love while repeating the matter separates friends. A rebuke reaches a wise man deeper than a hundred lashes reach a fool, and it is safer to meet a bear robbed of her cubs than a fool in his folly. Starting a quarrel is like breaching a dam, so stop it early. A friend loves at all times and a brother is born for adversity. A cheerful heart is good medicine. Even a fool is thought wise while he keeps his mouth shut.
PRO 18:1-24	The chapter is largely about talk and its consequences. A fool takes no delight in understanding, only in airing his own opinion, and answering before you have heard is folly and shame. A gossip's words go down like dainty morsels, and death and life are in the power of the tongue. Yahweh's name is a strong tower the righteous run into, while a rich man's wealth is a strong city only in his own imagination. Whoever pleads first sounds right until someone cross-examines him. An offended brother is harder to take than a fortified city. Finding a wife is finding a good thing; the poor plead and the rich answer harshly; and one friend can stick closer than a brother.
PRO 19:1-29	Poverty runs through this chapter. Better a poor man with integrity than a perverse fool; wealth adds friends while the poor lose even their relatives, who cannot be caught up with; and whoever pities the poor lends to Yahweh, who will repay him. Zeal without knowledge is no good, and hurrying your feet makes you miss the way. Discretion makes a man slow to anger, and overlooking an offence is his glory. A hot-tempered man rescued from the consequences will only need rescuing again. A quarrelsome wife is a continual dripping, while a prudent one comes from Yahweh. Many plans are in a man's heart but Yahweh's counsel prevails. The sluggard cannot get his hand from the dish to his mouth.
PRO 20:1-30	It opens with drink: wine is a mocker, beer is a brawler, and anyone led astray by them is not wise. Honest measurement returns twice, since differing weights and measures are both an abomination. Several sayings are about self-knowledge and its limits: who can say his heart is pure, a man's steps are from Yahweh so how can he understand his own way, and the spirit of man is Yahweh's lamp searching his innermost parts. Observational humour appears in the buyer who says it is no good and then boasts once he has left. Counsel in the heart is deep water a discerning man draws out. Do not repay evil; wait for Yahweh. Grey hair is the splendour of old men.
PRO 21:1-31	The king's heart is in Yahweh's hand like a watercourse, turned wherever he wishes, and doing righteousness and justice pleases him more than sacrifice. Diligent plans lead to profit while haste rushes to poverty. Whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor will himself cry out unheard. Two sayings recommend the corner of a roof, or even desert land, over a house shared with a contentious woman. Loving pleasure, wine and oil keeps a man poor, and the sluggard's own desire kills him because his hands refuse to work. Guarding your mouth keeps you out of trouble. No wisdom or counsel stands against Yahweh, and the last verse says the horse is prepared for battle but victory belongs to him.
PRO 22:1-29	A good name beats great riches, and rich and poor share one maker. The prudent see danger and hide while the simple walk on and suffer. Train up a child in the way he should go and he will not depart from it. The borrower is servant to the lender. A generous eye is blessed because it shares food with the poor, and the sluggard claims there is a lion in the street. Halfway through, the collection changes shape into longer instruction, introduced as thirty excellent sayings: do not exploit the poor in court, because Yahweh will plead their case; do not befriend a hot-tempered man in case you learn his ways; do not guarantee debts; do not move the ancient boundary stone. A skilled worker will serve kings.
PRO 23:1-35	Advice for eating with powerful people: watch what is in front of you, and treat a stingy host's delicacies as food you will end up vomiting, along with your compliments. Do not wear yourself out getting rich, since wealth sprouts wings like an eagle. Do not move a boundary stone or encroach on the fields of the fatherless, whose Defender is strong. Discipline a child with the rod and he will not die. Buy the truth and do not sell it. Then the long closing passage on wine, which asks who has woe, sorrow, strife, needless bruises and bloodshot eyes, warns against the wine that sparkles and goes down smoothly and then bites like a snake, and ends with the drunk who cannot feel his beating and wants another drink.
PRO 24:1-34	Do not envy evil men. A house is built by wisdom and its rooms filled by knowledge, and war is waged by wise guidance and many advisers. If you falter in trouble your strength is small. Then a demanding verse: rescue those being led away to death, and do not say you did not know, since the one who weighs hearts knows. Honey is offered as the model for wisdom's taste. A righteous man falls seven times and gets up. Do not rejoice when your enemy falls. Do not repay a man according to what he did. The chapter closes with the field of the sluggard, overgrown with thorns and nettles and its wall broken, and the same warning about a little sleep and a little folding of the hands.
PRO 25:1-28	A new collection, copied out by the men of Hezekiah. It opens at court: God's glory is to conceal a matter and a king's is to search it out, the hearts of kings are unsearchable, and it is better to be told to come up than to be moved down in front of a prince. Then a run of images. A word fitly spoken is apples of gold in settings of silver. A faithful messenger is like snow in harvest. A boaster is clouds and wind without rain. Singing to a heavy heart is like taking someone's coat in cold weather. Feed your hungry enemy and heap coals on his head. A man without self-restraint is a city with its walls broken down.
PRO 26:1-28	A chapter on fools, sluggards and troublemakers, built out of comparisons. Honour suits a fool as badly as snow in summer. Two consecutive verses contradict each other on purpose: do not answer a fool according to his folly, and answer a fool according to his folly. Sending a message by a fool is cutting off your own feet; a proverb in his mouth hangs like the legs of the lame; a fool repeating his folly is a dog returning to its vomit. The sluggard sees a lion in the road and turns on his bed like a door on its hinges. Meddling in someone else's quarrel is grabbing a dog by the ears. A quarrel dies without gossip as a fire dies without wood, and whoever digs a pit falls into it.
PRO 27:1-27	Do not boast about tomorrow, and let someone else praise you rather than your own mouth. A fool's provocation is heavier than stone or sand, and jealousy is worse than wrath. Open rebuke is better than hidden love; the wounds of a friend are faithful while an enemy's kisses are plentiful. A near neighbour is better than a distant brother. Blessing someone loudly early in the morning will be taken as a curse. A contentious wife is a continual dripping, and restraining her is like grasping oil. Iron sharpens iron. Sheol, Abaddon and human eyes are never satisfied. Grinding a fool in a mortar will not remove his folly. The chapter ends on husbandry: know the state of your flocks, since riches do not last forever.
PRO 28:1-28	The wicked flee when nobody is chasing them while the righteous are bold as a lion. Wealth and its uses dominate. A needy man who oppresses the poor is a driving rain that leaves no crops; interest gathered by extortion ends up with someone who pities the poor; a rich man is wise in his own eyes while a poor man with understanding sees through him. Better a poor man with integrity than a rich man who is crooked. Concealing sins does not prosper, and confessing and renouncing them finds mercy. A wicked ruler over helpless people is a roaring lion or a charging bear. Working your land brings food while chasing fantasies brings poverty. Whoever gives to the poor lacks nothing.
PRO 29:1-27	Politics runs through this chapter. When the righteous thrive people rejoice and when the wicked rule they groan; a king who judges the poor fairly has an established throne, while one who takes bribes tears the land down, and a ruler who listens to lies ends up with wicked officials. Flattery spreads a net for a man's feet. A fool vents all his anger while a wise man controls himself, and a wise man in court with a fool gets rage and scoffing instead of peace. Where there is no revelation the people cast off restraint. Being hasty in words is worse than being a fool. Pride brings a man low. The fear of man is a snare.
PRO 30:1-33	The words of Agur son of Jakeh, who opens by calling himself the most ignorant of men and asking who has gathered the wind in his fists. His prayer asks for two things: no falsehood, and neither poverty nor riches, in case wealth makes him deny God or poverty makes him steal. Then a series of numbered lists. Four things never say enough: Sheol, the barren womb, dry earth, and fire. Four are too amazing to understand: an eagle in the air, a snake on a rock, a ship at sea, and a man with a young woman. Four small things are exceedingly wise: ants, conies, locusts and the lizard in a king's palace. Forcing wrath produces strife as churning milk produces butter.
PRO 31:1-31	The words of King Lemuel, taught him by his mother. She warns him off women and wine, since drinking makes a king forget the law and pervert justice, though strong drink suits those who are perishing, and tells him to open his mouth for the mute and judge righteously for the poor. Then the closing poem on the worthy woman, whose price is above rubies. She seeks wool and flax, brings food from far off like a merchant ship, rises before dawn, buys a field and plants a vineyard, keeps her lamp burning at night, works the spindle, opens her hands to the needy, sells linen to merchants, and laughs at the time to come. Charm is deceitful and beauty vain; let her works praise her in the gates.
PSA 51:1-19	A plea for mercy and cleansing. The speaker admits his transgressions, says he has sinned against God alone, and asks to be washed whiter than snow and given a clean heart and a right spirit. He asks not to be cast from God's presence or lose the holy Spirit, promises to teach transgressors God's ways once restored, and says God wants a broken and contrite heart rather than sacrifice. It closes asking God to build the walls of Jerusalem, after which proper offerings will please him.
PSA 52:1-9	An accusation against a powerful man who boasts of mischief. His tongue is called a sharp razor that plots destruction, and he loves lying more than truth. God will uproot him from the land of the living, and the righteous will see it, fear, and laugh, saying this is the man who trusted his riches instead of God. The speaker contrasts himself as a green olive tree in God's house, trusting God's loving kindness and giving thanks before the assembly.
PSA 53:1-6	The fool says in his heart there is no God. God looks down from heaven to see if anyone understands or seeks him, and finds that all have turned back and become corrupt, with no one doing good. The wicked eat up God's people like bread and never call on him. They are seized by terror where no cause for fear exists, because God scattered the bones of their besiegers. The psalm ends wishing salvation would come out of Zion.
PSA 54:1-7	A short prayer for rescue. The speaker asks God to save him by his name and vindicate him, because strangers and violent men have risen against him and pay God no attention. He then states his confidence that God is his helper and sustains his soul, and asks that the evil his enemies intend be repaid to them. He promises a freewill offering and thanks to God's name, and says God has delivered him from all trouble.
PSA 55:1-23	A prayer from a man in terror, restless and moaning, wishing he had a dove's wings so he could fly away and rest in the wilderness. He asks God to confuse the language of the violent city, where malice and lies patrol the streets day and night. His deepest grievance is that the attacker is not an enemy but a close friend and worship companion, whose words were smoother than butter and oil while his heart was war. He calls on God evening, morning and noon, urges the hearer to cast their burden on Yahweh, and expects the bloodthirsty not to live out half their days.
PSA 56:1-13	The speaker says men hound him all day long, twisting his words and lurking to take his life. He answers his own fear with a refrain: when afraid, he trusts God, and asks what flesh can do to him. He asks God to cast down the peoples in anger, and says God counts his wanderings and keeps his tears in a bottle and in his book. He is confident his enemies will turn back when he calls, pays his vows with thank offerings, and says God kept his feet from falling.
PSA 57:1-11	The speaker takes refuge in the shadow of God's wings until disaster passes, crying out to the God who accomplishes his requests. He describes lying among lions whose teeth are spears and arrows and whose tongue is a sharp sword. His enemies dug a pit and fell into it themselves. Twice he asks that God be exalted above the heavens and his glory over all the earth. He declares his heart steadfast, wakes lute and harp, says he will wake the dawn, and sings thanks among the nations.
PSA 58:1-11	An attack on corrupt judges who claim to speak righteousness while plotting injustice. The wicked are said to go astray from the womb, poisonous as a deaf cobra that will not hear the charmer. The psalm asks God to break their teeth, to let them drain away like water, blunt their arrows, and make them like a snail that melts or a stillborn child. When vengeance comes the righteous will rejoice and wash their feet in the blood of the wicked, and people will say there is a God who judges the earth.
PSA 59:1-17	A prayer for deliverance from men lying in wait, and the speaker insists it is not for any sin of his. He asks God to rouse himself against the nations and show the traitors no mercy. The enemies are pictured returning at evening, howling like dogs and prowling the city, spewing swords from their lips and assuming nobody hears. God laughs at them. The speaker asks that they not be killed outright but scattered, so his people will not forget, and ends singing of God as his high tower and refuge.
PSA 60:1-12	A national complaint: God has rejected his people, broken them down, shaken the land and made them drink wine that leaves them staggering. The speaker asks him to mend the fractures. God speaks from his sanctuary claiming Shechem, Succoth, Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim and Judah as his own, and calls Moab his wash basin, throws his shoe on Edom and shouts over Philistia. The psalm asks who will bring him into the strong city, notes that God no longer marches with their armies, and says human help is worthless.
ROM 1:1-32	Paul introduces himself as an apostle set apart for the gospel of God's Son, descended from David and declared Son of God by the resurrection. He greets the Romans, says their faith is talked about everywhere, and explains that he has often planned to visit and been prevented. He is not ashamed of the gospel: it is God's power for salvation, for Jew first and also Greek, revealing a righteousness from faith to faith. Then the argument turns: God's wrath is revealed against people who knew God from what he made, refused to honour him, swapped his glory for images of humans, birds and animals, and were consequently handed over to their own desires, dishonoured bodies, and a mind full of every kind of wrong.
ROM 2:1-29	Paul turns on the reader who agreed with all that: if you judge others while doing the same, you condemn yourself, and God's kindness was meant to lead you to repentance rather than to confidence. God judges impartially by works, without favouritism between Jew and Greek. Gentiles who never had the law but do what it requires show it written on their hearts, their consciences accusing or defending them. He then addresses the person who relies on the law and boasts of teaching others: do you steal, commit adultery, rob temples? Circumcision counts only if the law is kept; an uncircumcised law-keeper effectively judges the circumcised law-breaker. The real Jew is inward, the real circumcision of the heart.
ROM 3:1-31	Paul asks what advantage the Jew has, and answers that they were entrusted with God's words, and that human unfaithfulness does not cancel God's faithfulness. He rejects the idea that sinning to make grace look better is acceptable reasoning. A chain of scripture quotations follows: no one is righteous, no one seeks God, their throats are open graves, their feet swift to shed blood. The law's job is to shut every mouth and give knowledge of sin, not to justify anyone. But now a righteousness from God has appeared apart from law, through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe without distinction, since all sinned. God set Jesus forth as an atoning sacrifice. Boasting is therefore excluded, and God is God of Gentiles as well as Jews.
ROM 4:1-25	Abraham is the test case. If he was justified by works he could boast, but scripture says he believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness, and a worker's pay is owed rather than given. David likewise blesses the man whose sin God does not count. Paul notes the sequence: Abraham was credited righteous while still uncircumcised, so circumcision was a seal on faith he already had, making him father of believing Gentiles as well as Jews. The promise came through the righteousness of faith, not the law, since law produces wrath. Abraham, roughly a hundred and facing Sarah's dead womb, did not waver but grew strong in faith. That crediting was written for our sake too, for those who believe in the God who raised Jesus.
ROM 5:1-21	Justified by faith, we have peace with God and access into grace. Paul says believers even rejoice in suffering, because suffering produces perseverance, perseverance character, character hope, and hope does not disappoint since God's love has been poured into our hearts by the Spirit. People rarely die for a righteous person, but Christ died for us while we were still sinners and enemies. He then sets Adam against Christ: sin and death entered through one man and spread to all, and death reigned even between Adam and Moses. The free gift is not like the trespass; through one man's disobedience many were made sinners, and through one man's obedience many will be made righteous. Law came in so the trespass would increase, but grace increased more.
ROM 6:1-23	Should we keep sinning so grace can abound? Paul says absolutely not, and argues from baptism: those baptised into Christ were baptised into his death and buried with him, so as to walk in newness of life. The old self was crucified so the body of sin would be broken, and a dead person is freed from sin. Christ, raised, dies no more, so death has no more power over him. Believers should count themselves dead to sin and alive to God, and stop offering their bodies to sin as instruments of wrongdoing. Being under grace rather than law is not licence: you are the slave of whatever you obey, either sin leading to death or obedience leading to righteousness. The wages of sin is death; the free gift of God is eternal life.
ROM 7:1-25	Paul argues from marriage law: death ends the binding, and believers likewise died to the law through Christ so they could belong to another. Is the law then sin? No: he would not have known coveting except that the law forbade it, and sin used the commandment to kill him. The law is holy; sin is what used it. He then describes an inner split, doing the evil he hates rather than the good he wants, delighting in God's law inwardly while another law in his body takes him captive. He cries out for deliverance and thanks God through Jesus Christ.
ROM 8:1-39	There is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. What the law could not do through weak flesh, God did by sending his own Son. Paul contrasts the mind set on the flesh, which is death, with the mind set on the Spirit, which is life and peace. Believers received a Spirit of adoption, cry "Abba, Father", and are heirs with Christ if they suffer with him. Creation and believers alike groan while the Spirit intercedes wordlessly. God works all things for good for those he called, justified and glorified, and nothing at all can separate them from Christ's love.
SIR 1:1-30	Sirach opens by asserting that all wisdom comes from the Lord and stays with him forever. Nobody can count the sand of the seas, the drops of rain or the days of eternity, and nobody can search out the height of heaven or the depth of wisdom. Wisdom was created before all things; God created her, saw and counted her, and poured her out on all his works, giving her freely to those who love him. The fear of the Lord is then described from every angle: it is glory, gladness and a crown of rejoicing, the beginning of wisdom, its fullness, its crown and its root. Practical warnings close the chapter: unjust anger is never justified, do not be a hypocrite, and do not exalt yourself lest your secrets be exposed.
SIR 2:1-18	A short chapter addressed to anyone starting out in God's service, telling him to prepare his soul for temptation, endure steadily and not act hastily in calamity. Gold is tried in fire and acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation. Three times he addresses those who fear the Lord: wait for his mercy, trust him, hope for good things and eternal gladness. He asks his readers to look at earlier generations and name anyone who trusted the Lord and was put to shame. Then a series of woes, aimed at fearful hearts, faint hands, the sinner who goes two ways and those who have lost patience. He ends preferring to fall into the hands of the Lord rather than of men, since his mercy matches his majesty.
SIR 3:1-31	A chapter on honouring parents. Honouring a father makes atonement for sins and giving glory to a mother is like storing up treasure; a father's blessing establishes his children's houses and a mother's curse tears out the foundations. He is specific about old age: help your father, do not grieve him, and if he fails in understanding be patient rather than dishonouring him while you are still strong. That kindness will not be forgotten and will melt sins away like fair weather on ice. The second half turns to humility: the greater you are, the more you should humble yourself, and do not seek out things too hard for you or too far above your strength. A stubborn heart fares badly, and almsgiving makes atonement for sins.
SIR 4:1-31	The first half concerns the poor. Do not deprive them of their living or make hungry eyes wait, do not add trouble to a provoked heart, do not turn your face from a poor man, and give no one occasion to curse you, since his maker will hear him. Be a father to the fatherless and a husband to their mother, and you will be like a son of the Most High. Then wisdom is described as a hard teacher: at first she walks with a man in crooked ways, brings fear and dread and torments him with her discipline until she can trust him, and only then returns by the straight way and reveals her secrets. He distinguishes shame that brings sin from shame that is grace, and urges striving for truth to the death.
SIR 5:1-15	A chapter of things not to say. Do not set your heart on your goods or call them sufficient, do not ask who has dominion over you, and above all do not say that you sinned and nothing happened, since the Lord is patient rather than indifferent. Do not say his compassion is great and he will overlook a multitude of sins, because mercy and wrath are both with him. Turn to the Lord without delay, since his wrath comes suddenly. Do not winnow with every wind or walk in every path, which is what the double-tongued sinner does. Be swift to hear and patient in answering, and if you have no understanding, keep your hand over your mouth. Do not be called a whisperer.
SIR 6:1-37	The chapter is mostly about friendship. Sweet words multiply friends, but let those at peace with you be many and your counsellors one in a thousand. Acquire a friend by testing him and do not be quick to trust, since some are friends for their own occasion, some turn to enmity and publicise the quarrel, and some are companions at the table who match your prosperity, order your servants about, and hide from you when you are brought low. A faithful friend is a strong defence, a treasure beyond price and a medicine of life. The second half turns to wisdom, describing her as harsh to the unlearned and heavy as a testing stone, and telling the son to put his feet in her fetters and neck in her chain, since those bonds become a robe of glory.
SIR 7:1-36	A long chain of prohibitions covering ambition, worship and household. Do not seek preeminence from the Lord or a seat of honour from the king, and do not seek to be a judge in case you fear a powerful man's face. Do not assume a large offering will be accepted on volume. Do not mock a man in the bitterness of his soul, do not lie against a brother or friend, do not chatter among elders or repeat words in prayer, and do not hate hard work or farming, which the Most High ordained. Then domestic instructions: correct your children, watch over your daughters and marry them to men of understanding, do not mistreat a servant who works truly, honour your parents, give the priest his portion, and visit the sick.
SIR 8:1-19	A chapter of conflicts to avoid. Do not contend with a mighty man, a rich man or a man full of tongue, since heaping wood on his fire only helps him, and do not joke with a rude man. Do not reproach a man turning from sin, dishonour the old or rejoice over the dead, since we all age and die. Attend instead to the discourse of the wise and the aged, who learned from their own fathers. Do not lend to a man mightier than yourself, and if you do, treat it as lost; do not go to law with a judge, whose honour decides the verdict. Do not travel through the desert with a wrathful man, take counsel with a fool, or open your heart to everyone.
SIR 9:1-18	A chapter of warnings about women and about company. Do not be jealous over your own wife, do not give your soul to a woman who would set her foot on your strength, avoid the harlot, the woman who sings, and gazing at a girl or another man's beautiful wife, since beauty has led many astray and kindles love like a fire. Do not sit or drink with a married woman. Then friendship again: never abandon an old friend, since a new one is like new wine and only good once it has aged. Do not envy a sinner's glory or share the delights of the ungodly. Keep well away from a man who has power to kill. A man full of tongue is dangerous in his city.
SIR 10:1-31	The chapter opens on government. A wise judge instructs his people, ministers resemble their judge and citizens their ruler, and an uninstructed king destroys his people, since the authority of the earth is in the Lord's hand. Then a sustained attack on pride, which is hateful to God and men: sovereignty passes from nation to nation because of injustice, violence and greed, and a man who is king today dies tomorrow and inherits creeping things and worms. God cast down the thrones of rulers and set the meek in their place, plucked up nations and planted the lowly. Pride was never created for humans. Honour belongs to those who fear the Lord, whether rich, honourable or poor, and a poor man with understanding should not be dishonoured.
SIR 11:1-34	The chapter argues that appearances mislead. Do not commend a man for his beauty or reject him for his looks, since the bee is small among flying things and produces the best of sweets. Many kings have ended sitting on the ground while someone nobody considered has worn a crown. Do not blame before examining or answer before hearing. Good and evil, life and death, poverty and riches all come from the Lord, who can make a poor man rich suddenly. A man who saves by pinching and finally decides to enjoy his goods does not know how little time is left. Call no one blessed before his death. Then a warning about who you let into your house, including the proud man who is like a decoy partridge in a cage.
SIR 12:1-18	On giving and on enemies. Know who you are giving to: help the godly man and the lowly and you will be repaid, if not by him then by the Most High, but keep back bread from the ungodly in case he uses it to overmaster you. Then a sustained warning never to trust an enemy, since his wickedness is like rust on brass. Even if he humbles himself and goes crouching, watch him: you will be like a man who has wiped a mirror and finds the rust still there. Do not seat him beside you or on your right, in case he takes your place. He speaks sweetly while planning a pit, weeps with his eyes, and if adversity comes he will be there first, tripping your heel and clapping his hands.
SIR 13:1-26	Whoever touches pitch is defiled, and whoever keeps company with a proud man becomes like him. Do not associate with someone mightier and richer than yourself, since the earthen pot and the kettle collide only one way. A rich man does wrong and threatens, while a poor man is wronged and has to plead. The rich patron is described in detail: he trades on you while you are useful, deceives you when he needs you, shames you with his food until he has stripped you two or three times, then laughs and shakes his head. Nature confirms it: wolf and lamb, hyena and dog, rich and poor. When a rich man falls there are many helpers; when a poor man falls he is rebuked, and his wisdom finds no place.
SIR 14:1-27	Blessed is the man who has not slipped with his mouth and whose soul does not condemn him. Then a portrait of the miser, whose eye is never satisfied with his portion, who grudges bread and is stingy at his own table, and who gathers by depriving himself so that others can revel in his goods. Against that, do well to yourself according to what you have, remember that death will not wait, be generous to your friend before you die, and do not let a good day pass, since there is no seeking luxury in the grave. All flesh wears out like a garment, and generations come and go like leaves on a thick tree. The chapter ends with wisdom pursued like game: peering in at her windows, camping beside her house and resting under her branches.
SIR 15:1-20	The man who fears the Lord and holds the law obtains wisdom, who meets him like a mother and receives him like a bride, feeds him bread of understanding and water of wisdom, exalts him above his neighbours and opens his mouth in the congregation. Fools and sinners will never obtain her, since she is far from pride. Then the sharpest section: do not say that it was through the Lord that you fell away or that he caused you to err, since he has no need of a sinful man. God made man and left him in the hand of his own counsel, setting fire and water before him to reach for whichever he chooses. He gave no one licence to sin.
SIR 16:1-30	The chapter begins with children: do not want a multitude of unprofitable ones or delight in ungodly sons, since one is better than a thousand and dying childless is better than having wicked children. Then a list of God's past judgments, on the giants of old, the people among whom Lot lived, the people of perdition and the six hundred thousand footmen who hardened their hearts. Mercy and wrath are both with him and his correction matches his mercy. Do not imagine you can be hidden in a boundless creation, since heaven, the deep and the earth shake when he visits. The last section turns to creation itself, where the works God made never hunger, never tire, never crowd each other out and never disobey his word.
SIR 17:1-32	A short account of humanity. The Lord created man from the earth and turns him back to it, giving him counted days, authority over what is on the earth, strength suited to him, and the image of God, along with counsel, tongue, eyes, ears and heart to understand with. He filled them with knowledge, showed them good and evil, gave them a law of life as an inheritance and made an everlasting covenant. Their ways are never hidden: all their works are like the sun before him. Almsgiving is kept like a signet and guarded as the apple of the eye. He grants a return to those who repent and comforts those losing patience, so turn back now, since thanksgiving perishes from the dead and only the living praise him.
SIR 18:1-33	God alone will be justified, and nobody has been given power to declare his works or trace them out: when a man has finished he is only at the beginning. Human days reach a hundred years at most, a drop from the sea or a pebble from the sand compared with eternity, which is why God is patient and multiplies forgiveness, reproving and teaching and bringing people back as a shepherd does his flock. Then practical advice. Add no blemish to your good deeds and no grief of words to your giving, since a word is better than a gift. Learn before you speak, examine yourself before judgment, and pay your vows in time rather than waiting until death. Remember hunger in days of plenty, and do not run up debts on banqueting.
SIR 19:1-30	A drunken workman will never get rich, and whoever despises small things falls little by little. Then a long section on keeping quiet. Never repeat what you are told, whether it came from a friend or an enemy, and let a word die with you, since it will not burst you: a fool labours with a word as a woman in childbirth, and it sticks in him like an arrow in the thigh. Reprove a friend or neighbour before threatening him, since he may not have done or said it, and everyone has sinned with the tongue. All wisdom is the fear of the Lord and the doing of the law, while knowledge of wickedness is not wisdom. Attire, laughter and gait reveal what a man is.
SIR 20:1-32	A chapter of paired opposites, mostly about silence and speech. There is a reproof that is unbecoming and a man who keeps silence and is wise; one man is silent because he has no answer and another because he knows his time, while the braggart misses his moment. Then a series of "there is" observations: prosperity found in misfortune, gain that turns to loss, a gift that profits nothing and a gift repaid double, a man who buys cheap and pays sevenfold. The fool's gift comes with reproach, is demanded back the next day, and is followed by complaints that he has no friends. A slip on the pavement is better than a slip of the tongue. Better to hide your folly than to hide your wisdom.
SIR 21:1-28	If you have sinned, add no more and pray about the old ones. Flee sin as from a serpent's face, since its teeth are a lion's, and all iniquity is a two-edged sword whose stroke has no healing. A poor man's prayer reaches God's ears and his judgment comes quickly. Building your house with other men's money is like gathering stones against winter. Most of the chapter contrasts the wise man with the fool: a fool's inward parts are a broken vessel that holds no knowledge, instruction is fetters on his feet but an ornament of gold on a prudent man's arm, and a fool laughs loudly where a clever man barely smiles. A fool is quickly inside another man's house and peers in at doors. The heart of fools is in their mouth.
SIR 22:1-27	The slothful man is compared to a defiled stone that everyone hisses at and to filth from a dunghill that people shake off their hands. An uninstructed son shames his father and a foolish daughter is his loss. Teaching a fool is gluing a potsherd or waking a deep sleeper who asks what it was. Weep for the dead seven days, the author says, but for a fool all his life, since a fool's life is worse than death, and sand, salt and a mass of iron are easier to carry than a man without understanding. Then friendship: a quarrel can be repaired, even after a drawn sword, except for arrogance, disclosing a secret and a treacherous blow. He ends asking who will set a watch over his own mouth.
SIR 23:1-28	The chapter opens with a prayer asking God not to give him a proud look and to turn away lust and a shameless mind. Then discipline of the mouth: do not get used to swearing oaths or naming the Holy One casually, since a man of many oaths fills his house with calamities, and avoid gross rudeness. He warns that two kinds of men multiply sins and a third brings wrath, naming the hot temper that burns until it is consumed and the fornicator who will not stop until he dies. The adulterer who reasons that darkness and walls hide him is answered directly: God's eyes are ten thousand times brighter than the sun and look into secret places. An unfaithful wife's case is described with the same conclusion and consequences for her children.
SIR 24:1-34	Wisdom praises herself in the congregation. She came forth from the mouth of the Most High, covered the earth like a mist, had her throne in the pillar of cloud, walked the circuit of heaven and the depth of the abyss, and looked for somewhere to rest until the Creator told her to make her tabernacle in Jacob and her inheritance in Israel. She took root in Zion, and describes herself through trees and spices: a cedar in Lebanon, a cypress on Hermon, a palm by the sea, roses in Jericho, cinnamon, myrrh, galbanum and frankincense. Those who eat her will still be hungry and those who drink her still thirsty. All this, the author says, is the book of the covenant, the law Moses commanded, flowing out like the Pishon, Tigris, Euphrates and Jordan.
SIR 25:1-26	Three things the author calls beautiful: harmony among relatives, friendship between neighbours, and a wife and husband who agree. Three he hates: a haughty poor man, a lying rich man, and an old adulterer without understanding. He praises the wisdom and counsel of the aged, then lists nine happy things and a tenth, including joy in your children, a wife of understanding, never slipping with the tongue, and finding prudence, with the fear of the Lord above all. The rest of the chapter is a sustained attack on wicked wives, saying he would rather live with a lion than keep house with one, blaming a woman for the beginning of sin and for death, and ending with instructions to allow her no freedom of speech and to cut her off.
SIR 26:1-29	The chapter begins by praising a good wife, who doubles her husband's days and lets him finish his years in peace, and calls her beauty in the ordering of a house like the rising sun and her face in ripe age like a lamp on the holy candlestick. A silent, well-instructed and modest wife is called a gift of the Lord beyond price. Between these come the author's fears, slander of a city, a hostile assembly and a false accusation, all worse than death, and a long series of complaints about jealous, drunken and headstrong women, with instructions to watch a daughter closely. At the end, two grievances and a third that angers him: a soldier suffering poverty, wise men treated as refuse, and a man turning back from righteousness. Traders, he adds, can scarcely avoid wrongdoing.
SIR 27:1-30	Sin thrusts itself in between buying and selling like a nail driven between stones, and many have sinned over something trivial while chasing profit. A sieve shows the refuse and a furnace tests the potter's vessels; a man is tested by his reasoning, so praise nobody before you have heard him argue. Then the long section on secrets. Whoever reveals a secret destroys trust and will not find a friend, and the friend he loses is like a bird let out of the hand or a gazelle out of a snare, gone beyond pursuit: a wound can be bound and reviling can be reconciled, but betraying a secret leaves no hope. The chapter closes on consequences: whoever throws a stone upward hits his own head, and whoever digs a pit falls in.
SIR 28:1-26	Whoever takes vengeance will find vengeance from the Lord, so forgive your neighbour and your own prayers will be answered. The argument is put as a question: a man nourishes wrath against someone like himself and then expects healing and atonement for his own sins. Remember your last end, remember death, and stop the quarrel. Strife burns according to its fuel, and a spark can be blown into flame or spat out, both of which come from your own mouth. Then the tongue: a third person's tongue has scattered nations, pulled down strong cities and driven women from their homes, and a whip marks the flesh while a tongue breaks bones. More have fallen by the tongue than by the sword. Make a balance for your words and a bar for your mouth.
SIR 29:1-28	On lending and dependence. Lending to a neighbour in need keeps the commandments, and repaying in due season is part of it, but many treat a loan as a windfall: the borrower kisses your hands until he has the money, then delays, complains about the times, and if he pays at all you may recover half and gain an enemy for nothing. So be patient with a poor man, help him for the commandment's sake, and treat almsgiving as treasure stored up, better than a shield and spear. Surety has ruined prosperous men and driven them from home. The essentials of life are water, bread, clothing and a house, and a poor man's own shelter of logs is better than fine food in someone else's house, where you dare not speak.
SIR 30:1-25	The chapter opens on discipline, arguing that a man who loves his son keeps laying stripes on him and will have joy of him in the end, while an indulged son becomes headstrong like an unbroken horse. Do not laugh with him or overlook his follies, and bow his neck while he is young. A well taught son continues his father, so that the father dies and yet has not died. The second half changes subject to health. A poor man with a sound constitution is better off than a rich man plagued in his body, health is better than all gold, and death is better than a bitter life. Do not give your soul over to sorrow, since gladness of heart is a man's life and envy and worry bring old age early.
SIR 31:1-31	The chapter opens on money and sleeplessness, since anxiety about riches consumes the flesh and drives away sleep, and many have been ruined for the sake of gold. He asks who has had the power to transgress and has not, and calls that man blessed. Then table manners: do not be greedy, do not reach where your eye looks or push into the dish, consider your neighbour's appetite by your own, and be first to stop eating. Moderate eating brings healthy sleep while an insatiable man gets colic. Stingy hosts are murmured at by the whole city. On wine, it is as good as life in measure, but bitterness of soul when drunk heavily.
SIR 32:1-24	Advice for a banquet and for the young. If you are made ruler of the feast, do not be exalted but take thought for the guests and take your place last. Elders should speak with sound knowledge and should not interrupt the music, since a concert at a banquet of wine is like a carbuncle set in gold. A young man should speak only if needed, scarcely even when asked twice, sum up much in few words, and be as one who knows and holds his tongue. Get up early, go home promptly and do not loiter. Then general rules: do nothing without counsel and do not regret what is done, avoid conflict, do not be confident on a smooth road, and trust your own soul in every work.
SIR 33:1-31	No evil happens to the man who fears the Lord, and a man of understanding trusts the law as though consulting an oracle, while a hypocrite in it is a ship in a storm. A fool's heart is a cartwheel and his thoughts a rolling axle. The author asks why one day is better than another when all daylight comes from the same sun, and answers that God distinguished them, exalting some and making others ordinary, and does the same with people, who are clay in the potter's hand. All the works of the Most High come two by two, opposites in pairs. He warns against handing over power or goods to family while still alive, and closes on servants: keep them working, but treat a servant as yourself, since you will need him.
SIR 34:1-26	Dreams and divination are dismissed as vain: setting your mind on dreams is catching at a shadow or chasing wind, and many have been led astray by hoping in them, unless they are sent from the Most High. Experience is better, and the author cites his own travels, in danger of death many times and preserved. Then a run of praise for those who fear the Lord, who are protected as by a cover from the noonday heat. The last section is severe about worship: a sacrifice from wrongly gotten goods is a mockery, and bringing an offering out of the goods of the poor is like killing a son before his father's eyes. Whoever deprives a hireling of his wages sheds blood, and fasting and then repeating the sin profits nothing.
SIR 35:1-20	Obedience is treated as sacrifice: keeping the law multiplies offerings, repaying a good turn is fine flour, giving alms is a thank offering, and departing from wickedness is itself an atoning sacrifice. Still, do not appear before the Lord empty, and give the firstfruits with a cheerful face and a good eye, since the Lord repays sevenfold. Do not imagine gifts can corrupt him, because he is judge and shows no favouritism: he will not accept anyone against a poor man, and will not despise the prayer of the fatherless or the widow whose tears run down her cheek. The prayer of the humble pierces the clouds and will not leave until God visits, crushes the loins of the unmerciful and breaks the sceptres of the unrighteous.
SIR 36:1-26	The chapter opens with a national prayer asking God to have mercy on his people, send his fear on the nations, show new signs and wonders, crush the heads of enemy rulers who say there is none but us, gather the tribes of Jacob and have compassion on Jerusalem, so that everyone on earth knows he is the eternal God. It then switches abruptly to discernment and marriage. The belly will eat any meat, but one is better than another, and an understanding heart tastes false speeches the way the mouth tastes game. Beauty cheers a man, and a wife with mercy and meekness on her tongue makes her husband unlike other men. Acquiring a wife is entering on a possession and a pillar of rest, while a man without one wanders, and nobody trusts a man with no nest.
SIR 37:1-31	Everyone claims to be your friend, but some are friends in name only, and it is a grief to death when a companion turns to enmity: one rejoices in your gladness and opposes you in affliction, another works alongside you for his stomach's sake. Then a careful treatment of advice. Every counsellor recommends taking counsel, but find out his interest first, since he may advise for himself and then stand nearby to watch what happens to you. He lists people not to consult: a woman about her rival, a coward about war, a merchant about exchange, a sluggard about work. Consult a godly man instead, and trust your own heart, which brings news better than seven watchmen. Also, test what is good for you, since not everything suits everyone.
SIR 38:1-34	Honour a physician, since the Lord created him and healing comes from the Most High, who made medicines out of the earth and gave men skill; pray in sickness, put away wrongdoing, make your offering, and then give place to the doctor. On mourning: weep for the dead, do not neglect the burial, wail for a day or two lest you be spoken ill of, and then be comforted, remembering that sorrow does the mourner no good and the dead no service. The rest of the chapter praises craftsmen while denying them wisdom's honours. The ploughman, the engraver of signets, the smith wrestling with iron in the furnace heat, and the potter turning his wheel with his feet all trust their hands. They maintain the fabric of the world, but they are not sought in council.
SIR 39:1-35	By contrast the scribe seeks out the wisdom of the ancients, studies prophecies and dark sayings, serves among great men, travels among foreign nations, and rises early to pray, and if the Lord wills he is filled with the spirit of understanding, so that his name lives from generation to generation. The author then breaks into praise, telling his hearers to bud like a rose by a brook and give a scent like frankincense. All the works of the Lord are exceedingly good and nobody may ask what this is or why that is, since everything is created for its use in its season. Water, fire, iron, salt, flour, honey, milk, wine, oil and clothing are the chief necessities. Winds, fire, hail, famine, wild teeth and the sword exist for vengeance.
SIR 40:1-30	Great travail is created for every man from birth until burial in the earth, the mother of all things, and the fear of death troubles everyone from the man on a throne of glory to the man in a hempen frock. Even sleep is disturbed, so that a man wakes like someone who has escaped from the front of a battle and marvels that the fear was nothing. Then a series of comparisons, each naming a good thing and then something better: children and a city are outdone by a blameless wife, wine and music by the love of wisdom, gold and silver by counsel, riches and strength by the fear of the Lord. The chapter closes bluntly on begging, saying it is better to die than to beg and live off another man's table.
SIR 41:1-24	The chapter opens on death from two sides: bitter to a man at peace in his possessions with strength still to eat, and welcome to a man who is needy, failing and out of patience. Do not fear the sentence, since it is the Lord's over all flesh and there is no inquisition of life in the grave. Then the children of the ungodly, whose inheritance perishes and whose name is blotted out, while a good name lasts forever and is worth more than a thousand treasures of gold. The rest is a catalogue of things to be ashamed of, arranged by audience: immorality before your parents, a lie before a prince, injustice before the congregation, theft where you are a guest, leaning your elbow on the table, silence when someone greets you, and repeating what you have heard.
SIR 42:1-25	A matching list of things not to be ashamed of: the law and the covenant, doing justice to the ungodly, settling accounts with a partner, exact weights and balances, and instructing the unwise. Put everything you hand over in writing, by number and weight. Then a father's anxiety about a daughter, who costs him sleep at every stage of her life, followed by more hostile lines about women. The second half turns to God's works: the Lord has not given the saints power to declare all his marvels, he searches out the deep and the heart, no thought escapes him, and he needed no counsellor. All things are double, one against another, and he has made nothing imperfect, each thing establishing the good of another.
SIR 43:1-33	A hymn to the sky and the weather. The firmament in its clearness is the pride of the height; the sun is a marvellous instrument that dries the country at noon and burns three times hotter than a man blowing a furnace; the moon marks feasts and seasons and gives the month its name. The stars keep their order and do not faint on watch. Then the rainbow encircling heaven with a circle of glory, snow sent flying like birds, hail broken small, thunder making the earth travail, hoar frost poured out like salt and freezing into points of thorns, and ice putting a breastplate on the water. Sailors report the dangers of the sea and its sea-monsters. Whatever is said falls short: the sum of our words is that he is all.
SIR 44:1-23	The praise of famous men begins. Rulers, prophets, counsellors, teachers, composers of music and verse, and wealthy men living peaceably were all honoured in their generations. Some left a name and some have no memorial at all, as though they had never been born, but the men of mercy are not forgotten and their descendants stand within the covenants. Then the roll call starts. Enoch pleased the Lord and was translated as an example of repentance. Noah was found perfect and was taken in exchange for the world, leaving a remnant when the flood came, with an everlasting covenant that flesh would not be destroyed by water again. Abraham kept the law, was proved faithful and received the oath about his seed. The blessing passed to Isaac and rested on Jacob's head.
SIR 45:1-26	The list continues with Moses, beloved of God and men, who caused the wonders to cease by his words, was led into the thick darkness and given commandments face to face. Then Aaron, given an everlasting covenant and the priesthood, described through his vestments in detail: linen breeches, long robe and ephod, golden pomegranates and bells to sound as he walked, the embroidered garment in gold and blue and purple, the Urim and Thummim, engraved stones for the twelve tribes, and a gold crown on the mitre engraved HOLINESS. When Dathan, Abiram and Korah's company opposed him they were consumed by fire. Aaron receives the firstfruits but no inheritance in the land, since God is his portion. Phinehas is third in glory, and a covenant was also made with David.
SIR 46:1-20	Joshua son of Nun, valiant in war and Moses' successor, is credited with the sun going back so that one day became two, and with hailstones breaking violently on the enemy. With Caleb he withstood the adversary and stilled the people's murmuring, and of six hundred thousand on foot only those two came into the land; Caleb kept his strength into old age and entered the high country. The judges whose hearts did not go astray are blessed, with a wish that their bones flourish again. Then Samuel, who established a kingdom and anointed princes, called on the Lord with a suckling lamb and was answered by thunder from heaven, and before his death protested that he had taken nobody's goods, not even a shoe. After he died he prophesied and showed the king his end.
SIR 47:1-25	Nathan prophesied in David's days, and David himself is described as fat separated from the peace offering: he played with lions as with kids, killed the giant with a sling stone as a youth, was praised for his ten thousands, destroyed the Philistines, set singers before the altar and ordered the feasts and seasons, and was given a covenant of kings. Then Solomon, who reigned in peace and built the house, filled the earth with dark parables, gathered gold like tin and silver like lead, and was marvelled at for his songs and proverbs. But he bowed his loins to women, blemished his honour and brought wrath on his children, so the kingdom was divided and Ephraim ruled disobediently. Rehoboam lacked understanding and Jeroboam made Israel sin.
SIR 48:1-25	Elijah arose like fire, his word burning like a torch: he brought a famine, shut up heaven, called down fire three times, raised a dead man, brought kings to destruction, anointed kings for retribution and prophets to succeed him, and was taken up in a tempest of fire in a chariot of fiery horses, appointed to turn the heart of the father to the son. Elisha was filled with his spirit, feared no ruler, and his body prophesied even after death. Still the people did not repent until they were carried off and scattered. Then Hezekiah, who fortified the city and brought water in by cutting sheer rock with iron, and when Sennacherib sent Rabshakeh and boasted, the people prayed and were delivered through Isaiah, whose angel destroyed the Assyrian camp.
SIR 49:1-16	Josiah's memory is compared to a compound of incense, sweet as honey and like music at a banquet, since he made godliness prevail in the days of wicked men. Apart from David, Hezekiah and Josiah, the kings of Judah all trespassed and failed, and the chosen city was burned as Jeremiah had written, though Jeremiah himself was sanctified in the womb to root out and to build. Ezekiel saw the vision of glory on the chariot of the cherubim. The bones of the twelve prophets are wished flourishing. Zerubbabel was like a signet on the right hand, and with Jesus son of Josedek he built the house; Nehemiah raised the fallen walls and set up gates and bars. Enoch, Joseph, Shem, Seth and above all Adam close the list.
SIR 50:1-29	Simon son of Onias, the high priest, repaired the house, built the double wall, worked on the water cistern and fortified the city against siege. His appearance coming out of the sanctuary is described through a run of images: the morning star in a cloud, the full moon, the sun on the temple, a rainbow, roses, lilies at a waterspring, frankincense in summer, a gold vessel set with stones, a budding olive, a cypress in the clouds. He puts on the robe of glory, is surrounded by his kindred like palm trees around a young cedar, pours the cup of the grape at the foot of the altar, and the sons of Aaron shout and sound the trumpets while all the people fall on their faces. The author names himself: Jesus son of Sirach Eleazar, of Jerusalem.
SIR 51:1-30	A closing thanksgiving. The author thanks God for delivering his body from destruction, from the snare of a slanderous tongue and forged lies, from gnashing teeth and from those who sought his life, and from slander taken to the king; his soul drew near to death, nobody helped, and he remembered God's mercy and prayed. Then a personal account of his search for wisdom: he asked for her before the temple while still young, tracked her from his youth, delighted in her as in a ripening grape, wrestled in her, and was given a tongue as his reward. He invites the unlearned to lodge in the house of instruction and to get her without money, putting their necks under the yoke, since he laboured only a little and found much rest.
SNG 1:1-17	The song opens with the woman's voice, asking to be kissed and saying his love is better than wine and his name is like poured out oil. She is taken into the king's rooms while friends join in praising him. She addresses the daughters of Jerusalem, telling them not to stare because the sun has darkened her: her brothers were angry and made her keep the vineyards, so she has not kept her own. She asks where he grazes his flock at noon, and he answers to follow the tracks of the sheep. He compares her to a steed in Pharaoh's chariots and praises her jewelled neck and dove eyes. She calls him a sachet of myrrh and henna blossoms from En Gedi. Their house has cedar beams.
SNG 2:1-17	She calls herself a rose of Sharon and a lily of the valleys, and he answers that she is a lily among thorns. To her he is an apple tree among the trees of the wood, whose shade she sits in and whose fruit is sweet. She is faint with love and asks for raisins and apples. Twice she charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up love until it desires. Then he arrives leaping on the mountains like a young deer, looks in at the window through the lattice, and calls her out: the winter is past, the rain is gone, the flowers are up, the turtledove is heard and the figs are ripening. He asks to see her face and hear her voice.
SNG 3:1-11	She searches for him at night from her bed, gets up and goes through the streets and squares of the city looking, and asks the watchmen who find her whether they have seen him. Just past them she finds him, holds him and will not let go until she brings him to her mother's house. Again she charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken love before it wishes. Then a procession: someone comes up from the wilderness like pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh, frankincense and merchants' spices. It is Solomon's carriage, made of Lebanon wood with silver pillars, a gold base and a purple seat, escorted by sixty armed men. The daughters of Zion are told to come and see him crowned on his wedding day.
SNG 4:1-16	He praises her at length, working downward. Her eyes are doves behind her veil, her hair a flock of goats coming down Mount Gilead, her teeth a newly washed flock where none is missing, her lips a scarlet thread, her temples a piece of pomegranate, her neck the tower of David hung with a thousand shields, and her breasts two fawns feeding among lilies. He calls her flawless and invites her down from Lebanon, from Amana, Senir and Hermon, from the lions' dens and the leopards' mountains. Her love is better than wine, her lips drip honeycomb, and she is a locked garden and a sealed fountain full of pomegranates, spikenard, saffron, cinnamon and myrrh. She calls the winds to blow the fragrance out.
SNG 5:1-16	He says he has come into his garden and gathered his myrrh, eaten his honeycomb and drunk his wine and milk, and the friends tell them to drink abundantly. Then she describes a night: asleep but her heart awake, she hears him knocking, his head wet with dew, and hesitates because she has undressed and washed her feet. By the time she opens the door, her hands dripping with myrrh, he has gone. She looks and calls but he does not answer. The watchmen find her, beat and bruise her and take her cloak. When the daughters of Jerusalem ask what makes him special, she answers with a full description: gold head, raven hair, dove eyes, cheeks like spice beds, ivory body, marble legs, and a face like Lebanon.
SNG 6:1-13	The daughters offer to help look for him, and she says he has gone down to his garden to gather lilies, then repeats that she is his and he is hers. He answers with praise: she is beautiful as Tirzah, lovely as Jerusalem and awesome as an army with banners, and he asks her to turn her eyes away because they have overcome him. He repeats the images of her hair like goats on Gilead and her teeth like a washed flock. Against sixty queens, eighty concubines and countless virgins, his dove is unique, her mother's only daughter, praised even by the queens. He describes going down to the nut grove to see whether the vines had budded. Voices call the Shulammite to return so they can look at her.
SNG 7:1-13	Another catalogue of praise, this one beginning at her feet in sandals and working up: thighs like jewels made by a skilled craftsman, a waist like a heap of wheat set about with lilies, breasts like twin fawns, an ivory tower for a neck, eyes like the pools of Heshbon, a nose like the tower of Lebanon looking toward Damascus, and hair in which the king is held captive. Her stature is a palm tree he intends to climb, her breath smells of apples and her mouth is the best wine. She answers that she is her beloved's and his desire is toward her, and invites him out to the fields and villages, up early to the vineyards, where she will give him her love among the mandrakes and stored fruit.
SNG 8:1-14	She wishes he were her brother so she could kiss him in public without reproach, and imagines bringing him to her mother's house and giving him spiced wine and pomegranate juice. Once more she charges the daughters not to awaken love before it wishes. Then the central declaration: set me as a seal on your heart, for love is strong as death and jealousy cruel as Sheol, its flashes a flame of Yahweh; many waters cannot quench it, and a man who offered all his wealth for it would be scorned. Her brothers debate what to do about their little sister, and she answers that she is a wall. Solomon's leased vineyard is contrasted with her own. She calls him away to the mountains of spices.
WIS 1:1-16	The book opens addressing the judges of the earth, telling them to love righteousness and seek the Lord in singleness of heart, since he is found by those who do not distrust him. Wisdom will not enter a soul that plans evil or a body held in pledge by sin. Because the spirit of the Lord fills the world and holds all things together, no unjust word goes unheard: there is an ear of jealousy that listens to everything, so murmuring and backbiting are dangerous. Then the central claim: God did not make death and takes no delight when the living perish. He created all things to exist, and righteousness is immortal. Ungodly men called death to themselves and made a covenant with him, treating him as a friend.
WIS 2:1-24	The author quotes the reasoning of the ungodly at length. Life is short and sorrowful, they say, nobody returns from Hades, we were born by chance, the breath in our nostrils is smoke and reason a spark that goes out. Therefore enjoy everything now: costly wine, perfumes, rosebuds crowned before they wither, revelry everywhere. Then it turns cruel: oppress the righteous poor, spare no widow, respect no grey hair, and let our strength be our law, since weakness is useless. They resolve to trap the righteous man, who reproves them by existing, calls himself God's servant and claims God as his father, and to test his patience with outrage, torture and a shameful death. They are wrong, the author says: God made man for incorruption, and death entered through the envy of the devil.
WIS 3:1-19	The souls of the righteous are in God's hand and no torment will touch them. What looked to fools like death and ruin is peace. Their brief chastening was a test, gold proved in the furnace and accepted as a whole burnt offering, and at their visitation they will shine and run like sparks among stubble, judging nations. The ungodly are repaid according to their own reasoning, their hope void and their works useless. Two surprising blessings follow: the childless woman who has not conceived in transgression is happy and will have fruit when God visits souls, and the eunuch who has done no lawless deed receives a place in the sanctuary better than wife or children. The end of an unrighteous generation, it concludes, is always grievous.
WIS 4:1-20	Virtue matters more than numbers of descendants, since the memory of virtue is immortality, imitated when present and longed for once gone. The offspring of the ungodly strike no deep root, flourish briefly and are torn out by wind, their fruit never ripening. A righteous man who dies young is at rest, because honourable old age is not measured in years: understanding is grey hair and an unspotted life is ripe old age. Such a man was taken away early precisely so wickedness would not change his mind. Made perfect quickly, he fulfilled long years. The dead righteous man will condemn the living ungodly, who will see a wise man's end and not understand what God intended. Their own lawless deeds will convict them to their faces.
WIS 5:1-23	The righteous man stands boldly before those who afflicted him, and they are terrified. The author gives them a speech of regret: this is the man we mocked and made a byword, whose life we called madness, and now he is counted among the sons of God. What did our arrogance profit us? Their lives passed like a shadow, like a ship leaving no track in the water, a bird leaving no mark in the air, an arrow whose path closes behind it. Their hope was chaff and vanishing foam. The righteous live forever and receive a royal crown. Then God arms himself: jealousy as armour, righteousness as a breastplate, judgment as a helmet, holiness as a shield, wrath as a sword, with lightning as arrows and hailstones hurled from a siege engine.
WIS 6:1-25	The address to rulers continues. Kings and judges are told that their dominion was given by the Lord, who will examine their works and counsels, and that judgment on the powerful is stricter: a man of low estate may be pardoned in mercy, but mighty men will be searched out mightily, since God shows no deference to greatness. Then the tone turns inviting. Wisdom is radiant and does not fade, is easily seen by those who love her, and makes herself known first to those who want her, so the man who rises early finds her already sitting at his gates. A chain of steps follows, from desire of discipline to love of her laws to incorruption and nearness to God. A multitude of wise men is salvation to the world.
WIS 7:1-30	The speaker insists on his own ordinariness: mortal, descended from the first man formed of earth, moulded in a womb over ten months, and born crying the same first wail as everyone, since no king has any other beginning. He prayed, and a spirit of wisdom came. He preferred her to sceptres and thrones, counted gold as sand and silver as clay beside her, and loved her above health and beauty, and with her came all good things. He lists what she taught him: the structure of the world, the working of the elements, solstices and seasons, star positions, the natures of animals, the violence of winds, the thoughts of men, the virtues of roots. She is a breath of God's power, an unspotted mirror of his working, fairer than the sun.
WIS 8:1-21	Wisdom reaches from one end of the world to the other and orders all things graciously. The speaker describes seeking her from his youth and wanting to take her as his bride, enamoured of her beauty and of her noble birth, since she lives with God. He argues her value under headings: riches, since she works all things; understanding, since she is the architect of what exists; virtue, since her fruits are soberness, understanding, righteousness and courage; and experience, since she knows the past and divines the future. With her he expects glory among crowds, honour from elders despite his youth, admiration from princes, immortality and an eternal memory, rule over nations, and rest at home. Realising he could not have her unless God gave her, he prayed.
WIS 9:1-18	The prayer itself. He addresses the God who made all things by his word and formed man by wisdom to rule the world in holiness, then asks for wisdom, the one who sits beside God on his throne. He calls himself God's servant, the son of a handmaid, weak and short-lived and of small power to understand judgment. Even a man perfect among men counts for nothing without her. He recalls being chosen as king and commanded to build the sanctuary, a copy of the tabernacle prepared from the beginning, and asks God to send wisdom from the throne of glory to toil alongside him. Mortal thoughts are timid, a corruptible body weighs down the soul, and only wisdom sent from on high corrected the ways of those on earth.
WIS 10:1-21	A retelling of Genesis and Exodus with Wisdom as the actor throughout, and with no names given. She guarded the first formed father and delivered him from his own transgression; a man who fell away from her in anger perished in the rage in which he killed his brother; she saved the earth from the flood by steering the righteous man with a poor piece of wood. She knew the righteous man among confounded nations, delivered another from fire falling on Pentapolis, where a smoking waste, fruit that never ripens and a pillar of salt still stand. She guided a fugitive from his brother's anger, went down into a dungeon with a man who had been sold and brought him a kingdom, withstood terrible kings through a servant of the Lord, and brought the people over the Red Sea.
WIS 11:1-26	Wisdom prospered the people's works through a holy prophet, guiding them through an uninhabited desert, and when they thirsted God gave them water out of flinty rock. The author's controlling idea is that the same means punished the enemy and helped Israel: the Egyptians got clotted blood instead of a river, rebuking the decree to kill infants, while the thirsty Israelites got abundant water. The Egyptians who worshipped reptiles and vermin were sent a multitude of irrational creatures, since a man is punished by the very things he sins with. God could have sent bears, lions or new-made beasts breathing fire, but he ordered everything by measure, number and weight. The whole world before him is a grain in a balance, and he overlooks sins so people may repent, loving all he has made.
WIS 12:1-27	God's incorruptible spirit is in all things, so he convicts the straying little by little, reminding them through the very things they sin with. The old inhabitants of the land, who practised enchantments, child sacrifice and cannibal feasts, were destroyed by Israel's ancestors, but even then God sent hornets ahead of the army so they would perish gradually and have a place of repentance, though he knew their wickedness was inborn. Nobody can ask what he has done or accuse him for the perishing of nations. Because he is sovereign over his own strength, he judges gently, and by such works he taught his people that the righteous must love other people. He chastens Israel but scourges its enemies far more, so mercy may be expected.
WIS 13:1-19	An argument against idolatry, starting mildly. People who had no perception of God failed to recognise the architect from his works, and took fire, wind, air, stars or water to be the gods ruling the world. If they were captivated by beauty, the author says, they should recognise how much better the first author of beauty is, and their blame is small since they were at least searching. Worse are those who hope in dead things made by hands. A woodcutter shapes a useful vessel from good timber, burns the offcuts to cook his dinner, then carves a crooked knotty leftover into a human shape, paints it red, and bolts it to a wall so it will not fall. Then he prays to it for children.
WIS 14:1-31	The subject stays with wood. A man about to sail prays to a piece of wood more rotten than the ship carrying him, though it was God's providence that made a path through the sea; a raft once carried the hope of the world when the giants were perishing. Blessed is wood through which righteousness comes; cursed is the idol and its maker. Then a history of how idols began: a grieving father made an image of a dead child and honoured it as a god, princes commanded worship of statues, absent kings were flattered by their portraits, and craftsmen forced the likeness toward greater beauty until the crowd worshipped a man. The consequences listed are child sacrifice, secret rites, frenzied revels, murder, perjury and adultery, and idol worship is called the beginning and end of every evil.
WIS 15:1-19	The author turns from idols to God, who is gracious, longsuffering and orders all things in mercy, and says that knowing him is perfect righteousness and knowing his dominion the root of immortality. Israel, he insists, was not led astray by painters' work or dead images. Then the potter: from the same clay he makes vessels for clean uses and vessels for the opposite, deciding himself which is which, and then makes a god out of the same clay, though he is earth himself and will hand back the borrowed soul. His heart is ashes and his life less honourable than clay. Worst are those who count the idols of nations as gods, things with no eyes, nostrils, ears, fingers or working feet, made by a man whose own spirit is borrowed.
WIS 16:1-29	The contrast is pressed further. Egypt was tormented by vermin while Israel was given quails of rare taste; the enemies lost their appetite at the sight of what was sent among them. When Israel was bitten by serpents, God's wrath did not last, since they had a token of salvation to remind them of the law, and it was not herb or plaster that cured them but God's word. Strange rains, hail and fire pursued the ungodly, and the fire burned more fiercely in water because creation fights for the righteous. Israel meanwhile received angels' food from heaven that tasted like whatever the eater wanted. Snow and ice survived that fire without melting, yet the same bread melted in a faint sunbeam, teaching them to rise before the sun to give thanks.
WIS 17:1-21	A long treatment of the plague of darkness, told as psychology rather than event. The Egyptians, thinking they held a holy nation in their power, became prisoners of darkness themselves, shut under their roofs and separated from each other by a curtain of forgetfulness. Sounds rushed down around them, phantoms appeared with unsmiling faces, and no fire or star could light that night, only a self-kindled glimmering which frightened them more than what they could not see. Their magicians, who promised to drive terrors away, were themselves sick with fear. The author names the mechanism: wickedness condemned by a witness within is cowardly, and fear is the surrender of the help reason offers. Farmer, shepherd and labourer alike were bound by one chain of darkness while the rest of the world had clear light.
WIS 18:1-25	For the holy ones there was great light, and the Egyptians, hearing their voices without seeing them, called them fortunate. Israel had a pillar of fire to guide an unknown journey. Egypt deserved to lose the light, having imprisoned the people through whom the law's incorruptible light would come, and having planned to kill their infants, so their own children were taken and their army destroyed in a flood. Then the Passover night: children of good men sacrificed in secret and sang, while the enemy's lament for children answered in discord, servant and master and king suffering alike with corpses beyond burying. God's word leaped from the royal throne as a stern warrior with a sharp sword. When the righteous too were struck in the wilderness, a blameless man stopped the wrath with prayer and incense.
WIS 19:1-22	Indignation without mercy came on the ungodly, because God foreknew that after urging Israel to leave they would change their minds and pursue them, which they did while still mourning at their graves. Creation was refashioned to serve: the cloud shadowed the camp, dry land rose out of the Red Sea, a grassy plain came out of the surge, and the people crossed roaming like horses and skipping like lambs. They remembered the land producing lice instead of cattle and the river throwing up frogs instead of fish, and then quails coming out of the sea. The author compares Sodom's refusal of strangers with Egypt enslaving its benefactors, and notes both were struck blind. The elements changed order like notes on a lute while remaining themselves.
