1KI 19:1-21	Ahab tells Jezebel what happened and she swears to kill Elijah within a day. He runs to Beersheba and asks to die under a juniper tree. An angel wakes him twice with a cake and a jar of water, and on that food he walks forty days to Horeb. Asked what he is doing, he says Israel has broken the covenant and killed the prophets and he alone is left. Wind, earthquake and fire pass without Yahweh in them; then a still small voice. He is sent to anoint Hazael, Jehu and Elisha, and told seven thousand have not bowed to Baal.
1KI 20:1-23	Ben Hadad of Syria besieges Samaria with thirty-two allied kings and demands Ahab's silver, gold, wives and children. Ahab agrees until the demand becomes a search of every house, and the elders tell him to refuse. Ben Hadad swears there will not be a handful of dust left per soldier; Ahab answers that a man putting on armour should not boast like one taking it off. A prophet promises victory through the young men of the provincial officials, and two hundred and thirty-two of them rout the Syrians at noon while Ben Hadad is drunk. Syria decides Israel's god is a god of the hills.
1KI 20:24-43	Syria replaces its kings with captains and rebuilds the army to fight in the plain. At Aphek, Israel camps like two little flocks of goats against a country full of Syrians. A man of God says that because Syria called Yahweh a god of the hills and not the valleys, the multitude will be handed over. Israel kills a hundred thousand Syrian foot soldiers in a day, and the wall of Aphek falls on twenty-seven thousand more. Ben Hadad hides, then sends his servants out in sackcloth and ropes to beg for his life, and Ahab calls him his brother and lets him go on terms. A prophet has himself wounded, disguises himself, and traps Ahab into sentencing a man who let a prisoner escape, then reveals Ahab has done exactly that.
ACT 9:1-21	Saul gets letters to the Damascus synagogues so he can bring back anyone of the Way in chains. Near the city a light knocks him down and a voice asks why he is persecuting it; told it is Jesus, he is sent into the city for instructions. His companions hear the sound but see no one. Blind three days, he neither eats nor drinks. Ananias, sent to him, objects that the man arrests believers, and is told Saul is a chosen vessel who will suffer much. Scales fall from Saul's eyes; he is baptized and preaches at once.
ACT 9:22-43	Saul grows stronger and confounds the Damascus Jews, who plot to kill him and watch the gates, so his disciples lower him through the wall in a basket. In Jerusalem the disciples are afraid of him until Barnabas takes him to the apostles and explains what happened. He preaches boldly, disputes with the Hellenists, and when they try to kill him the brothers send him from Caesarea to Tarsus. The churches then have peace and grow. Peter, travelling, comes to Lydda and tells Aeneas, paralyzed and bedridden eight years, to get up and make his bed, and the whole district turns to the Lord. At Joppa, Tabitha, known for good works, dies; the widows show the clothes she made, and Peter puts them out, prays, tells her to get up, and presents her alive.
ACT 10:1-25	In Caesarea a devout centurion named Cornelius sees an angel who tells him his prayers and gifts have been remembered and to send to Joppa for Simon called Peter. Next day Peter, praying hungry on the roof, sees a sheet let down holding every kind of animal and a voice telling him to kill and eat. He refuses as unclean, and is told not to call unclean what God has cleansed; this happens three times. Cornelius's men arrive, the Spirit tells him to go with them, and he travels to Caesarea, where Cornelius falls at his feet.
ACT 10:26-48	Peter raises Cornelius up, saying he is only a man, and explains that although a Jew does not associate with a foreigner, God has shown him not to call anyone unclean. Cornelius recounts his vision. Peter says God shows no favouritism and accepts those in every nation who fear him and do right, then summarises Jesus of Nazareth: anointed with the Spirit, doing good and healing, killed on a tree, raised on the third day, seen by chosen witnesses, appointed judge of the living and the dead. The Spirit falls on the listeners mid-sentence, and Peter has them baptized.
JER 51:1-31	God raises a destroying wind against Babylon and sends strangers to winnow her. His people are told to flee and save their own lives, because Babylon, a golden cup in his hand that made all the earth drunk, has suddenly fallen and cannot be healed. The kings of the Medes are stirred up and a standard set against her walls. Babylon had been God's battle axe, used to break horses, chariots and governors alike; now she is paid for what she did in Zion. Runners meet runners telling the king his city is taken.
JER 51:32-64	The fords are seized and the reeds burned, and Babylon is a threshing floor at treading time. Zion is quoted: Nebuchadnezzar swallowed me like a monster, so let my blood be on Chaldea. God answers that he will plead her cause, dry her sea and fountain, and set a feast that puts them to sleep for good. Jeremiah then writes it all in a book and sends it with Seraiah son of Neriah, who is to read it in Babylon, tie a stone to it and throw it into the Euphrates.
JER 52:1-17	Zedekiah became king at twenty one and reigned eleven years, doing evil as Jehoiakim had and rebelling against Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem from the tenth day of the tenth month of his ninth year into the eleventh, by which time the famine had left no bread. The wall was breached, the soldiers fled by night, and Zedekiah was overtaken in the plains of Jericho. At Riblah he watched his sons killed, was blinded, and died imprisoned in Babylon. Nebuzaradan burned the temple and the palace, broke down the walls, and deported all but the poorest.
JER 52:18-34	An inventory of what was carried off: the bronze service vessels, the gold and silver cups and lamp stands, the two pillars, the sea and the twelve bronze bulls, whose bronze was beyond weighing. Each pillar is measured out, eighteen cubits high and hollow, with a capital of network and pomegranates. Nebuzaradan also took Seraiah the chief priest, palace officials and sixty men of the city, all put to death at Riblah. Deportation totals come to four thousand six hundred. The book ends with Evilmerodach releasing Jehoiachin after thirty seven years.
1KI 21:1-29	Ahab offers to buy Naboth's vineyard, next door to the palace, and Naboth refuses to hand over his fathers' inheritance. Ahab goes home sullen and will not eat. Jezebel writes letters in his name to the elders of Jezreel, arranging a fast with Naboth seated in the place of honour and two scoundrels to accuse him of cursing God and the king. Naboth is stoned to death and Ahab goes down to take the vineyard. Elijah meets him there: where dogs licked Naboth's blood they will lick Ahab's, his house will end like Jeroboam's and Baasha's, and dogs will eat Jezebel by the rampart of Jezreel. Ahab tears his clothes and fasts, and God defers the disaster to his son's day.
1KI 22:1-26	After three years of peace, Jehoshaphat of Judah visits Ahab, who proposes retaking Ramoth Gilead. Jehoshaphat agrees but asks for a word from Yahweh. Four hundred prophets say go, and Zedekiah makes iron horns to act it out. Jehoshaphat asks whether there is another prophet; Ahab names Micaiah, whom he hates for never prophesying good. Micaiah first parrots the others, then, pressed, reports Israel scattered on the mountains like sheep without a shepherd, and a vision of Yahweh's court where a spirit volunteers to be a lying spirit in the mouths of Ahab's prophets. Zedekiah strikes him. Ahab orders him taken back to the governor.
1KI 22:27-53	Ahab orders Micaiah held on prison rations until he returns in peace, and Micaiah answers that if he returns at all, Yahweh has not spoken by him. The two kings go up to Ramoth Gilead. Ahab disguises himself and sends Jehoshaphat out in royal robes; the Syrian chariot captains, ordered to fight only the king of Israel, chase Jehoshaphat until they realise their mistake. A man draws his bow at random and hits Ahab between the joints of his armour. Propped up in his chariot, he dies at evening, and the army disperses. The chariot is washed at the pool of Samaria and dogs lick his blood. Ahaziah succeeds him. Jehoshaphat's twenty-five year reign is summarised: right in Yahweh's eyes, high places left standing, a wrecked fleet at Ezion Geber. Ahaziah of Israel serves Baal.
2KI 1:1-18	Moab rebels after Ahab's death. Ahaziah falls through the lattice of his upper room and sends messengers to ask Baal Zebub, god of Ekron, whether he will recover. Elijah intercepts them: because the king consulted a foreign god as though there were none in Israel, he will not leave his bed. The messengers describe a hairy man with a leather belt, and Ahaziah names him. He sends a captain with fifty men to fetch Elijah; fire from the sky consumes them, and a second fifty as well. The third captain kneels and begs for his life, and an angel tells Elijah to go with him. Elijah repeats the sentence to the king's face. Ahaziah dies, and because he has no son, Jehoram reigns in his place.
2KI 2:1-25	Knowing Elijah is about to be taken, Elisha refuses three times to be left behind, at Bethel, Jericho and the Jordan. Elijah rolls up his mantle, strikes the water, and the two cross on dry ground. Asked what he wants, Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah's spirit, and is told he will have it if he sees the departure. A chariot and horses of fire separate them and Elijah goes up in a whirlwind. Elisha tears his clothes, takes the fallen mantle, and parts the Jordan with it. Fifty prophets search three days for Elijah and find nothing. Elisha heals Jericho's bad water with salt from a new jar. At Bethel youths jeer at his baldness, he curses them, and two bears maul forty-two of them.
2KI 3:1-27	Jehoram of Israel removes his father's pillar of Baal but keeps the sins of Jeroboam. Mesha of Moab, a sheep breeder who paid tribute in wool, rebels. Jehoram allies with Jehoshaphat of Judah and the king of Edom, and after seven days through the wilderness the army has no water. At Jehoshaphat's insistence they consult Elisha, who says he would not look at Jehoram but for Jehoshaphat. With a musician playing, he orders the valley dug full of trenches and promises water without rain and victory over Moab. Water arrives at morning sacrifice; the Moabites see it red as blood, assume the kings have killed each other, and rush the camp. Israel drives them back and ruins the land. Besieged at Kir Hareseth, the king of Moab sacrifices his eldest son on the wall, and the invaders withdraw.
2KI 4:1-24	A widow of one of the prophets tells Elisha a creditor is coming for her two sons as slaves. She has one pot of oil, and he tells her to borrow every empty container she can, shut the door and pour. The oil runs until the last jar is filled, and she sells it to clear the debt and live on the rest. At Shunem a prominent woman feeds Elisha whenever he passes and builds him a roof room. Offered a favour she asks for nothing; Gehazi points out she has no son and an old husband, and Elisha tells her she will hold a son within the year. She does. The boy grows, cries out about his head in the harvest field, and dies on her knees at noon. She lays him on Elisha's bed and rides for Carmel.
2KI 4:25-44	Elisha sees the Shunammite coming and sends Gehazi to ask if all is well; she says it is well, then takes hold of Elisha's feet and asks whether she ever requested a son. He sends Gehazi ahead with his staff, telling him to greet no one, but laying it on the child's face does nothing. Elisha shuts himself in with the boy, prays, and stretches himself over him twice until the flesh warms; the child sneezes seven times and opens his eyes. The mother takes up her son. At Gilgal, in a famine, someone shreds unknown wild gourds into the stew pot and the men cry that there is death in the pot; Elisha throws in meal and it is safe. A man brings twenty barley loaves and fresh grain, and a hundred men eat with some left over.
2KI 5:1-14	Naaman, commander of Syria's army and a great man with his master, has leprosy. A captive Israelite girl serving his wife says the prophet in Samaria could heal him. The king of Syria sends him with a letter, ten talents of silver, six thousand pieces of gold and ten changes of clothing. The king of Israel tears his clothes, taking the letter as a pretext for a quarrel, and Elisha sends word to let the man come. Elisha does not come out; a messenger tells Naaman to wash seven times in the Jordan. Naaman leaves in a rage, expecting a ceremony and preferring the rivers of Damascus. His servants point out that he would have done something difficult if asked. He dips seven times and his flesh is restored like a child's.
2KI 5:15-27	Naaman returns and declares there is no God in all the earth but in Israel, then presses a gift on Elisha, who refuses under oath. Naaman asks instead for two mules' load of Israelite earth, since he will sacrifice to Yahweh alone from now on, and asks pardon in advance for bowing in the temple of Rimmon when his master leans on his arm. Elisha sends him off in peace. Gehazi runs after him, says two young prophets have arrived and asks for a talent of silver and two changes of clothing; Naaman insists on two talents and sends servants to carry them. Gehazi hides the goods and tells Elisha he went nowhere. Elisha says his heart went with him, and that Naaman's leprosy will cling to him and his offspring. Gehazi leaves white as snow.
2KI 6:1-18	The company of prophets tells Elisha their quarters are too small and asks to build by the Jordan. A borrowed axe head flies into the water, and Elisha throws in a stick and makes the iron float. Meanwhile Syria is at war with Israel, and every time the king of Syria fixes a camp Elisha warns Israel's king away from it. Suspecting a traitor, the king is told that Elisha reports even what he says in his bedroom. Learning the prophet is at Dothan, he surrounds the city by night with horses and chariots. Elisha's servant panics; Elisha says those with them are more, and prays until the servant sees the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire. Then he prays the Syrians blind.
2KI 6:19-33	Elisha tells the blinded Syrians they are at the wrong city and leads them into Samaria, where their eyes are opened. The king asks twice whether to kill them; Elisha says no, feed them, and they are sent home, and the Syrian raids stop. Later Ben Hadad besieges Samaria until a donkey's head sells for eighty pieces of silver and a little dove's dung for five. A woman calls to the king from the wall: she and another woman agreed to eat their sons, hers was boiled and eaten, and the other has hidden her child. The king tears his clothes, showing sackcloth underneath, and swears to have Elisha's head that day. Elisha tells the elders to bar the door against the messenger. The king says the disaster is from Yahweh and asks why he should wait any longer.
2KI 7:1-20	Elisha says that by this time tomorrow flour and barley will sell cheaply in Samaria's gate. The captain the king leans on scoffs that not even windows in heaven could do it, and is told he will see it but not eat it. Four men with leprosy at the gate reason that they will die either way and go to surrender to Syria, whose army has fled at the sound of a great host, leaving the camp standing. The four eat, loot two tents, hide the spoil, then decide that keeping quiet on a day of good news is wrong and tell the gatekeepers. The king suspects an ambush and sends chariots, which find the road strewn with discarded gear. The people plunder the camp, prices fall as promised, and the captain, posted at the gate, is trampled to death.
2KI 8:1-29	Warned by Elisha of a seven year famine, the Shunammite woman lives in Philistine territory, then returns to petition for her house and land. Gehazi is telling the king about the boy raised from the dead as she arrives, and the king restores her property with its income. In Damascus the sick Ben Hadad sends Hazael with forty camel loads of gifts to ask whether he will recover. Elisha says to tell him he will recover, though God has shown he will die, then weeps over the atrocities Hazael will commit in Israel, and tells him he will be king. Next day Hazael smothers his master with a wet cloth. In Judah, Jehoram marries Ahab's daughter and does evil, and Edom and Libnah revolt. His son Ahaziah joins Joram of Israel against Hazael, who wounds Joram at Ramoth Gilead.
2KI 9:1-18	Elisha sends a young prophet to Ramoth Gilead with a vial of oil, telling him to anoint Jehu privately and then run. The young man pours the oil, declares Jehu king over Israel, and gives him the commission: strike down the house of Ahab to avenge the prophets' blood, and dogs will eat Jezebel at Jezreel. Then he flees. Jehu's fellow officers ask what the madman wanted; when he tells them, they spread their cloaks on the stairs, blow the trumpet and proclaim him king. Jehu orders the city sealed so no news reaches Jezreel, where the wounded Joram is recovering and Ahaziah of Judah is visiting. A watchman sees the company coming; a rider sent to ask whether it is peace is told to fall in behind, and does not return.
2KI 9:19-37	A second rider is sent and also does not come back, and the watchman recognises the driving as Jehu's, which is furious. Joram and Ahaziah drive out and meet him on Naboth's land. Asked whether he comes in peace, Jehu answers that there is none while Jezebel's idolatry and witchcraft continue. Joram turns to flee and Jehu shoots him through the heart, ordering the body thrown onto Naboth's field in fulfilment of the word spoken against Ahab. Ahaziah is struck as he flees and dies at Megiddo, and is buried in Jerusalem. At Jezreel, Jezebel paints her eyes and calls Jehu a murderer of his master from the window. At his word, eunuchs throw her down, and he tramples her. When he sends men to bury her, only her skull, feet and hands remain.
2KI 10:1-17	Jehu writes to the guardians of Ahab's seventy sons in Samaria, daring them to pick one and fight. Terrified, they answer that they will do whatever he says. His second letter demands the heads of the seventy by the next day, and they are sent to Jezreel in baskets. Jehu has them piled in two heaps at the gate, then tells the people that he alone conspired against his master but that someone else killed these, and that nothing of Yahweh's word against Ahab's house will fail. He kills the rest of Ahab's household in Jezreel with its officials, friends and priests, then kills forty-two of Ahaziah's brothers met on the road, at the shearing house pit. He takes Jehonadab son of Rechab into his chariot to watch his zeal, then destroys what is left of Ahab's house in Samaria.
2KI 10:18-36	Jehu announces that Ahab served Baal a little but he will serve him much, and summons every prophet, priest and worshipper of Baal to a great sacrifice, threatening death for absence. The temple fills, robes are issued, and Jehu has the crowd checked to be sure no servant of Yahweh is among them. He posts eighty men outside and tells them that anyone who lets a man escape will pay with his own life. As the burnt offering ends, the guards go in and kill everyone; the pillars are burned, the temple pulled down and made a latrine. Jehu ends Baal in Israel but keeps the golden calves at Bethel and Dan. He is promised four generations on the throne. In his time Hazael begins taking Israelite territory east of the Jordan. Jehu reigns twenty-eight years.
2KI 11:1-21	When Athaliah learns her son Ahaziah is dead, she destroys the royal family. Jehosheba, Joram's daughter, steals away the infant Joash with his nurse and hides him in the temple for six years while Athaliah reigns. In the seventh year the priest Jehoiada summons the captains of the Carites and the guard, shows them the king's son, and assigns them shifts to surround him with David's spears and shields from the temple. Joash is crowned, given the covenant, anointed and acclaimed. Athaliah hears the noise, comes in, sees the king by the pillar, and cries treason; Jehoiada has her taken out through the horses' entry and killed away from the temple. Covenants are made between Yahweh, king and people; the people tear down the house of Baal and kill its priest Mattan. Joash, aged seven, takes the throne.
2KI 12:1-21	Jehoash reigns forty years and does right while Jehoiada instructs him, though the high places remain. He tells the priests to use the temple's dedicated money for repairs, but by his twenty-third year nothing is repaired, so he takes the collection out of their hands. Jehoiada bores a hole in a chest lid and sets it by the altar. When it fills, the king's scribe and the high priest count the money and pay it straight to the carpenters, masons and stonecutters. No silver or gold vessels are made from it, and no accounting is demanded of the foremen, who deal honestly. Guilt and sin offering money stays with the priests. When Hazael takes Gath and turns toward Jerusalem, Jehoash buys him off with the temple and palace gold. His servants conspire and kill him at the house of Millo.
2KI 13:1-25	Jehoahaz son of Jehu reigns seventeen years in Israel, does evil, and is given into the hands of Hazael and Ben Hadad; when he pleads, Israel is granted a deliverer, but the sins of Jeroboam and the Asherah in Samaria remain, and his army is reduced to fifty horsemen, ten chariots and ten thousand foot. His son Jehoash reigns sixteen years and also does evil. Elisha, dying, has Jehoash shoot an arrow eastward as the arrow of victory over Syria, then tells him to strike the ground; he strikes three times and stops, and Elisha is angry, because five or six would have finished Syria. Elisha dies, and later a body thrown into his tomb revives on touching his bones. Hazael dies, and Jehoash retakes from Ben Hadad the cities lost by his father, beating him three times.
2KI 14:1-29	Amaziah of Judah does right but not like David, and the high places remain. He executes his father's assassins but spares their children, citing the law that each man dies for his own sin. He kills ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt. He then challenges Jehoash of Israel, who replies with a fable of a thistle proposing marriage to a cedar and being trampled by a wild animal, and tells him to stay home. Amaziah insists; Judah is beaten at Beth Shemesh, Amaziah is captured, four hundred cubits of Jerusalem's wall come down, and the temple and palace treasures go to Samaria. Amaziah is later killed by conspirators at Lachish, and Azariah, aged sixteen, succeeds him. Jeroboam son of Joash reigns forty-one years, does evil, and restores Israel's borders as Jonah son of Amittai had said.
2KI 15:1-19	Azariah becomes king of Judah at sixteen and reigns fifty-two years, doing right except that the high places remain. He is struck with leprosy and lives in a separate house while his son Jotham runs the household and judges the people. In Israel the throne changes hands fast. Zechariah son of Jeroboam reigns six months, does evil, and is struck down in public by Shallum, which completes the promise of four generations to Jehu. Shallum reigns one month before Menahem comes up from Tirzah and kills him. Menahem attacks Tiphsah for refusing to open its gates and rips open its pregnant women. He reigns ten years and does evil. When Pul of Assyria invades, Menahem pays him a thousand talents of silver to secure his hold on the kingdom.
2KI 15:20-38	Menahem raises the Assyrian tribute by taxing every wealthy man fifty shekels, and Assyria withdraws. His son Pekahiah reigns two years, does evil, and is killed in the palace fortress by his captain Pekah with fifty Gileadites. Pekah reigns twenty years and does evil. In his time Tiglath Pileser of Assyria takes Ijon, Abel Beth Maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead and Galilee, all Naphtali, and deports the people to Assyria. Hoshea son of Elah then conspires against Pekah, kills him and takes the throne. In Judah, Jotham reigns sixteen years and does right, though the high places remain, and he builds the upper gate of the temple. In his days God begins sending Rezin of Syria and Pekah against Judah. Ahaz succeeds him.
2KI 16:1-20	Ahaz reigns sixteen years in Jerusalem and does not do right: he walks in the way of the kings of Israel, makes his son pass through the fire, and sacrifices at the high places and under every green tree. Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel besiege Jerusalem without taking it, and Rezin recovers Elath. Ahaz sends silver and gold from the temple and palace to Tiglath Pileser of Assyria, calling himself his servant and son; Assyria takes Damascus, deports its people and kills Rezin. Visiting Damascus, Ahaz sends home a drawing of an altar there, and Urijah the priest builds a copy before he returns. Ahaz sacrifices on it, moves the bronze altar aside for his own use, and strips the temple bases, sea and Sabbath entrance because of the king of Assyria.
ACT 11:1-30	Back in Jerusalem, Peter is criticised for eating with uncircumcised men, and answers by retelling the vision of the sheet, the three men from Caesarea, the six brothers who came with him, Cornelius's angel, and the Spirit falling on the household as it had on them at the beginning; his critics fall silent and praise God for granting the Gentiles repentance. Meanwhile believers scattered by the persecution over Stephen reach Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, and some men of Cyprus and Cyrene preach to Greeks there. Jerusalem sends Barnabas, who is glad, encourages them, and fetches Saul from Tarsus; they teach for a year, and the disciples are first called Christians in Antioch. The prophet Agabus predicts a worldwide famine, and the church sends relief to Judea by Barnabas and Saul.
ACT 12:1-25	Herod kills James the brother of John with the sword and, seeing that it pleases people, arrests Peter during the days of unleavened bread under four squads of soldiers. The night before the trial an angel wakes Peter, his chains fall off, and they pass both guards and an iron gate that opens by itself; Peter thinks it is a vision until the angel leaves him in the street. At the house of Mary, mother of John Mark, the maid Rhoda recognises his voice and is so glad she leaves him outside while she reports it, and the praying group tell her she is crazy. He explains, sends word to James, and leaves. Herod executes the guards, and at Caesarea, hailed as a god after a speech, is struck by an angel and dies eaten by worms.
ACT 13:1-25	In Antioch the prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen and Saul, are fasting when the Spirit sets Barnabas and Saul apart for a work. They sail to Cyprus with John as attendant, preach at Salamis, and at Paphos meet the sorcerer Bar Jesus, called Elymas, who tries to turn the proconsul Sergius Paulus from the faith. Saul, also called Paul, denounces him and he goes blind, and the proconsul believes. At Perga John leaves for Jerusalem. In Antioch of Pisidia, invited to speak in the synagogue, Paul begins with the history: the exodus, forty years in the wilderness, seven nations destroyed, judges until Samuel, Saul son of Kish, then David, from whose offspring came the promised saviour, announced beforehand by John's baptism of repentance.
ACT 13:26-52	Paul continues: the rulers in Jerusalem fulfilled the prophets they read each Sabbath by condemning Jesus, asked Pilate for his death without cause, and buried him, but God raised him and he was seen for many days by witnesses from Galilee. Quoting the second psalm and the promise that the Holy One would not see decay, he argues that David died and decayed while Jesus did not, and that forgiveness comes through him where the law of Moses could not justify. He closes with a prophetic warning against scoffers. Almost the whole city gathers the next Sabbath; the synagogue leaders, jealous, contradict him, so Paul and Barnabas turn openly to the Gentiles. Persecution is stirred up through prominent women and city leaders, and they shake off the dust and go to Iconium.
ACT 14:1-28	At Iconium many Jews and Greeks believe, but the city divides and a plot to stone them sends Paul and Barnabas to Lystra and Derbe. At Lystra Paul sees a man lame from birth who has faith to be healed and tells him to stand; he leaps up. The crowd calls Barnabas Jupiter and Paul Mercury, and the priest of Jupiter brings oxen and garlands, so the apostles tear their clothes and insist they are only men, pointing to the God who made everything and gave rains and harvests. Then Jews from Antioch and Iconium persuade the crowd, and Paul is stoned and dragged out for dead, but rises and goes on to Derbe. They retrace their route, appointing elders, then sail to Antioch and report a door of faith opened to the nations.
ACT 15:1-41	Men from Judea teach at Antioch that circumcision is required for salvation, so Paul and Barnabas are sent to Jerusalem to put the question to the apostles and elders. Believing Pharisees argue for circumcision and the law. After much debate Peter says God gave the Gentiles the Spirit and cleansed their hearts by faith, and asks why they would impose a yoke no one could bear. James, citing the prophecy about rebuilding David's fallen tent, proposes requiring only abstention from idol pollution, sexual immorality, strangled meat and blood. A letter goes to Antioch with Judas Barsabbas and Silas and is received gladly. Later Barnabas wants to take John Mark on a return visit, Paul refuses because Mark left them in Pamphylia, and they part, Barnabas sailing to Cyprus and Paul taking Silas through Syria and Cilicia.
ACT 16:1-18	At Derbe and Lystra Paul meets Timothy, son of a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father, and circumcises him because of the Jews in the area. They deliver the Jerusalem decrees as they travel, and the assemblies grow. The Spirit forbids them to speak in Asia and blocks Bithynia, so they reach Troas, where Paul sees a Macedonian begging him to come and help. They sail to Philippi, a Roman colony, and on the Sabbath speak to women at a riverside place of prayer. Lydia, a seller of purple from Thyatira, is baptized with her household and presses them to stay with her. A slave girl with a spirit of divination follows them shouting for days until Paul, annoyed, casts it out.
ACT 16:19-40	Seeing their profit gone, the girl's owners drag Paul and Silas to the magistrates, accusing them of advocating unlawful customs. The crowd joins in, and the two are beaten with rods and jailed, the jailer putting them in the inner prison with their feet in stocks. Around midnight they are praying and singing while the prisoners listen when an earthquake opens every door and loosens everyone's bonds. The jailer, assuming escape, is about to kill himself when Paul calls out that they are all there. He asks what he must do to be saved, washes their wounds, is baptized with his household and feeds them. In the morning the magistrates send word to release them quietly, but Paul, noting they were beaten publicly and untried as Romans, makes them come in person. They apologise and ask them to leave.
ACT 17:1-34	At Thessalonica Paul argues in the synagogue for three Sabbaths that the Christ had to suffer and rise; some believe, along with devout Greeks and leading women. A mob attacks Jason's house and drags him before the rulers, charging that these men say there is another king, Jesus. Sent on to Beroea, they find people who examine the scriptures daily, until Thessalonian agitators arrive and Paul is escorted to Athens. Provoked by the idols, he argues in the synagogue and marketplace, and Epicurean and Stoic philosophers bring him to the Areopagus. He begins from an altar inscribed to an unknown god, argues that God does not live in temples or need service, quotes their own poets, and calls for repentance before a judgment by a man raised from the dead. Some mock; Dionysius, Damaris and others believe.
ACT 18:1-28	In Corinth Paul meets Aquila and Priscilla, recently expelled from Rome by Claudius, and works with them as a fellow tentmaker while reasoning in the synagogue each Sabbath. Opposed, he shakes out his clothes, turns to the Gentiles, and moves next door to the house of Justus. Crispus the synagogue ruler believes with his household and many Corinthians are baptized. A night vision tells Paul not to be afraid, and he stays a year and a half. The proconsul Gallio refuses to hear a dispute about words and names and drives his accusers off, ignoring the beating of Sosthenes. Paul sails for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila, shaving his head at Cenchreae for a vow, and leaves them at Ephesus. Apollos arrives there knowing only John's baptism, is corrected privately by the couple, and goes on to Achaia.
ACT 19:1-21	At Ephesus Paul finds disciples who have not heard of the Holy Spirit and were baptized only into John's baptism; he baptizes the twelve or so in the name of Jesus, and when he lays hands on them they speak in other languages and prophesy. He argues in the synagogue three months, then teaches daily in the school of Tyrannus for two years, so that all Asia hears. Cloths taken from him heal the sick. Seven sons of Sceva try the name of Jesus as a formula; the evil spirit says it knows Jesus and Paul but not them, and the man drives them out naked and wounded. Believers burn magic books worth fifty thousand pieces of silver. Paul plans to reach Jerusalem through Macedonia and Achaia, and afterwards to see Rome.
ACT 19:22-41	Paul sends Timothy and Erastus into Macedonia and stays in Asia. Demetrius, a silversmith who makes silver shrines of Artemis, gathers the craftsmen and warns that Paul's preaching against handmade gods threatens their income and the temple's standing. They shout that Artemis of the Ephesians is great, and the city rushes into the theatre, seizing Paul's companions Gaius and Aristarchus. Paul is stopped from going in by the disciples and by friendly Asiarchs. The assembly is confused, most not knowing why they came; Alexander is pushed forward but, recognised as a Jew, is shouted down for two hours. The town clerk quiets them, notes that no one disputes the city's role as temple keeper, that these men have robbed no temple, that courts exist for grievances, and that they risk being charged with rioting, then dismisses them.
ACT 20:1-38	After the uproar Paul travels through Macedonia into Greece, spends three months there, and on learning of a plot returns overland. Seven named companions go ahead to Troas. Talking until midnight on the first day of the week, Paul is interrupted when Eutychus, asleep in a third-floor window, falls and is taken up dead; Paul embraces him, says his life is in him, then talks until daybreak, and the boy is brought in alive. Paul walks to Assos and rejoins the ship, sailing past Ephesus to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost. From Miletus he summons the Ephesian elders, recalls his work among them, says the Spirit warns of bonds ahead, that they will not see his face again, and that wolves will come from among themselves. They pray, weep, and see him to the ship.
ACT 21:1-22	The voyage runs by Cos, Rhodes and Patara to Tyre, where disciples tell Paul through the Spirit not to go up to Jerusalem. The whole company, with wives and children, sees them off and they pray on the beach. By way of Ptolemais they reach Caesarea and stay with Philip the evangelist, one of the seven, whose four unmarried daughters prophesy. The prophet Agabus takes Paul's belt, binds his own hands and feet, and says its owner will be bound in Jerusalem and handed to the Gentiles. Everyone begs Paul not to go; he answers that he is ready to die there, and they yield. In Jerusalem James and the elders welcome his report but raise the rumour that he teaches Jews abroad to abandon Moses.
ACT 21:23-40	The elders propose that Paul join four men under a vow, purify himself with them and pay their expenses, so everyone can see he keeps the law; the Gentile believers remain bound only by the earlier four rules. Paul does it. Near the end of the seven days Jews from Asia see him in the temple and rouse the crowd, claiming he teaches against the people, the law and the place, and has brought Greeks inside, an assumption drawn from seeing Trophimus with him in the city. He is dragged out, the doors shut, and the crowd is beating him when the Roman commander arrives and binds him with two chains. Unable to hear anything over the shouting, he has Paul carried up the steps. Paul asks to speak, surprising the officer, who had taken him for an Egyptian rebel.
ACT 22:1-30	Speaking in Hebrew, which quiets the crowd, Paul says he is a Jew born in Tarsus, raised in Jerusalem under Gamaliel, and that he persecuted the Way with letters from the high priest. He describes the light near Damascus at noon, the voice asking why he persecutes it, and the answer that it is Jesus of Nazareth; his companions saw the light but did not understand the voice. Blinded, he was led into Damascus, where Ananias restored his sight and told him to be baptized. He adds that in a temple trance he was sent to the Gentiles. At that word the crowd erupts, throwing dust and demanding his death. The commander orders him scourged, and Paul asks whether it is lawful to scourge an uncondemned Roman; the officer, who bought his citizenship, learns Paul was born to it.
ACT 23:1-35	Paul tells the council he has lived with a good conscience, and the high priest Ananias orders him struck; Paul calls him a whitewashed wall, then withdraws it on learning who he is. Noticing the council is split, he declares himself a Pharisee on trial over the resurrection, and the Pharisees and Sadducees fall to arguing until the commander pulls him out by force. That night the Lord tells him he will testify in Rome as he has in Jerusalem. More than forty men swear not to eat or drink until Paul is dead and ask for another hearing as a trap. Paul's nephew tells the commander, who sends Paul to Caesarea by night under heavy guard with a letter to Felix saying the dispute concerns their law and carries no capital charge.
ACT 24:1-27	Five days later the high priest Ananias comes down with elders and the orator Tertullus, who flatters Felix and then calls Paul a plague, an agitator among Jews worldwide and a ringleader of the Nazarenes who tried to defile the temple. Paul answers that it is only twelve days since he came up to worship, that no one found him disputing or stirring crowds, and that they cannot prove their charges. He says he serves the God of his fathers after the Way, believing the law and prophets and hoping in a resurrection, and notes that his Asian accusers are absent. Felix defers the case until Lysias comes. Hearing him later with his wife Drusilla, he is alarmed at talk of judgment and hopes for a bribe. Two years on, Festus succeeds him and Paul is left in bonds.
ACT 25:1-27	Three days after arriving, Festus goes up to Jerusalem, where the chief priests ask him to send Paul there, intending to kill him on the road. He refuses, telling them to come to Caesarea. At the hearing they bring charges they cannot prove, and Paul answers that he has offended neither the law nor the temple nor Caesar. When Festus, wanting to please them, asks whether he will be tried in Jerusalem, Paul says he is already at Caesar's judgment seat and appeals to Caesar; Festus confers and grants it. King Agrippa and Bernice arrive, and Festus lays out the case, admitting the accusers brought only disputes about their religion and about one Jesus who died and whom Paul says is alive. Agrippa asks to hear him, and Paul is brought in the next day with great ceremony.
ACT 26:1-32	Invited by Agrippa to speak, Paul says he is glad to answer before a king expert in Jewish customs. He recounts living as a strict Pharisee, says he is on trial for the hope the twelve tribes serve for, and asks why a resurrection should be thought incredible. He describes imprisoning believers and voting for their deaths, then the noon light brighter than the sun, the voice in Hebrew about kicking against goads, and the commission to turn people from darkness to light. He preached repentance in Damascus, Jerusalem, Judea and to the Gentiles, saying nothing beyond Moses and the prophets. Festus shouts that learning has driven him mad; Agrippa asks whether Paul means to make him a Christian. Afterwards they agree he deserves no death, and could have been freed had he not appealed.
ACT 27:1-21	Paul and other prisoners are handed to a centurion named Julius for the voyage to Italy, with Aristarchus along. Julius treats Paul kindly at Sidon, letting him visit friends. Contrary winds take them under Cyprus to Myra, where they transfer to an Alexandrian ship, then slowly past Cnidus and under Crete to Fair Havens. The season is late and Paul warns the voyage will cost cargo, ship and lives, but the centurion follows the captain and owner, and the majority vote to try for Phoenix. A soft south wind seems to confirm it until a north-easter called Euroclydon drives them off. They secure the ship's boat with difficulty, undergird the hull with cables, lower the sea anchor for fear of the Syrtis sands, and throw over cargo and tackle. After days without sun or stars all hope is gone.
ACT 27:22-44	Paul tells them to take heart: an angel has said he must stand before Caesar and that God has granted him everyone sailing with him, so only the ship will be lost, though they must run aground on an island. On the fourteenth night the sailors sense land, sound twenty fathoms then fifteen, and drop four anchors. When they try to escape in the ship's boat, Paul warns the centurion and the soldiers cut it loose. At dawn Paul urges everyone to eat, takes bread, gives thanks and eats; all two hundred and seventy-six are encouraged, and the wheat goes overboard. They run for an unknown beach, strike a shoal, and the stern breaks up. The soldiers want to kill the prisoners, but the centurion, wanting to save Paul, sends swimmers ashore first and the rest on planks.
ACT 28:1-31	The island is Malta, and the islanders build a fire in the rain and cold. A viper driven out by the heat fastens on Paul's hand; the locals conclude he is a murderer Justice will not let live, then, when he shakes it off unharmed, decide he is a god. Publius, the chief man, hosts them three days, and Paul heals his father of fever and dysentery, after which the island's sick come and are cured. Three months later they sail on to Rome, where believers meet them on the road. Under guard in his own quarters, Paul argues from Moses and the prophets all day; some believe, some do not, and he quotes Isaiah on dull ears before declaring the salvation of God sent to the nations. He stays two years, preaching without hindrance.
EXO 7:1-25	God tells Moses he will be like God to Pharaoh with Aaron as his prophet, and that he will harden Pharaoh's heart so the signs multiply. Moses is eighty and Aaron eighty-three. Aaron throws down his rod and it becomes a serpent; the Egyptian magicians duplicate it, but Aaron's rod swallows theirs. Pharaoh is unmoved. At the river the next morning Aaron strikes the Nile and all the water in Egypt turns to blood, killing the fish and fouling the river. The magicians duplicate that too. Pharaoh goes home unbothered while Egypt digs beside the river for water. Seven days pass.
EXO 8:1-32	Aaron stretches out his rod and frogs cover Egypt, into houses, beds, ovens and kneading troughs. The magicians produce frogs too. Pharaoh asks for relief and lets Moses set the time; he chooses tomorrow, and the frogs die and are piled in stinking heaps. With the pressure off, Pharaoh refuses. Aaron strikes the dust and it becomes lice on people and animals; this time the magicians fail and tell Pharaoh it is God's finger. Then swarms of flies fill Egypt but not Goshen. Pharaoh offers a sacrifice inside Egypt, then a short trip, then goes back on it once the flies are gone.
EXO 9:1-18	A pestilence is announced on Egyptian livestock in the field, with Israel's animals spared. It happens the next day; Pharaoh checks, finds not one Israelite animal dead, and still refuses. Moses then throws furnace ashes toward the sky and boils break out on people and animals across Egypt, so badly that the magicians cannot stand before him. God hardens Pharaoh's heart. Moses is sent out early the next morning with a longer message: God could have wiped Egypt out already, but has kept Pharaoh standing to display his power, and tomorrow will bring unprecedented hail.
EXO 9:19-35	Pharaoh is warned to bring livestock and workers under shelter. Some of his officials take the warning and some do not. Moses stretches out his rod and hail falls with thunder and lightning across Egypt, striking every person, animal, plant and tree left in the field, but not Goshen. Pharaoh admits he has sinned and that Yahweh is righteous. Moses leaves the city, spreads his hands, and the storm stops, though he says he knows Pharaoh still does not fear God. Flax and barley are destroyed but wheat and spelt survive, being late. Pharaoh hardens his heart again.
EXO 10:1-29	Locusts are threatened, and Pharaoh's own officials ask him how long this will go on, saying Egypt is destroyed. He offers to let the men go but not the children, and drives Moses and Aaron out. An east wind brings locusts that strip everything the hail left, leaving nothing green in Egypt. Pharaoh admits sin and asks for prayer; a west wind drives the locusts into the Red Sea. Three days of darkness follow that can be felt, while Israel has light. Pharaoh offers to release everyone but the livestock. Moses refuses, saying not a hoof will stay. Pharaoh banishes him on pain of death.
EXO 11:1-10	God tells Moses one more plague is coming, after which Pharaoh will drive Israel out entirely, and instructs the people to ask their Egyptian neighbours for silver and gold. Israel has favour in Egyptian eyes, and Moses himself is held in high regard by Pharaoh's officials. Moses announces that at about midnight every firstborn in Egypt will die, from Pharaoh's heir to the servant girl's child to the livestock, and that there will be a cry like no other, while not even a dog will bark at Israel. He leaves Pharaoh in hot anger.
EXO 12:1-22	God makes this month the first of the year and gives the Passover instructions. On the tenth each household takes a year-old male lamb without defect, sharing with a neighbour if the household is small, and kills it at evening on the fourteenth. Blood goes on the two doorposts and the lintel; the meat is roasted whole, eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, nothing left till morning, eaten dressed to travel. Seven days of unleavened bread follow, with holy assemblies on the first and seventh. Moses tells the elders to apply the blood with hyssop and stay indoors until morning.
EXO 12:23-51	Israel is told the blood will keep the destroyer out, and that the rite is to be explained to their children forever. At midnight every firstborn in Egypt dies, from Pharaoh's heir to the prisoner in the dungeon to the livestock, and there is not a house without a death. Pharaoh summons Moses in the night and orders them all out, asking to be blessed. The Egyptians push them to hurry, so the dough leaves unleavened, and Israel asks for and receives silver, gold and clothing. About six hundred thousand men plus families and a mixed multitude leave Rameses after four hundred and thirty years. Further Passover rules follow.
EXO 13:1-22	Every firstborn male, human and animal, is set apart as God's. Moses tells the people to remember this day, keep the seven days of unleavened bread when they reach Canaan, and treat it as a sign on the hand and a memorial between the eyes. A firstborn donkey is redeemed with a lamb or else has its neck broken; every firstborn son is redeemed. Children who ask are to be told the story. God avoids the short Philistine road in case war makes them turn back, and routes them by the wilderness toward the Red Sea. Moses carries Joseph's bones. A pillar of cloud leads by day and fire by night.
EXO 14:1-31	Israel is told to camp by the sea at Pihahiroth so Pharaoh will think them trapped. Pharaoh regrets releasing them and pursues with six hundred chosen chariots. Seeing the army, the people panic and tell Moses they would rather have stayed slaves. Moses tells them to stand still and watch. The pillar moves behind them and stands between the two camps all night. Moses stretches out his hand, an east wind divides the sea, and Israel crosses on dry ground with walls of water either side. The Egyptians follow, their chariot wheels come off, and the sea returns and drowns every one of them. Israel sees the bodies and believes.
EXO 15:1-27	Moses and Israel sing a victory song: God threw horse and rider into the sea, sank Pharaoh's chosen captains like stone, piled the waters up with the blast of his nostrils, and answered the enemy's boast about dividing plunder with a wind. It goes on to say the surrounding peoples, Philistia, Edom, Moab and Canaan, will hear and be terrified while Israel passes through to God's sanctuary. Miriam the prophetess leads the women with tambourines and dancing. Three days later in the wilderness of Shur they find no water, then bitter water at Marah. Moses throws in a tree and it turns sweet. They camp at Elim, twelve springs and seventy palms.
EXO 16:1-16	A month and a half out of Egypt, in the wilderness of Sin, the whole congregation complains that they should have died in Egypt where there were meat pots and bread. God tells Moses he will rain bread from the sky, a day's portion at a time, doubled on the sixth day, as a test. Moses and Aaron point out the grumbling is really against God, not them. God's glory appears in the cloud. That evening quail cover the camp, and in the morning a fine flaky substance is left when the dew lifts. The people ask what it is. Moses tells them to gather an omer each.
EXO 16:17-36	Some gather more and some less, but measured out everyone has exactly enough. Told to keep nothing overnight, some do anyway and it breeds worms and stinks. What is left on the ground melts in the sun. On the sixth day they gather double, and Moses explains the seventh is a Sabbath; that portion keeps overnight without spoiling. Some go out looking on the seventh day and find nothing, and God asks how long they will refuse to keep his commands. They call it manna, white like coriander seed, tasting of honey wafers. An omer of it is stored in a pot as a keepsake. They eat it forty years.
EXO 17:1-16	At Rephidim there is no water, and the people quarrel with Moses, who tells God they are nearly ready to stone him. God has him take the elders and the rod that struck the Nile, and strike a rock at Horeb; water comes out. He names the place Massah and Meribah, because they tested God by asking whether he was among them. Then Amalek attacks. Joshua leads the fighting while Moses watches from the hilltop with the rod raised; Israel wins while his hands are up, so Aaron and Hur sit him on a stone and hold his arms steady until sunset. Joshua wins. Moses builds an altar named Yahweh our Banner.
EXO 18:1-27	Jethro, priest of Midian, hears what God has done and brings Moses his wife Zipporah and their two sons, Gershom and Eliezer, to the camp at the mountain. Moses tells him everything, and Jethro blesses God, declares him greater than all gods, and offers sacrifices, eating with Aaron and the elders. The next day he watches Moses judge disputes alone from morning to evening and tells him plainly that this is not good and will wear him out. He advises appointing capable, God-fearing, honest men as officers over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens, to handle small cases and pass hard ones up. Moses does exactly that, and Jethro goes home.
EXO 19:1-25	Three months out of Egypt, Israel camps in the wilderness of Sinai in front of the mountain. God tells Moses to remind them he carried them on eagles' wings, and offers a covenant: obey and they will be his own possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. The people agree to everything. They are told to wash their clothes and be ready on the third day, with a boundary around the mountain and death for anyone or any animal that touches it. On the third morning there is thunder, lightning, thick cloud, a loud trumpet, fire and smoke, and the whole mountain shakes. Moses goes up and is sent straight back down to warn them again.
EXO 20:1-26	God speaks the ten commandments: no other gods, no carved images to bow to, do not misuse God's name, keep the Sabbath holy because God rested on the seventh day, honour father and mother, and no murder, adultery, theft, false testimony or coveting a neighbour's house, wife, servants or animals. The people, seeing the thunder, lightning, trumpet and smoke, stand back and beg Moses to speak instead of God, and Moses tells them the fear is meant to keep them from sinning. God then adds altar rules: earth or uncut stone, no tool marks, and no steps up to it.
EXO 21:1-36	Case law begins. A Hebrew servant serves six years and goes free in the seventh, though a wife given by the master stays behind with her children; a servant who chooses to stay has his ear bored through with an awl at the doorpost. Rules follow for a daughter sold as a servant, who must keep her food, clothing and marital rights. Death penalties cover murder, striking or cursing a parent, and kidnapping, with a place of refuge for accidental killing. Injury cases set the eye for eye, tooth for tooth standard. The chapter ends on goring bulls: a first offence stones the bull, a known gorer condemns the owner too.
EXO 22:1-31	Property law. A stolen ox is repaid fivefold and a sheep fourfold, but only double if found alive. A thief killed breaking in at night carries no bloodguilt; the same killing after sunrise does. Restitution covers grazing damage, fires spread through thorns, goods left for safekeeping, borrowed animals and disputed claims, several of which are settled by an oath before God. Seducing an unbetrothed woman requires the bride price whether or not her father allows the marriage. Then abrupt capital clauses on sorceresses, bestiality and sacrificing to other gods, followed by protections: do not wrong the foreigner, the widow or the orphan, charge no interest to the poor, and return a cloak taken as collateral before sunset.
EXO 23:1-33	Rules for justice and the calendar. No false reports, no siding with a crowd against justice, no favouritism to the poor either, no bribes, no oppressing foreigners. An enemy's stray ox is to be returned and his fallen donkey helped up. Land lies fallow every seventh year so the poor and the wild animals can eat, and the seventh day rests so servants and animals are refreshed. Three annual feasts are required: unleavened bread, harvest and ingathering. Do not boil a young goat in its mother's milk. God promises an angel to lead them in, and to drive out the inhabitants little by little rather than all at once, so the land does not go wild.
EXO 24:1-18	Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu and seventy elders are summoned up the mountain, but only Moses may come near. Moses reports all the words and ordinances and the people agree to do them. He writes them down, builds an altar with twelve pillars for the twelve tribes, and has young men offer sacrifices. Half the blood goes on the altar; he reads the book of the covenant aloud, the people agree again, and he sprinkles the rest on them. The seventy go up, see the God of Israel standing on what looks like sapphire pavement, and eat and drink unharmed. Moses and Joshua climb higher into the cloud, and Moses stays forty days and nights.
EXO 25:1-40	God asks for a freewill offering of gold, silver, brass, dyed yarns, linen, goats' hair, skins, acacia wood, oil, spices and gemstones, so that a sanctuary can be built and he can dwell among them, made exactly to the pattern shown. Specifications follow for the ark of acacia overlaid with gold inside and out, with carrying poles that are never to be removed from its rings, and a solid gold mercy seat with two hammered cherubim facing each other, where God will meet and speak with Moses. Then the gold-covered table for the bread of the presence, and a lampstand hammered from a single talent of gold, seven lamps, branches shaped like almond blossoms.
EXO 26:1-18	The tabernacle itself: ten linen curtains in blue, purple and scarlet worked with cherubim, twenty-eight cubits by four, joined in two sets of five with fifty loops and fifty gold clasps so the whole thing counts as one. Over it goes a tent of eleven goats' hair curtains, one more than the layer beneath, the extra one doubled back over the front and the surplus hanging down the back and sides. Two more coverings go on top, rams' skins dyed red and sea cow hides. Then the frame begins: upright acacia boards ten cubits tall, each with two tenons, twenty of them along the south side.
EXO 26:19-37	Forty silver sockets take the twenty south boards, two per board, and the same on the north; six boards close the west end with two more shaped for the corners, doubled from bottom to top. Five acacia bars run along each side, with a middle bar passing the whole length from end to end, everything overlaid with gold. It is to be assembled exactly as shown on the mountain. A veil of blue, purple and scarlet linen worked with cherubim hangs on four gold-covered pillars and divides the holy place from the most holy, where the ark and mercy seat go. Table to the north, lampstand to the south, and an embroidered screen on five pillars at the door.
EXO 27:1-21	The bronze altar is five cubits square and three high, with horns of one piece at the corners, all overlaid with brass, hollow-planked, with brass pots, shovels, basins, hooks and fire pans, a bronze grating halfway up, and poles through rings for carrying. The courtyard is a hundred cubits by fifty, walled with fine linen hangings five cubits high on sixty pillars in brass sockets, with silver hooks and bands, and a twenty-cubit embroidered screen for the east gate. Every peg is brass. Finally, Israel is to supply beaten olive oil so Aaron and his sons can keep a lamp burning from evening to morning, permanently.
EXO 28:1-24	Aaron and his sons Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar are appointed priests, and skilled craftsmen are to make holy garments for glory and beauty: a breastplate, ephod, robe, checkered coat, turban and sash. The ephod is woven of gold, blue, purple, scarlet and linen with two shoulder straps, and carries two onyx stones engraved like signets with the twelve tribal names, six per stone in birth order, so Aaron carries Israel on his shoulders. The breastplate of judgment is square, folded double, a span each way, set with twelve named stones in four rows, and fitted with gold rings and braided gold chains.
EXO 28:25-43	The chains and rings tie the breastplate to the ephod with a blue cord so it cannot swing loose, and Aaron carries the tribes' names over his heart. Into it go the Urim and the Thummim. The blue robe has a reinforced neck opening and a hem alternating gold bells with pomegranates, so Aaron can be heard going in and out and does not die. A gold plate engraved HOLY TO YAHWEH is tied to the front of the turban, and Aaron bears the guilt of the holy things. His sons get coats, sashes and headbands, and all of them get linen undergarments from waist to thigh, on pain of death.
EXO 29:1-23	The ordination ceremony. A young bull, two unblemished rams and a basket of unleavened bread, cakes and wafers are brought to the door of the Tent of Meeting. Aaron and his sons are washed, dressed in the garments, and Aaron is anointed with oil poured on his head. They lay hands on the bull, which is killed as a sin offering, its blood put on the altar horns and its carcass burned outside the camp. The first ram is burned whole. The second is killed and its blood put on their right ear tips, right thumbs and right big toes, then sprinkled with oil over them and their clothes.
EXO 29:24-46	The fat, thigh and bread are placed in their hands and waved before God, then burned. The breast becomes Moses' portion, and the waved breast and thigh become the priests' permanent share of Israel's peace offerings. Aaron's garments pass to his successors, worn seven days on taking office. The ram is boiled and eaten with the bread at the tent door by the priests only, and anything left by morning is burned. The whole ordination runs seven days, with a bull each day to purify the altar. After that, two year-old lambs are offered every day, morning and evening, with flour, oil and wine, forever. God says he will dwell among them.
EXO 30:1-18	A gold-covered acacia incense altar, one cubit square and two high, with horns and carrying poles, goes in front of the veil. Aaron burns fragrant incense on it every morning and evening when he tends the lamps, and nothing else may be offered on it, no strange incense, no burnt offering, no drink offering. Once a year its horns get atonement blood. Then a census rule: everyone counted, twenty and over, pays a ransom of half a shekel, rich and poor exactly the same, to prevent a plague, and the money funds the tent's service. Then a bronze basin with a bronze stand, set between the tent and the altar and filled with water.
EXO 30:19-38	Aaron and his sons must wash hands and feet at the basin before entering the tent or approaching the altar, so that they do not die. The anointing oil recipe follows: five hundred shekels of liquid myrrh, two hundred and fifty each of cinnamon and fragrant cane, five hundred of cassia, and a hin of olive oil, blended by a perfumer. It anoints the tent, the furniture, the altars, the basin and the priests. Nobody may make it or use it on an outsider. The incense is equal weights of gum resin, onycha, galbanum and pure frankincense, salted, and copying its scent for personal use also gets a person cut off.
EXO 31:1-18	God names the craftsmen: Bezalel son of Uri son of Hur, of Judah, filled with the Spirit of God in wisdom, understanding, knowledge and every kind of workmanship, in gold, silver, brass, stonecutting and wood carving, with Oholiab son of Ahisamach of Dan alongside him and skill given to every willing worker. Between them they will make the tent, the ark, the furniture, the altars, the basin, the priestly garments, the anointing oil and the incense. God then insists on the Sabbath as a perpetual sign, with death for anyone who works on it. He hands Moses the two stone tablets, written with God's finger.
EXO 32:1-16	With Moses long delayed on the mountain, the people ask Aaron to make them gods to go before them. He collects their gold earrings, casts a calf, and they declare it the god that brought them out of Egypt. Aaron builds an altar and announces a feast to Yahweh; the next day they sacrifice, eat, drink and revel. God tells Moses to go down, calls Israel a stiff-necked people, and offers to destroy them and start again from Moses. Moses argues on three grounds: they are God's own people, the Egyptians will talk, and the promise to Abraham, Isaac and Israel stands. God relents. Moses goes down with the two tablets, written on both sides by God.
EXO 32:17-35	Joshua hears the noise and takes it for war; Moses says it is singing. Seeing the calf and the dancing, he throws down the tablets and breaks them, burns the calf, grinds it to powder, scatters it on water and makes Israel drink it. Aaron blames the people and claims the calf came out of the fire by itself. Moses calls for whoever is on God's side, and the Levites answer; on his orders about three thousand are killed. The next day Moses goes back up to seek atonement, offering to be blotted out of God's book instead. God refuses that trade, sends him on with an angel, and strikes the people over the calf.
EXO 33:1-23	God tells Moses to lead the people to the promised land with an angel ahead of them, but says he will not go among them himself, since they are stiff-necked and he would destroy them. The people mourn and strip off their jewellery. Moses pitches a tent outside the camp, the Tent of Meeting, where the pillar of cloud comes down and God speaks with him face to face as a friend, while everyone watches from their tent doors and Joshua stays behind inside. Moses presses for God's presence to go with them, and wins. He then asks to see God's glory, and is told he may see God's back but not his face and live.
EXO 34:1-18	Moses cuts two new stone tablets and goes back up alone at dawn, with nobody and no livestock allowed near the mountain. God descends in the cloud and proclaims his name: merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving kindness and truth, forgiving sin yet by no means clearing the guilty, visiting iniquity to the third and fourth generation. Moses worships and asks God to go with them and take them as his inheritance. God makes a covenant promising unheard-of wonders, drives out the six nations, and forbids treaties with them: break their altars, smash their pillars, cut down their Asherah poles, since his name is Jealous.
EXO 34:19-35	The covenant terms continue: every firstborn belongs to God, a donkey's firstborn is redeemed with a lamb or its neck broken, sons are redeemed, and nobody appears before God empty-handed. Rest on the seventh day even in ploughing and harvest. Keep the feast of weeks and the feast of ingathering, and appear before God three times a year, with a promise that nobody will covet the land while they are away. No leaven with sacrificial blood, no Passover meat left till morning, firstfruits brought in, and no boiling a young goat in its mother's milk. Moses spends forty days without food or water writing the covenant. Coming down, his face shines so brightly that people are afraid, so he wears a veil except when speaking with God.
EXO 35:1-35	Moses assembles the congregation and restates the Sabbath, adding one specific ban: no fire kindled anywhere on that day. He then calls for a freewill offering of gold, silver, brass, dyed yarn, linen, goats' hair, skins, acacia, oil, spices and gemstones, and lists everything to be made, from the tabernacle down to the tent pegs and cords. Everyone whose heart moves them comes, men and women, bringing brooches, earrings, signet rings and armlets. Skilled women spin the blue, purple, scarlet and linen, and others spin goats' hair. The rulers bring the onyx and setting stones, spices and oil. Moses names Bezalel and Oholiab, noting that God has also given them the ability to teach.
EXO 36:1-38	Bezalel, Oholiab and every skilled worker take the offerings and begin, and the people keep bringing more every morning. The craftsmen come to Moses and report that there is far more than the job requires, so a proclamation goes out through the camp telling everyone to stop, and the people are restrained from giving. The work then follows the earlier instructions exactly: ten linen curtains with cherubim joined by fifty gold clasps, eleven goats' hair curtains joined by fifty brass ones, two outer coverings, acacia boards in silver sockets, gold-covered bars with a middle bar running the full length, the embroidered veil on four pillars, and the door screen on five.
EXO 37:1-29	Bezalel makes the ark of acacia overlaid with gold inside and out, with gold rings and gold-covered poles, and the mercy seat of pure gold with two cherubim of beaten work at its ends, made from one piece with it, wings spread and faces turned toward each other. He makes the gold-overlaid table with its rim, rings, poles and pure gold dishes, spoons, bowls and pitchers. The lampstand is beaten from a single talent of pure gold, base, shaft, six branches, almond-blossom cups, buds and flowers all in one piece, with seven lamps and gold snuffers. He also makes the gold incense altar with its horns and poles, and the anointing oil and pure incense.
EXO 38:1-31	The bronze altar is built five cubits square and three high, hollow, with horns, a bronze grating and carrying poles, plus its pots, shovels, basins, forks and fire pans. The basin and its base are made from the bronze mirrors of the women who served at the door of the Tent of Meeting. The courtyard is hung with linen on sixty pillars in bronze sockets with silver hooks and bands, and an embroidered screen at the gate. Then an audit, recorded under Ithamar: twenty-nine talents and seven hundred and thirty shekels of gold, a hundred talents and 1,775 shekels of silver from 603,550 men at half a shekel each, and seventy talents and 2,400 shekels of brass.
EXO 39:1-21	The priestly garments are made from the blue, purple and scarlet. Gold is beaten into thin plates and cut into wires so it can be woven in with the yarn and linen. The ephod is made with joined shoulder straps and a woven band of the same piece, and the two onyx stones are engraved like signets with the tribal names and set in gold on the straps. The breastplate is made square and doubled, a span each way, set with twelve engraved stones in four rows, then fitted with braided gold chains and four gold rings and tied to the ephod with a blue cord so it cannot come loose.
EXO 39:22-43	The blue robe is woven in one piece with a reinforced neck opening, and its hem alternates woven pomegranates with pure gold bells. Linen coats, turban, headbands, breeches and an embroidered sash are made for Aaron and his sons, and the gold plate engraved HOLY TO YAHWEH is tied to the turban with a blue cord. With that the work is finished. Everything is carried to Moses: the tent and its frame, the coverings, the veil, the ark and mercy seat, the table and bread, the lampstand and oil, both altars, the basin, the courtyard hangings, the pegs and cords, and the garments. Moses inspects it all, finds it done as commanded, and blesses them.
EXO 40:1-38	God tells Moses to raise the tabernacle on the first day of the first month, place the ark behind the veil, set out the table and light the lamps, put the incense altar in place, set the burnt offering altar and the water basin outside, hang the courtyard, anoint everything, then wash, dress and anoint Aaron and his sons for a perpetual priesthood. Moses does all of it, and the tabernacle goes up in the first month of the second year. When it is finished the cloud covers the tent and God's glory fills it so completely that Moses cannot enter. From then on Israel travels only when the cloud lifts, with fire in it by night.
EZK 1:1-28	By the river Chebar among the exiles, in the fifth year of Jehoiachin's captivity, Ezekiel sees a storm wind out of the north carrying fire and glowing metal. Inside it are four living creatures, each with four faces, human, lion, ox and eagle, four wings and calf-like feet, moving straight ahead wherever the spirit goes. Beside each is a wheel within a wheel, its rims full of eyes, and the wheels rise when the creatures rise because the spirit of the creatures is in them. Above their heads is a crystal expanse, and above that a sapphire throne with a figure like a man on it, fire and rainbow brightness around him. Ezekiel falls on his face and hears a voice.
EZK 2:1-10	The voice calls him son of man and tells him to stand; the Spirit sets him on his feet. He is sent to Israel, described as a rebellious nation of stubborn, hard-faced people, and told to say Thus says the Lord Yahweh whether they listen or not, so that they will at least know a prophet was among them. He is told not to fear their words or their looks even though he lives among briers, thorns and scorpions, and not to be rebellious himself. A hand holds out a scroll, written on both sides, and its writing is lamentations, mourning and woe.
EZK 3:1-27	Ezekiel is told to eat the scroll, and it tastes as sweet as honey. He is sent not to foreigners whose speech he could not understand, who would have listened, but to Israel, who will not, so God makes his forehead harder than flint. The Spirit lifts him, he hears the noise of the wings and wheels, and he arrives at Tel Aviv among the exiles, sitting overwhelmed for seven days. After that God appoints him watchman: if he fails to warn the wicked, their blood is on his hands; if he warns and they refuse, he is clear. Sent out to the plain, he sees the glory again, then is told to shut himself in his house, where he will be bound with ropes and made mute except when God opens his mouth.
EZK 4:1-17	Ezekiel is told to act out the siege of Jerusalem. He scratches the city on a clay tile, builds siege works against it, and sets an iron pan between himself and it as a wall. Then he lies on his left side 390 days for the guilt of Israel and on his right 40 for Judah, a day per year. His food is a rationed loaf of mixed grains baked over human dung, a sign that Israel will eat unclean bread among the nations; when he objects, God allows cow dung instead.
EZK 5:1-17	Ezekiel is told to shave his head and beard with a sword used as a razor, then weigh the hair and divide it in three. A third is burned in the city, a third struck with the sword around it, a third scattered to the wind, with a sword sent after it; a few hairs are tucked into his robe and some of those burned too. The explanation follows: this is Jerusalem, set among the nations and more rebellious than any of them. God says he is against her and will do what he has never done before, so that fathers eat sons and sons eat fathers. A third will die by plague and famine, a third by the sword, a third scattered. She will become a horror and a warning to the nations around her.
EZK 6:1-14	Ezekiel is told to face the mountains of Israel and prophesy against them, along with the hills, ravines and valleys. God will bring a sword against the high places, break the incense altars, and lay the dead in front of the idols they worshipped, scattering their bones around the altars. A remnant will survive scattered among the nations, and there they will remember God, loathing themselves for what they did. He is told to clap his hands, stamp his foot and say Alas, because Israel will fall by sword, famine and plague: the distant by plague, the near by the sword, the besieged by hunger. The bodies will lie among the idols on every high hill and under every green tree.
EZK 7:1-27	A short, hammering oracle announcing that the end has arrived on all four corners of the land. God says his eye will not spare and there will be no pity. Trade becomes pointless, since buyer should not celebrate and seller should not grieve; the trumpet sounds but nobody goes out to fight. Sword outside, plague and famine inside. Survivors moan on the mountains like doves, hands limp and knees like water. They throw their silver into the streets and treat their gold as filth, because neither can buy food or rescue. The temple ornaments they filled with idols will be handed to foreigners to plunder. They will look for a vision and find none, and priests and elders will have nothing left to say.
EZK 8:1-18	In the sixth year, with the elders of Judah sitting in front of him, Ezekiel is seized by a fiery figure who takes him by a lock of hair and carries him in vision to Jerusalem. At the north gate stands the image of jealousy. God shows him four things in escalating order: that image; a hidden room reached by digging through a wall, its walls covered with creeping things and idols, where seventy elders including Jaazaniah son of Shaphan burn incense saying Yahweh does not see us; women at the north gate weeping for Tammuz; and twenty-five men between the porch and the altar with their backs to the temple, worshipping the sun. God says he will act in wrath and will not listen even when they shout.
EZK 9:1-11	God calls the city's executioners forward. Six men arrive with weapons, and with them a seventh dressed in linen carrying a writer's inkhorn. The glory of God moves from the cherub to the threshold, and the man in linen is sent through Jerusalem to mark the foreheads of everyone who grieves over the city's abominations. The six are told to follow him and kill without pity, old and young, women and children, sparing only those with the mark, and to begin at the sanctuary. They start with the elders in front of the temple. Ezekiel falls on his face and asks whether God will destroy everyone left of Israel. God answers that the land is full of blood because they said he does not see. The man in linen reports the marking done.
EZK 10:1-22	Ezekiel sees the sapphire throne again above the cherubim. The man in linen is told to go in among the whirling wheels, take handfuls of burning coals from between the cherubim, and scatter them over the city; a cherub hands him the fire and he carries it out. The cloud fills the inner court and the brightness of the glory fills it, and the sound of the wings carries to the outer court. Ezekiel describes the wheels again, beryl coloured, wheel within wheel, covered with eyes, moving with the cherubim because the spirit is in them. He notes that each has four faces, cherub, man, lion and eagle. The glory leaves the temple threshold, settles over the cherubim, and they rise and stop at the east gate. He now recognises them as the creatures he saw at the Chebar.
EZK 11:1-25	The Spirit brings Ezekiel to the east gate, where twenty-five men, among them Jaazaniah and Pelatiah, are giving bad counsel and saying the city is the cauldron and they are the meat. Ezekiel answers that the dead they filled the streets with are the meat, and that they will be taken out of the pot and killed at the border. Pelatiah drops dead while he speaks. God promises the exiles that he is their sanctuary abroad, and will replace their heart of stone with a heart of flesh. The glory then leaves the city.
EZK 12:1-28	Ezekiel packs an exile's baggage and carries it out in daylight where everyone can see, then at evening digs through the wall with his hands and goes out with his face covered. Asked what he is doing, he explains: this is the prince in Jerusalem, who will leave through a hole in the wall, be caught in God's net, and die in a Babylon he never sees. Eating and drinking in visible fear is a second sign. Two sayings are answered: that visions never come true, and that this one is far off.
EZK 13:1-23	An oracle against prophets who prophesy out of their own imagination. They are called foxes among ruins who never went up to the gaps or repaired the wall. They say Yahweh says when he has not spoken, and they promise peace where there is none. The image is a flimsy wall someone whitewashes: God sends a downpour, hailstones and a storm wind to knock it down, and when it falls the question will be what happened to the plaster, and the plasterers will die in the collapse. Then he turns to women who prophesy, sewing magic bands for the wrists and veils for the head to trap people, working for handfuls of barley and scraps of bread, condemning the innocent and sparing the guilty. God says he will tear the bands and veils off and free those they hunted.
EZK 14:1-23	Elders of Israel come to sit before Ezekiel to consult God. God says they have taken idols into their hearts, and that anyone who comes to a prophet in that condition will be answered by God himself according to those idols, cut off as a warning; and that if the prophet gives an answer, God deceived that prophet, and prophet and inquirer bear the same guilt.
