Then a second ruling: if a land sins and God sends famine, wild animals, sword or plague, even Noah, Daniel and Job standing in it would save only themselves, not a son or daughter. Jerusalem gets all four judgments at once. Yet a remnant of sons and daughters will come out to the exiles, and seeing how they behaved will make plain that God did not act without cause.
EZK 15:1-8	A short parable about wood. Vine wood is no better than any other wood in the forest; nobody builds with it, and you cannot even carve a peg from it to hang a pot on. It is fuel, and once the fire has eaten both ends and charred the middle it is less useful than it already was, which was not at all. God says the inhabitants of Jerusalem are that piece of vine. They will come out of one fire only for another to consume them, and the land will be left desolate because of their treachery.
EZK 16:1-33	God confronts Jerusalem with her history as an allegory. Born to an Amorite father and a Hittite mother, she was abandoned in a field until God passed by and told her to live. He raised her, washed her, dressed her in fine linen, gave her gold and a crown, and her beauty became famous. She then trusted that beauty, used his gifts to make shrines and idols, and sacrificed the children she had borne him. She took Egypt, Assyria and Chaldea as lovers, and unlike other prostitutes she paid them rather than being paid.
EZK 16:34-63	The sentence follows the crime. God will gather every lover she took, and everyone she hated, and expose her to them, judge her as an adulteress and a murderer, let them tear down her shrines, strip her jewelry and clothing, stone her and burn her houses, after which his anger will finally be spent. He quotes a proverb against her: like mother, like daughter. Her older sister is Samaria and her younger sister is Sodom, whose sin is named as pride, plenty of food, comfortable ease and no help for the poor; Jerusalem has outdone both and so made them look righteous. Yet the oracle ends with restoration: God will bring back Sodom, Samaria and Jerusalem alike, remember the covenant of her youth, establish an everlasting one, and forgive her so completely that she is left silent with shame.
EZK 17:1-24	Ezekiel poses a riddle. A great eagle snaps the top shoot off a cedar in Lebanon and plants it in a city of merchants, then sows seed that grows into a low spreading vine turned toward him. When a second eagle appears, the vine bends its roots that way instead, and is told it will wither when the east wind hits. The meaning is plain: Babylon installed a royal relative under oath, who broke it by sending to Egypt for horses. God will then plant his own shoot on a high mountain in Israel.
EZK 18:1-32	God bans the proverb about fathers eating sour grapes and children's teeth being set on edge. Every soul belongs to him, and the soul that sins is the one who dies. He works it through three generations: a just man lives, his son who does the opposite dies, and that son's son, refusing to copy his father, lives. To the objection that this is unfair, he answers that a wicked man who turns will live and a righteous man's record will not save him. Make a new heart, he says: turn and live.
EZK 19:1-14	A funeral song for the princes of Israel, in two images. First a lioness raises a cub who learns to devour men, until the nations trap him and drag him with hooks to Egypt; she raises a second, who is netted, caged and taken to Babylon. Then a vine planted by water, fruitful enough for rulers' scepters, torn up in fury, dried by the east wind and replanted in a wilderness. Fire came out of its own branches, and no branch is left for a scepter. The text says twice that this is a lament.
EZK 20:1-26	In the seventh year the elders come to inquire, and God refuses to be inquired of. Instead he has Ezekiel recite their history. In Egypt he swore to bring them to a land flowing with milk and honey and told them to throw away their idols; they refused, and he acted for the sake of his own name rather than destroying them. In the wilderness he gave statutes and Sabbaths; they rebelled and profaned them, and he swore they would not enter the land, but spared them again. He told their children not to copy their fathers; the children rebelled too, and he swore to scatter them among the nations. He says he also gave them statutes that were not good and let their own offerings defile them, including making their firstborn pass through the fire.
EZK 20:27-49	The history continues into the land, where they found every high hill and leafy tree to sacrifice on, which is where the name Bamah comes from. God asks whether they are polluting themselves the same way, and again refuses to be consulted. Their plan of becoming like the nations will not happen: he will gather them from the countries, judge them face to face, and purge out the rebels. Afterwards they will serve him and loathe themselves. Told to prophesy against the forest of the south, Ezekiel complains that people call him a parable-teller.
EZK 21:1-18	Ezekiel faces Jerusalem and the sanctuaries and announces that God is drawing his sword against righteous and wicked alike, and it will not go back. He is to groan aloud with a broken heart, and when asked why, to say it is the news coming: every heart melting, every knee weak as water. Then the sword song itself, a blade sharpened for slaughter and polished to flash like lightning, handed to a killer. He beats his thigh and claps his hands while the sword doubles again. Then God's wrath will rest.
EZK 21:19-32	Ezekiel marks out two roads for the king of Babylon's sword, with a signpost at the fork: one to Rabbah of the Ammonites, one to Jerusalem. At the junction the king takes omens, shaking arrows and inspecting a liver, and the lot says Jerusalem. Those who swore oaths will call the divination false, but their own guilt delivers them. The prince of Israel is told to take off his turban and crown, since the low goes up and the high comes down until the one comes whose right it is.
EZK 22:1-31	Three oracles against Jerusalem, called the bloody city. The first is a charge sheet: princes shedding blood, contempt for parents, oppression of foreigners and widows, profaned Sabbaths and extortion. The second is a smelting image, in which Israel has become the dross left over from silver, gathered into the city as into a furnace until it melts. The third names each class in turn: prophets conspiring like a lion, priests who erased the line between holy and common, princes like wolves. God looked for one man to stand in the gap and found nobody.
EZK 23:1-25	An allegory of two sisters, daughters of one mother, who both prostituted themselves in Egypt in their youth. Oholah is Samaria and Oholibah is Jerusalem. Oholah pursued the Assyrians, their governors and cavalry in blue, and defiled herself with their idols, so God handed her over to those same lovers, who killed her and took her children. Her sister watched and did worse. She chased the Assyrians too, then saw Babylonians drawn in red on a wall, sashes and turbans, and sent messengers to Chaldea for them; they came, and she turned against them in disgust, then went back to remembering Egypt. God says he will bring all those lovers against her, Babylonians, Chaldeans, Pekod, Shoa, Koa and Assyrians, with chariots and shields, and let them judge her: her nose and ears cut off, her children taken, the rest burned.
EZK 23:26-49	The judgment continues. She is stripped of clothes and jewels, handed to the people she hates, left bare, her Egyptian obsession finally ended. She is given her sister's cup to drink, deep and wide and full, a cup of drunkenness, grief, horror and desolation, drained to the point of gnawing its broken pieces. God asks Ezekiel to judge both sisters and lists the charges: adultery with idols, blood on their hands, sons passed through the fire, and then entering the sanctuary the same day to defile it. He describes them sending for men from far away, washing, painting their eyes and sitting on a couch with his own incense and oil set out on the table. A mob will stone them, cut them down, kill their children and burn their houses, so that no one imitates them again.
EZK 24:1-27	On the day Babylon reaches Jerusalem, Ezekiel records the date and tells a parable: set the pot on the fire, load in the choice cuts and boil it hard. Then the pot itself is the problem, corroded beyond cleaning, so it is set on the coals until the metal glows. Ezekiel's wife, the desire of his eyes, dies that evening, and he is forbidden to mourn her. Asked why, he explains that God will profane the sanctuary they love, and they too will not mourn. When a fugitive brings the news, he will speak again.
EZK 25:1-17	Four short oracles against neighbours who enjoyed Judah's fall. Ammon said Aha over the profaned sanctuary, the ruined land and the exile, so it will be handed to the people of the east, who will camp there and eat its fruit; Rabbah becomes a camel stable and the country a sheep pasture. Ammon also clapped and stamped in contempt, so it will be plundered and wiped out. Moab and Seir said Judah is just like every other nation, so Moab's frontier cities, Beth Jeshimoth, Baal Meon and Kiriathaim, are opened to the same easterners. Edom took revenge on Judah, so it will be made desolate from Teman to Dedan, with Israel carrying out the vengeance. The Philistines acted out of long standing spite, so the Cherethites and the rest of the coast will be cut off.
EZK 26:1-21	Tyre celebrated Jerusalem's fall as good for business, so God brings nations against her like the sea bringing up waves. Walls and towers come down, the dust is scraped off, and the island is left as bare rock where fishermen spread their nets. Nebuchadnezzar is named: siege mounds, battering rams, hooves in the streets, and her stones and timber dumped in the water. The songs and the harps stop. The princes of the sea come off their thrones, sit trembling on the ground, and sing a lament. Tyre goes down to the pit.
EZK 27:1-36	A lament for Tyre, built as a shipwreck. The city is described as a ship: cypress planks from Senir, a cedar mast, oars of Bashan oak, an embroidered Egyptian sail, rowers from Sidon and caulkers from Gebal. Then the trade register, running from Tarshish with silver and tin through Judah's wheat and honey to the spices and gold of Sheba. Then the east wind breaks her in the heart of the seas, cargo and crew go down together, and the sailors on shore throw dust on their heads and ask who was ever like Tyre.
EZK 28:1-26	Two oracles about Tyre's ruler and one about Sidon. The prince of Tyre said I am a god and grew rich by real commercial skill; God answers that he is a man, and asks whether he will still say it in front of the man killing him. The second is a lament for the king of Tyre, in Eden covered in precious stones, the guardian cherub walking among the stones of fire, blameless until violence came in through his trade. He is burned to ash before watching kings. Sidon gets plague.
EZK 29:1-21	An oracle against Pharaoh, pictured as the great crocodile lying in his own river saying the Nile is mine and I made it. God will put hooks in his jaws, drag him out with the fish stuck to his scales, and leave him in the field for animals and birds. The charge is that Egypt was a reed staff that splintered when Israel leaned on it. Egypt will lie uninhabited forty years, then return as the lowest of kingdoms. Since Nebuchadnezzar got no pay for besieging Tyre, God gives him Egypt as wages.
EZK 30:1-26	A wail for the day of Yahweh over Egypt: clouds, a sword, and anguish in Ethiopia. Egypt's allies fall with her, and Nebuchadnezzar is named as the instrument. God will dry the rivers, destroy the idols of Memphis and leave Egypt without a prince. A list of cities follows, from fire in Zoan to daylight withdrawing at Tehaphnehes. A separate dated oracle says one of Pharaoh's arms is already broken and unhealed, and God will break both so the sword drops from his hand, while strengthening the arms of the king of Babylon.
EZK 31:1-18	Pharaoh is asked who he resembles, and is given Assyria as the answer: a cedar taller than every tree in Lebanon, watered by the deep, sheltering every bird and nation under its shade, so beautiful the trees of Eden envied it. Because its heart grew proud of its height, God handed it to the mightiest of the nations, who cut it down, and everyone living in its shade left. The lesson is spelled out: no well watered tree should exalt itself, since all go down to the pit. Pharaoh lies in the same place.
EZK 32:1-18	A lament over Pharaoh, who thought himself a young lion but is really a sea monster thrashing in the rivers and fouling the water with his feet. God will throw a net over him, haul him onto dry land, and leave his flesh on the mountains and the valleys filled with him. When he is put out, the sky goes dark, stars, sun and moon all covered. The sword of the king of Babylon comes, Egypt's pride is ended, and afterwards the rivers run clear like oil.
EZK 32:19-32	A tour of Sheol, where the nations who terrified the living lie in ranks. Egypt is told to go down and lie with the uncircumcised. Assyria is there, graves in the far corners of the pit, everyone slain by the sword. Elam is there, bearing its shame, a bed made among the slain. Meshech and Tubal are there with their crowds around them, and there is a note about warriors buried with their weapons and their swords under their heads. Edom with its kings and princes is there, along with all the princes of the north and the Sidonians, ashamed of the terror they once caused. Pharaoh will look at them and be comforted by the company. The chapter ends by naming him among the slain with all his multitude.
EZK 33:1-16	The watchman image is set out as a rule. When a country appoints a watchman and he blows the trumpet at the sight of the sword, anyone who hears and ignores it is responsible for his own death; if the watchman sees the sword and does not blow, the victim still dies but his blood is charged to the watchman. God applies this to Ezekiel directly. Then he answers the people's complaint that their sins are wasting them away and they cannot live: he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked and tells them to turn. The principle from chapter 18 is restated. Past righteousness does not cover a man who turns to wrong, and past wickedness is not counted against a man who turns back, restores what he took by robbery and returns the pledge.
EZK 33:17-33	The people again say the Lord's way is not fair, and God repeats that each is judged by his own conduct. Then a man escaped from Jerusalem arrives with the news that the city has fallen, and Ezekiel's muteness ends. Those living in the ruins argue that if Abraham inherited the land alone, they are many and it must be theirs; the sword, the animals and the plague are shared out among them instead. Finally God says people invite each other to hear Ezekiel as though he were a singer: they listen and do nothing.
EZK 34:1-15	An oracle against the shepherds of Israel, who feed themselves instead of the flock. They eat the fat, wear the wool and slaughter the fattened animals, but have not healed the sick, bandaged the injured or looked for the lost, ruling by force instead. With no shepherd the sheep scattered and became food for wild animals. God is against the shepherds and will take the flock out of their mouths, then do the job himself: search for his sheep, gather them from the countries, and feed them on good pasture on the mountains of Israel.
EZK 34:16-31	God will seek the lost, bandage the broken and strengthen the sick, but destroy the fat and the strong, feeding the flock with justice. He then turns on the sheep themselves: some eat the good grass and trample the rest, foul the water with their feet, and shove the weak aside with shoulder and horns. He will save the flock from them and set one shepherd over them, his servant David. He promises a covenant of peace, rain in season, and no more famine.
EZK 35:1-15	An oracle against Mount Seir, that is Edom. Its cities will be laid waste and its hills, valleys and watercourses filled with the slain, with travellers cut off entirely. The reasons are given: an unending hostility, and handing Israel over to the sword at the time of their disaster. Since Edom did not hate bloodshed, blood will pursue it. Edom also said that both nations and both countries would become its own, ignoring that Yahweh was there. God says he heard every insult spoken against the mountains of Israel, including the claim that the desolate land was theirs to swallow. When the whole earth is rejoicing, Edom will be made desolate, the same way it rejoiced over Israel's ruin.
LAM 1:1-22	The city that was once full of people sits alone like a widow, a princess reduced to forced labor. Her roads mourn because nobody comes to the festivals, her priests groan, her children have gone into captivity. None of her former lovers comfort her; her friends have turned enemy. Jerusalem herself speaks: she admits she rebelled, describes fire sent into her bones and a net spread for her feet, and reports that her priests and elders died in the streets searching for food. She asks passers-by whether any sorrow is like hers, and asks God to deal with her enemies as he has dealt with her.
LAM 2:1-22	The poem catalogues what the Lord himself has done to Zion. He bent his bow like an enemy, tore down her strongholds, wrecked his own tabernacle and made festival and Sabbath forgotten. Her king and princes are among the nations, her prophets get no vision, her elders sit on the ground in sackcloth and silence. The poet's eyes fail with weeping as infants faint in the streets and ask their mothers for bread that is not there. Passers-by hiss at the city once called the perfection of beauty. The chapter closes with the worst of it: women eating their own children, priests and prophets killed in the sanctuary, nobody left alive who escaped.
LAM 3:1-66	A single man speaks: he has been walked into darkness, walled in, set up as a target for arrows, fed bitterness and gravel. He says his hope in God has perished, then turns and says the one thing he can recall, that God's mercies are new every morning and his faithfulness is great. He argues that it is good to wait quietly, that God does not afflict from the heart, and that a living man has little standing to complain. He calls the people to examine their ways and return, admits the nation's rebellion, then returns to weeping. He recalls being thrown into a pit with a stone over him, calling out from the lowest dungeon, and hearing the answer, Don't be afraid. He ends asking God to judge his enemies and repay them.
LAM 4:1-22	Gold has gone dull and the sanctuary stones lie scattered at every street corner. The sons of Zion, once worth their weight in gold, are treated as clay pots. Nursing children go thirsty and no one gives the young ones bread; those raised in purple now sit on ash heaps. The poet says the starving are worse off than those killed by the sword, and reports that women have boiled their own children. He blames the prophets and priests who shed innocent blood, now driven from the streets as unclean. Judah watched in vain for a nation that could not save, and the anointed king was caught in the enemy's pit. The poem ends turning to Edom: your turn with the cup is coming.
LAM 5:1-22	A closing prayer that simply lists the conditions. The inheritance belongs to strangers, they buy their own water and firewood, they are orphans and their mothers are widows. They beg bread from Egypt and Assyria, bear the sins of fathers who are gone, and get food at the risk of their lives. Women are raped, princes hanged, elders dishonored, boys carrying millstones. The music has stopped and dancing has turned to mourning; foxes walk on the deserted mountain of Zion. They confess they sinned, affirm that God's throne endures forever, and ask why he has forgotten them. The book ends unresolved, with the fear that he has rejected them entirely.
NUM 1:1-30	A year and a fortnight after leaving Egypt, in the Tent of Meeting at Sinai, God orders a census of every male aged twenty and over who can fight, counted by family and ancestral house. One chief per tribe assists: Elizur, Shelumiel, Nahshon, Nethanel, Eliab, Elishama, Gamaliel, Abidan, Ahiezer, Pagiel, Eliasaph and Ahira. The whole congregation assembles on the first day of the second month and registers their ancestry one by one. The tallies begin: Reuben 46,500, Simeon 59,300, Gad 45,650, Judah 74,600, Issachar 54,400, and Zebulun is reached.
NUM 1:31-54	The remaining tallies: Zebulun 57,400, Ephraim 40,500, Manasseh 32,200, Benjamin 35,400, Dan 62,700, Asher 41,500, Naphtali 53,400. The total counted by Moses, Aaron and the twelve tribal heads is 603,550. The Levites are deliberately left out. Instead of being counted with the rest, they are put in charge of the Tabernacle of the Testimony and everything belonging to it: they carry it, take it down, set it up and camp around it, and any outsider who comes near is to be put to death. The other tribes camp under their own standards, and the Levite ring around the tent is there to keep wrath off the congregation.
NUM 2:1-34	The camp is laid out as a square around the Tent of Meeting, each tribe under its own banner. East is Judah with Issachar and Zebulun, 186,400 in all, and they march first. South is Reuben with Simeon and Gad, 151,450, marching second. The Tent of Meeting and the Levites travel in the middle. West is Ephraim with Manasseh and Benjamin, 108,100, marching third. North is Dan with Asher and Naphtali, 157,600, marching last. The total is again 603,550 with the Levites excluded, and Israel camps and moves exactly in that order.
NUM 3:1-27	Aaron's sons were Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar; Nadab and Abihu died before God for offering strange fire and left no children, so Eleazar and Ithamar serve. The Levites are given to Aaron and his sons as assistants for the tent and its furnishings, with death for any outsider who approaches. God claims the Levites in place of every Israelite firstborn, since all firstborn became his the day he struck Egypt. Levite males are counted from one month old, by the three clans of Gershon, Kohath and Merari. Gershon numbers 7,500, camps west, and handles the tabernacle coverings, screens, court hangings and cords.
NUM 3:28-51	Kohath numbers 8,600, camps south under Elizaphan, and carries the ark, table, lampstand, altars, sanctuary vessels and screen, with Eleazar as chief of the Levite chiefs. Merari numbers 6,200, camps north under Zuriel, and takes the boards, bars, pillars, sockets, pegs and cords. Moses, Aaron and his sons camp on the east side, and any outsider approaching dies. The Levite total is 22,000. God has Moses count Israel's firstborn males from one month old, and they come to 22,273. The Levites substitute one for one, leaving 273 extra, who are redeemed at five shekels each. Moses collects 1,365 shekels and gives it to Aaron and his sons.
2KI 17:1-20	Hoshea, the last king of Israel, reigns nine years and does evil, though less than those before him. He becomes Assyria's vassal, then sends messengers to So of Egypt and stops paying tribute. Shalmaneser imprisons him, overruns the land, besieges Samaria three years and takes it, deporting Israel to Halah, the Habor river of Gozan and the cities of the Medes. The narrator then explains why: Israel feared other gods, built high places in every town, set up pillars and Asherah poles on every hill and under every green tree, served idols, and would not listen to the prophets sent to both kingdoms. They made two calves and an Asherah, worshipped the host of heaven, served Baal, passed their children through the fire and used divination. So God removed them, leaving Judah alone, and Judah too kept Israel's practices.
2KI 17:21-41	The account continues: Israel was torn from David's house, made Jeroboam king, followed his sin without turning from it, and was finally carried to Assyria. The king of Assyria resettles Samaria's cities with people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath and Sepharvaim. Not fearing Yahweh, they are attacked by lions, and Assyria sends back one of the deported priests, who settles at Bethel and teaches them how to fear Yahweh. Each nation nevertheless makes its own gods and installs them in the high places: Succoth Benoth, Nergal, Ashima, Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burn their children to Adrammelech and Anammelech. They appoint their own priests and both fear Yahweh and serve their images. The chapter restates the covenant command against fearing other gods, and reports that they did not listen, and their descendants do the same.
2KI 18:1-20	Hezekiah becomes king of Judah at twenty-five and reigns twenty-nine years. He does right as David did, removes the high places, breaks the pillars and the Asherah, and destroys the bronze serpent Moses made, which was being burned incense to, calling it Nehushtan. No king of Judah before or after is like him. He rebels against Assyria and strikes the Philistines as far as Gaza. Samaria falls in his sixth year and Israel is deported. In his fourteenth year Sennacherib takes the fortified cities of Judah, and Hezekiah submits at Lachish and pays three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold, stripping the temple doors of their gold. Assyria then sends three officers with a large army to Jerusalem, and Rabshakeh, meeting Hezekiah's officials by the upper pool, asks what his confidence rests on.
2KI 18:21-37	Rabshakeh continues: Egypt is a broken reed that pierces the hand that leans on it, and if Judah claims to trust Yahweh, it was Hezekiah who removed his high places and altars. He offers two thousand horses if Judah can find riders, and claims Yahweh himself sent him against the city. The officials ask him to speak Aramaic rather than Hebrew, since the men on the wall can hear; he answers that his message is for those men, who face eating and drinking their own filth in a siege. He then shouts in Hebrew that Hezekiah cannot save them, offers terms of surrender and resettlement in a land like their own, and asks which nation's gods ever delivered it from Assyria. The people keep silent as ordered, and the officials return to Hezekiah with torn clothes.
2KI 19:1-20	Hezekiah tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and goes into the temple, sending Eliakim, Shebna and the senior priests to Isaiah with the message that this is a day of trouble, like children come to birth with no strength to deliver them, and a request for prayer for the remnant. Isaiah answers not to fear the blasphemy, since God will put a spirit in Sennacherib so that he hears news, returns home and falls by the sword there. Rabshakeh finds his king fighting Libnah. Hearing that Tirhakah of Ethiopia has marched out, Sennacherib sends a letter repeating that no nation's gods have saved it. Hezekiah takes the letter into the temple, spreads it before Yahweh, and prays that God save them so all kingdoms may know he alone is God. Isaiah sends word that the prayer is heard.
2KI 19:21-37	Isaiah delivers the oracle against Sennacherib. The daughter of Zion shakes her head at him; he has defied the Holy One of Israel, boasting of chariots on Lebanon's heights, of felling its cedars and drying up Egypt's rivers. But God planned it long ago, which is why fortified cities fell and their people were like grass on a housetop. For his raging, God will put a hook in his nose and a bridle in his lips and turn him back the way he came. The sign to Judah is two years of volunteer growth, then sowing again, and a remnant taking root. Assyria will not shoot an arrow at the city. That night the angel of Yahweh strikes a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp. Sennacherib goes home to Nineveh, where his sons kill him at worship.
2KI 20:1-21	Hezekiah falls mortally ill and Isaiah tells him to set his house in order. He turns to the wall, prays that his faithfulness be remembered, and weeps bitterly. Before Isaiah has crossed the city, God sends him back: the prayer is heard, Hezekiah will go up to the temple on the third day, fifteen years are added, and the city will be defended. A cake of figs is laid on the boil and he recovers. Asked for a sign, Hezekiah chooses the harder option, and the shadow goes back ten steps on the sundial of Ahaz. Berodach Baladan of Babylon sends letters and a gift, and Hezekiah shows the envoys everything he owns. Isaiah says it will all go to Babylon, with sons of his as eunuchs there. Hezekiah calls the word good, since peace will last his days.
2KI 21:1-26	Manasseh becomes king at twelve and reigns fifty-five years, longer than anyone. He rebuilds the high places his father destroyed, raises altars to Baal, makes an Asherah as Ahab did, worships the host of heaven, and builds altars to it in both courts of the temple, setting the carved Asherah inside the house God had named for himself. He passes his son through the fire, practises sorcery and consults mediums, and leads Judah into worse evil than the nations displaced before them. The prophets announce a disaster that will make ears tingle: Jerusalem measured by the line of Samaria and wiped like a dish turned upside down. He also fills Jerusalem with innocent blood. His son Amon reigns two years the same way and is killed by his servants; the people execute the conspirators and make Josiah king.
2KI 22:1-20	Josiah becomes king at eight and reigns thirty-one years, doing right and turning neither right nor left. In his eighteenth year he sends Shaphan the scribe to have Hilkiah the high priest count the money collected at the threshold and pay the workmen repairing the temple, with no accounting demanded, since they deal honestly. Hilkiah tells Shaphan he has found the book of the law in the temple. Shaphan reads it, reports the repairs to the king, then reads the book to him, and Josiah tears his clothes. He sends five men to inquire of Yahweh. They go to Huldah the prophetess, who says the disaster written in the book will come on this place, but that because Josiah's heart was tender and he wept, he will be gathered to his grave in peace and will not see it.
2KI 23:1-16	Josiah gathers the elders and all the people to the temple and reads the book of the covenant aloud, then stands by the pillar and makes a covenant to keep it, and the people join. He has the vessels made for Baal, the Asherah and the host of heaven burned in the fields of Kidron and their ashes carried to Bethel, removes the idolatrous priests, burns the Asherah from the temple and scatters its dust on common graves, and pulls down the shrine prostitutes' quarters. He defiles the high places from Geba to Beersheba and Topheth in the valley of Hinnom, removes the horses dedicated to the sun and burns the sun chariots, destroys the altars of Ahaz and Manasseh, and defiles Solomon's high places. At Bethel he breaks Jeroboam's altar and burns bones from the tombs on it.
2KI 23:17-37	Seeing a monument, Josiah is told it marks the man of God who foretold what he has just done, and orders his bones left undisturbed. He removes the high place shrines throughout Samaria, kills their priests on their altars, and returns to Jerusalem. He orders a Passover kept as the book requires, and none like it had been kept since the days of the judges. He clears out mediums, wizards, teraphim and idols, and no king before or after turned to Yahweh as he did. Even so, God does not turn from his anger over Manasseh, and says Judah will be removed as Israel was. Pharaoh Necoh kills Josiah at Megiddo. Jehoahaz reigns three months before Necoh jails him at Riblah, imposes tribute, and makes his brother Eliakim king as Jehoiakim, who taxes the land to pay it.
2KI 24:1-20	Nebuchadnezzar comes up and Jehoiakim serves him three years, then rebels. Raiding bands of Chaldeans, Syrians, Moabites and Ammonites are sent against Judah, and the narrator says this came at Yahweh's command because of Manasseh's sins and the innocent blood he shed. Jehoiakim dies and Jehoiachin succeeds him at eighteen, reigning three months. Babylon besieges Jerusalem, Jehoiachin surrenders with his mother, servants, princes and officers, and is taken. Nebuchadnezzar carries off the treasures of the temple and palace and cuts up the gold vessels Solomon made. He deports ten thousand, including the princes, the fighting men, the craftsmen and the smiths, leaving only the poorest. Jehoiachin, his mother, his wives and the leading men go to Babylon. Mattaniah, his uncle, is made king and renamed Zedekiah; he reigns eleven years, does evil, and rebels against Babylon.
2KI 25:1-16	In Zedekiah's ninth year Nebuchadnezzar's army encamps against Jerusalem and builds siege works. The siege runs into the eleventh year, and by the fourth month the famine is severe and there is no bread. The wall is breached, the soldiers flee by night through the gate between the two walls, and the king heads for the Arabah. The Chaldeans overtake him near Jericho, his army scatters, and he is sentenced at Riblah: his sons are killed in front of him, his eyes put out, and he is taken to Babylon in chains. A month later Nebuzaradan burns the temple, the palace and every great house, and the army pulls down the walls. The rest of the people are deported, the poorest left to work the fields, and the temple's bronze and gold carried off.
2KI 25:17-30	The two pillars are described, eighteen cubits high with bronze capitals of three cubits worked with network and pomegranates. Nebuzaradan takes Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, three keepers of the threshold, an officer over the soldiers, five of the king's counsellors, the scribe who mustered the people and sixty men of the land, and brings them to Riblah, where the king of Babylon has them put to death. Gedaliah is made governor over those left, and tells the captains who come to Mizpah to settle down and serve Babylon. In the seventh month Ishmael of the royal line kills him with the Jews and Chaldeans there, and the people flee to Egypt. In the thirty-seventh year of his captivity Jehoiachin is released by Evilmerodach, given a seat above the other kings and a daily allowance for life.
DAN 1:1-21	Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem, takes Jehoiakim and some temple vessels to Shinar, and orders that promising young Israelite nobles be trained three years in Chaldean language and learning. Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah are renamed Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. Daniel refuses the king's food and wine and proposes a ten day test on vegetables and water. They come out healthier than the rest, so the diet stands. God gives all four learning and gives Daniel understanding of visions. At their examination the king finds them ten times better than his magicians.
DAN 2:1-26	Nebuchadnezzar has a dream that takes his sleep away and demands that his magicians tell him both the dream and its meaning. They protest that no king has ever asked such a thing and that only the gods could do it. Enraged, he orders every wise man in Babylon killed. Daniel asks Arioch, the captain sent to carry it out, why the decree is so urgent, then requests time from the king. He and his three friends pray, the secret is revealed to him at night, and he blesses God for removing and setting up kings. Arioch hurries him in to the king.
DAN 2:27-49	Daniel says no wise man can reveal the secret, but a God in heaven does. The dream was a huge statue: head of gold, chest and arms of silver, belly and thighs of bronze, legs of iron, feet of iron mixed with clay. A stone cut without hands smashed the feet, the whole image blew away like chaff, and the stone became a mountain filling the earth. Nebuchadnezzar is the head of gold, followed by three kingdoms, the last divided and part strong, part brittle. God will set up a kingdom that lasts forever. The king honours Daniel and makes him ruler of Babylon.
DAN 3:1-15	Nebuchadnezzar erects a gold image sixty cubits high on the plain of Dura and summons every official in the empire to its dedication. At the sound of horn, flute, zither, lyre, harp and pipe, everyone must fall down and worship it or be thrown into a burning furnace at once. The crowd complies. Some Chaldeans then accuse the Jews the king appointed over the province, naming Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. Brought in, they are offered one more chance when the music plays, and asked what god could rescue them from his hand.
DAN 3:16-30	The three answer that they need no defence: their God can rescue them, and even if he does not, they will not worship the image. Nebuchadnezzar has the furnace heated seven times hotter and has them thrown in fully clothed; the flames kill the soldiers carrying them. Then he sees four men walking loose in the fire, the fourth like a son of the gods. He calls them out, and the officials see no burn, no singed hair, not even the smell of smoke. He decrees protection for their God and promotes all three.
DAN 4:1-20	Nebuchadnezzar writes an open letter to all peoples describing what God did to him. Comfortable in his palace, he dreamed of an enormous tree reaching the sky, feeding everyone, sheltering animals and birds. A watcher came down from heaven and ordered it cut down, its branches stripped and its fruit scattered, but the stump left bound with iron and bronze in the grass, wet with dew, its mind changed to an animal's for seven times. His magicians could not interpret it, so he called Daniel, who stood silent and troubled before beginning.
DAN 4:21-37	Daniel says the tree is the king, and the sentence is that he will be driven out to live with animals, eating grass and soaked with dew for seven times until he learns that the Most High rules. The stump means his kingdom will be kept for him. Daniel advises him to break off his sins and show mercy to the poor. Twelve months later, admiring the Babylon he built, the king hears a voice from heaven and it happens the same hour. His hair grows like eagle feathers and his nails like claws. When he finally looks up, his reason returns and he praises God, who can humble the proud.
DAN 5:1-14	Belshazzar throws a feast for a thousand nobles and calls for the gold and silver vessels Nebuchadnezzar took from the temple, so that he, his lords, his wives and his concubines can drink from them while praising gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood and stone. A human hand appears and writes on the plaster wall by the lampstand. The king goes pale, his knees knock, and he offers purple, a gold chain and third place in the kingdom to anyone who can read it. No one can. The queen comes in and recommends Daniel, who is brought before the king.
DAN 5:15-31	Daniel tells the king to keep his gifts, then reminds him what happened to Nebuchadnezzar, who was brought down and driven out among wild donkeys until he learned who rules. Belshazzar knew all this and still exalted himself, drinking from the temple vessels and praising gods that cannot see or hear. The writing reads MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN: God has counted the kingdom and ended it, the king has been weighed and found wanting, and the kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians. He is robed in purple anyway. That night Belshazzar is killed and Darius the Mede takes the kingdom.
DAN 6:1-28	Darius appoints 120 satraps under three presidents, one of them Daniel, and plans to promote him over the whole realm. Unable to find any fault in his work, the officials trick the king into signing an unalterable decree that for thirty days petitions may be made only to him, on pain of the lion pit. Daniel keeps praying three times a day at his open window toward Jerusalem. The king, distressed, works until sunset to save him but cannot change the law, and Daniel is thrown in and the stone sealed. In the morning Daniel reports that an angel shut the lions' mouths. The accusers are thrown in with their families, and Darius decrees reverence for Daniel's God.
DAN 7:1-13	In Belshazzar's first year Daniel dreams of four winds stirring the great sea and four beasts coming up out of it: a lion with eagle's wings whose wings are plucked so it stands like a man, a lopsided bear with three ribs in its teeth told to eat much flesh, a four headed leopard with four wings, and a fourth beast with iron teeth and ten horns that crushes everything. A small horn comes up among them with human eyes and a boastful mouth, uprooting three. Then thrones are set, the Ancient of Days sits in white with hair like wool on a throne of fire, the books are opened, and the beast is burned. One like a son of man comes with the clouds.
DAN 7:14-28	The one like a son of man is given everlasting dominion over all peoples. Daniel, troubled, asks a bystander what it means and is told the four beasts are four kings, and that the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom forever. He asks specifically about the fourth beast and the boastful horn, which he has seen making war on the saints and winning until the Ancient of Days gives judgment to them. The answer is that ten kings arise from that kingdom, then another who subdues three, speaks against the Most High and wears out the saints for a time, times and half a time, until his dominion is taken away. Daniel keeps it to himself.
DAN 8:1-27	By the river Ulai at Susa, Daniel sees a two horned ram, the second horn taller and later, charging west, north and south unopposed. A male goat with one horn between its eyes comes from the west without touching the ground, smashes the ram's horns and tramples it. At its strongest the great horn breaks and four grow in its place, and out of one comes a little horn that grows toward the glorious land, throws down some of the stars, stops the daily offering and casts truth to the ground. A holy one asks how long, and the answer is 2,300 evenings and mornings. Gabriel explains that the ram is Media and Persia and the goat is Greece. Daniel is left sick for days.
DAN 9:1-15	In the first year of Darius, Daniel reads in Jeremiah that the desolation of Jerusalem is to last seventy years, and turns to God in prayer with fasting, sackcloth and ashes. He confesses on behalf of the whole nation: they have sinned, done wrong, rebelled and refused to listen to the prophets sent to their kings and fathers. Righteousness belongs to God and shame to them, wherever they have been scattered. The curse written in the law of Moses has been poured out, and even then they did not seek God's favour.
DAN 9:16-27	Daniel asks God to turn his anger from Jerusalem, to look at the desolate sanctuary, and to act not because they deserve it but for the sake of his own mercy and name. While he is still praying, Gabriel arrives in swift flight at the time of the evening offering, saying the order went out the moment Daniel began. He announces seventy weeks decreed to end sin and bring everlasting righteousness: seven weeks and sixty-two from the word to rebuild Jerusalem, after which the Anointed One is cut off, and a coming prince's people destroy the city and sanctuary, with sacrifice stopped in the middle of a final week.
EZK 36:1-18	Ezekiel prophesies to the mountains of Israel, which the surrounding nations have claimed for themselves, saying the ancient high places are ours. God speaks in jealousy against them and against Edom, and swears they will bear their own shame. Then he addresses the land directly: the mountains will bear fruit for an Israel about to come home, the ground will be ploughed, and the ruined cities will do better than at first. The land will no longer be called a devourer of men. A new oracle then recalls how Israel defiled it with bloodshed.
EZK 36:19-38	Scattered among the nations, the exiles profaned God's name simply by being there, since people said these are Yahweh's people and they left his land. So what he is about to do is not for their sake but for his own name's. He will gather them, sprinkle clean water to cleanse them of their idols, exchange their heart of stone for a heart of flesh, and put his own Spirit in them. They will then loathe themselves for what they did. The wasteland will be called like the garden of Eden.
EZK 37:1-28	God sets Ezekiel down in a valley of very dry bones and asks whether they can live; he answers that God knows. Told to prophesy, he does, and bone joins bone with a rattling, then sinew, flesh and skin, but no breath. Called from the four winds, the breath comes and they stand up as a huge army. The bones are the house of Israel, who say their hope is gone. Then two sticks, one for Judah and one for Joseph, are joined into one: the two kingdoms become one nation.
EZK 38:1-23	An oracle against Gog of the land of Magog, prince of Rosh, Meshech and Tubal. God will turn him around with hooks in his jaws and bring out his whole army in full armour, joined by Persia, Cush, Put and Togarmah. In the latter years Gog will come against a land living securely in unwalled villages, and will plan to plunder it. Merchants ask whether he has come for silver and livestock. Since God brings him there, his fury rises when Gog arrives: an earthquake, plague, hailstones, fire and sulphur.
EZK 39:1-14	God brings Gog down from the far north onto the mountains of Israel, knocks the bow from his left hand and the arrows from his right, and leaves him and his hordes in the open for birds and animals. Fire goes out on Magog and the coastlands. Israel burns the abandoned weapons for fuel for seven years and needs no firewood. Gog is buried in a valley east of the sea, renamed the Valley of Hamon Gog, and the burial takes seven months.
EZK 39:15-29	Searchers keep walking the land marking any human bone they find so the gravediggers can collect it, and a city is named Hamonah. Then Ezekiel summons the birds and animals to a sacrificial feast on the mountains, where they eat the flesh of warriors and princes and drink blood until they are full. God says the nations will finally understand that Israel went into exile for its own guilt, not his weakness, and that he will now bring them home, hide his face no longer, and pour out his Spirit on them.
EZK 40:1-23	Twenty-five years into the exile, Ezekiel is set down on a high mountain in Israel where a man like bronze, holding a flax line and a measuring reed, tells him to watch closely and report everything to Israel. The man measures the outer wall, then the east gate with its steps, threshold, guardrooms, porch and palm tree carvings, then the outer court with its pavement and thirty rooms, then the north gate to the same dimensions. Gate to gate measures a hundred cubits.
EZK 40:24-49	The tour continues to the south gate, then the inner court's south, east and north gates, each matching the earlier measurements and each reached by eight steps instead of seven. At the north gate are a room for washing burnt offerings and eight tables for slaughtering the burnt, sin and trespass offerings, with hooks fixed around the walls. Rooms are pointed out for the priests who keep the temple and for the sons of Zadok who keep the altar. The inner court is a hundred cubits square with the altar in front of the house.
EZK 41:1-26	The man measures the temple building itself: the nave forty by twenty cubits, then an inner room twenty by twenty that he identifies as the most holy place. Around the house are side rooms in three storeys, thirty in all, resting on ledges rather than cutting into the wall, and widening at each level. A separate building stands to the west. The walls and doors are carved throughout with palm trees between cherubim, each cherub having a human face on one side and a lion's face on the other. A wooden altar is called the table before Yahweh.
EZK 42:1-20	The guide shows Ezekiel the chambers north and south of the temple yard, built in three storeys with the upper rooms set back because the galleries take space from them. He explains that these are the holy rooms where the priests eat the most holy offerings and store the grain, sin and trespass offerings, and where they must leave their ministering garments before going out to the people. He then measures the whole complex, five hundred by five hundred, walled to separate the holy from the common.
EZK 43:1-27	Ezekiel is brought to the east gate and sees the glory of God returning from the east with a voice like many waters, the same vision he saw at the Chebar and when the city was destroyed. The glory enters by the east gate and fills the house, and a voice calls this the place of his throne where he will live among Israel forever, no longer defiled by their kings. Ezekiel is told to show them the plan so they are ashamed. Then the altar is measured and a seven day consecration is prescribed, a bull and goats for sin offerings, blood on its horns, salt cast on the offerings.
EZK 44:1-14	The outer east gate is shut, and God says it stays shut because he entered by it; only the prince may sit there to eat bread. Brought to the north gate, Ezekiel again sees the glory filling the house and falls on his face. God complains that Israel brought in foreigners uncircumcised in heart and flesh to keep charge of his sanctuary, and bans it. The Levites who went after idols will bear their guilt: they keep the gates, slaughter the offerings and serve the people, but never act as priests.
EZK 44:15-31	The sons of Zadok, who stayed faithful when Israel strayed, come near to minister. They wear linen inside the inner court, nothing woollen and nothing that makes them sweat, and must change out of those clothes before going out to the people. They neither shave their heads nor let their hair grow long, drink no wine on duty, and marry only virgins of Israel or a priest's widow. They teach the difference between holy and common, judge disputes and keep the Sabbaths. They may attend only their closest relatives' funerals. They get no land: God himself is their inheritance, and they live on the offerings.
EZK 45:1-25	When the land is divided, a holy strip is set aside: a portion for the priests with the sanctuary at its centre, a matching portion for the Levites, land for the city, and territory on either side for the prince. The princes are told to stop dispossessing people and to keep honest weights and measures, and the standard ephah, bath, shekel and mina are defined. The people bring set contributions of wheat, barley, oil and lambs to the prince, who supplies the offerings at every feast, new moon and Sabbath. A yearly cleansing of the sanctuary and the observances for Passover and the autumn feast are prescribed.
EZK 46:1-24	The inner east gate stays shut on working days and opens on Sabbaths and new moons, when the prince worships at its threshold while the priests prepare his offerings, and it stays open until evening. Worshippers entering by the north gate must leave by the south and the other way round, never doubling back. A lamb is offered every morning with flour and oil. The prince may give land to his sons permanently but to a servant only until the year of release, and he may not seize anyone's inheritance. Ezekiel is shown the kitchens where priests boil the offerings and the four corner courts where the people's sacrifices are cooked.
EZK 47:1-23	Water flows out from under the temple threshold on its south side and runs east. The man measures a thousand cubits four times, and the water goes from ankle deep to knee deep to waist deep to a river too deep to cross. Trees line both banks. The stream runs down to the Arabah and into the sea, healing the water so that fish swarm and fishermen spread nets from En Gedi to En Eglaim, though the marshes stay salty. The trees fruit every month and their leaves heal. The boundaries of the land are then listed, with resident foreigners inheriting alongside the tribes.
EZK 48:1-17	The land is allotted in parallel strips running east to west. From the north down: Dan, Asher, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim, Reuben and Judah. Then the holy offering, twenty-five thousand wide, with the sanctuary at its centre: one section for the Zadokite priests who did not go astray, one alongside for the Levites, which may never be sold or exchanged, and a five thousand strip of common land for the city with its pasture. The city measures four thousand five hundred on each side.
EZK 48:18-35	The land beside the holy portion is farmed to feed the city's workers, who come from all the tribes. The whole offering is a twenty-five thousand square, and the land on either side of it belongs to the prince. The remaining tribes follow south of it: Benjamin, Simeon, Issachar, Zebulun and Gad, down to the boundary at Tamar and Meribath Kadesh. The city has twelve gates, three on each side, each named for a tribe, and measures eighteen thousand round. Its name from that day is Yahweh is there.
NUM 4:1-25	A second Levite census counts only men aged thirty to fifty, the ones fit for actual service. The Kohathites' work is the most holy things, but they may not touch or even look at them: before every move Aaron and his sons take down the veil, wrap the ark in it, add sealskin and a blue cloth, and fit the poles, then cover the table, lampstand, golden altar, service vessels and bronze altar in blue, scarlet or purple cloth under sealskin. Only then may the Kohathites lift them, or they will die. Eleazar is responsible for the oil, incense, meal offering and anointing oil. The Gershonites are counted next and given the curtains and coverings.
NUM 4:26-49	The Gershonites also carry the court hangings, the gate screen and all the cords, working under Ithamar's direction. The Merarites, counted the same way, take the boards, bars, pillars, sockets, pegs and cords, each item assigned to a man by name, also under Ithamar. The counts follow: Kohath 2,750, Gershon 2,630, Merari 3,200, giving a total of 8,580 Levites aged thirty to fifty available for the work of carrying and serving at the Tent of Meeting. Everything is done exactly as God commanded through Moses, each man assigned according to his service and his load.
NUM 5:1-31	Anyone with a skin disease, a discharge, or contact with a corpse is put outside the camp, male or female, because God dwells in it. Someone who wrongs another must confess, repay in full plus a fifth, and if the wronged party has no kinsman the payment goes to the priest. Then the ordeal for a suspected unfaithful wife where there is no witness: the husband brings her and a barley offering without oil or incense, the priest loosens her hair, makes her swear an oath, writes the curses down and washes the ink into holy water mixed with tabernacle dust, and makes her drink it. Guilt shows in her body; innocence means she is free and will conceive.
NUM 6:1-27	The Nazirite vow, open to men and women, requires abstaining from wine, vinegar, grape juice, fresh or dried grapes, and anything from the vine down to the seeds and skins, leaving the hair uncut, and avoiding any dead body, including a parent's or sibling's. If someone dies suddenly beside them, the vow is void: they shave on the seventh day, bring two birds on the eighth, and start over. At the end of the term they offer a lamb, a ewe, a ram and unleavened bread, shave their head at the tent door and burn the hair under the peace offering, and may drink wine again. The chapter closes with the priestly blessing.
NUM 7:1-29	On the day the tabernacle is finished and anointed, the twelve tribal chiefs bring six covered wagons and twelve oxen. Moses gives two wagons and four oxen to Gershon and four wagons and eight oxen to Merari under Ithamar, but nothing to Kohath, because they carry the holy things on their shoulders. God then orders each chief to bring his dedication offering for the altar on his own day, one a day. Nahshon of Judah goes first, then Nethanel of Issachar, then Eliab of Zebulun, each bringing a silver platter of 130 shekels and a bowl of 70 filled with flour and oil, a gold ladle of incense, a bull, ram and lamb, a goat, and peace offerings of two cattle, five rams, five goats and five lambs.
NUM 7:30-61	The dedication continues, one chief a day, in the order the camps march rather than by birth. Day four is Elizur of Reuben, then Shelumiel of Simeon, Eliasaph of Gad, Elishama of Ephraim, Gamaliel of Manasseh, and on the ninth day Abidan of Benjamin. Each brings exactly the same gift as the last: a silver platter weighing 130 shekels and a silver bowl of 70, both full of fine flour mixed with oil, a gold ladle of ten shekels full of incense, a young bull, a ram and a year-old lamb for a burnt offering, a male goat for a sin offering, and two cattle, five rams, five goats and five lambs for peace offerings.
NUM 7:62-89	The last three days: Ahiezer of Dan, Pagiel of Asher and Ahira of Naphtali, each bringing the identical set. Then the totals for the whole dedication: twelve silver platters and twelve bowls weighing 2,400 shekels of silver together, twelve gold ladles of incense weighing 120 shekels, twelve bulls, twelve rams, twelve lambs and twelve goats for the burnt and sin offerings, and for the peace offerings twenty-four bulls, sixty rams, sixty goats and sixty lambs. The chapter ends with Moses entering the Tent of Meeting and hearing the voice speaking to him from above the mercy seat, between the two cherubim.
NUM 8:1-26	Aaron is told to set the seven lamps so they shine forward, and the lampstand is described again as beaten gold made to the pattern shown on the mountain. The Levites are then dedicated: sprinkled with the water of cleansing, shaved all over, clothes washed, and presented before the whole congregation, who lay their hands on them. Aaron waves them before God as an offering from Israel, and two bulls are offered, one for sin and one as a burnt offering. They are taken in place of Israel's firstborn and given to Aaron so that no plague falls on Israel at the sanctuary. Their working life runs from twenty-five to fifty, after which they assist but do no service.
NUM 9:1-23	In the first month of the second year God orders the Passover kept at its appointed time, and Israel keeps it on the fourteenth at evening in the wilderness of Sinai. Some men who are unclean from contact with a corpse ask why they should be excluded; Moses waits for an answer. God rules that anyone unclean or away on a long journey keeps it a month later, on the fourteenth of the second month, with the same rules, and that a foreigner living among them keeps it the same way. Anyone clean and at home who skips it is cut off. From the day the tabernacle went up, the cloud covered it, looking like fire at night, and Israel moved only when it lifted, whether after a night or a year.
NUM 10:1-36	Two silver trumpets are made from beaten work: both together summon the whole congregation, one summons the chiefs, and an alarm blast moves the camps out, east first, then south. Only Aaron's sons may blow them, in war and at feasts and new moons. On the twentieth day of the second month of the second year the cloud lifts and Israel leaves Sinai for the wilderness of Paran, marching in the set order under Judah, Reuben, Ephraim and Dan, with Gershon and Merari carrying the tent and the Kohathites the sanctuary. Moses asks Hobab the Midianite to come as their guide; he declines, and Moses presses him. The ark goes three days ahead, and Moses speaks a formula whenever it sets out and rests.
NUM 11:1-18	The people complain, and fire from God burns the edge of the camp until Moses prays; the place is named Taberah. Then the mixed multitude craves meat, and Israel weeps for the fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic of Egypt, saying there is nothing but manna. The manna is described as coriander-like, ground or beaten and boiled into cakes tasting of fresh oil, falling with the dew each night. Moses, hearing them weeping at every tent door, tells God the burden is too heavy and asks to be killed rather than carry it. God tells him to gather seventy elders at the tent to share the Spirit and the load, and to tell the people they will have meat tomorrow.
NUM 11:19-35	The meat will last not a day or ten but a month, until it comes out of their nostrils, because they rejected God and wished themselves back in Egypt. Moses objects that there are six hundred thousand men and asks whether all the flocks or all the fish would be enough; God answers by asking whether his hand has grown short. The seventy elders receive the Spirit and prophesy once. Eldad and Medad, who stayed in the camp, prophesy there too, and when Joshua asks Moses to stop them Moses wishes all God's people were prophets. A wind brings quail piled around the camp, and while the meat is still between their teeth a severe plague strikes. The place is named Kibroth Hattaavah.
NUM 12:1-16	Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses over the Cushite woman he married, and ask whether God has spoken only through him. The narrator notes that Moses was the humblest man on earth. God summons all three to the tent, comes down in the cloud, and says that he speaks to other prophets in visions and dreams but to Moses mouth to mouth, plainly, and asks why they were not afraid. When the cloud lifts Miriam is leprous, white as snow. Aaron begs Moses, Moses cries out for her healing, and God says she must be shut outside the camp seven days, as after a father's rebuke. The whole nation waits until she returns.
NUM 13:1-33	Twelve leaders, one per tribe, are sent to scout Canaan, among them Caleb of Judah and Hoshea of Ephraim, whom Moses renames Joshua. They are told to assess the people, the cities and the soil, and to bring back fruit. They travel from the wilderness of Zin to the entrance of Hamath, pass Hebron where the children of Anak live, and cut a single cluster of grapes so large it is carried on a pole between two men, plus pomegranates and figs. After forty days they report the land does flow with milk and honey, but the people are strong and the cities fortified. Caleb urges going up at once; the others say the land devours its inhabitants and that beside the Nephilim they felt like grasshoppers.
NUM 14:1-22	The congregation weeps all night, tells Moses and Aaron they wish they had died in Egypt or in the wilderness, and proposes appointing a captain and going back. Moses and Aaron fall on their faces. Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes and insist the land is exceedingly good and that its people have lost their protection, but the crowd threatens to stone them. God's glory appears, and he asks how long these people will despise him, offering to strike them with plague and make Moses a greater nation. Moses argues from reputation, that Egypt and Canaan will say God could not finish what he started, and quotes God's own words about being slow to anger.
NUM 14:23-45	God pardons but rules that none of that generation will see the land, except Caleb, who followed fully. Everyone counted at twenty and over will die in the wilderness; the children they said would be taken captive are the ones who will enter, after forty years of wandering, a year for each of the forty days of scouting. Joshua is named alongside Caleb as the exception. The ten spies who brought the bad report die of plague. When Moses reports this, the people mourn and then try to march up the mountain anyway. Moses warns them God is not with them, and the ark and Moses stay in the camp. The Amalekites and Canaanites drive them back to Hormah.
NUM 15:1-22	Offering measures for when they are in the land: with a lamb, a tenth of an ephah of flour with a quarter hin of oil and a quarter hin of wine; with a ram, two tenths and a third of a hin of each; with a bull, three tenths and half a hin of each, scaled by the number of animals. The same rules apply to native Israelites and to resident foreigners, stated three times over as one law for both. When they eat the bread of the land they are to give a cake from the first of the dough as a wave offering. The section then turns to what happens when the commandments are broken by mistake.
NUM 15:23-41	An unintentional community-wide failure is covered by one bull as a burnt offering and one male goat as a sin offering, and the congregation and the foreigners among them are forgiven. An individual's unwitting sin takes a year-old female goat. But anyone who sins deliberately, native or foreigner, has blasphemed and is cut off. Then a case with no precedent: a man is found gathering sticks on the Sabbath, held in custody until God rules, and stoned outside the camp. Finally, Israel is told to put fringes with a blue cord on the corners of their garments, to look at and remember the commandments rather than follow their own eyes.
NUM 16:1-25	Korah the Levite, with Dathan, Abiram and On of Reuben and 250 prominent leaders, confronts Moses and Aaron, arguing that the whole congregation is holy and they have no right to elevate themselves. Moses falls on his face and proposes a test: everyone brings a censer with fire and incense tomorrow, and God will show whom he chooses. He asks Korah whether Levite service is not enough without the priesthood too. Dathan and Abiram refuse to come, calling Egypt the land flowing with milk and honey. The 250 stand with their censers at the tent door, God's glory appears, and he tells Moses and Aaron to stand clear so he can consume the congregation.
NUM 16:26-50	Moses warns the congregation to move away from the tents of Korah, Dathan and Abiram and touch nothing of theirs. He says that if these men die ordinary deaths God has not sent him, but if the ground opens they have despised God. As he finishes, the earth splits, swallows the men, their households and all their goods alive, and closes over them, while Israel flees at the sound. Fire then consumes the 250 who offered incense. Eleazar collects their bronze censers and hammers them into a covering for the altar as a warning. The next day the congregation blames Moses and Aaron for the deaths, a plague breaks out, and Aaron runs with incense and stands between the dead and the living until it stops, after 14,700 have died.
NUM 17:1-13	To end the argument over who is chosen, God has each of the twelve tribal chiefs bring a rod with his name on it, Aaron's name written on Levi's, and all twelve are laid up in the Tent of the Testimony. The next day Aaron's rod has sprouted, budded, blossomed and produced ripe almonds. Moses brings all twelve out and each man takes his own back. Aaron's is put back in front of the testimony as a permanent sign against rebellion, so that the murmuring stops and the people do not die. The people respond in panic, saying that everyone who comes near the tabernacle dies and asking whether they are all going to perish.
NUM 18:1-15	God answers that fear by assigning responsibility. Aaron, his sons and his father's house bear the guilt attached to the sanctuary and the priesthood, and the Levites are joined to them as assistants who may serve the tent but must never approach the sanctuary vessels or the altar, on pain of death for both parties. Any outsider who comes near is put to death. In return the priests receive the offerings: every meal, sin and trespass offering as most holy food for the males, the wave offerings for the whole clean household, the best of the oil, wine and grain, the firstfruits, everything devoted, and everything that opens the womb, with human firstborn and unclean animals redeemed.
NUM 18:16-32	Human firstborn are redeemed from a month old at five shekels; firstborn cattle, sheep and goats are not redeemed but sacrificed, their meat going to the priests. All of this is called a covenant of salt forever. The priests get no land at all, because God himself is their portion. The Levites receive Israel's tithe as their inheritance in exchange for the tent service and the risk it carries, and they too hold no land. The Levites must then tithe their own tithe, giving the best tenth of it to Aaron, after which the rest is theirs to eat anywhere as ordinary wages for their work.
NUM 19:1-22	The red heifer: a flawless red cow that has never been yoked is taken outside the camp and killed in front of Eleazar, who sprinkles her blood toward the tent seven times. She is burned whole, skin, meat, blood and dung, with cedar, hyssop and scarlet thrown into the fire. Everyone involved becomes unclean until evening, including the priest, while the ashes are stored to make water for cleansing. Anyone touching a corpse, entering a tent where someone has died, or touching a bone or a grave is unclean seven days, and is sprinkled on the third and seventh days. Failure to purify defiles the tabernacle and gets the person cut off.
NUM 20:1-29	Israel reaches Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin, where Miriam dies and is buried. There is no water, and the people quarrel with Moses and Aaron, saying they should have died with their brothers. God tells Moses to take the rod, gather the people, and speak to the rock. Moses calls them rebels, asks whether he and Aaron should bring water out, and strikes the rock twice. Water pours out, but God tells both men they will not bring the assembly into the land. Edom refuses to let Israel pass along the king's highway even for payment, and comes out armed, so Israel turns aside. At Mount Hor Aaron's garments are transferred to Eleazar, Aaron dies there, and Israel mourns him thirty days.
NUM 21:1-35	The Canaanite king of Arad attacks and takes captives; Israel vows to destroy his cities, does so, and names the place Hormah. Detouring around Edom, the people complain again about the food, calling the manna disgusting, and venomous snakes are sent among them. When they confess, Moses makes a bronze serpent on a pole, and anyone bitten who looks at it lives. The march continues through Oboth, the Arnon and Beer, where they sing a song to the well. Sihon king of the Amorites refuses passage and attacks, and Israel takes his land and cities including Heshbon. Og king of Bashan comes out at Edrei and is destroyed with his sons and all his people.
NUM 22:1-21	Camped on the plains of Moab across from Jericho, Israel alarms Balak king of Moab, who has seen what happened to the Amorites and says they will lick up everything like an ox eating grass. He sends elders of Moab and Midian with payment to Balaam son of Beor at Pethor, asking him to curse Israel, since whoever he blesses is blessed. Balaam has them stay the night and consults God, who says not to go, because the people are blessed. Balak sends a larger and more distinguished delegation with promises of honour. Balaam says he cannot go beyond God's word for a house full of silver and gold, asks them to stay again, and is told he may go but must speak only what he is given.
NUM 22:22-41	God is angry that Balaam goes, and his angel stands in the road with a drawn sword. The donkey sees the angel and turns into a field, and Balaam beats her. In a walled lane she crushes his foot against the wall, and he beats her again. In a place too narrow to pass she lies down, and he beats her a third time. God opens the donkey's mouth and she asks what she has done; Balaam says he would kill her if he had a sword. She points out she has never behaved this way before. Balaam's eyes are opened, he sees the angel and falls on his face, and is told to go on but speak only what he is given. Balak takes him up to the high places of Baal.
NUM 23:1-30	Balaam has Balak build seven altars and offer a bull and a ram on each, then goes off alone. God gives him words, and instead of a curse he says he cannot curse whom God has not cursed, describes Israel as a people dwelling alone and uncountable as dust, and wishes he could die their death. Balak protests, so they move to the field of Zophim on Pisgah and repeat the seven altars. The second oracle says God is not a man that he should lie, that he has seen no iniquity in Jacob, and that Israel rises like a lion. Balak asks him to at least stop blessing them, then takes him to the top of Peor for a third attempt.
NUM 24:1-25	Seeing that God intends to bless Israel, Balaam stops using enchantments and simply looks toward the wilderness. The Spirit comes on him, and he praises Israel's tents spread out like gardens and cedars by water, promises a king higher than Agag, and repeats that whoever blesses Israel is blessed. Balak strikes his hands together in fury, says he has blessed them three times, and sends him away without payment. Before leaving, Balaam delivers a final set of oracles: a star out of Jacob and a sceptre out of Israel that strikes Moab, Edom possessed, Amalek destroyed, the Kenites eventually carried off by Asshur, and ships from Kittim afflicting Asshur and Eber.
NUM 25:1-18	At Shittim the people begin sleeping with Moabite women and are drawn into the sacrifices of their gods, joining themselves to Baal Peor. God's anger burns, and Moses is told to have the chiefs executed and orders the judges to kill everyone who joined the cult. While the congregation is weeping at the tent door, an Israelite brings a Midianite woman in openly. Phinehas, son of Eleazar, takes a spear and kills them both, and the plague stops, but 24,000 have died. Phinehas is granted a covenant of peace and a lasting priesthood. The pair are named as Zimri, a Simeonite chief, and Cozbi, daughter of a Midianite chief, and Israel is told to attack Midian.
NUM 26:1-34	After the plague a second census is taken, this time by Moses and Eleazar, on the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho, of all men twenty and over able to fight, listed by clan. Reuben comes to 43,730, and the list pauses to recall that Dathan and Abiram of that tribe were swallowed with Korah's company, noting that Korah's own sons did not die. Simeon is 22,200, Gad 40,500, Judah 76,500 with a note that Er and Onan died in Canaan, Issachar 64,300, Zebulun 60,500, and Manasseh 52,700, where Zelophehad is recorded as having no sons but five daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah.
NUM 26:35-65	The remaining tallies: Ephraim 32,500, Benjamin 45,600, Dan 64,400, Asher 53,400 with a daughter named Serah recorded, and Naphtali 45,400, for a total of 601,730. God says the land is to be divided in proportion to these numbers, larger tribes receiving more, but allotted by lot. The Levites are counted separately by their clans and come to 23,000 males from a month old, and receive no inheritance. The genealogy notes Amram and Jochebed as the parents of Aaron, Moses and Miriam, and that Nadab and Abihu died offering strange fire. Not one man counted at Sinai remains alive except Caleb and Joshua.
NUM 27:1-23	The five daughters of Zelophehad, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah, stand at the tent door and argue that their father died in his own sin, not with Korah, left no sons, and that his name should not vanish from his family. Moses brings the case to God, who rules that they are right and establishes an order of inheritance: daughter, then brothers, then uncles, then nearest kinsman. God then tells Moses to climb Abarim, see the land, and be gathered to his people like Aaron, because of Meribah. Moses asks for a successor so the congregation is not like sheep without a shepherd, and Joshua is commissioned before Eleazar and the people with the laying on of hands.
NUM 28:1-31	A calendar of offerings. Every day, two year-old lambs, one morning and one evening, each with a tenth of an ephah of flour, a quarter hin of beaten oil and a quarter hin of drink offering. On the Sabbath, two extra lambs with two tenths of flour. At each new moon, two bulls, a ram and seven lambs with three tenths, two tenths and one tenth of flour respectively, wine in proportion, and a goat for sin. Passover on the fourteenth, then seven days of unleavened bread with the same bull, ram and lamb offering daily and holy assemblies on the first and seventh. At the feast of weeks, the same again with a goat for atonement.
NUM 29:1-40	The seventh month's calendar. On the first, a day of trumpet blasts with one bull, one ram, seven lambs and a goat. On the tenth, a day of self-affliction with the same offering plus the atonement sin offering. On the fifteenth begins a seven-day feast whose bull count descends day by day, thirteen on the first, then twelve, eleven, ten, nine, eight and seven, always with two rams, fourteen lambs and a goat, and always in addition to the continual burnt offering. The eighth day is a solemn assembly with a single bull, one ram, seven lambs and a goat. All of this is on top of any vows, freewill offerings and peace offerings.
NUM 30:1-16	The law of vows. A man who vows or swears an oath must do exactly what he said. A young woman still in her father's house is bound by her vow if he says nothing when he hears it, but the vow is annulled if he forbids it that same day, and she is forgiven. The same applies to a married woman and her husband, including a rash promise made on impulse. A widow or divorced woman is bound by whatever she vows. If a husband hears and stays silent day after day, he has confirmed the vow, and if he annuls it later, after already hearing it, he bears her guilt himself.
BAR 1:1-22	Baruch son of Nerias writes in Babylon five years after the Chaldeans burned Jerusalem, and reads the book aloud to the exiled king Jechonias and all the people by the river Sud. They weep, fast and pray, then collect money and send it with the returned temple vessels to the high priest for offerings, asking prayers for Nabuchodonosor and his son Baltasar and for themselves. Enclosed is a confession for the feast: righteousness belongs to God, shame to them, since they have disobeyed since Egypt.
BAR 2:1-18	The confession says God has done exactly what he warned through Moses: plagues worse than any under heaven, a siege in which parents ate their own children, and Israel left a reproach among the nations it was scattered into. Even then nobody turned from a wicked heart. The prayer appeals to the God who brought them out of Egypt: turn your wrath away, we are few, hear us for your own name's sake, since the dead cannot praise you but a hungry, failing soul can.
BAR 2:19-35	The plea rests not on the merits of their fathers or kings but on God's own words. The prophets told them to bow to the king of Babylon and stay in the land, warning that refusal would end all mirth and marriage; they refused, the land was emptied, royal bones were turned out to lie in heat and frost, and the temple was ruined. Moses also promised that exile would teach the stiff necked people, who would be given new hearts, the land sworn to Abraham, and an everlasting covenant.
BAR 3:1-37	The prayer closes with the anguished soul asking God to forget the sins of the fathers. Then the book turns to wisdom and asks Israel why it has grown old in a foreign country among the dead: it forsook the fountain of wisdom. Foreign princes, hoarders of silver, the merchants of Merran and Teman and the giants of old all missed her and went to the grave. Nobody fetched her from heaven or across the sea. Only God, who calls the stars, knows her, and he gave her to Jacob.
BAR 4:1-37	Wisdom is identified with the law that endures: hold it and live, leave it and die, and do not give its glory to a foreign nation. Israel was sold for correction, not destruction, having sacrificed to demons and forgotten God. Jerusalem then speaks as a widow, telling her neighbours to see the captivity of her children, taken by a shameless nation of strange speech.
