She wears sackcloth now, but tells her children to take heart: the one who brought the plagues will deliver them, and their enemy's city will burn.
BAR 5:1-9	Jerusalem is told to take off her mourning clothes and put on the glory that comes from God, a robe of righteousness and a crown of the Everlasting, and will be called The peace of righteousness. She is to stand on the height and look east and see her children gathered from every direction at the word of the Holy One. They left on foot as prisoners and are carried back high as if on a royal throne, with mountains levelled and valleys filled to make the road plain.
BAR 6:1-36	A letter Jeremiah sends to those about to be taken to Babylon, telling them they will stay seven generations before being brought out peaceably. They will see gods of silver, gold and wood carried on shoulders, and must not fear the crowds worshipping them. The letter then argues that these images are not gods: their tongues are polished by a craftsman and cannot speak, their priests steal their gold, they cannot save themselves from rust, dust, bats or thieves, and they must be carried because they have no feet.
BAR 6:37-73	The letter keeps listing what the idols cannot do: heal the blind, help the widow or the fatherless, make or unmake a king, give rain, judge a case or save anyone from death. Even the Chaldeans dishonour them, bringing a mute man to Bel as though it could hear, and the priests hide them or flee when war or fire comes. They are the work of carpenters and goldsmiths, while sun, moon, stars, wind and fire obey God. A just man with no idols is better off.
DAN 10:1-21	After three weeks of mourning without rich food, meat or wine, Daniel is by the Tigris when he sees a man in linen with a face like lightning and eyes like torches. His companions flee without seeing it, and Daniel collapses until a hand raises him. He is told his prayer was heard on the first day, but the prince of Persia delayed the messenger twenty-one days until Michael came to help. Strengthened, he hears that the fight with Persia, and then Greece, continues.
DAN 11:1-21	The messenger sets out the future as a line of kings: three more in Persia, then a rich fourth who provokes Greece, then a mighty king whose empire breaks toward the four winds and passes to strangers rather than his heirs. The rest is the king of the south against the king of the north: a failed marriage alliance, campaigns both ways, gods and treasure carried to Egypt, a fortified city taken. One king dies over taxes, and a contemptible man gains the kingdom by flattery.
DAN 11:22-45	The contemptible king wins by deceit and broken treaties, defeats the king of the south, whose own table companions betray him, and returns home hostile to the holy covenant. Ships of Kittim turn back his second southern campaign, so he profanes the sanctuary, stops the daily offering and sets up the abomination that makes desolate. The wise instruct many and fall by sword and captivity, which refines them. He exalts himself above every god, then dies camped between the sea and the holy mountain, with no one to help him.
DAN 12:1-13	Michael arises, unequalled trouble comes, and everyone whose name is in the book is delivered. Many who sleep in the dust awake, some to everlasting life and some to everlasting contempt, and the wise shine like stars. Daniel is told to seal the book until the end. Two figures at the river ask how long, and the man in linen swears it will be a time, times and a half. Daniel does not understand; he is given 1,290 and 1,335 days and sent to rest.
DEU 1:1-22	Forty years after Egypt, on the plains of Moab, Moses begins a long address to Israel. He recalls God's order at Horeb to leave the mountain and take the land promised to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Unable to bear the people's disputes alone, he had them choose wise men as captains of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens, and charged the judges to show no partiality and fear no man. They reached Kadesh Barnea, where the people asked to send scouts ahead.
DEU 1:23-46	Moses recalls the twelve scouts, who brought back fruit and a good report, and the people's refusal to go up. They complained that God hated them and that the Anakim held cities walled to the sky. His reminder of Egypt and of the fire and cloud did not persuade them. God swore that none of that generation but Caleb would see the land, told Moses he too would not enter, and named Joshua and the children instead. They attacked anyway, were chased like bees to Hormah, and wept unheard.
DEU 2:1-20	Moses recounts the years spent circling Mount Seir and God's order to turn north and pass Esau's territory without provoking it, buying food and water for money. Edom's land, and Moab's, are not Israel's to take, having been given to Esau and to Lot's descendants. He notes the Emim and Rephaim who lived there before. Thirty-eight years passed between Kadesh Barnea and crossing the brook Zered, until the whole generation of fighting men was gone. Ammon is off limits too.
DEU 2:21-37	After more notes on displaced peoples, God tells Israel to cross the Arnon and take Sihon's land. Moses sends messengers to Sihon of Heshbon asking only for passage along the highway and offering to buy food and water. Sihon refuses, his spirit hardened by God, and comes out to fight at Jahaz. Israel destroys him, his sons and every inhabited city, keeping the livestock and plunder. They take everything from Aroer to Gilead, but do not approach Ammonite land.
DEU 3:1-29	Og of Bashan attacks at Edrei and is destroyed with all sixty of his fortified cities, his people killed and the livestock taken. Moses notes Og's iron bed, nine cubits long. He assigns the conquered land east of the Jordan to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh, on condition their fighting men cross over armed ahead of the others. He charges Joshua not to fear, then asks to see the land himself. God refuses and tells him to climb Pisgah and look.
DEU 4:1-24	Moses urges Israel to keep the statutes without adding or subtracting, pointing to the men destroyed at Baal Peor. Obedience will make other nations call them wise, and no nation has a god so near. He warns them not to forget Horeb, where the mountain burned and they heard a voice but saw no form, and so not to make an image of anything, or worship sun, moon or stars. He repeats that he himself will die outside the land.
DEU 4:25-49	Moses predicts that once settled, Israel will make images and be scattered among the nations, left few in number, serving gods of wood and stone that cannot see or hear. Even then, if they seek God wholeheartedly they will find him, because he is merciful and keeps the covenant. He argues that no nation has heard God speak from fire and lived, so they should know there is no other God. He then sets apart Bezer, Ramoth and Golan as cities of refuge east of the Jordan.
DEU 5:1-33	Moses recites the Ten Commandments, insisting the covenant at Horeb was made with the people standing there. The list runs from no other gods and no images through the name, the Sabbath, parents, murder, adultery, theft, false testimony and coveting. Here the Sabbath is grounded in the slavery in Egypt, and extends to servants, livestock and foreigners. God spoke these from the fire and added nothing more. The people, terrified, asked Moses to listen on their behalf, and God approved.
DEU 6:1-25	Moses gives the central command: Yahweh is one, and Israel is to love him with all their heart, soul and might. These words are to be taught to children, spoken at home and on the road, bound on the hand and forehead, and written on doorposts and gates. He warns that once they live in cities they did not build and eat from vineyards they did not plant, they will be tempted to forget. When a son asks what the laws mean, the answer is the story of Egypt.
DEU 7:1-26	Israel is told to destroy the seven nations of Canaan, make no covenant with them and not intermarry, since that would draw their children to other gods, and to smash the altars, pillars, poles and images. They were chosen not for their size, being the fewest of peoples, but because God loves them and keeps his oath. Obedience brings fertility, health and freedom from Egypt's diseases. They should not fear larger nations, but the conquest will be gradual, so that wild animals do not overrun the land.
DEU 8:1-20	Moses tells Israel to remember the forty years in the wilderness, where hunger and manna taught them that man does not live by bread alone, and where their clothes did not wear out and their feet did not swell. God disciplined them as a father disciplines a son. He describes the land ahead: brooks and springs, wheat, barley, vines, figs, pomegranates, olives and honey, stones of iron and hills with copper. The warning is against claiming, once rich, that their own strength earned it.
DEU 9:1-29	Israel is about to cross and dispossess taller peoples in walled cities, but Moses insists it is not for their righteousness. They are stiff-necked, and he reviews the evidence: the golden calf while he was on the mountain forty days without food, God's offer to destroy them and start again with him, the tablets thrown down and broken, the calf burned, ground to dust and thrown into the brook. He fasted another forty days for them and prayed for Aaron.
DEU 10:1-22	Moses recounts cutting two new tablets and making an acacia ark to hold them, God rewriting the ten commandments, and Levi being set apart to carry the ark and serve, with God as its only inheritance. He notes Aaron's death at Moserah and Eleazar's succession. The requirement is stated simply: fear God, love him, walk in his ways, serve with all the heart. God takes no bribes, defends the fatherless and widow, and loves the foreigner, so Israel must love foreigners too, having been foreigners in Egypt.
DEU 11:1-32	Moses says he is speaking to the adults who saw the plagues, the Red Sea and the earth swallowing Dathan and Abiram, not to their children. He contrasts Egypt, watered by foot, with a land of hills that drinks rain, so obedience brings the early and late rains and disobedience shuts the sky. The words are again to be bound on the hand and written on doorposts. He sets before them a blessing and a curse, to be placed on Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal.
DEU 12:1-16	The law of a single sanctuary. Israel is to destroy every high place, altar, pillar and pole where the nations worshipped, and not treat their own God that way. Sacrifices, tithes, vows and firstborn are to be brought only to the one place God chooses, and eaten there with rejoicing, the Levite included. Everyone doing what seems right in his own eyes is to end. Ordinary meat may be killed and eaten at home like game, but the blood must be poured out on the ground.
DEU 12:17-32	Tithes, firstborn and vow offerings may not be eaten at home but only at the chosen place, with the household and the Levite present, and the Levite is not to be neglected. If that place is far away, ordinary meat may be killed and eaten locally by clean and unclean alike, as with gazelle or deer. The blood is never eaten, because the blood is the life, and is poured out like water. Israel is warned not to copy the nations, who burned their children.
GEN 4:1-26	Eve bears Cain and then Abel. Abel keeps sheep, Cain farms. Both bring offerings; God respects Abel's and not Cain's, and warns Cain that sin crouches at his door. Cain lures Abel into a field and kills him. Asked where his brother is, he says he is not his brother's keeper. God curses his farming, makes him a wanderer, and marks him against reprisal. Cain settles in Nod, and his line runs down to Lamech, who boasts of killing a man. Eve bears Seth.
GEN 5:1-32	A genealogy from Adam to Noah, ten generations, each entry giving the age at fatherhood, the years lived afterward, and the total before death. Adam lives 930 years, Methuselah 969, the longest. Two entries break the pattern: Enoch walks with God for three hundred years and is taken rather than dying, and Lamech names his son Noah as a comfort against the cursed ground. The list closes with Noah at five hundred fathering Shem, Ham and Japheth.
GEN 6:1-22	God's sons take human women as wives, and the Nephilim are on the earth. God limits human life to a hundred and twenty years. Seeing that human wickedness and violence fill the earth, God regrets making humanity and resolves to destroy all flesh, but Noah finds favour. God tells Noah to build a ship of gopher wood, three hundred cubits by fifty by thirty, sealed with pitch, with three decks and a door in the side, and to bring his family, two of every creature, and food. Noah does it all.
GEN 7:1-24	God tells Noah to enter the ship with seven pairs of every clean animal and two of the unclean, since rain will come in seven days and last forty days and nights. Noah is six hundred years old. On the seventeenth day of the second month the fountains of the deep burst and the sky opens. The family and the animals go in and God shuts the door. The waters rise until every mountain is covered and everything on dry land dies. Only those in the ship survive. The flood stands for a hundred and fifty days.
GEN 8:1-22	God remembers Noah and sends a wind; the waters fall and the ship comes to rest on the mountains of Ararat. Noah sends out a raven, then a dove that finds no footing, then the dove again, which returns with an olive leaf, then a third time, and it does not come back. The ground dries and God tells them all to leave the ship and multiply. Noah builds an altar and offers burnt offerings. God resolves never again to curse the ground or destroy all life, and promises the seasons will not cease.
GEN 9:1-29	God blesses Noah and his sons, gives them every living thing for food but forbids eating blood, and requires a reckoning for human bloodshed, since man is made in God's image. He makes a covenant never again to flood the earth and sets the rainbow as its sign. Noah plants a vineyard, gets drunk and lies uncovered. Ham sees him and tells his brothers, who cover him walking backwards. Waking, Noah curses Canaan to servitude and blesses Shem and Japheth. Noah dies at nine hundred and fifty.
GEN 10:1-32	A table of the nations descended from Noah's three sons. Japheth's line spreads to the coastlands. Ham's includes Cush, Egypt, Put and Canaan, and Cush fathers Nimrod, a mighty hunter whose kingdom begins at Babel and who builds Nineveh and other Assyrian cities; Canaan's descendants are the peoples of Canaan, with their borders described. Shem's line runs through Arpachshad to Eber, whose son Peleg is named for the earth being divided. From these families the nations spread after the flood.
GEN 11:1-32	The whole earth speaks one language. Settling in Shinar, the people make bricks and set out to build a city and a tower reaching the sky so they will not be scattered. God comes down, sees that nothing will be beyond them, and confuses their speech, so they stop building and scatter; the place is called Babel. A genealogy then runs from Shem through Arpachshad, Eber and Peleg to Terah, who fathers Abram, Nahor and Haran. Sarai is barren. Terah takes the family from Ur toward Canaan, settles in Haran, and dies there.
GEN 12:1-20	God tells Abram to leave his country for a land he will be shown, promising to make him a great nation through whom all families of the earth will be blessed. Abram, seventy-five, sets out from Haran with Sarai and Lot, reaches Canaan, and builds altars at Shechem and near Bethel. Famine drives him to Egypt, where he tells Sarai to pass as his sister. Pharaoh takes her into his house and enriches Abram. Plagues follow, Pharaoh works out why, and sends them all away.
GEN 13:1-18	Abram comes up from Egypt rich in livestock, silver and gold, and returns to his altar between Bethel and Ai. He and Lot have too many herds for the land to carry them both, and their herdsmen quarrel, so Abram offers Lot the first choice of territory. Lot picks the well-watered Jordan plain and settles near Sodom, whose people are wicked. God tells Abram to look in every direction: all of it will belong to his offspring, who will be as countless as dust. Abram settles at Hebron.
GEN 14:1-24	Four kings under Chedorlaomer put down a revolt by five kings of the plain, sweeping through the region and defeating Sodom and Gomorrah in the tar-pit valley of Siddim. They carry off the goods and Lot with them. Hearing of it, Abram arms three hundred and eighteen men of his household, attacks by night, pursues past Damascus and recovers everyone and everything. Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings bread and wine and blesses him, and Abram gives him a tenth. He refuses to keep anything of Sodom's.
GEN 15:1-21	God tells Abram not to fear, and Abram objects that he is childless and his servant Eliezer stands to inherit. God says the heir will be his own child and tells him to count the stars; Abram believes, and it is credited as righteousness. Asked for assurance about the land, God has him cut three animals in half. Abram drives off the birds of prey, then in a dark, terrified sleep hears that his descendants will be enslaved four hundred years. A furnace and torch pass between the pieces, sealing the covenant.
GEN 16:1-16	Childless, Sarai gives Abram her Egyptian servant Hagar as a wife in the hope of getting children through her. Hagar conceives and looks down on Sarai, who blames Abram; he tells her to do as she likes, and she treats Hagar so harshly that Hagar runs into the wilderness. An angel finds her at a spring, tells her to go back, and promises her a son called Ishmael, who will live at odds with everyone. She names God as the one who sees. Ishmael is born when Abram is eighty-six.
GEN 17:1-27	At ninety-nine Abram is renamed Abraham, father of a multitude, and promised nations, kings and all Canaan as an everlasting possession. The covenant sign is circumcision of every male at eight days old, household slaves included. Sarai becomes Sarah and is promised a son. Abraham laughs at the idea of a child at a hundred and asks for Ishmael instead; God insists on Isaac, born within the year, while blessing Ishmael with twelve princes. Abraham circumcises his whole household that day.
GEN 18:1-33	Three men appear at Mamre in the heat of the day, and Abraham rushes to serve them cakes, curds, milk and a dressed calf. They say Sarah will have a son within the year; she laughs to herself in the tent, is called out on it and denies it. As they set off toward Sodom, God decides not to hide his plans from Abraham. Abraham then bargains him down: he will spare the city for fifty righteous, then forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, and finally ten.
GEN 19:1-17	Two angels reach Sodom at evening and Lot presses them to stay in his house. The men of the city surround it and demand he bring them out to be raped. Lot offers his two virgin daughters instead; the crowd turns on him and moves to break down the door. The angels pull him inside and strike the men blind, then tell Lot to gather his family and leave. His sons-in-law think he is joking, and at dawn the angels take the four of them by the hand and set them outside the city.
GEN 19:18-38	Lot begs to shelter in the nearby small town rather than the mountains, and is allowed it; the place is called Zoar. As the sun rises, sulphur and fire fall on Sodom and Gomorrah and destroy the cities, the plain and everything growing on it. Lot's wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. Abraham sees the smoke rising from where he had stood the day before. Afraid to stay in Zoar, Lot moves into a cave with his daughters, who get him drunk on successive nights and conceive by him. Their sons are Moab and Ben Ammi.
GEN 20:1-18	Living as a foreigner in Gerar, Abraham again calls Sarah his sister, and King Abimelech takes her. God warns Abimelech in a dream that he is a dead man, though he has not touched her, and tells him to return the woman and ask her husband to pray for him. Abimelech confronts Abraham, who explains that he feared for his life and that Sarah is in fact his half-sister. Abimelech returns her with livestock, servants and a thousand pieces of silver. Abraham prays, and the closed wombs of Abimelech's household open.
GEN 21:1-34	Sarah bears Isaac in Abraham's hundredth year and says God has made her laugh. At the weaning feast she sees Ishmael mocking and demands that Hagar and her son be sent away. Abraham is distressed, but God tells him to do it, promising to make Ishmael a nation too. Hagar's water runs out in the wilderness and she leaves the boy under a shrub to die; God hears him and shows her a well. Ishmael grows up an archer in Paran. Abraham and Abimelech then swear a treaty over a disputed well at Beersheba.
GEN 22:1-24	God tests Abraham, telling him to offer Isaac as a burnt offering in the land of Moriah. Abraham sets out with two servants, wood and a knife. Isaac carries the wood and asks where the lamb is; his father says God will provide it. Abraham builds the altar, binds Isaac and raises the knife, and an angel stops him, saying his fear of God is proved. He finds a ram caught in a thicket and offers it instead, naming the place Yahweh Will Provide. The promise of offspring is sworn again. A note lists Nahor's children, including Rebekah's father Bethuel.
GEN 23:1-20	Sarah dies at a hundred and twenty-seven in Hebron, and Abraham mourns her. Owning no land, he asks the Hittites for a burial place. They offer him the best of their tombs free, and Ephron offers the field and cave of Machpelah as a gift. Abraham insists on paying, and Ephron names four hundred shekels of silver, which Abraham weighs out in front of the whole assembly at the gate. The field and its cave are deeded to him, and he buries Sarah there.
GEN 24:1-32	Old and blessed, Abraham makes his senior servant swear not to take a Canaanite wife for Isaac but to fetch one from his own relatives, and not to take Isaac back there. The servant travels to the city of Nahor with ten camels and waits at the well, asking God for a sign: the right woman will offer to water his camels. Rebekah, granddaughter of Abraham's brother, arrives and does exactly that. He gives her a gold ring and bracelets, learns whose daughter she is, and worships. Her brother Laban brings him home and unloads the camels.
GEN 24:33-67	The servant refuses to eat until he has told his errand. He recounts Abraham's wealth, the oath, his prayer at the well and how Rebekah answered it, then asks for a decision. Laban and Bethuel agree that this is from God and hand Rebekah over. He gives out silver, gold and clothing. Asked to stay ten days, he insists on leaving at once, and Rebekah, when asked, says she will go. She rides off with her nurse, sees Isaac walking in a field at evening and veils herself. Isaac marries her and is comforted after his mother's death.
GEN 25:1-34	Abraham takes another wife, Keturah, and has six more sons, but leaves everything to Isaac and sends the others east with gifts. He dies at a hundred and seventy-five, and Isaac and Ishmael bury him beside Sarah at Machpelah. Ishmael's twelve sons are listed; he dies at a hundred and thirty-seven. Rebekah, barren, conceives after Isaac prays, and is told the two struggling in her womb are two nations, the elder to serve the younger. Esau is born red and hairy, Jacob gripping his heel. Esau later sells his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of lentil stew.
GEN 26:1-35	Famine sends Isaac to Gerar, where God tells him to stay put and repeats Abraham's promises. Afraid, he calls Rebekah his sister until Abimelech sees them together and orders that nobody touch either of them. Isaac's harvest is a hundredfold and the Philistines envy him, stopping up his father's wells. He redigs them, and moves on twice after quarrels over water before finding a well nobody contests. At Beersheba he builds an altar and swears a treaty with Abimelech. Esau marries two Hittite women, to his parents' grief.
GEN 27:1-26	Old and blind, Isaac asks Esau to hunt venison so he can bless him before he dies. Rebekah overhears and sends Jacob to bring goat meat instead. Jacob objects that his brother is hairy and he is not, so she covers his hands and neck in goatskins and dresses him in Esau's clothes. He brings the food to his father, claiming to be Esau. Isaac questions the speed of the hunt, then feels his hands and says the voice is Jacob's but the hands are Esau's. He eats, drinks, and asks for a kiss.
GEN 27:27-46	Smelling Esau's clothes, Isaac blesses Jacob with grain, wine and mastery over his brothers. Esau arrives moments later with his own meal, and Isaac trembles as he realises what has happened, but says the blessing stands. Esau cries out bitterly and asks for one of his own; Isaac can only promise him a life by the sword, serving his brother until he breaks the yoke. Esau decides to kill Jacob once their father is mourned. Rebekah hears, and sends Jacob to her brother Laban in Haran until the anger passes.
GEN 28:1-22	Isaac sends Jacob to Paddan Aram to find a wife among Laban's daughters rather than in Canaan, blessing him with Abraham's promise. Esau, seeing that Canaanite wives displease his father, marries Ishmael's daughter Mahalath. On the road Jacob sleeps with a stone for a pillow and dreams of a stairway between earth and heaven with angels going up and down it, and God standing above promising him the land, countless offspring and protection. He wakes afraid, calls the place Bethel, sets the stone up as a pillar, and vows a tenth of everything.
GEN 29:1-35	Jacob reaches a well near Haran, meets Rachel, rolls the stone away for her flock and weeps as he tells her who he is. Laban takes him in, and Jacob agrees to seven years' work for Rachel. On the wedding night Laban substitutes Leah, defending it as local custom, and Jacob must serve another seven years for Rachel, whom he loves more. Leah, unloved, bears Reuben, Simeon, Levi and Judah, while Rachel remains childless.
GEN 30:1-25	Rachel, still childless, demands children of Jacob, who answers that he is not God. She gives him her servant Bilhah, who bears Dan and Naphtali; Leah gives her servant Zilpah, who bears Gad and Asher. Reuben finds mandrakes, and Rachel trades a night with Jacob for them, after which Leah bears Issachar, then Zebulun, then a daughter, Dinah. At last God opens Rachel's womb and she bears Joseph. Jacob then asks Laban to let him go home.
GEN 30:26-43	Jacob asks for his wives and children and leave to go, but Laban, who knows he has prospered because of him, asks him to name his wages. Jacob takes as his pay only the speckled, spotted and black animals, and Laban separates those out and puts three days' distance between the flocks. Jacob then peels streaks into fresh rods and sets them in the watering troughs where the flocks breed, working the stronger animals into his own share and leaving Laban the feeble. He grows very rich.
GEN 31:1-29	Hearing Laban's sons complain and seeing Laban's face turn against him, Jacob is told by God to go home. He tells Rachel and Leah how their father changed his wages ten times and how God kept giving him the flocks, and recounts a dream at mating season telling him to leave. They agree that nothing is left for them there. While Laban is shearing, Rachel steals his household gods and the family slips away toward Gilead. Laban pursues for seven days, warned in a dream to say nothing to Jacob either way.
GEN 31:30-55	Laban demands to know why his gods were stolen. Jacob, who does not know Rachel took them, invites a search on pain of death; she has hidden them in her camel saddle and stays seated, pleading her period. Nothing is found. Jacob rounds on Laban with twenty years of grievance: losses he absorbed, nights without sleep, wages changed ten times. Laban proposes a covenant instead. They raise a heap of stones as a witness that neither will cross it to harm the other, eat together, and part in the morning.
GEN 32:1-32	Angels meet Jacob on the road, and he sends word ahead to Esau. The messengers come back saying Esau is coming with four hundred men. Frightened, Jacob splits his people into two companies so one can escape, prays for deliverance, and sends ahead a graded procession of livestock as a gift. That night he sends his family over the Jabbok and is left alone, wrestling a man until daybreak. His hip is strained, but he refuses to let go without a blessing and is renamed Israel. He calls the place Peniel and walks away limping.
GEN 33:1-20	Esau approaches with his four hundred men. Jacob arranges the women and children by rank, goes ahead and bows to the ground seven times, and Esau runs to embrace him; they weep. Esau asks who everyone is and refuses the gift until Jacob presses it on him, saying that seeing his face was like seeing the face of God. Offered an escort, Jacob pleads the pace of the children and the nursing flocks and follows separately. Esau returns to Seir. Jacob settles at Succoth, then buys land at Shechem and builds an altar.
GEN 34:1-31	Shechem son of Hamor rapes Dinah, then wants to marry her, and his father comes to negotiate a match and a general intermarriage. Jacob's sons answer with deceit: they will agree only if every male in the city is circumcised. Hamor and Shechem sell the plan to their townsmen on the promise of gain, and all the men submit. On the third day, while the city is still sore, Simeon and Levi kill every male in it, take Dinah back, and the rest of the brothers plunder the town and carry off its wives and children. Jacob says they have made him hated and vulnerable; they answer that their sister was treated as a prostitute.
GEN 35:1-29	Told to go up to Bethel, Jacob has his household surrender their foreign gods and earrings, which he buries under an oak, and they travel unpursued. He builds an altar there. Rebekah's nurse Deborah dies and is buried nearby. God appears again, confirms the name Israel, and repeats the promise of nations, kings and land, and Jacob sets up a stone pillar. On the road to Ephrath, Rachel dies bearing Benjamin and is buried there. Reuben sleeps with Bilhah. The twelve sons are listed, and Isaac dies at a hundred and eighty.
GEN 36:1-43	A register of Esau's descendants, who are the Edomites. His wives and sons are named, and he moves to the hill country of Seir because the land cannot support both brothers' herds. The chiefs descended from each of his sons are listed, then the sons and chiefs of Seir the Horite, including the Anah who found the hot springs while pasturing donkeys. Eight kings who reigned in Edom before Israel had any king are named in succession, and a final list of Edomite chiefs closes the chapter.
GEN 37:1-36	Seventeen-year-old Joseph, his father's favourite and owner of a coloured coat, reports on his brothers and tells them two dreams in which their sheaves, then the sun, moon and eleven stars, bow to him. Their hatred grows and even his father rebukes him. Sent to check on them at Dothan, he is seized; Reuben talks them out of killing him and they throw him into a dry pit. On Judah's suggestion they sell him to passing traders for twenty pieces of silver and he is taken to Egypt. They dip his coat in goat's blood, and Jacob, believing a wild animal killed him, refuses all comfort.
GEN 38:1-30	Judah marries a Canaanite woman and has three sons. His firstborn Er marries Tamar and dies; Onan refuses to father a child for his brother and dies too; Judah sends Tamar home a widow rather than give her Shelah. Widowed himself, he goes to the sheep shearing, and Tamar veils herself at the roadside. Taking her for a prostitute, he pays with his signet, cord and staff as a pledge. Told three months later that she is pregnant, he orders her burned, until she produces the pledge. He admits she is more in the right than he is. She bears twins, Perez and Zerah.
GEN 39:1-23	Potiphar, captain of Pharaoh's guard, buys Joseph, and everything he touches prospers, so his master puts the whole household in his hands and stops watching it. Potiphar's wife propositions him repeatedly and he refuses, calling it a sin against God. Catching him alone, she grabs his garment; he runs, leaving it behind, and she uses it to accuse him of assault. Potiphar has him jailed with the king's prisoners. There too he prospers, and the warden puts every prisoner under his charge and stops checking on him.
GEN 40:1-23	Pharaoh's chief cup bearer and chief baker are jailed and put in Joseph's charge. Both dream on the same night and find nobody to interpret. Joseph says interpretations belong to God and listens: three vine branches mean three days until the cup bearer is restored, and three baskets of bread the birds eat mean three days until the baker is hanged. He asks the cup bearer to mention him to Pharaoh. On his birthday Pharaoh restores one man and hangs the other, exactly as Joseph said. The cup bearer forgets him.
GEN 41:1-30	Two years later Pharaoh dreams of seven fat cattle eaten by seven thin ones, then seven good heads of grain swallowed by seven withered ones, and no magician can explain it. The cup bearer finally remembers Joseph, who is brought from the dungeon, shaved and dressed. Joseph says the answer belongs to God, and that both dreams mean one thing: seven years of great plenty across Egypt, followed by seven years of famine so severe that the plenty will be forgotten.
GEN 41:31-57	Joseph explains that the dream came twice because God has fixed it, and advises Pharaoh to appoint a wise administrator and store a fifth of the harvest through the good years. Pharaoh gives him his signet ring, fine linen, a gold chain and authority over all Egypt, renames him Zaphenath-Paneah and marries him to Asenath. At thirty he tours the country and stockpiles grain beyond counting. Two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, are born. When the famine comes, Egypt alone has bread, and every country comes to Joseph to buy.
GEN 42:1-21	Hearing there is grain in Egypt, Jacob sends ten of his sons to buy, keeping Benjamin at home. They bow before the governor without recognising him. Joseph knows them, speaks harshly and accuses them of spying. They protest that they are twelve brothers, the youngest at home and one gone. He swears they will not leave unless the youngest is brought, and holds them three days. Then he offers a different test: one brother stays behind, the rest carry grain home and return with Benjamin. Among themselves they say this is punishment for what they did to their brother.
GEN 42:22-38	Reuben reminds them that he warned against harming the boy. Joseph, who has been using an interpreter, understands every word, turns away and weeps, then binds Simeon in front of them. He orders their sacks filled with grain, their money returned inside, and provisions for the road. One brother finds his silver at the lodging place and they are terrified, asking what God has done to them. At home they report everything to Jacob, and all the money turns up in the sacks. Jacob refuses to let Benjamin go, despite Reuben pledging his own sons.
GEN 43:1-34	With the grain gone, Jacob tells his sons to buy more, and Judah insists they cannot go without Benjamin, offering himself as surety. Jacob relents, sending gifts of balm, honey, spices, nuts and double money. In Egypt Joseph orders a meal prepared. Fearing arrest over the returned silver, the brothers explain themselves to the steward, who reassures them and brings out Simeon. Joseph asks after their father, sees Benjamin, and has to leave the room to weep. He eats apart from them, seats them by age, and gives Benjamin five times as much as anyone else.
GEN 44:1-34	Joseph has their sacks filled and his own silver cup hidden in Benjamin's. Once they have left the city his steward overtakes them and accuses them of theft. Confident, they agree that whoever has it should die; the search runs from oldest to youngest and the cup is in Benjamin's sack. They return and fall on the ground, and Joseph says only the guilty man will be his slave. Judah then makes a long plea: their father has already lost one son of that mother, and losing this one would kill him. He offers himself as a slave in Benjamin's place.
GEN 45:1-28	Joseph clears the room and tells his brothers who he is, weeping aloud. They are too terrified to answer. He tells them not to blame themselves, since God sent him ahead to preserve life, with five years of famine still to come, and has made him ruler of Egypt. They are to fetch their father at once and settle in Goshen. He embraces Benjamin and then all of them. Pharaoh, pleased, sends wagons and promises them the best of Egypt. Loaded with gifts, they carry the news home, and Jacob revives when he sees the wagons.
GEN 46:1-34	At Beersheba, Jacob sacrifices and God tells him in a night vision not to fear going down to Egypt, where he will become a great nation and Joseph will close his eyes. The family travels in Pharaoh's wagons, and the household is listed son by son: thirty-three from Leah, sixteen from Zilpah, fourteen from Rachel, seven from Bilhah, seventy in all. Judah goes ahead to Goshen, where Joseph meets his father and weeps on his neck. Joseph coaches them to say they are herdsmen, since Egyptians despise shepherds, so they will be given Goshen.
GEN 47:1-17	Joseph tells Pharaoh his family has arrived and presents five of his brothers, who say they are shepherds and ask to live in Goshen. Pharaoh grants them the best of the land and offers work managing his own livestock. Jacob is brought in, blesses Pharaoh, and says his hundred and thirty years have been few and hard. Joseph settles them in Rameses and provides food. As the famine bites, he collects all the money in Egypt and Canaan for grain, and when that runs out he takes horses, flocks, herds and donkeys in payment.
GEN 47:18-31	The next year the Egyptians have nothing left but their bodies and their fields, and ask to sell both for bread. Joseph buys all the land for Pharaoh, moves the population into the cities, and leaves only the priests' land untouched. He hands out seed and sets a permanent rule that a fifth of the harvest goes to Pharaoh. Israel prospers in Goshen. Jacob lives seventeen years in Egypt, reaching a hundred and forty-seven, and makes Joseph swear not to bury him there but in his fathers' burial place.
GEN 48:1-22	Told his father is ill, Joseph brings Manasseh and Ephraim. Jacob recalls God's promise at Luz and claims the two boys as his own sons, equal to Reuben and Simeon, then mentions Rachel's death and burial near Ephrath. Nearly blind, he embraces them, and crosses his hands so that his right rests on the younger, Ephraim. Joseph tries to correct him and is refused: Manasseh will be great, but Ephraim greater. Jacob blesses them both, says God will bring the family back to Canaan, and gives Joseph an extra portion.
GEN 49:1-33	Jacob gathers his sons and speaks over each in turn. Reuben loses his standing for defiling his father's bed; Simeon and Levi are cursed for their violence and will be scattered. Judah gets the lion, the scepter and the wine. Zebulun gets the coast, Issachar the burdened donkey, Dan the snake in the path, Gad, Asher and Naphtali brief words each. Joseph is a fruitful vine, shot at but unbroken, and Benjamin a ravenous wolf. Jacob then charges them to bury him at Machpelah with Abraham, Isaac and Leah, and dies.
GEN 50:1-26	Joseph weeps over his father and has him embalmed, which takes forty days, and Egypt mourns seventy. With Pharaoh's leave he takes a great procession of officials, chariots and horsemen to Canaan, mourning seven days at the threshing floor of Atad, and buries Jacob in the cave of Machpelah. Back in Egypt the brothers fear reprisal and offer themselves as slaves. Joseph weeps and tells them that what they meant for evil God meant for good, and promises to provide for them. He lives to a hundred and ten, makes them swear to carry his bones out of Egypt, and is embalmed and coffined.
LEV 1:1-17	God speaks to Moses from the Tent of Meeting and sets out the rules for the burnt offering. Cattle must be an unblemished male, presented at the tent door, with the offerer laying a hand on its head and killing it while the priests handle the blood at the altar. The carcass is flayed, cut up, the innards and legs washed, and the whole thing burned. Sheep and goats follow the same pattern, killed on the north side. A bird offering is a dove or pigeon, its head wrung off and its crop discarded.
LEV 2:1-16	Rules for the grain offering. Fine flour with oil and frankincense, of which the priest burns a handful as a memorial portion and Aaron's sons keep the rest as something most holy. Baked versions are permitted: unleavened cakes from the oven, wafers, griddle bread or pan bread, all of fine flour with oil. Yeast and honey are forbidden on the altar, salt is required on every offering, and a first fruits offering is fresh grain parched and bruised, with oil and frankincense.
LEV 3:1-17	The peace offering. It may be from the herd or the flock, male or female, but unblemished, killed at the tent door with a hand laid on its head while the priests sprinkle the blood around the altar. What burns is the fat: the fat over the innards, the two kidneys with their fat, and the covering of the liver, with a lamb's whole tail fat added. The same procedure covers cattle, sheep and goats. A standing rule closes the chapter: never eat fat or blood.
LEV 4:1-19	Rules for unintentional sin. If the anointed priest sins and brings guilt on the people, he offers a young bull, sprinkling its blood seven times before the veil, daubing the horns of the incense altar and pouring out the rest at the base of the burnt offering altar; the fat is burned and the rest of the carcass taken outside the camp and burned where the ashes go. If the whole congregation sins in ignorance, the assembly brings a bull, the elders lay hands on it, and the priest handles the blood the same way.
LEV 4:20-35	The congregation's bull is treated like the priest's and burned outside the camp, and the people are forgiven. A ruler who sins unwittingly brings a male goat, its blood put on the horns of the burnt offering altar and the rest poured at the base, its fat burned. A commoner brings a female goat, or else a female lamb, handled by the same procedure. In each case the priest makes atonement and the person is forgiven.
LEV 5:1-19	Cases requiring a guilt offering: staying silent as a witness under oath, touching something unclean without realising, or swearing a rash oath. On discovering it, the person confesses and brings a female sheep or goat. Those who cannot afford one bring two doves or pigeons, one for sin and one for burnt offering; those who cannot afford birds bring a tenth of an ephah of flour without oil or frankincense. Wrongs against holy things require an unblemished ram, plus restitution with a fifth added.
LEV 6:1-30	Fraud against a neighbour, robbery, a false oath or a kept deposit require full restitution plus a fifth, then an unblemished ram as a guilt offering. Then come the priests' instructions. The burnt offering stays on the altar overnight and the fire must never go out; the priest clears the ashes in linen, changes clothes and carries them outside the camp. Grain offerings are eaten unleavened in the courtyard by Aaron's male descendants, but a priest's own grain offering is burned entirely. Sin offering meat is eaten in a holy place, its earthen pot broken afterwards.
LEV 7:1-19	The guilt offering follows the sin offering's law: killed where the burnt offering is, its fat burned, the meat eaten by the priests in a holy place. Priestly portions are set out: the hide of a burnt offering and every baked grain offering go to the officiating priest. A peace offering given in thanksgiving comes with leavened and unleavened cakes and must be eaten the same day; one given for a vow or freely may be eaten the next day, but anything left on the third day is burned. Meat that touches something unclean is burned.
LEV 7:20-38	Anyone unclean who eats peace offering meat is cut off from the people. Fat and blood are forbidden entirely, whether from cattle, sheep, goats or birds, though fat from an animal found dead may be used for other purposes. The offerer brings the fat and breast himself; the breast is waved and goes to Aaron's family, and the right thigh goes to the priest who handled the blood. These portions are theirs permanently. A summary closes the section, naming the laws given to Moses at Sinai.
LEV 8:1-21	With the whole congregation assembled at the tent door, Moses ordains Aaron and his sons. He washes them, dresses Aaron in the coat, sash, robe, ephod and breastplate with the Urim and Thummim, and sets the turban with its gold plate on his head. He anoints the tabernacle, its furnishings and the altar, sprinkling it seven times, then pours oil on Aaron's head and dresses his sons. A bull is offered for sin, its blood daubed on the altar horns and the carcass burned outside the camp, then a ram is offered whole as a burnt offering.
LEV 8:22-36	The second ram, the ram of consecration, is killed and its blood put on the right ear, right thumb and right big toe of Aaron and each of his sons. The fat, the right thigh and three kinds of bread from the basket are placed in their hands and waved before God, then burned; Moses takes the breast as his own portion. He sprinkles anointing oil and altar blood over the men and their garments. They are to boil and eat the meat at the tent door, burn the leftovers, and stay there seven days on pain of death. They do everything as commanded.
LEV 9:1-24	On the eighth day Moses has Aaron begin his ministry. Aaron offers a calf for his own sin and a ram as a burnt offering, then the people's goat, calf and lamb, a grain offering, and a bull and ram as peace offerings, handling the blood at the altar and waving the breast and right thigh. He blesses the people, and after he and Moses come out of the Tent of Meeting the glory of God appears. Fire comes out and consumes the offering on the altar, and the people shout and fall on their faces.
LEV 10:1-20	Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorised fire before God and are killed by fire. Moses tells Aaron this is what it means for God to be treated as holy, and Aaron says nothing. Cousins carry the bodies out of the camp, and the surviving priests are forbidden to mourn or leave the tent. God bans wine for priests on duty and charges them to distinguish holy from common and to teach the law. Moses is angry that the sin offering goat was burned rather than eaten, and accepts Aaron's answer that eating it on such a day would not have been right.
LEV 11:1-28	Clean and unclean creatures. Land animals must both have split hooves and chew the cud, which rules out the camel, the cony, the hare and the pig. Water creatures must have fins and scales. A list of birds is banned, from eagles and vultures to the stork, hoopoe and bat. Flying insects are out except hopping ones: locusts, katydids, crickets and grasshoppers. Touching a forbidden carcass makes a person unclean until evening, and carrying one requires washing clothes as well.
LEV 11:29-47	Eight small creatures are listed unclean, among them the weasel, the rat, the gecko and the chameleon. If one dies on a utensil the object must be washed, an earthen vessel broken, and an oven or stove smashed; a spring or cistern stays clean, and dry seed stays clean but wet seed does not. Touching or carrying the carcass of an animal that was otherwise edible also brings uncleanness until evening. Anything that crawls is forbidden as food. The reason given is that God is holy, so Israel is to be holy too.
LEV 12:1-8	Purification after childbirth. A woman who bears a son is unclean seven days, the boy is circumcised on the eighth, and she waits another thirty-three days before touching anything holy or entering the sanctuary. For a daughter both periods double, to two weeks and sixty-six days. At the end she brings a year-old lamb as a burnt offering and a pigeon or dove as a sin offering, and the priest makes atonement. If she cannot afford a lamb, two birds will do.
LEV 13:1-30	Diagnostic rules for skin disease. A swelling, scab or bright spot is brought to a priest, who looks for whitened hair and a sore deeper than the skin; uncertain cases are isolated seven days and re-examined, sometimes twice. Chronic disease with raw flesh is unclean at once, while a condition that has turned entirely white is declared clean, and raw flesh reappearing makes it unclean again. Similar tests apply to spots arising in a healed boil or burn, and to sores on the head or beard, where thin yellow hair is the sign.
LEV 13:31-59	An itch on the head or beard is isolated and the surrounding hair shaved, and black hair growing back means healing. Dull white patches are a harmless rash, and baldness itself is clean, though a reddish-white sore on a bald scalp is not. A person declared leprous wears torn clothes, leaves his hair loose, covers his lip, calls out "Unclean" and lives outside the camp. The same procedure covers mould in wool, linen or leather: isolate it, wash it, watch whether it spreads, cut out or burn the affected part.
LEV 14:1-25	The ritual for a healed leper. The priest goes outside the camp to inspect him, then takes two birds, cedar wood, scarlet yarn and hyssop; one bird is killed over running water, the other dipped in its blood and released, and the man is sprinkled seven times. He washes, shaves and bathes, waits seven days, shaves everything again, and on the eighth day brings two male lambs, a ewe lamb, flour and oil. Blood from the guilt offering and then oil are put on his right ear, thumb and big toe. The poor bring one lamb and two birds instead.
LEV 14:26-57	The reduced ritual runs the same way: oil sprinkled seven times, dabbed on ear, thumb and toe over the blood, the rest poured on his head, and two birds offered for sin and burnt offering. Then comes mould in a house. The owner reports it, the priest empties and inspects the house and shuts it seven days; spreading mould means removing the stones, scraping and replastering, and if it returns the house is demolished and carted outside the city. A clean house is purified with the same two birds, cedar, scarlet and hyssop.
LEV 15:1-33	Rules about bodily discharges. A man with a discharge makes unclean any bed, seat or saddle he uses, and anyone touching him, his spit or his things must wash and wait until evening; earthenware he touches is broken. After it stops he counts seven days, bathes, and on the eighth brings two birds for sin and burnt offerings. An emission of semen requires bathing, and so does intercourse. A woman is unclean seven days during her period, with the same rules for what she lies or sits on, and a prolonged discharge is treated the same way, ending with seven days and two birds.
LEV 16:1-17	After the death of Aaron's two sons, God restricts entry to the Most Holy Place. Once prepared, Aaron bathes, dresses in plain linen, and brings a bull for his own sin, a ram, and two goats from the people. Lots decide which goat is for God and which is sent away. He offers the bull, carries a censer of coals and incense inside the veil so the cloud covers the mercy seat, and sprinkles the bull's blood on and before it seven times. The people's goat is killed and its blood used the same way. Nobody else may be in the tent.
LEV 16:18-34	Aaron then puts blood from both animals on the horns of the altar and sprinkles it seven times to cleanse it. He lays both hands on the live goat, confesses over it all Israel's sins, and has a man lead it into the wilderness. He leaves the linen garments in the tent, bathes, changes, and offers the burnt offerings. The man who released the goat and the man who burns the carcasses outside the camp must wash. The tenth day of the seventh month is fixed as a permanent day of self-denial and complete rest, atoning for the nation once a year.
LEV 17:1-16	All slaughter of cattle, sheep or goats must be brought to the Tent of Meeting, and anyone who kills an animal elsewhere is treated as having shed blood and is cut off. The point is to stop sacrifices in the open field and to end offerings to goat idols. Eating blood of any kind is forbidden, because the life is in the blood and the blood is what makes atonement on the altar. A hunter must pour out an animal's blood and cover it with earth. Eating something found dead or torn requires washing and lasts unclean until evening.
LEV 18:1-30	Israel is told not to copy the practices of Egypt or Canaan. A long list of forbidden sexual relationships follows, covering mother, stepmother, sister and half-sister, granddaughter, aunt by blood or marriage, daughter-in-law, sister-in-law, a woman and her daughter or granddaughter, and a wife's sister while the wife lives. Also forbidden are sex during menstruation, adultery, sacrificing children to Molech, sex between men, and sex with animals. The reason given is that these things defiled the previous inhabitants until the land vomited them out, and the same will happen to Israel.
LEV 19:1-37	A mixed collection of laws under the heading that Israel must be holy because God is holy. It covers respect for parents, Sabbath, avoiding idols, eating peace offerings within two days, leaving field corners and fallen grapes for the poor and the foreigner, honest dealing, prompt wages, fair judgment, not cursing the deaf or tripping the blind, not slandering, not bearing a grudge, and loving your neighbour as yourself. Then mixed breeding and mixed cloth, fruit trees left unharvested three years, bans on divination, certain haircuts, tattoos and mediums, respect for the old, equal treatment of foreigners, and honest weights.
LEV 20:1-27	Penalties for the offences already named. Giving a child to Molech means death by stoning, and a community that looks away is implicated. Consulting mediums, cursing a parent, adultery, sex with a father's wife or a daughter-in-law, sex between men, and taking both a woman and her mother all carry death, in the last case by burning. Sex with an animal means death for both. Other cases bring being cut off, or childlessness. Israel is told to keep these laws so the land will not vomit them out, to distinguish clean from unclean animals, and to be holy because God is holy.
NUM 31:1-23	Yahweh tells Moses to avenge Israel on Midian, after which he will die. Twelve thousand men, a thousand per tribe, go out with Phinehas and the sanctuary trumpets. They kill every Midianite male, the five kings, and Balaam son of Beor, burn the towns, and bring back the women, children and livestock. Moses is angry the women were spared and orders the boys and every woman who has known a man killed. The soldiers stay outside the camp seven days, and metal plunder is purified by fire.
NUM 31:24-54	The soldiers wash their clothes on the seventh day and return to camp. Moses, Eleazar and the family heads count the plunder and halve it between the fighters and the congregation. One in five hundred of the soldiers' half goes to Eleazar, one in fifty of the people's half to the Levites. The totals are 675,000 sheep, 72,000 cattle, 61,000 donkeys and 32,000 captive women. The officers report not one Israelite missing and bring 16,750 shekels of gold.
NUM 32:1-20	Reuben and Gad, who own huge herds, see that Jazer and Gilead are good grazing land and ask Moses to give them that territory instead of crossing the Jordan. Moses accuses them of discouraging Israel exactly as the spies did at Kadesh Barnea, which cost that generation the land and forty years of wandering. They answer that they will build sheepfolds and cities for their families, then go armed ahead of Israel and not return home until every tribe has its inheritance. Moses begins to set terms.
NUM 32:21-42	Moses sets the condition: every armed man must cross the Jordan and fight until the land is subdued, after which they may return and hold Gilead. If they refuse, they have sinned, and their sin will find them out. Gad and Reuben agree, and Moses puts Eleazar, Joshua and the tribal heads in charge of enforcing it. He assigns Gad, Reuben and half of Manasseh the kingdoms of Sihon and Og. The two tribes rebuild and rename the cities, and Machir, Jair and Nobah take towns in Gilead.
NUM 33:1-56	Moses records the whole itinerary out of Egypt: some forty camps from Rameses, through the sea, Marah, Elim with its twelve springs and seventy palms, Sinai, Kadesh and Mount Hor, where Aaron died at a hundred and twenty-three in the fortieth year, ending in the plains of Moab. Yahweh then orders Israel, on crossing the Jordan, to drive out the inhabitants, destroy their idols and high places, and divide the land by lot. Any inhabitants left will be thorns in their sides.
NUM 34:1-29	Yahweh dictates the borders of Canaan: south from the wilderness of Zin along Edom, west the great sea, north from the sea to Mount Hor and Hazar Enan, east down past Chinnereth to the Jordan and the Salt Sea. Moses notes this is for the nine and a half tribes, since Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh already hold land east of the Jordan. Eleazar and Joshua will divide it, with one named prince from each remaining tribe, Caleb first.
NUM 35:1-17	The Levites, who get no tribal territory, are to receive forty-eight cities with pasture measured two thousand cubits out on each side. Six of those are cities of refuge, three east of the Jordan and three in Canaan, open to Israelites and foreigners alike, where anyone who kills a person accidentally can flee the avenger of blood until the assembly judges the case. A killer who used an iron tool or a stone is a murderer and is put to death.
NUM 35:18-34	The law continues: killing with a wooden weapon, or out of hatred, ambush or hostility, makes a man a murderer, and the avenger of blood executes him. If the death was sudden and without enmity, the assembly judges and returns him to his city of refuge, where he must stay until the high priest dies. If he leaves early, the avenger may kill him without guilt. Conviction needs more than one witness, and no ransom may be taken for a murderer.
NUM 36:1-13	The heads of Gilead's family raise a problem with the inheritance of Zelophehad's daughters: if they marry outside the tribe, their land goes with them and Manasseh loses it at the jubilee. Moses rules that they are right. The daughters may marry whom they choose, provided it is within their father's tribe, and the same applies to any heiress, so no inheritance moves between tribes. Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah and Noah marry their cousins, and Numbers ends in the plains of Moab.
DEU 13:1-18	Three cases of enticement to other gods. A prophet whose sign comes true but who urges worship of other gods is a test, and is to be put to death. A brother, child, spouse or closest friend who suggests it in private must not be pitied or hidden but stoned, the hearer's hand first. A whole city led astray is to be investigated carefully, then destroyed with its livestock, its plunder burned in the street, and left a ruin that is never rebuilt.
DEU 14:1-29	Israel is not to gash itself or shave its head for the dead. Food laws follow: cloven-hoofed cud-chewers may be eaten, but not camel, hare, rabbit or pig; fish need fins and scales; birds of prey, the bat, winged insects and anything found dead are forbidden. A kid is not to be boiled in its mother's milk. Tithes are eaten at the chosen place, or sold for money if the journey is long, and every third year stored locally for the Levite, foreigner, orphan and widow.
DEU 15:1-23	Every seventh year debts between Israelites are cancelled, though a foreigner's may still be collected. Lenders are warned not to refuse a loan because the year of release is near, since the poor will never cease out of the land. A Hebrew slave goes free in the seventh year and must be sent off supplied from flock, threshing floor and winepress. One who chooses to stay has his ear pierced to the door with an awl. Firstborn animals are dedicated, but a defective one is eaten at home.
DEU 16:1-22	The three annual festivals. Passover is kept in Abib at the chosen place only, at sunset, with unleavened bread for seven days and no meat left overnight. Weeks is counted seven weeks from the first sickle and kept with a freewill offering. Tents lasts seven days after the harvest. All three include servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans and widows, and every male appears three times a year, never empty-handed. Judges are appointed who take no bribes, since a bribe blinds the wise.
DEU 17:1-20	No defective animal may be sacrificed. Anyone who worships other gods or the sun, moon or stars is stoned after diligent inquiry, on the word of two or three witnesses and never one, with the witnesses casting first. Cases too hard for local judges go to the priests and the judge at the chosen place, whose verdict is binding on pain of death. If Israel asks for a king, he must be an Israelite, must not accumulate horses, wives or silver, and must write out and read this law daily.
DEU 18:1-22	The Levites hold no land and live on the offerings, receiving the shoulder, cheeks and inner parts of sacrifices, plus first fruits and the first fleece. A Levite who moves to the chosen place shares equally. Israel must not imitate the nations: child sacrifice, divination, sorcery, charms, mediums or consulting the dead. God will raise up a prophet like Moses, since the people asked at Horeb not to hear the voice again. A prophet who speaks presumptuously dies, and the test is whether his word comes true.
DEU 19:1-21	Three cities of refuge are to be set apart, with roads prepared, and three more if the territory grows. The example given is an axe head flying off its handle and killing a companion. A man who killed out of hatred and ambush is handed over by the elders to the avenger of blood. Boundary markers may not be moved. No one is convicted on one witness, and a witness proved false suffers what he intended, life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth.
DEU 20:1-20	Rules for war. A priest addresses the army, and officers send home anyone with a new house, a new vineyard or a fiancee, and anyone who is afraid, so his fear does not spread. Distant cities are offered peace first, and if they refuse, the men are killed and the rest taken as plunder. The cities of the seven Canaanite nations are to be destroyed entirely, so their practices are not learned. Fruit trees may not be cut down during a siege.
DEU 21:1-23	An unsolved killing is expiated by the nearest city's elders breaking a heifer's neck in an unploughed valley and washing their hands over it, declaring their innocence. A captive woman a soldier wishes to marry shaves her head, trims her nails and mourns her parents a month first, and if he rejects her she goes free and may not be sold. A firstborn son's double portion holds even if his mother is the unloved wife. A rebellious son is stoned, and an executed body is buried the same day.
DEU 22:1-30	A lost ox, sheep, donkey or garment must be returned, and a fallen animal helped up. Clothing of the other sex is forbidden, as are mixed seed, ploughing with ox and donkey together, and wool woven with linen. Cloaks get fringes, roofs get railings, and a mother bird must be let go. Sexual offences follow: a false accusation against a bride costs a hundred shekels, adultery is capital for both, and a betrothed woman forced in open country is held guiltless while the man dies.
DEU 23:1-25	Rules on who may enter the assembly: not the emasculated, not those of a forbidden union, and not Ammonites or Moabites to the tenth generation, because they refused bread and water and hired Balaam. Edomites and Egyptians may enter in the third generation. The camp must be kept clean, with a latrine outside and a trowel among the weapons. An escaped slave must not be handed back, no interest may be charged to an Israelite, and vows must be paid.
DEU 24:1-22	Divorce requires a written bill, and a woman who has remarried may not return to her first husband. A newly married man is exempt from war and business for a year. A millstone may not be taken as a pledge, kidnapping is capital, and a poor man's cloak taken in pledge must be returned by sunset. Wages are paid the same day. Children are not executed for their fathers' sins. Forgotten sheaves, olives and grapes are left for the foreigner, the orphan and the widow.
DEU 25:1-19	A flogging is capped at forty stripes so the man is not degraded, and an ox is not muzzled while treading grain. If a man dies childless, his brother marries the widow and her first son carries the dead man's name. A brother who refuses is summoned before the elders, has his sandal pulled off and is spat at. A woman who seizes a fighting man's genitals loses her hand. Weights and measures must be honest, and Amalek, who struck the stragglers, is to be blotted out.
DEU 26:1-19	On entering the land, the first fruits are brought in a basket to the priest with a recital: my father was a wandering Syrian, we went to Egypt, were oppressed, cried out, and were brought here with signs and wonders. The offering is set down, and the household, the Levite and the foreigner rejoice. In the third year the tithe goes to the Levite, foreigner, orphan and widow, with a declaration that it was handled properly. Israel and God each declare the other their own.
DEU 27:1-26	Moses orders that on crossing the Jordan, great plastered stones be set up on Mount Ebal with the law written plainly on them, and an altar of uncut stones built there for offerings and a meal. Six tribes stand on Gerizim for the blessing, six on Ebal for the curse. The Levites shout twelve curses, against secret idols, dishonouring parents, moving landmarks, misleading the blind, denying justice, incest, bestiality, secret murder and bribes to kill, and the people answer amen to each.
DEU 28:1-25	Obedience brings blessing, listed in pairs: in the city and in the field, in body, ground and livestock, in basket and kneading trough, coming in and going out. Enemies flee seven ways, rain comes in season, Israel lends and does not borrow, and is the head and not the tail. Disobedience reverses every item. Then the curses proper begin: pestilence, consumption, fever, blight and mildew, a sky of brass and earth of iron, rain of dust, and defeat before enemies.
DEU 28:26-50	The curses continue: unburied bodies eaten by birds, incurable boils and tumours, madness and blindness, groping at noon. Everything built or planted is taken by others, wife, house, vineyard, ox, donkey and sheep, and children are carried off while their parents watch. Locusts and worms eat the crops. The foreigner rises while Israel sinks to the tail. Israel and its king are carried to an unknown nation and serve their enemies in hunger under an iron yoke.
DEU 28:51-68	The final curses describe a siege: the walls Israel trusted come down, and famine drives parents to eat their own children in secret. Plagues of long duration follow, including all the diseases of Egypt, and a nation once numerous as the stars is left few. They are uprooted and scattered from one end of the earth to the other, with trembling hearts and no rest, longing in the morning for evening and in the evening for morning. The last verse returns them to Egypt in ships, unsold.
DEU 29:1-29	Moses makes a second covenant in Moab, in addition to the one at Horeb. He recalls Egypt, the forty years in which clothes and sandals did not wear out, and the defeat of Sihon and Og. Everyone stands to enter the oath: leaders, wives, children, and the foreigners who cut wood and draw water, along with those not present. Anyone who secretly turns to other gods will be blotted out, and the land left sulphur and salt like Sodom. The secret things belong to God.
DEU 30:1-20	Moses looks past the exile: when the scattered people remember and return with all their heart, God will gather them from the ends of the heavens, bring them back, circumcise their hearts, and put the curses on their enemies. He insists the command is not remote, not in heaven or across the sea, but in their mouth and heart. He sets before them life and death, blessing and curse, calls heaven and earth as witnesses, and tells them to choose life.
DEU 31:1-16	At a hundred and twenty, Moses tells Israel he cannot cross the Jordan, but God and Joshua will go ahead of them. He charges Joshua publicly to be strong and courageous. He writes the law, gives it to the Levitical priests and the elders, and commands that it be read aloud to the whole assembly, women, children and foreigners included, every seventh year at the feast of tents. God tells him he is about to die and summons Joshua to the Tent, appearing in a pillar of cloud.
DEU 31:17-30	God predicts that once fat and settled, Israel will turn to other gods, and he will hide his face until they ask whether these evils came because God is not among them. He tells Moses to write a song and teach it as a witness. Moses writes it, commissions Joshua, finishes the book of the law, and has the Levites place it beside the ark as a witness. He says plainly that they rebelled while he lived and will corrupt themselves after his death, then recites the song.
EST 1:1-22	King Ahasuerus, ruler of a hundred and twenty-seven provinces, throws a hundred and eighty days of display for his officials, followed by a seven-day feast in the palace garden with marble pillars, gold couches and unlimited wine. Queen Vashti holds her own feast for the women. On the seventh day the king, merry with wine, sends seven eunuchs to bring Vashti out so the guests can admire her beauty. She refuses, and he is furious. His advisers, led by Memucan, warn that other wives will follow her example, and propose an irrevocable decree barring her from his presence and giving her position to someone else. Letters go out across the empire.
EST 2:1-23	The king's servants propose gathering beautiful young women into the harem so he can choose a new queen. Among them is Esther, an orphaned Jew brought up by her cousin Mordecai, who tells her to keep her people secret. Hegai, keeper of the women, favours her and gives her the best quarters. After twelve months of prescribed beauty treatments each woman goes in to the king; Esther pleases him more than any other and is crowned in place of Vashti. Mordecai, sitting at the palace gate, learns of a plot by two eunuchs, Bigthan and Teresh, reports it through Esther, and they are hanged.
EST 3:1-15	Ahasuerus promotes Haman the Agagite above all his officials and orders everyone to bow to him. Mordecai will not, and when Haman learns he is a Jew he decides to destroy not just Mordecai but every Jew in the empire. Lots are cast and the twelfth month, Adar, is chosen. Haman tells the king of a scattered people who keep their own laws, and offers ten thousand talents of silver for permission to wipe them out. The king hands over his signet ring and tells him to do as he likes. Couriers carry the decree to every province, and the king and Haman sit down to drink while Susa is bewildered.
EST 4:1-17	Mordecai tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and ashes and wails in the city, as Jews mourn and fast across the provinces. Esther, told of it, sends clothes, which he refuses, then sends the eunuch Hathach to ask what is wrong. Mordecai sends back the details, a copy of the decree, and a demand that she plead with the king. Esther answers that anyone entering the king's presence uncalled is put to death, and she has not been summoned for thirty days. Mordecai replies that she will not escape either, and asks who knows whether she came to the throne for this moment. She asks for a three-day fast and says that if she dies, she dies.
EST 5:1-14	On the third day Esther puts on her royal robes and enters the inner court. The king holds out the golden scepter and offers her anything up to half the kingdom. She asks only that he and Haman come to a banquet she has prepared. At the banquet he asks again, and she asks them both back the following day, promising to state her request then. Haman leaves pleased until he passes Mordecai at the gate, who will not rise for him. At home he boasts of his wealth and his invitations, then complains that Mordecai spoils it all. His wife Zeresh and his friends tell him to build a gallows fifty cubits high, and he does.
EST 6:1-14	Sleepless, the king has the royal chronicles read aloud and hears how Mordecai exposed the assassination plot without ever being rewarded. Haman happens to be waiting outside, intending to ask permission to hang Mordecai, and is called in. Asked what should be done for a man the king wishes to honour, he assumes he is the man and proposes royal robes, the king's horse and a herald. The king orders him to do exactly that for Mordecai. Haman leads the horse through the square, then goes home covering his head, and his wife and advisers tell him he is going to fall.
EST 7:1-10	At the second banquet the king again offers Esther whatever she asks. She asks for her own life and the lives of her people, saying they have been sold for destruction. Asked who is responsible, she names Haman. The king storms out into the garden, and Haman throws himself on Esther's couch to beg for his life. Returning, the king takes this as an assault on the queen, and Haman's face is covered. The eunuch Harbonah mentions the fifty-cubit gallows standing at Haman's house, and the king has Haman hanged on it.
EST 8:1-17	The king gives Haman's estate to Esther and his signet ring to Mordecai, whom Esther puts in charge of the household. She then falls at the king's feet in tears, begging him to undo Haman's decree. Since a sealed royal order cannot be revoked, he tells her and Mordecai to write whatever they wish in his name. Letters go out to all hundred and twenty-seven provinces granting the Jews the right to assemble and defend themselves against attackers on the thirteenth of Adar. Mordecai comes out in blue and white with a gold crown, Susa cheers, and many people in the provinces become Jews out of fear.
EST 9:1-17	On the thirteenth of Adar, the day meant for their destruction, the Jews assemble in their cities and strike at those who meant to harm them, with provincial officials assisting because Mordecai's power is now feared. Five hundred men die in the citadel of Susa, including Haman's ten sons, who are named, and no plunder is taken. Told the numbers, the king asks Esther what else she wants; she asks for another day in Susa and for the ten sons' bodies to be hanged. Three hundred more die there, and seventy-five thousand in the provinces. The fourteenth becomes a day of feasting.
EST 9:18-32	Because the Jews of Susa fought on two days and rested on the fifteenth, while those in the unwalled towns rested on the fourteenth, both days are kept. Mordecai writes to every province instructing an annual observance of the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar as days of feasting, gladness, presents of food and gifts to the poor, marking the turn from mourning to celebration. The name Purim comes from the lot Haman cast. The Jews take the custom on themselves and their descendants permanently, and Esther and Mordecai send a second letter confirming it, which is written down.
EST 10:1-3	A short closing note. Ahasuerus imposes tribute across the land and the coastal islands. His achievements and the full account of Mordecai's greatness are said to be recorded in the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia. Mordecai stands second to the king himself, holds high standing among the Jews, is respected by his own people, and works for their welfare and for peace for those who come after him.
JOS 1:1-18	After Moses dies, God tells Joshua to cross the Jordan and take the land, promising that nobody will withstand him and that he will not be abandoned. He is repeatedly told to be strong and courageous, to keep the whole law without deviating, and to keep the book of the law constantly in mind. Joshua orders the people to prepare provisions for a crossing in three days, and reminds Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh that their fighting men must cross armed ahead of the others. They promise to obey him as they obeyed Moses.
JOS 2:1-24	Joshua sends two spies into Jericho, and they lodge with a prostitute named Rahab. When the king's men come looking, she hides them under flax on the roof and sends the search toward the Jordan fords. She tells the spies she knows the land is theirs, having heard about the Red Sea and the defeat of Sihon and Og, and asks that her family be spared. They agree, on condition she keeps quiet and gathers her household inside the house marked by a scarlet cord in the window. She lowers them from the wall, and they hide three days before reporting back.
JOS 3:1-17	The camp moves to the Jordan. After three days the officers tell the people to follow the ark at a distance of two thousand cubits, and Joshua tells them to consecrate themselves for the wonder to come. God says he will begin to raise Joshua's standing before Israel, and instructs that the priests carrying the ark stop at the water's edge. When their feet touch the Jordan, which is in full flood at harvest, the water upstream piles up at Adam near Zarethan and the flow to the Salt Sea stops. The priests stand in the riverbed while the whole nation crosses on dry ground.
JOS 4:1-24	Twelve men, one from each tribe, take twelve stones from where the priests stood and carry them out, and Joshua also sets up twelve stones in the riverbed itself. The stones are to prompt children in future to ask what they mean. Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh cross armed at the head of about forty thousand fighting men, and Joshua's standing with the people is confirmed. When the priests come up out of the Jordan the water returns and floods its banks again. The people camp at Gilgal, where the stones are set up as a memorial.
JOS 5:1-15	News of the dried-up Jordan leaves the Amorite and Canaanite kings without courage. God tells Joshua to circumcise the nation, since the men who left Egypt died in the wilderness and their sons born on the way were never circumcised. It is done with flint knives at Gibeath Haaraloth, and the camp waits while they heal; the place is named Gilgal. They keep the Passover on the plains of Jericho, eat produce of the land the next day, and the manna stops. Near Jericho Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword who says he is commander of God's army, and tells him to take off his sandals.
JOS 6:1-27	Jericho is shut tight. God tells Joshua to march the army around it once a day for six days, with seven priests carrying seven ram's horn trumpets before the ark, then seven times on the seventh day. The people march in silence, and on the seventh day at Joshua's word they shout, the wall falls flat and they take the city. Everything in it is destroyed, people and animals alike, and burned, with the metal put into the treasury. The two spies fetch Rahab and her whole family out alive, as promised. Joshua puts a curse on anyone who rebuilds the city.
JOS 7:1-26	Achan of Judah takes some of the plunder that was to be destroyed. Joshua, told Ai is weakly held, sends only three thousand men, who are routed with thirty-six dead, and the people lose heart. Joshua tears his clothes and lies before the ark until evening, and God tells him to get up: Israel has broken the covenant and will not stand until the offence is removed.
