Lots narrow it down by tribe, family and household to Achan, who admits taking a Babylonian robe, silver and gold and burying them in his tent. He and his household are stoned and burned in the valley of Achor.
JOS 8:1-18	God tells Joshua to attack Ai, this time keeping the livestock and goods, and to set an ambush behind the city. Joshua sends thirty thousand men out by night to hide west of Ai between it and Bethel, with a further five thousand in ambush, and camps the main force north of the city across a valley. His plan is to feign the earlier rout and draw the defenders out. The king of Ai takes the bait, and every man in Ai and Bethel leaves the city open and chases Israel toward the wilderness. God tells Joshua to stretch out his javelin toward the city, and he does.
JOS 8:19-35	The ambush runs into Ai and sets it on fire. Seeing the smoke behind them, the men of Ai are trapped between two forces and cut down, with twelve thousand killed and none escaping. Joshua holds out the javelin until it is done. Only the livestock and goods are taken, and the city is left a permanent ruin. The king is hanged until sundown, then buried under a heap of stones. Joshua builds an altar of uncut stones on Mount Ebal, writes a copy of the law on stones, and reads out the whole law with its blessing and curse to the entire assembly.
JOS 9:1-27	The kings of the region unite against Israel, but Gibeon tries a different approach. Its people arrive at Gilgal in worn clothes and patched sandals with dry, mouldy bread, claiming to have travelled from a distant country because of God's reputation, and ask for a treaty. The Israelites inspect the provisions but do not consult God, and Joshua swears a covenant to let them live. Three days later the truth comes out, and the people complain, but the oath holds. Joshua confronts them, and they admit they lied out of fear. He spares them and makes them woodcutters and water carriers.
JOS 10:1-23	Alarmed by Gibeon's treaty with Israel, Adoni-Zedek of Jerusalem brings the kings of Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish and Eglon to attack it. Gibeon appeals to Joshua, who marches all night from Gilgal. God throws the Amorites into confusion, and Israel cuts them down from Gibeon to Azekah and Makkedah; more die from hailstones out of the sky than by the sword. Joshua calls on the sun to stand still over Gibeon and the moon over Aijalon, and the day is held. The five kings hide in a cave at Makkedah, and Joshua has it sealed with stones until the pursuit is finished, then has them brought out.
JOS 10:24-43	Joshua has his commanders put their feet on the necks of the five kings, tells them not to be afraid, then kills them and hangs the bodies until sunset before throwing them into the cave and sealing it with stones. He then takes Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron and Debir in turn, killing every inhabitant and each king, and destroys the king of Gezer's relief force as well. The account concludes that he struck the whole region from Kadesh Barnea to Gaza and left nobody alive, because God fought for Israel, then returned to Gilgal.
JOS 11:1-23	Jabin of Hazor gathers a northern coalition with horses and chariots as numerous as sand, camped at the waters of Merom. God tells Joshua not to fear and to hamstring the horses and burn the chariots. Joshua attacks suddenly, drives them as far as Sidon, and leaves no survivors. He takes Hazor, kills its king and burns the city, the only one on its mound he burns, while sparing the others' structures and taking their livestock and goods as plunder. No city made peace except Gibeon. He clears the Anakim from the hill country, and the land, divided among the tribes, has rest from war.
JOS 12:1-24	A summary of conquests. East of the Jordan, Moses defeated Sihon king of Heshbon, whose territory ran from the Arnon to the Jabbok, and Og king of Bashan, the last of the Rephaim, and gave that land to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh. West of the Jordan, Joshua's conquests from Baal Gad to Mount Halak are set out as a roll call of defeated kings, one apiece, beginning with Jericho and Ai and running through Jerusalem, Hebron, Lachish, Megiddo, Hazor and Tirzah. The total is thirty-one kings.
JOS 13:1-33	Joshua is old, and much land is still unconquered: Philistine territory from the Shihor to Ekron, the Geshurites, Sidonian country, Lebanon and the land of the Gebalites. God tells him to allocate it anyway and promises to drive out the inhabitants. The eastern allotments made by Moses are then restated. Reuben gets the plain around Heshbon and Medeba, in the account of which Balaam is noted among the killed. Gad gets Jazer, Gilead and the Jordan valley up to the Sea of Chinnereth, and half of Manasseh gets Bashan. Levi receives no land, only the offerings.
JOS 14:1-15	Eleazar, Joshua and the tribal heads divide Canaan by lot among the nine and a half tribes, since Moses had already settled the two and a half east of the Jordan, and the Levites get only towns and pasture. Caleb then comes forward: he was forty when he scouted the land and reported honestly while the others frightened the people, and Moses swore the land he walked on would be his. Now eighty-five and still fit for war, he asks for the hill country where the Anakim and their fortified cities are. Joshua blesses him and gives him Hebron.
JOS 15:1-14	Judah's allotment is traced by its borders. The southern line runs from the end of the Salt Sea past the ascent of Akrabbim, Zin and Kadesh Barnea to the brook of Egypt and the sea. The east border is the Salt Sea, and the northern line goes up through Beth Hoglah and the valley of Achor, past Jerusalem and the valley of Hinnom, on to Kiriath Jearim, Beth Shemesh and Ekron before reaching the sea. The Mediterranean is the western limit. Caleb receives Hebron within Judah's territory and drives out Anak's three sons, Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai.
JOS 15:15-63	Caleb offers his daughter Achsah to whoever takes Debir, and his relative Othniel does it; she then asks her father for springs to go with her dry southern land, and gets the upper and lower springs. The rest of the chapter lists Judah's towns by region: twenty-nine in the far south, then groups of fourteen, sixteen and nine in the lowland, the Philistine coast around Ekron, Ashdod and Gaza, several groups in the hill country, and six in the wilderness including En Gedi. Judah could not drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem, and they still live there.
JOS 16:1-10	The allotment for Joseph's descendants starts at the Jordan by Jericho and runs up through the hill country to Bethel, then west past Beth Horon and Gezer to the sea. Ephraim's own border is described in detail, from Ataroth Addar and upper Beth Horon westward to the brook of Kanah and the sea, and eastward back down to the Jordan, along with towns set aside for Ephraim inside Manasseh's territory. Ephraim did not drive the Canaanites out of Gezer; they remain there as forced labour.
JOS 17:1-18	Manasseh's allotment. Machir's line already holds Gilead and Bashan, so the remaining families are listed, and the daughters of Zelophehad, who had no brothers, come to Eleazar and Joshua and are given land alongside their father's kinsmen, making ten portions west of the Jordan. The border with Ephraim is described, with several towns in Issachar and Asher belonging to Manasseh, whose people could not expel the Canaanites and later put them to forced labour. Joseph's descendants complain that one allotment is too small, and Joshua tells them to clear the forest and take the valleys despite the iron chariots.
JOS 18:1-28	The assembly gathers at Shiloh and sets up the Tent of Meeting, with seven tribes still unsettled. Joshua asks how long they will delay taking possession, and has three men from each tribe survey the remaining land and write it up in seven portions, Judah holding the south and Joseph the north. He casts lots for them at Shiloh. Benjamin's lot falls between Judah and Joseph, its border traced from the Jordan past Jericho and Bethel and back down past Jerusalem to the Salt Sea. Its towns are listed in two groups, twelve and fourteen, Jericho, Gibeon and Jerusalem among them.
JOS 19:1-51	The remaining lots. Simeon gets thirteen towns and then four more inside Judah's territory, which was larger than Judah needed. Zebulun gets twelve towns around Sarid, Issachar sixteen around Jezreel, Asher twenty-two reaching to Carmel, Sidon and Tyre, and Naphtali nineteen fortified towns including Hazor and Kedesh. Dan gets Zorah, Aijalon, Ekron and the coast near Joppa, and later takes Leshem by force and renames it Dan. With the division finished, Israel gives Joshua the town he asked for, Timnath Serah in the hill country of Ephraim, and he rebuilds and settles there.
JOS 20:1-9	God tells Joshua to designate the cities of refuge promised through Moses. A person who kills someone accidentally may flee to one, state his case at the city gate, and be taken in and given a place to live; the elders are not to hand him over to the avenger of blood. He stays until he has stood trial before the assembly and until the death of the serving high priest, after which he may go home. Six cities are set apart: Kedesh, Shechem and Hebron west of the Jordan, and Bezer, Ramoth and Golan to the east. Resident foreigners may use them too.
JOS 21:1-20	The Levite family heads ask Eleazar and Joshua for the towns and pasture promised through Moses. Lots assign thirteen towns to Aaron's descendants from Judah, Simeon and Benjamin, ten to the rest of the Kohathites from Ephraim, Dan and half of Manasseh, thirteen to the Gershonites from the northern tribes, and twelve to the Merarites from Reuben, Gad and Zebulun. The priestly towns are then named, beginning with Hebron, which is also a city of refuge, though its outlying fields stay with Caleb, and continuing through Libnah, Debir, Beth Shemesh, Gibeon and Anathoth.
JOS 21:21-45	The rest of the Levite towns are listed by clan: Shechem, Gezer and Beth Horon in Ephraim, four in Dan and two in Manasseh for the Kohathites; Golan, Kishion, Mishal and Kedesh in Galilee among the Gershonites' thirteen; Jokneam, Bezer, Ramoth in Gilead and Heshbon among the Merarites' twelve. Four of them, Shechem, Golan, Kedesh and Ramoth, are cities of refuge. The total is forty-eight towns with their pasture. The chapter closes by stating that God gave Israel all the land he had sworn to their ancestors and that none of his promises failed.
JOS 22:1-18	Joshua commends Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh for staying with their brothers throughout the campaign, and sends them home across the Jordan with a charge to keep the law and a large share of plunder. On reaching the Jordan they build a large altar there. Hearing of it, the rest of Israel assembles at Shiloh ready for war and sends Phinehas with ten tribal chiefs to Gilead. The delegation accuses them of rebellion, invoking the sin at Peor and warning that God's anger will fall on the whole nation.
JOS 22:19-34	The eastern tribes swear that the altar was never meant for sacrifice. They built it out of fear that later generations west of the Jordan would tell their children they had no share in God, so it stands as a witness, a copy of the real altar rather than a rival to it. Phinehas and the chiefs are satisfied, and Phinehas says their innocence shows God is among them. The report pleases Israel, talk of war ends, and the eastern tribes name the altar A Witness Between Us that Yahweh is God.
JOS 23:1-16	Old and with the fighting over, Joshua summons Israel's leaders. He reminds them that God fought for them, that the remaining nations have already been allotted to them and will be driven out, and that one of them can chase a thousand. He tells them to keep the whole law of Moses without deviating, to avoid the surviving nations, and not to name or serve their gods. If they intermarry with them, those nations will become a snare, a whip on their sides and thorns in their eyes. Just as every promised good has come, so will the promised ruin if they break the covenant.
JOS 24:1-16	At Shechem Joshua recites Israel's history as God's own words: Terah served other gods, Abraham was brought from beyond the river, Isaac and Jacob followed, Egypt was plagued and the sea closed over the pursuing chariots, the Amorites were defeated, Balaam was made to bless rather than curse, and the land was given complete with towns, vineyards and olive groves they never planted. He tells them to serve God sincerely and discard the old gods, and offers them the choice, saying that he and his household will serve God. The people refuse to forsake him.
JOS 24:17-33	The people recount the exodus and the driving out of the Amorites as their reason for choosing God. Joshua warns them that they cannot serve him lightly, since he is holy and jealous and will not overlook their sins, and that abandoning him will bring ruin after all the good. They insist twice, and he makes them witnesses against themselves, tells them to get rid of their foreign gods, and cuts a covenant at Shechem, writing it down and setting up a great stone as a witness. Joshua dies at a hundred and ten. Joseph's bones are buried at Shechem, and Eleazar dies too.
LEV 21:1-24	Rules for priests. A priest may not make himself unclean for the dead except for his closest relatives, and may not shave his head, trim his beard or cut his flesh in mourning. He may not marry a prostitute or a divorced woman, and a priest's daughter who turns to prostitution is burned. The high priest is stricter still: no mourning at all, not even for his parents, no leaving the sanctuary, and marriage only to a virgin of his own people. Any descendant of Aaron with a physical defect may eat the holy food but may not officiate at the altar.
LEV 22:1-33	Priests must keep clear of the holy offerings while unclean, whether from disease, discharge, contact with a corpse or with a creeping thing, and may eat again only after bathing and sunset. Outsiders, hired workers and a priest's daughter married outside the family may not eat the holy food, though bought slaves and a widowed daughter who has come home may. Eating it accidentally requires restitution plus a fifth. Sacrifices must be unblemished males, with a list of disqualifying defects, must be at least eight days old, and a thanksgiving offering must be eaten the same day.
LEV 23:1-21	The calendar of appointed festivals. Every seventh day is a Sabbath of complete rest. Passover falls on the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month, followed by seven days of unleavened bread with holy assemblies on the first and last. When the harvest begins, the first sheaf is waved before God with a year-old lamb, flour, oil and wine, and no new grain may be eaten until then. Fifty days are counted from that day to a new grain offering of two leavened loaves, with lambs, a bull, two rams, a goat and a holy assembly.
LEV 23:22-44	Field corners and gleanings are again left for the poor and the foreigner. The first day of the seventh month is a day of rest marked by trumpet blasts. The tenth is the Day of Atonement, a Sabbath of self-denial kept from evening to evening, with anyone working or refusing to deny himself cut off. The fifteenth begins the seven-day Feast of Tents, with assemblies on the first and eighth days. The people take palm and willow branches and fruit and rejoice, living in temporary shelters for a week to remember the shelters of the exodus.
LEV 24:1-23	Israel supplies pure olive oil so the lamps burn continually before the veil, and twelve cakes of fine flour are set in two rows with frankincense on the gold table each Sabbath, to be eaten by the priests in a holy place. Then a case: the son of an Israelite woman and an Egyptian father, quarrelling in the camp, curses the Name. He is held in custody until God's ruling comes, which is death by stoning by the whole assembly. The law that follows sets out life for life and fracture for fracture, applied equally to foreigner and native. The man is stoned.
LEV 25:1-29	The land keeps a Sabbath. After six years of sowing and pruning, the seventh year is left uncultivated, and whatever grows on its own feeds the household, the workers, the foreigner and the livestock. After seven such cycles, the fiftieth year is a jubilee, announced by trumpet on the Day of Atonement: liberty is proclaimed, and everyone returns to his own property and family. Land sales are therefore priced by the number of harvests left until the jubilee. God promises a sixth-year harvest large enough to cover the gap. Land cannot be sold permanently, since it belongs to God, and a poor man's relative may redeem it.
LEV 25:30-55	A house in a walled city not redeemed within a year stays with the buyer permanently, while village houses count as farmland and return at the jubilee, and Levites may always redeem theirs. A poor Israelite is to be supported without interest or profit on food. One who sells himself is to be treated as a hired worker, not a slave, and released with his children at the jubilee. Slaves may be bought from surrounding nations and held permanently, but not fellow Israelites, who may be redeemed by a relative or themselves at a price prorated to the jubilee.
LEV 26:1-25	No idols, no sacred pillars, keep the Sabbaths. Obedience brings rain in season, harvests that run into each other, safety, sleep without fear, the removal of dangerous animals, and enemies routed by a handful of men, with God's presence walking among the people. Disobedience brings escalating punishment in stages, each seven times worse than the last: wasting disease and fever, crops eaten by enemies, defeat and rule by those who hate them, a sky like iron and soil like bronze, wild animals taking their children and livestock, and then the sword, siege and plague.
LEV 26:26-46	The punishments continue: bread rationed by weight and never enough, hunger reaching the point of eating their own children, the high places destroyed, corpses thrown on the idols, cities and sanctuaries laid waste, and the people scattered among the nations while the land at last enjoys the Sabbaths it was denied. Survivors will be so afraid that a blown leaf will send them running. But if they confess their guilt and humble themselves, God says he will remember the covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham, and will not utterly reject them even in exile.
LEV 27:1-17	A schedule of valuations for things vowed to God. A person is assessed by age and sex, from fifty shekels for a man between twenty and sixty down to three for an infant girl, with the priest setting a lower figure for anyone who cannot pay. A dedicated animal fit for sacrifice becomes holy and cannot be swapped; an unclean animal is valued by the priest and may be bought back with a fifth added. A house is likewise valued, with a fifth added to redeem it, and a field is valued by how much barley seed it takes.
LEV 27:18-34	A field dedicated after the jubilee is valued only for the years remaining. Redeeming it costs a fifth extra; leaving it unredeemed or selling it means it passes permanently to the priests at the jubilee. A bought field returns to its original owner then. All valuations use the sanctuary shekel of twenty gerahs. Firstborn animals cannot be dedicated, since they already belong to God, and anything irrevocably devoted may never be redeemed. A tenth of crops, fruit and livestock is holy, redeemable only with a fifth added, and animals must not be sorted or substituted.
PSA 1:1-6	A short poem contrasting two kinds of life. The person who avoids the advice, company and mockery of the wicked and instead dwells on God's law day and night is compared to a tree planted by streams, fruitful in season and never withering. The wicked are chaff blown away by the wind, unable to stand in judgment or among the righteous. The closing line states the difference: God knows the way of the righteous, while the way of the wicked comes to nothing.
PSA 2:1-12	A psalm about rebellion against God and his anointed king. Nations conspire and rulers plot to throw off their bonds, and the response from heaven is laughter, then anger. God declares he has installed his king on Zion, and the king recites the decree naming him God's son, promising him the nations as an inheritance and the power to smash them like pottery. The psalm ends by advising the kings and judges of the earth to serve with fear and pay homage, and calls those who take refuge in him blessed.
PSA 3:1-8	A prayer under attack. The writer complains that his enemies have multiplied and that many are saying God will not help him, then turns to call God a shield around him and the one who lifts his head. He notes that he cries out and is answered, that he can lie down and sleep and still wake up, and that he will not fear tens of thousands surrounding him. He asks God to rise and save him, recalling enemies struck on the jaw, and ends by saying salvation belongs to God.
PSA 4:1-8	An evening prayer for relief. The writer asks God to answer and have mercy, then addresses those turning his honour into shame and chasing lies, telling them God hears the godly. He advises them to be in awe rather than sin, to examine themselves in bed and be quiet, and to trust God. Against the many who ask who will show them any good, he says God has put more gladness in his heart than a good harvest brings, and that he can lie down and sleep in safety.
PSA 5:1-12	A morning prayer. The writer lays his requests out at daybreak and waits, on the grounds that God takes no pleasure in wickedness and cannot live with evil, hating liars and the bloodthirsty. He asks to be led straight because of his enemies, whose mouths have no truth in them and whose throats are open graves, and asks that they be held guilty and fall by their own schemes. He closes asking that those who take refuge in God rejoice, since God surrounds the righteous with favour like a shield.
PSA 6:1-10	A plea from illness and exhaustion. The writer asks not to be disciplined in anger but healed, saying his bones are troubled and his whole self in anguish, and asks how long this will go on. He argues that the dead cannot praise God from Sheol. He describes flooding his bed with tears every night and his eyes wasting with grief. Then the tone shifts: God has heard his weeping and accepted his prayer, so he tells the wrongdoers to leave and expects his enemies to be shamed.
PSA 7:1-17	A prayer for vindication. Pursued and afraid of being torn apart like prey by a lion, the writer offers to accept defeat and disgrace if he is actually guilty of what he is accused of. He asks God to rise up and judge, appealing to his own integrity, and describes God as a righteous judge with a sharpened sword, a strung bow and flaming arrows ready. The central image is the trap that rebounds: the enemy digs a pit and falls into it, and his violence lands on his own head. It ends in thanks and praise.
PSA 8:1-9	A short hymn of praise, opening and closing with the same line about the majesty of God's name in all the earth. Strength is established even from the mouths of infants, silencing the enemy. Looking at the moon and stars as the work of God's fingers, the writer asks why God should give any thought to human beings at all, then answers that he made them a little lower than the angels, crowned them with glory and put everything under their feet: flocks, herds, wild animals, birds and fish.
RUT 1:1-22	Famine drives Elimelech of Bethlehem to Moab with his wife Naomi and two sons. He dies, the sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth, and after about ten years both sons die too. Hearing that there is food in Judah again, Naomi sets out home and urges her daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers, since she has no more sons to give them. Orpah goes, but Ruth refuses, saying she will go where Naomi goes and that Naomi's people and God will be hers. They reach Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest, and Naomi tells the town to call her Mara.
RUT 2:1-23	Ruth asks leave to glean and happens into a field belonging to Boaz, a wealthy relative of Elimelech. Boaz asks who she is, learns she came back with Naomi, and tells her to stay in his field, drink from his water and keep near his women, having ordered the men not to touch her. He credits her with leaving her homeland for her mother-in-law's sake. He shares his meal with her and quietly tells the reapers to let her glean among the sheaves and pull out extra for her. She takes home an ephah of barley, and Naomi names Boaz as one of their near kinsmen.
RUT 3:1-18	Naomi tells Ruth to wash and dress, go down to the threshing floor where Boaz is winnowing, wait until he has eaten and lain down, then uncover his feet and lie there. Ruth does it, and at midnight Boaz wakes to find a woman at his feet. She asks him to spread his garment over her as a near kinsman. He blesses her, agrees, and says the whole town knows her worth, but that a nearer kinsman has the first claim and must be given the chance. She leaves before dawn with six measures of barley, and Naomi says he will settle the matter that day.
RUT 4:1-22	Boaz sits at the town gate, stops the nearer kinsman and gathers ten elders as witnesses. He offers the man Naomi's field, and the man agrees to redeem it until he hears that Ruth comes with it, at which point he hands over the right, sealing it by taking off his sandal. Boaz declares before everyone that he has bought Elimelech's property and taken Ruth as his wife to keep the dead man's name alive. The town blesses them, Ruth bears a son, and Naomi nurses him. He is named Obed, the father of Jesse, the father of David.
1CH 10:1-14	The Philistines rout Israel on Mount Gilboa, killing Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchishua. Saul, hard pressed by archers, asks his armor bearer to run him through; the man refuses, so Saul falls on his own sword, and the armor bearer does the same. The Philistines strip the bodies, fasten Saul's head in the house of Dagon and carry the news to their idols. Men of Jabesh Gilead recover the bodies, bury the bones under an oak and fast seven days. Saul died, the text says, for his unfaithfulness and for consulting a medium rather than Yahweh.
1CH 11:1-18	All Israel gathers to David at Hebron, makes a covenant with him and anoints him king, as Yahweh had said through Samuel. He takes Jerusalem, also called Jebus, after its inhabitants tell him he cannot enter; the first man to strike the Jebusites is promised command, and Joab goes up first. David builds up the city and grows greater. His chief warriors are named: Jashobeam, who killed three hundred at once, and Eleazar, who held a barley field. Three of the thirty break through the Philistine lines for water from Bethlehem's well.
1CH 11:19-47	David refuses to drink the water, calling it the blood of men who risked their lives, and pours it out to Yahweh. Abishai killed three hundred and captained the three without being counted among them. Benaiah killed two sons of Ariel of Moab, killed a lion in a pit on a snowy day, and killed an Egyptian five cubits tall with the man's own spear; David set him over his guard. The chapter then lists the mighty men by name and home town, Uriah the Hittite among them.
1CH 12:1-20	Men join David at Ziklag while he is a fugitive from Saul: Benjaminites of Saul's own tribe who could sling and shoot with either hand. Gadites come to his wilderness stronghold, faces like lions and swift as gazelles, the least of them equal to a hundred, and cross the Jordan at flood. When men of Benjamin and Judah arrive, David asks whether they come to help or betray; the Spirit comes on Amasai, who declares for him, and David makes them captains. Manassites join him on the road to Ziklag.
1CH 12:21-40	The men who came to David at Hebron are counted by tribe: six thousand eight hundred from Judah, seven thousand one hundred from Simeon, four thousand six hundred Levites with Jehoiada and the young Zadok, and three thousand from Benjamin, most of that tribe having stayed with Saul's house until then. Issachar sends two hundred chiefs who understood the times. From east of the Jordan come a hundred twenty thousand. They spend three days eating and drinking, supplies brought in on donkeys, camels, mules and oxen.
1CH 13:1-14	David consults the commanders and the whole assembly about bringing back the ark, noting it was not sought in Saul's day, and they agree. All Israel gathers from the brook of Egypt to the entrance of Hamath, and the ark is carried from Kiriath Jearim on a new cart driven by Uzza and Ahio, with singing and instruments. At Chidon's threshing floor the oxen stumble, Uzza puts out his hand to the ark, and God strikes him dead. David, displeased and afraid, names the place Perez Uzza and leaves the ark with Obed-Edom, whose house is blessed for three months.
1CH 14:1-17	Hiram of Tyre sends cedar, masons and carpenters to build David a house, and David understands that his kingdom is established. He takes more wives in Jerusalem, and thirteen more children are named. Hearing he is king, the Philistines raid the valley of Rephaim; David asks God, is told to go up, and defeats them at Baal Perazim, and the gods they abandon are burned. On a second raid God tells him to circle to the mulberry trees and attack when he hears marching in the treetops. He does, and drives them from Gibeon to Gezer.
1CH 15:1-29	David prepares a place and pitches a tent for the ark, then rules that only Levites may carry it, since Yahweh chose them. He gathers Aaron's sons and six Levite families by name and number, tells them to sanctify themselves, and says the earlier disaster came of not carrying it according to the ordinance. They bear it on their shoulders with poles as Moses commanded. Singers and players are appointed, Chenaniah over the singing. Seven bulls and seven rams are sacrificed. Michal watches David dancing from a window and despises him.
1CH 16:1-43	The ark is set in its tent, burnt and peace offerings are made, and David blesses the people and gives every man and woman bread, meat and a cake of raisins. He appoints Levites under Asaph to minister before the ark, and gives them a psalm of thanks: call on his name, remember the covenant with Abraham, the gods of the peoples are idols, let the sea roar and the trees sing for joy. The people say Amen. Asaph stays with the ark, Zadok is left at the tabernacle in Gibeon for the daily offerings, and everyone goes home.
1CH 17:1-27	David tells Nathan it is wrong that he lives in a house of cedar while the ark sits in a tent, and Nathan tells him to do as he wishes. That night God tells Nathan otherwise: he has lived in tents since Egypt and never asked any judge of Israel for a house of cedar. Instead Yahweh will build David a house. A son of David will build the temple, his throne established forever, with God as his father. David sits before Yahweh, asks who he is to be brought this far, and prays that the promise stand.
1CO 1:1-31	Paul thanks God for the Corinthians' gifts, then names the problem: Chloe's household has reported factions, with people claiming to follow Paul, Apollos, Cephas or Christ. He asks whether Christ is divided and points out he baptised almost none of them. He argues that the message of the cross looks like foolishness, since Jews want signs and Greeks want wisdom, but God's foolishness is wiser than human wisdom. He notes that few of them were wise, powerful or well born, because God chose the lowly and despised so nobody could boast.
1CO 2:1-16	Paul recalls arriving in Corinth without polished speech or clever argument, in weakness and fear, determined to talk about nothing but Christ crucified, so that their faith would rest on God's power rather than human persuasion. The wisdom he does teach is a hidden wisdom, prepared before the world and unknown to its rulers, who would not have crucified the Lord of glory had they recognised him. Only God's Spirit knows God's mind, and only those with that Spirit can discern such things.
1CO 3:1-23	Paul says the Corinthians are still infants, fed milk rather than solid food, and their jealousy and factions prove it. He and Apollos are only workers: one planted, one watered, God gave the growth. Switching to construction, he says he laid the foundation, which is Christ, and warns that whatever is built on it will be tested by fire, so that gold survives and straw does not, though the builder himself is saved. They are God's temple. Nobody should boast in human leaders, since everything already belongs to them.
1CO 4:1-21	Paul describes himself and Apollos as servants and stewards who answer to the Lord, not to the Corinthians, and asks them to postpone judgment until Christ comes. He then contrasts their self-satisfaction with the apostles' condition: hungry, thirsty, beaten, homeless, working with their hands, treated as the world's rubbish and made a spectacle. He says he writes as their father rather than to shame them, has sent Timothy ahead, and will come himself soon, asking whether they would prefer he arrive with a rod or with gentleness.
1CO 5:1-13	Paul reports a case of a man living with his father's wife, something he says even the Gentiles do not tolerate, and is angrier that the church is proud rather than grieving. Though absent, he has already judged the case and tells them to hand the man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh so his spirit may be saved. A little yeast leavens the whole lump, so the old yeast must be purged. He clarifies his earlier letter: the ban on association concerns members of the church, not outsiders, whom God judges.
1CO 6:1-20	Paul is appalled that believers are suing each other in pagan courts, when people who will one day judge the world and angels ought to settle small matters themselves. Better to be wronged, he says, than to litigate against a brother. He lists those who will not inherit the kingdom, then reminds the Corinthians that some of them were such people and were washed and justified. Against the slogan that all things are lawful, he argues the body belongs to the Lord, joining oneself to a prostitute makes one body with her, and their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, bought at a price.
1CO 7:1-22	Answering a written question, Paul says celibacy is good but marriage is the remedy for lack of self-control, and that husband and wife each have authority over the other's body, so neither should withhold except by mutual consent for prayer. He wishes everyone were single like him, but says it is better to marry than to burn. Married couples should not separate, and a believer married to an unbeliever should stay if the unbeliever is willing, though a departing unbeliever releases them. Each person should remain in the condition in which they were called, circumcised or not, slave or free.
1CO 7:23-40	On virgins Paul says he has no command from the Lord, only his own judgment: given the present distress, people should stay as they are. Marrying is not a sin, but it brings trouble, and the time is short, so those who have wives should live as though they had none, and buyers as though they owned nothing, since this world is passing away. The unmarried are free to attend to the Lord undistracted. A father who gives his virgin daughter in marriage does well; not giving her does better. A widow may remarry, though he thinks she is happier as she is.
1CO 8:1-13	The question is meat sacrificed to idols. Paul grants their argument that knowledge shows there is only one God and that idols are nothing, but notes that knowledge puffs up while love builds up. Food itself does not make anyone better or worse before God. The danger is that a believer with a weak conscience, seeing someone eating in an idol's temple, may be drawn into eating as if to an idol and be destroyed. Wounding such a conscience is sinning against Christ, so Paul says he would give up meat permanently rather than trip up a brother.
1CO 9:1-27	Paul defends his apostleship and then his refusal to be paid for it. He argues at length that he has every right to support, citing soldiers, vinedressers, shepherds, the law against muzzling a threshing ox, temple servants living from the altar, and the Lord's own instruction. Then he says he has never used the right, because preaching free of charge is his only boast. He makes himself a Jew to Jews and weak to the weak in order to win people, and compares himself to an athlete training under discipline for an imperishable crown.
1CO 10:1-33	Paul uses Israel in the wilderness as a warning: all of them passed through the sea and ate the same spiritual food, yet most fell, through idolatry, immorality that killed twenty-three thousand in a day, testing God, and grumbling. Anyone confident of standing should watch out, though God always provides a way of escape. Returning to idol meat, he argues that sharing the cup and loaf makes one body, and that pagan sacrifices are offered to demons, so one cannot drink both cups. Market meat is fine; if a host names it as idol food, refrain for the other person's conscience.
1CO 11:1-34	Paul addresses head coverings, arguing from an order of headship and from creation that a man should pray uncovered and a woman covered, adding that nature gives a woman her hair as a covering and that neither sex is independent of the other. He then turns to the Lord's supper, which he says they are not really eating: they divide by wealth, some going hungry while others get drunk. He repeats the words of Jesus over the bread and cup on the night he was betrayed, warns that eating unworthily brings judgment, and tells them to wait for one another or eat at home.
1CO 12:1-31	On spiritual gifts, Paul says nobody can call Jesus Lord except by the Spirit, and that the varieties of gifts, service and working all come from one Spirit: wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment, tongues and interpretation, distributed as the Spirit chooses. He develops the body image at length, with the foot and ear insisting they do not belong and the eye telling the hand it is unnecessary, and argues that the apparently weaker and less honourable parts get the greater honour, so that all suffer and rejoice together. He lists roles in the church and points ahead to a better way.
1CO 13:1-13	Paul says that tongues without love are only noise, and that prophecy, complete knowledge, mountain-moving faith, giving away everything and even being burned all count for nothing without it. He describes love as patient, kind, not envious or boastful, not easily provoked, keeping no record of wrong, bearing and enduring everything. Prophecy, tongues and knowledge will all end, because they are partial, as childhood is put away and a dim reflection gives way to seeing face to face. Faith, hope and love remain, and love is the greatest.
1CO 14:1-40	Paul ranks prophecy above tongues because prophecy builds up the whole assembly while tongues without interpretation edify only the speaker. He compares unclear speech to an instrument with no distinct notes or a trumpet giving an uncertain signal, and says he would rather speak five intelligible words in church than ten thousand unintelligible ones. An outsider walking into a room where everyone speaks in tongues will think them mad. He then sets rules: two or three speakers at a time, in turn, with an interpreter, prophets yielding to one another, wives silent, and everything done decently and in order.
1CO 15:1-29	Paul restates the gospel he received: Christ died for our sins, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Cephas, the twelve, more than five hundred at once, James, all the apostles, and last of all to Paul himself, whom he calls the least, since he persecuted the church. He then confronts those denying the resurrection of the dead, arguing that if the dead are not raised then Christ is not raised, the preaching is empty, the faith is empty and the dead have perished. Christ is the first fruits; the last enemy destroyed is death.
1CO 15:30-58	Paul asks why he would risk his life daily, including fighting beasts at Ephesus, if the dead are not raised, since eating and drinking would make more sense. To the question of what kind of body rises, he answers with a seed that must die, and notes that flesh differs from flesh and star from star in glory. The body is sown perishable and raised imperishable, natural then spiritual, bearing first the image of the man of dust and then the heavenly. At the last trumpet the dead will rise and the living be changed, and death will be swallowed up.
1CO 16:1-24	Paul gives instructions for the collection for Jerusalem: each person setting aside money weekly so nothing has to be gathered when he arrives, with approved delegates carrying the gift. He plans to come through Macedonia and perhaps winter in Corinth, but will stay at Ephesus until Pentecost because a great door has opened and there are many opponents. He asks them to receive Timothy without contempt, notes Apollos declined to come now, commends Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus, and sends greetings from Aquila and Priscilla before signing in his own hand.
1JN 1:1-10	The letter opens without a greeting, insisting instead on firsthand contact: what was from the beginning, heard, seen with their eyes and touched with their hands, is what is being reported so the readers can share the same fellowship with the Father and the Son. The message itself is stated simply: God is light and there is no darkness in him. Claiming fellowship while walking in darkness is a lie. Two more claims are ruled out: saying we have no sin deceives ourselves, and saying we have not sinned makes God a liar. Confession brings forgiveness.
1JN 2:1-29	John writes so they will not sin, but names Jesus as advocate and atoning sacrifice if they do. The test of knowing God is keeping his commandments, and the commandment is both old and new: whoever hates his brother is in the dark and blind, while whoever loves him stays in the light. He addresses children, fathers and young men in turn, then warns against loving the world, which is passing away along with its desires. He calls this the final hour, noting that many antichrists have already gone out from among them, and identifies the liar as anyone denying that Jesus is the Christ.
1JN 3:1-24	The chapter marvels that they are called children of God, unrecognized by the world, and says that when he appears they will be like him. Everyone with that hope purifies himself. Sin is defined as lawlessness, and the Son came to destroy the devil's work. Cain is the counterexample, killing his brother because his own deeds were evil. Hating a brother is called murder, and love is defined by Christ laying down his life, which means laying down theirs. A concrete test follows: seeing a brother in need and closing your heart. Love should be in deed rather than words, and a condemning heart is smaller than God.
1JN 4:1-21	John tells them to test the spirits, since many false prophets are out in the world, and gives the test: whether a spirit confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. The rest of the chapter is about love. Love comes from God, so whoever loves has been born of God, and God is love. This was shown by God sending his Son as the atoning sacrifice, before anyone loved him. Since no one has seen God, mutual love is where he becomes visible. Perfect love casts out fear, and claiming to love God while hating a visible brother is called a lie.
1JN 5:1-21	Belief that Jesus is the Christ marks birth from God, and loving God means keeping commandments that are not burdensome, since faith is the victory that overcomes the world. John points to three witnesses that agree: the Spirit, the water and the blood, and says God's testimony is that eternal life is in his Son. He states his purpose in writing: so they may know they have eternal life. Prayer according to God's will is heard, including prayer for a sinning brother, though he distinguishes a sin leading to death. The letter ends abruptly: keep yourselves from idols.
1PE 1:1-25	Peter writes to scattered believers across five provinces of Asia Minor, calling them foreigners in the Dispersion. He blesses God for a new birth into a living hope through the resurrection and an inheritance kept in heaven. Their present griefs are trials that test faith the way fire tests gold. The prophets searched for the time this salvation pointed to, and even angels want to look into it. He tells them to be sober, set their hope on the coming revelation, and be holy, since they were ransomed not with silver or gold but with the blood of a lamb without blemish. Flesh is grass; the word endures.
1PE 2:1-25	Peter tells them to crave the word like newborns wanting milk, and describes Christ as a living stone rejected by builders but chosen by God, with believers built into a spiritual house and a holy priesthood. They are called a chosen race and a holy nation, once no people and now God's. As foreigners they should behave well in front of outsiders and submit to the emperor and governors, silencing ignorance by doing good. Slaves are told to endure even harsh masters, following the example of Christ, who did not curse back, bore sins on the tree, and is called the Shepherd of their souls.
1PE 3:1-22	Household instructions come first: wives are to win unbelieving husbands by conduct rather than argument, adorning the hidden person of the heart instead of braided hair and gold, as Sarah did, and husbands are to honor their wives as joint heirs so their prayers are not hindered. Everyone is told to be like-minded and to bless rather than repay insult, quoting a psalm about keeping the tongue from evil. They should always be ready to explain their hope, with humility. Christ suffered once for sins, preached to the spirits in prison, and Noah's eight rescued through water are compared to baptism.
1PE 4:1-19	Since Christ suffered in the flesh, Peter says, arm yourselves with the same intention and stop living for human desires; enough time was spent on drunkenness, orgies and idolatry, and former companions find the change strange. Because the end of all things is near, they should be sober in prayer, love each other earnestly since love covers many sins, be hospitable without grumbling, and use their gifts to serve. He then addresses their fiery trial directly: suffering as a Christian is no disgrace, but suffering as a thief or a meddler is, and judgment begins with God's own household.
1PE 5:1-14	Peter closes by addressing the elders as a fellow elder and witness of Christ's sufferings, telling them to shepherd the flock willingly rather than for gain, and by example rather than domineering, with a crown of glory promised when the chief Shepherd appears. Younger members should defer, and everyone should clothe themselves in humility and cast their worries on God. The devil is described prowling like a roaring lion, to be resisted in the knowledge that others suffer the same. He signs off through Silvanus, sends greetings from Babylon and from Mark, and asks for a kiss of love.
1TH 1:1-10	Paul, Silvanus and Timothy greet the Thessalonians and give thanks for their work of faith, labour of love and perseverance of hope. Paul says the gospel came to them not in words only but in power and the Holy Spirit, and that they became imitators of the apostles and of the Lord, receiving the word in affliction with joy. Their example has spread through Macedonia and Achaia and beyond, so that others report how the Thessalonians turned from idols to serve the living God and to wait for his Son from heaven.
1TH 2:1-20	Paul recalls that he came to them after being shamefully treated at Philippi, and insists his preaching involved no deception, flattery or greed, and that he sought no honour from them although he could have claimed apostolic authority. He was gentle as a nursing mother and worked night and day so as not to burden anyone, exhorting each of them as a father does. He notes they suffered from their own countrymen as the churches in Judea did, says he tried repeatedly to visit but was hindered by Satan, and calls them his crown and joy.
1TH 3:1-13	Unable to bear the separation any longer, Paul stayed behind at Athens and sent Timothy to strengthen them, worried that the afflictions he had warned them about might have shaken them and that his labour would prove wasted. Timothy has now returned with good news of their faith and love and their longing to see him, which comforted Paul in his own distress. He prays night and day to see them, asks God to direct his way to them, and prays their love will increase so their hearts are blameless at the coming of the Lord.
1TH 4:1-18	Paul urges them to please God more and more, naming sexual purity as God's will, with each person controlling his own body and nobody wronging a brother in this matter. On brotherly love he says they need no instruction, but should aim at a quiet life, mind their own business and work with their hands so that outsiders respect them and they need nothing. He then addresses grief over those who have died: since Jesus rose, God will bring them with him. The Lord will descend with a shout, a trumpet and the archangel's voice, the dead in Christ rising first.
1TH 5:1-28	Paul says the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night, sudden destruction arriving just as people say peace and safety, but the Thessalonians are children of light and should stay awake and sober, wearing faith and love as a breastplate and hope of salvation as a helmet. He asks them to respect their leaders, admonish the disorderly, encourage the fainthearted and never repay evil with evil. Then a run of short commands: rejoice always, pray constantly, give thanks, do not quench the Spirit, test everything. He asks that the letter be read to everyone.
1TI 1:1-20	Paul writes to Timothy, whom he left at Ephesus to stop certain men teaching a different doctrine and occupying themselves with myths and endless genealogies. The point of the instruction is love from a pure heart. The law, he says, is good when used properly, and was made for the lawless, whom he lists. He thanks Christ for appointing him despite having been a blasphemer and persecutor, calls himself the chief of sinners, and offers himself as a display of divine patience. He hands Timothy the charge, naming Hymenaeus and Alexander as men who made shipwreck of the faith.
1TI 2:1-15	Paul asks that prayers be made for everyone, including kings and those in authority, so that believers can live quiet and godly lives, since God wants all people saved and there is one God and one mediator, Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all. He wants men everywhere to pray with lifted hands, without anger or argument, and women to dress modestly rather than relying on braided hair, gold and pearls, and to be known for good works. He then directs that a woman learn quietly and not teach or hold authority over a man, arguing from Adam and Eve.
1TI 3:1-16	Paul sets out qualifications for church office. An overseer must be above reproach, married once, temperate, sensible, hospitable, able to teach, not a drinker or violent or greedy, gentle, managing his own household well, not a recent convert, and well regarded by outsiders. Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued or greedy, tested before serving, with their wives dignified and trustworthy. He says he writes in case his visit is delayed, so Timothy knows how people should behave in God's household, and closes by quoting a hymn about God revealed in the flesh.
1TI 4:1-16	Paul warns that some will fall away, following liars who forbid marriage and certain foods, and answers that everything God created is good if received with thanksgiving. Timothy should refuse profane fables and train himself in godliness, since physical training has limited value while godliness has value for this life and the next. Nobody should look down on his youth; instead he should set an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity, attend to public reading, exhortation and teaching, and not neglect the gift given him by prophecy and the elders' laying on of hands.
1TI 5:1-25	Paul tells Timothy to treat older men as fathers, younger as brothers, older women as mothers and younger as sisters. On widows he distinguishes those genuinely alone from those with families who should support them, sets sixty as the age for enrolment, requires a record of good works, and advises younger widows to marry rather than drift into idleness and gossip. Elders who lead well deserve double honour, and he cites the ox and the labourer's wages. Accusations need two or three witnesses, ordination should not be hurried, and he advises a little wine for Timothy's stomach.
1TI 6:1-21	Slaves should honour their masters, including believing ones, so the teaching is not slandered. Anyone teaching otherwise is conceited and addicted to arguments, and supposes godliness is a way to make money. Paul answers that godliness with contentment is the real gain, since we bring nothing in and take nothing out, and that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. He charges Timothy to flee these things and fight the good fight, then tells the rich to hope in God rather than their wealth and to be generous, and warns against so-called knowledge.
2CO 1:1-24	Paul opens by blessing God as the Father of mercies who comforts the afflicted so that they can comfort others. He describes a crisis in Asia so severe that he despaired of life and felt under a death sentence, which taught him to rely on God who raises the dead, and he thanks the Corinthians for their prayers. He then defends his conscience and his travel plans, denying that he changed his route out of fickleness, since God's promises in Christ are all Yes rather than yes and no. He says he stayed away to spare them.
2CO 2:1-17	Paul explains why he did not visit: he did not want another painful trip, and the harsh letter he sent came out of anguish and many tears, written to show his love rather than to hurt them. The offender has been punished enough, and Paul urges them to forgive and comfort him before grief swallows him, forgiving him himself so Satan gains no advantage. He describes his restlessness at Troas when Titus failed to appear, then thanks God for leading him in triumph and spreading a fragrance that is life to some and death to others.
2CO 3:1-18	Asked for letters of recommendation, Paul says the Corinthians themselves are his letter, written not in ink but by the Spirit, on hearts rather than stone tablets. He contrasts two ministries: the letter kills, the Spirit gives life. If the covenant carved on stone came with such glory that Israel could not look at Moses' face, the ministry of the Spirit has far more, and its glory does not fade. Moses veiled his face; a veil still lies over the reading of the old covenant, removed when a person turns to the Lord.
2CO 4:1-18	Paul says he does not lose heart and has renounced underhanded methods and any tampering with God's word. If the gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those blinded by the god of this world. He preaches Christ rather than himself, and the treasure is carried in clay pots so the power is plainly God's. He lists his condition in pairs: pressed but not crushed, perplexed but not despairing, struck down but not destroyed, always carrying Jesus' death in his body. The outer self decays while the inner is renewed daily, and present affliction is light beside eternal glory.
2CO 5:1-21	Paul compares the body to a tent that will be dissolved and replaced by an eternal building from God, and says believers groan for that covering, walking by faith rather than sight and preferring to be at home with the Lord. All must appear before Christ's judgment seat. Christ's love compels him, since one died for all, so those who live should live for him. Anyone in Christ is a new creation, and God has committed to them the ministry of reconciliation, making them ambassadors who beg others to be reconciled.
2CO 6:1-18	Paul urges them not to receive God's grace in vain, since now is the day of salvation, and defends his ministry with a long list of what he has endured: beatings, imprisonments, riots, sleeplessness and fasting, along with purity, knowledge and sincere love. He describes his position in paradoxes, treated as a deceiver yet true, unknown yet well known, dying yet alive, poor yet making many rich. He tells them his heart is wide open and asks the same of them, then warns against being unequally yoked with unbelievers, since they are the temple of the living God.
2CO 7:1-16	Paul asks them again to open their hearts, insisting he has wronged, corrupted and exploited nobody. He recalls arriving in Macedonia with no rest, harassed outside and afraid inside, until Titus came with news of their longing and zeal for him. His harsh letter caused grief, which he does not regret, because it was godly sorrow that produced repentance rather than the sorrow of the world, which produces death. He lists the earnestness it stirred in them, says he wrote to test their care for him, and reports that his boasting about them to Titus proved true.
2CO 8:1-24	Paul holds up the churches of Macedonia, who gave beyond their means out of deep poverty and begged for the privilege. He asks the Corinthians, who excel in everything else, to excel in giving too, not as a command but as a test of sincerity, citing Christ who became poor to make them rich. They began a year ago and should now finish; the aim is equality, not hardship, with abundance supplying lack. He is sending Titus with two other brothers, and explains that the arrangement protects him from any accusation about handling the money.
2CO 9:1-15	Paul says he hardly needs to write about the collection, since Achaia has been ready for a year and their zeal stirred up the Macedonians, but he is sending the brothers ahead so the gift is prepared as generosity rather than something squeezed out at the last minute, and so his boasting is not embarrassed. Sparse sowing means a sparse harvest. Each should give as he has decided, without reluctance, since God loves a cheerful giver. The result is not only relief for the poor but thanksgiving to God, and he ends thanking God for his indescribable gift.
2CO 10:1-18	Paul answers the charge that he is bold in letters and feeble in person. He says his warfare is not fought with worldly weapons but demolishes strongholds and takes every thought captive to Christ. He quotes his critics directly: his letters are weighty, his presence weak, his speech contemptible, and warns that he will act in person as he writes when absent. He refuses to compare himself with people who measure themselves by themselves, insists he stays within the territory God assigned him rather than boasting in another's work, and says approval comes from the Lord's commendation.
2CO 11:1-33	Paul asks them to bear with a little foolishness. He compares himself to a father who betrothed them to Christ as a pure bride and fears they are being seduced as Eve was by the serpent. He notes bitterly that they tolerate a different gospel, and that his refusal of payment is held against him while other churches supported him. He calls his rivals false apostles, since Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light. Then he boasts as they do, listing floggings, beatings, a stoning, three shipwrecks, constant danger, hunger and cold, and his escape from Damascus in a basket.
2CO 12:1-21	Paul describes a man caught up fourteen years ago to the third heaven and Paradise, who heard words he is not permitted to repeat, and declines to boast about it. To keep him from pride he was given a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan, and three times asked for its removal, receiving instead the answer that grace is sufficient and power is perfected in weakness. He argues that he performed the signs of an apostle among them, that his only offence was refusing their money, and says he fears finding them quarrelling and unrepentant when he arrives.
2CO 13:1-14	Paul says he is coming a third time and will not spare them, invoking the rule about two or three witnesses. Since they demand proof that Christ speaks through him, he tells them to examine themselves instead, to see whether Christ is in them. He would rather appear weak while they are strong, and says he writes in advance so he will not have to be severe in person, since his authority was given for building up rather than tearing down. He closes with instructions to live in peace and a benediction naming grace, love and fellowship.
2PE 1:1-21	Peter opens by saying God's power has supplied everything needed for godliness, then gives a chain of qualities to add to faith: moral excellence, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly affection and love. Anyone lacking them is short-sighted and has forgotten being cleansed. He explains why he keeps repeating himself: he knows he will soon put off his tent, and wants them to remember after he is gone. He insists the message is not invented, since he was on the holy mountain and heard the voice call Jesus his beloved Son, and adds that prophecy came by the Spirit, not private interpretation.
2PE 2:1-22	A chapter against false teachers who smuggle in destructive teachings for profit. Peter stacks up precedents for their punishment: the angels who sinned and were thrown into Tartarus, the flood that spared only Noah and seven others, and Sodom and Gomorrah reduced to ashes while Lot was rescued. He describes the teachers as unreasoning animals, feasting with the congregation, eyes full of adultery, following Balaam, who was stopped by a talking donkey. They are wells without water and storm-driven clouds who promise freedom while enslaved themselves, and he ends with proverbs about a dog returning to its vomit and a washed pig going back to the mud.
2PE 3:1-18	Peter writes a second time to answer mockers asking where the promised coming is, since everything carries on as always. He replies that they deliberately forget the flood, and that the present world is stored up for fire. With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and his apparent slowness is patience meant to allow repentance. The day will arrive like a thief, with the heavens dissolving and the elements melting, and what follows is a new heaven and earth where righteousness lives. He mentions Paul's letters, some of which are hard to understand and get twisted, and ends telling them to grow in grace.
2TH 1:1-12	Paul, Silvanus and Timothy thank God that the Thessalonians' faith is growing and their love for one another increasing, and say they boast about their endurance under persecution in other churches. Paul treats their suffering as evidence of God's righteous judgment, since it is just for God to repay those who afflict them and to give the afflicted relief when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with mighty angels in flaming fire, punishing those who do not know God with eternal destruction. He prays that God will count them worthy of their calling and fulfil every good purpose in them.
2TH 2:1-17	Paul tells them not to be shaken by any spirit, word or forged letter claiming the day of the Lord has already arrived. First must come the rebellion and the revealing of the man of sin, the son of destruction, who opposes every god and seats himself in God's temple claiming to be God. Something is restraining him for now; when that is removed he will appear with Satanic power and lying signs, and the Lord will destroy him with the breath of his mouth. Those who refused the truth will be given over to believing a lie. He tells them to stand firm.
2TH 3:1-18	Paul asks for prayer that the word spread quickly and that he be rescued from unreasonable and evil men. He then commands them to keep away from any brother living in idleness, pointing to his own example of working night and day and paying for his food rather than burdening them, though he had the right to be supported. He repeats the rule he gave them in person: anyone unwilling to work should not eat. Some are not working at all but meddling; they should work quietly. Such a person should be shamed but treated as a brother, not an enemy.
2TI 1:1-18	Paul writes to Timothy as his beloved child, remembering his tears and the faith he inherited from his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, and tells him to stir up the gift given through the laying on of hands, since God gave a spirit of power, love and self-control rather than fear. Timothy should not be ashamed of the gospel or of Paul's imprisonment, but guard the pattern of sound words. Paul notes that everyone in Asia deserted him, naming Phygelus and Hermogenes, and asks mercy for Onesiphorus, who searched Rome until he found him.
2TI 2:1-26	Paul tells Timothy to pass on what he has heard to faithful people who can teach others, and offers three pictures: a soldier who avoids distractions, an athlete who competes by the rules, a farmer who gets the first share. He quotes a saying about dying, enduring and denying, then warns against arguing about words, comparing empty talk to gangrene and naming Hymenaeus and Philetus, who say the resurrection has already happened. In a large house some vessels are gold and some clay. The Lord's servant should not quarrel but correct opponents gently.
2TI 3:1-17	Paul describes the last days with a long list of vices: lovers of self and money, boastful, ungrateful, without self-control, treacherous, lovers of pleasure rather than God, keeping the form of godliness while denying its power. Some prey on vulnerable households and oppose the truth as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, but their folly will become obvious. Timothy has followed Paul's teaching and knows his persecutions at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, and everyone who wants to live godly will suffer. He has known the Scriptures from infancy, and all Scripture is God-breathed and useful.
2TI 4:1-22	Paul charges Timothy to preach the word in season and out, patiently, because a time is coming when people with itching ears will collect teachers who suit their own desires and turn to fables. He says his own departure is at hand: he has fought the good fight, finished the course and kept the faith. Then personal notes. Demas deserted him for the world, only Luke is with him, and he asks Timothy to bring Mark, his cloak from Troas and the books. Nobody supported him at his first defence, but the Lord stood by him.
BEL 1:1-20	Under Cyrus, Daniel is the king's most honored friend, and the king asks why he will not worship Bel, whose idol consumes twelve measures of flour, forty sheep and six firkins of wine daily. Daniel says the thing is clay inside and bronze outside and has never eaten anything. The king puts it to the test with his seventy priests, on pain of death for whoever is wrong. The priests, who have a secret entrance under the table, are unconcerned. After the food is set out, Daniel has ashes scattered across the floor, and the door is sealed with the king's signet.
BEL 1:21-42	The footprints in the ashes convict the priests, who show the king their hidden doors and are executed, and Daniel destroys Bel and his temple. The king then points to a great dragon the Babylonians worship as unquestionably alive. Daniel kills it without a weapon by feeding it lumps of boiled pitch, fat and hair until it bursts. The furious populace forces the king to hand him over, and he is thrown into a den of seven starved lions for six days. An angel carries the prophet Habakkuk by the hair from Judea to bring him a meal. On the seventh day the king finds him alive, and the accusers go in instead.
COL 1:1-29	Paul thanks God for the Colossians' faith, reported to him by Epaphras, and prays they will grow in the knowledge of God's will and endure with joy. He describes Christ as the image of the invisible God and the firstborn of all creation, through whom everything visible and invisible was made, in whom all things hold together, and who is head of the church and first from the dead, reconciling all things by the blood of his cross. Once enemies, they are now reconciled. Paul says he rejoices in his sufferings and serves the mystery now revealed: Christ in you, the hope of glory.
COL 2:1-23	Paul tells the Colossians how hard he struggles for them and for Laodicea, people who have never met him, and warns them not to be talked out of their faith by persuasive speech or by philosophy following human tradition, since the fullness of deity dwells in Christ bodily. Buried and raised with him in baptism, they had the record of debts against them nailed to the cross, and the powers were stripped and paraded. So nobody should judge them over food, festivals or Sabbaths, or rob them with angel worship and self-imposed severity, which look wise but do not curb the flesh.
COL 3:1-25	Since they were raised with Christ, Paul tells them to set their minds on things above, where Christ is seated. They should put to death immorality, evil desire and greed, and put away anger, slander and lying, having taken off the old self and put on the new, in which there is no Greek or Jew, barbarian, Scythian, slave or free. Instead they should put on compassion, kindness, humility and patience, forgive one another as Christ forgave them, and let peace rule, teaching each other with psalms and hymns. Then instructions for wives, husbands, children, fathers and slaves.
COL 4:1-18	Masters are told to treat their slaves justly, since they have a Master in heaven. Paul asks for steady prayer, including for a door to open for his message, and tells them to be wise with outsiders and to keep their speech gracious and seasoned with salt. Tychicus and Onesimus will bring news. Greetings come from Aristarchus, Mark, Jesus called Justus, Epaphras, Luke the physician and Demas. He asks that the letter be read in Laodicea and their letter read in Colossae, sends a message to Archippus, and signs in his own hand, asking them to remember his chains.
DEU 32:1-26	Moses recites his song. He calls heaven and earth to listen, praises God as the Rock whose ways are just, and accuses Israel of being a crooked generation that repaid its father badly. He recounts how God found Jacob in the wilderness, carried him as an eagle carries its young, and fed him honey, oil and the finest wheat. Grown fat, Israel kicked, abandoned the Rock and sacrificed to demons. God vows to hide his face, spend his arrows and scatter them.
DEU 32:27-52	God holds back total destruction only so that enemies will not claim the credit. He declares that vengeance is his, that he alone kills and makes alive, and that no other god can rescue from his hand. Moses and Joshua finish reciting the song, and Moses tells Israel these words are their life. That same day God tells Moses to climb Mount Nebo, see Canaan and die there, barred from entering because of Meribah.
DEU 33:1-29	Before his death Moses blesses the tribes. God comes from Sinai with ten thousands of holy ones. Reuben is asked to live and not dwindle, Judah to be helped against his adversaries, Levi to keep the Urim and Thummim and teach the law, Benjamin to dwell in safety, Joseph to receive the richest land, and Gad, Dan and Naphtali are likened to lions or given territory. Moses ends by calling Israel happy, a people saved by Yahweh, with the everlasting arms underneath.
DEU 34:1-12	Moses climbs Nebo to the top of Pisgah, and God shows him the whole land, from Gilead to Dan, Naphtali, Ephraim, Manasseh, Judah and the valley of Jericho, then repeats that he will not cross into it. Moses dies in Moab at a hundred and twenty, his eyesight and strength intact, and is buried in a grave no one has ever found. Israel mourns thirty days. Joshua takes over, and no prophet like Moses has arisen since.
EPH 1:1-23	Paul blesses God for choosing believers before the foundation of the world, predestining them for adoption, redeeming them by Christ's blood and making known the mystery of his will, which is to sum up all things in Christ. Those who believed were sealed with the Holy Spirit as a pledge of their inheritance. He then prays that they be given wisdom and revelation, with the eyes of their hearts enlightened, so they grasp the power that raised Christ and seated him above every rule and authority, head over all things for the church, which is his body.
EPH 2:1-22	Paul says his readers were dead in their sins, following the prince of the power of the air, and that God made them alive with Christ out of mercy, saving them by grace through faith as a gift rather than by works, so nobody can boast. They are God's workmanship, made for good works. He then reminds the Gentiles that they were once outside Israel's covenants and without hope, and are now brought near, since Christ broke down the dividing wall and made one new humanity out of two, reconciling both in one body. They are fellow citizens, a temple built on Christ the cornerstone.
EPH 3:1-21	Writing as a prisoner for the Gentiles, Paul describes the mystery revealed to him: that Gentiles are fellow heirs and fellow members of the same body. He calls himself the least of all the saints, given the task of preaching the unsearchable riches of Christ and of making God's wisdom known even to the powers in the heavenly places. He asks them not to lose heart over his sufferings. Then he prays that they be strengthened inwardly, rooted in love, able to grasp its width, length, height and depth, and closes with a doxology.
EPH 4:1-32	Paul urges them to live worthily of their calling with humility and patience, keeping the unity of the Spirit, and lists what they share: one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God. Christ ascended and gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers to equip the saints, so the church grows up instead of being blown about by every wind of doctrine. They should put off the old self and put on the new: no lying, no anger carried past sunset, no stealing, no corrupt talk, no bitterness, but kindness and forgiveness.
EPH 5:1-33	Believers should imitate God and walk in love, avoiding immorality, greed and coarse talk, since such people have no inheritance in the kingdom. Once darkness, they are now light, and should expose the deeds of darkness rather than share them. Paul tells them to use the time well because the days are evil, and to be filled with the Spirit rather than drunk, speaking in psalms and hymns and giving thanks. Then household instruction: wives subject to husbands as the church to Christ, and husbands loving their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself for it.
EPH 6:1-24	Children should obey their parents, which Paul notes is the first commandment with a promise attached, and fathers should not provoke their children. Slaves should serve sincerely rather than only when watched, and masters should stop threatening, since both answer to the same impartial Master. He then tells them to put on the whole armour of God, because the struggle is against spiritual powers rather than flesh and blood: the belt of truth, breastplate of righteousness, shoes of the gospel, shield of faith, helmet of salvation and sword of the Spirit. He asks prayer for his own boldness as an ambassador in chains, and says Tychicus will bring news.
GAL 1:1-24	Paul skips the usual thanksgiving and says he is astonished that the Galatians are so quickly deserting the gospel for a different one, which is no gospel at all. Anyone preaching another message should be cursed, even an angel from heaven. He insists he did not receive his gospel from any human being but by revelation, and gives his history: he persecuted the church violently and was zealous for ancestral tradition, then went to Arabia rather than to Jerusalem, and only after three years met Peter for fifteen days, seeing no other apostle except James.
GAL 2:1-21	Fourteen years later Paul went to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus, presenting his gospel privately to the leaders. Titus, a Greek, was not required to be circumcised despite pressure from people he calls false brothers. James, Cephas and John recognised his mission to the Gentiles and asked only that he remember the poor. He then reports confronting Peter publicly at Antioch, because Peter had eaten with Gentiles until visitors came from James and then withdrew, taking even Barnabas with him. Paul argues nobody is justified by works of law, and says he has been crucified with Christ.
GAL 3:1-29	Paul calls the Galatians foolish and asks whether they received the Spirit by law or by faith. Abraham believed and was counted righteous, so those of faith are his children, while those relying on law are under the curse the law itself pronounces, a curse Christ absorbed by hanging on a tree. He argues that a promise made to Abraham cannot be annulled by a law arriving four hundred and thirty years later. The law was a guardian until Christ came. Now all are one in Christ, with no Jew or Greek, slave or free, male or female.
GAL 4:1-31	Paul compares the situation before Christ to an heir who is still a minor under guardians, and says God sent his Son so they could be adopted as children who cry Abba, Father, no longer slaves but heirs. He is dismayed that they are turning back to observing days and seasons. He recalls that he first preached to them during an illness and they received him as an angel, and asks whether telling the truth has made him their enemy. He then reads Hagar and Sarah as an allegory of two covenants, and tells them they are children of the free woman.
GAL 5:1-26	Paul tells them to stand firm in freedom, warning that anyone accepting circumcision is obliged to keep the entire law and has cut himself off from grace, since what counts is faith working through love. They were running well until someone interfered, and he wishes his opponents would cut themselves off. Freedom is not licence for the flesh but service to one another, since the whole law is fulfilled in loving your neighbour. He lists the works of the flesh, from immorality to drunkenness, and against them the fruit of the Spirit, beginning with love and ending with self-control.
GAL 6:1-18	Paul asks the spiritual to restore a person caught in a fault gently, watching themselves, and to carry each other's burdens while also bearing their own. Whatever a person sows they will reap, so they should not tire of doing good. He then takes up the pen himself, noting his large handwriting, and says those pushing circumcision want to avoid persecution and to boast about Galatian flesh, without keeping the law themselves. He boasts only in the cross, says what matters is a new creation, and points to the marks branded on his body.
HEB 1:1-14	The letter opens by contrasting how God once spoke through prophets with how he has now spoken through his Son, who is heir of all things, the one through whom the worlds were made, the radiance of God's glory, who purified sins and sat down at God's right hand. The writer then argues from a series of scripture quotations that the Son is superior to the angels: no angel was ever called Son, angels are told to worship him, angels are made winds and fire, and the Son is addressed as God with an everlasting throne. Angels are serving spirits.
HEB 2:1-18	Since the message came through the Son rather than through angels, the writer warns against drifting away, arguing that if the law delivered through angels carried penalties, neglecting this greater salvation is worse.
