He quotes the psalm about man being made a little lower than the angels and crowned with glory, and applies it to Jesus, who tasted death for everyone and was made perfect through suffering. Because the children share flesh and blood, he shared it too, to destroy the devil's power over death and free those enslaved by fear of it, becoming a merciful high priest who has been tempted himself.
HEB 3:1-19	Jesus is compared with Moses: both were faithful, but Moses was a servant in the house while Christ is a Son over it, and the builder deserves more honour than the house. The readers are that house if they hold their confidence to the end. The writer then quotes the psalm warning against hardening hearts as in the wilderness rebellion, where God was displeased with that generation for forty years and swore they would not enter his rest. He works through the questions in order: who rebelled, with whom was God displeased, who was barred, and answers that unbelief kept them out.
HEB 4:1-16	The argument continues that the promise of rest still stands, since the earlier generation failed to enter through unbelief, and since David speaks of a today long after Joshua, meaning Joshua's conquest was not the rest in question. A Sabbath rest remains for God's people, and they should be diligent to enter it. The word of God is described as living and sharper than a two-edged sword, dividing soul and spirit and exposing everything. Because their great high priest has passed through the heavens and was tempted in every way without sin, they can approach the throne of grace boldly.
JAS 1:1-27	James writes to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion and opens by telling them to count trials as joy, since testing produces endurance. Anyone lacking wisdom should ask God, but without doubting, since a doubter is a wave driven by the wind. The rich fade like a flower withered by scorching wind. Temptation, he insists, does not come from God but from one's own desire, which conceives sin and then death. He tells them to be quick to hear and slow to anger, and to be doers rather than hearers who forget their own face in a mirror. Real religion is caring for orphans and widows.
JAS 2:1-26	The chapter opens against favouritism, imagining a man with a gold ring seated well while a poor man is told to stand, and points out that God chose the poor to be rich in faith. Loving your neighbour is the royal law, and breaking the law at one point makes a person guilty of it all, since mercy triumphs over judgment. James then argues that faith without works is dead: telling a hungry person to go be warmed feeds nobody, and even demons believe God is one. He cites Abraham offering Isaac and Rahab hiding the messengers as faith completed by action.
JAS 3:1-18	A warning to would-be teachers, who face heavier judgment, and then a chapter about the tongue. Small things steer big ones: a bit controls a horse and a small rudder a ship. The tongue is a small member that boasts greatly, a fire that can burn a forest, an untameable evil full of poison even though people have tamed every kind of animal. James objects that blessing and cursing come out of the same mouth, when no spring gives both fresh and salt water. He contrasts earthly wisdom, which is jealous and ambitious, with wisdom from above, which is pure, peaceable and merciful.
JAS 4:1-17	James traces quarrels back to cravings: they want, do not get, and fight, and when they do ask their motives are wrong. He calls friendship with the world hostility toward God, quotes that God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble, and tells them to submit, resist the devil, draw near, and turn their laughter into mourning. He forbids speaking against one another, since judging a brother means setting oneself above the law. Then he mocks confident business plans, saying life is a vapour and they should say if the Lord wills, and ends noting that knowing the good and not doing it is sin.
JAS 5:1-20	The chapter opens by telling the rich to weep, describing corroded gold, moth-eaten clothes, and the withheld wages of harvesters crying out to the Lord of Armies. The others are told to be patient like a farmer waiting for the early and late rain, and not to grumble, since the judge is at the door; the prophets and Job are given as examples of endurance. He forbids oaths, telling them to let yes be yes. The sick should call the elders to pray and anoint with oil, and they should confess to one another, since Elijah's prayer stopped and restarted the rain.
JDT 1:1-16	The book opens with a war between two kings: Nebuchadnezzar, here ruling the Assyrians from Nineveh, and Arphaxad of the Medes, who has fortified Ecbatana with enormous hewn stone walls, towers and gates whose measurements are given. Nebuchadnezzar summons the nations from Persia to Egypt and Ethiopia to join him, and they refuse and send his messengers home in disgrace. He swears vengeance on the whole western region. In his seventeenth year he defeats Arphaxad anyway, sacks Ecbatana, kills the king with darts in the mountains of Ragau, and returns to Nineveh to feast for a hundred and twenty days.
JDT 2:1-28	In his eighteenth year Nebuchadnezzar convenes his court and decides to punish everyone who ignored his summons. He gives Holofernes, his commander in chief, a hundred and twenty thousand infantry and twelve thousand cavalry, orders him to demand earth and water from the west, and to spare those who surrender for the king's own later judgment while destroying the rest. Holofernes marches out with a baggage train and a horde compared to locusts and sand, and works his way through Put, Lud, Mesopotamia and Cilicia, burning the fields of Damascus at harvest, until the coastal cities are terrified.
JDT 3:1-10	The coastal peoples send envoys with words of complete surrender, offering their land, crops, flocks, cities and inhabitants for Holofernes to use as he pleases. He comes down to the coast, garrisons the fortified towns and conscripts their best men, and is welcomed with garlands, dancing and drums. He then demolishes their shrines and cuts down their sacred groves, since he has been authorized to destroy all local gods so that every nation will worship Nebuchadnezzar alone. He moves on to Esdraelon near Dothan, opposite the ridge of Judea, and camps a month to gather supplies.
JDT 4:1-15	Hearing what Holofernes has done to the temples of other nations, the Israelites in Judea panic, especially for Jerusalem, since they have only recently returned from captivity and rededicated the altar and vessels. They fortify the hilltop villages and stockpile supplies from a harvest just gathered. Joakim the high priest writes to Bethulia and Betomesthaim to hold the mountain passes, which are narrow enough for two men to block. Everyone puts on sackcloth, including children, servants and livestock, and they throw ashes on their heads and drape the altar. The Lord hears them, and the fasting continues for days.
JDT 5:1-24	Told that the Israelites have blocked the passes, Holofernes angrily demands to know who these hill people are and why they alone did not come out to meet him. Achior, leader of the Ammonites, gives him a summary of Israel's history: descent from the Chaldeans, the move to Mesopotamia over their fathers' gods, Canaan, the famine and Egypt, the plagues, the Red Sea, the conquest of the Amorites and the hill country, then exile when they sinned, and their recent return to Jerusalem. His advice is to check whether they have sinned, and if not, to pass by rather than be humiliated. The council calls for his death.
JDT 6:1-21	Holofernes rejects Achior's advice with the question who is God but Nebuchadnezzar, and predicts mountains drunk with Israelite blood. As punishment Achior is told he will not see his face again until the vengeance is done, and is handed over to the Israelites so he will die with them. Guards take him to the springs below Bethulia, where slingers on the hill drive them off, so they tie him up and leave him at the foot of the slope. The men of Bethulia untie him and bring him to their rulers, Ozias, Chabris and Charmis. He repeats Holofernes's words to the assembly, and the people worship and pray all night.
JDT 7:1-17	Holofernes moves the whole army against Bethulia: a hundred and seventy thousand infantry and twelve thousand cavalry, spread from Dothan to Belmaim and from Bethulia to Cyamon. The defenders light fires on their towers and watch all night. Next day Holofernes rides out to inspect the approaches and the springs, and seizes them. His Edomite and Moabite allies then propose a siege rather than a battle: hold the water source at the foot of the mountain, since all Bethulia's water comes from there, and let thirst and famine finish the city. He agrees, and Ammonite and Assyrian troops occupy the springs.
JDT 7:18-32	With Edomites and Ammonites in the hills and the main army filling the plain, Bethulia is completely surrounded for thirty-four days, and every water vessel runs dry. Water is rationed by measure, and children, women and young men collapse from thirst in the streets and gateways. The whole population turns on Ozias and the rulers, blaming them for not making peace with the Assyrians, and demands that the city be surrendered, arguing that slavery is better than watching their children die. Ozias asks them to hold out five more days for God to show mercy, and promises to do as they say if nothing comes.
JDT 8:1-17	Judith is introduced with a long genealogy back to Israel. Her husband Manasses died of sunstroke while supervising the barley harvest, leaving her wealthy in land, livestock and servants, and she has been a widow three years and four months, living in a tent on her roof, wearing sackcloth and fasting except on Sabbaths and feasts. She is described as very beautiful and of unblemished reputation. Hearing that Ozias has promised to surrender the city in five days, she summons the three elders and tells them the promise was wrong: setting a deadline for God is putting themselves in his place.
JDT 8:18-36	Judith continues her rebuke. This generation, she says, worships no idols, unlike the fathers who were handed over for it, so they may hope God will not despise them; and if Bethulia falls, all Judea and the sanctuary fall with it, and their blood will be required. She calls their situation a test like those of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, a scourging meant to admonish. Ozias grants she has always been wise but says the thirsty people forced the oath and asks her to pray for rain. She answers that she will do something that will be remembered for generations, and refuses to say what.
JDT 9:1-14	At the hour of the evening incense in Jerusalem, Judith prostrates herself in ashes and sackcloth and prays. She begins with her ancestor Simeon, to whom God gave a sword to avenge the defiling of a virgin, then affirms that God plans events before they happen. She describes the Assyrians trusting in horses, shields, spears and slings without knowing that the Lord breaks battles, and asks that their arrogance be broken by the hand of a woman, with her lips and her deceit as the weapon. God, she says, is the helper of the oppressed and the savior of the hopeless, not a God of large numbers.
JDT 10:1-23	Judith gets up, washes, anoints herself, braids her hair, puts on a tiara and the festival clothes she wore while her husband lived, and adds every piece of her jewellery, explicitly to catch the eyes of the men who will see her. She packs her own kosher food and wine and leaves through the gate with her maid, watched by the astonished elders. The Assyrian patrol stops her; she says she is fleeing her doomed people and will show Holofernes a way to take the hill country without a single casualty. A hundred men escort her, the camp crowds round to stare, and she bows before Holofernes.
JDT 11:1-23	Holofernes reassures her that nobody who serves Nebuchadnezzar is harmed, and asks why she fled. Judith flatters him and then builds her lie on Achior's argument: Israel cannot be defeated unless they sin against their God, and she claims the starving people of Bethulia are about to eat forbidden food and consume the tithes reserved for the priests. She offers to pray in the valley each night and report the moment the sin is committed, after which he can march to Jerusalem unopposed. Holofernes and his officers are delighted, praise her beauty and wisdom, and he promises her a place in the king's house.
JDT 12:1-20	Offered the general's own food and wine, Judith refuses and insists on eating only what she brought, saying it will not run out before God has done what he intends. She is allowed out of the camp each night to pray and wash at the spring. On the fourth day Holofernes throws a private banquet and sends the eunuch Bagoas to persuade her to attend, admitting it would be a disgrace to let her go untouched. She agrees at once, dresses up, and reclines on her own fleeces beside him. He is captivated, watching for his chance, and drinks more wine than on any day of his life.
JDT 13:1-20	The servants leave and Bagoas closes the tent, leaving Judith alone with Holofernes lying drunk on his bed. She prays for strength, takes his own scimitar from the bedrail, grips his hair and strikes his neck twice, cutting off the head. She rolls the body off the bed, takes the canopy, puts the head in her food bag and walks out with her maid as if going to pray, straight through the camp and up to Bethulia. She calls to the watchmen, praises God at the gate, and shows the head, saying he did not defile her. Ozias blesses her above all women.
JDT 14:1-19	Judith gives the plan: hang the head on the wall, and at dawn march out as if to attack, so the Assyrians rouse their commander and find him missing. First she has Achior brought in; he faints at the sight of the head, then bows to her and asks to hear everything, and afterwards he is circumcised and joins Israel. At sunrise the head goes up and the men take the mountain passes. The Assyrian officers send Bagoas to wake his master, and he assumes Judith is inside. He finds the body on the threshold without its head, tears his clothes, and shouts through the camp that one Hebrew woman has disgraced the king.
JDT 15:1-13	Panic empties the camp: the soldiers scatter across the plain and hill country without waiting for orders, and the Israelites chase them down. Ozias sends word to the surrounding towns, and men from Jerusalem, the hill country, Gilead and Galilee join the pursuit past Damascus. Bethulia loots the abandoned camp and grows rich. Joakim the high priest and the elders come from Jerusalem to bless Judith as the glory of Israel. The plundering lasts thirty days, and Holofernes's tent, silver and furniture are given to her. The women of Israel gather to dance for her, and she leads the procession in olive garlands.
JDT 16:1-25	Judith leads a victory song. It recounts the Assyrian advance from the north with threats to kill the young men and enslave the virgins, and insists the enemy commander fell not to young warriors or giants but was undone by a widow's beauty: her sandal caught his eye and the scimitar went through his neck. The song praises God as creator whose voice nothing resists, and ends warning the nations who attack Israel. In Jerusalem she dedicates Holofernes's goods and the canopy to the Lord. She refuses remarriage, frees her maid, dies at a hundred and five, and Israel is left unthreatened for years after.
MAN 1:1-15	A short penitential prayer put in the mouth of King Manasseh. It opens by addressing the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who made heaven and earth and shut up the deep, and whose glory is unbearable and whose anger toward sinners is unendurable, but whose promise of mercy cannot be measured. The speaker argues that repentance was appointed not for the righteous patriarchs but for sinners like himself. He says his sins outnumber the sands of the sea, that he is bowed down under iron bands and cannot lift his head, and that he set up abominations. He bows the knee of his heart and asks not to be destroyed.
MRK 1:1-45	Mark opens with no birth story. John the Baptist appears in the wilderness in camel hair, eating locusts and wild honey, baptizing crowds and announcing someone mightier. Jesus is baptized, sees the Spirit descend like a dove and hears a voice call him beloved Son, then spends forty days in the wilderness tempted by Satan. After John's arrest he preaches in Galilee, calls Simon, Andrew, James and John from their nets, drives an unclean spirit out of a man in the Capernaum synagogue, heals Simon's mother in law and a whole town at the door, and cleanses a leper who then publicizes it.
MRK 2:1-28	Four men carry a paralytic to a crowded house and dig through the roof to lower him in. Jesus forgives his sins, which the scribes call blasphemy, then tells him to pick up his mat and walk. He calls Levi the tax collector and eats with tax collectors and sinners, saying a physician is for the sick. Asked why his disciples do not fast, he answers that groomsmen cannot fast while the bridegroom is present, and adds sayings about unshrunk cloth and new wine. Challenged over grain plucked on the Sabbath, he cites David eating the show bread.
MRK 3:1-35	Watched in the synagogue, Jesus asks whether it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath, gets silence, and heals a man's withered hand in anger and grief at their hard hearts. The Pharisees and Herodians begin plotting to kill him. Crowds from as far as Tyre and Idumaea press in so hard he needs a boat offshore. He appoints twelve, named in full. His family come to seize him, thinking him insane, and scribes say he casts out demons by Beelzebul. He answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand, warns about blaspheming the Spirit, and redefines his family as whoever does God's will.
MRK 4:1-41	Teaching from a boat, Jesus tells the parable of the sower: seed lost to the path, the rocky ground and the thorns, and seed on good soil yielding thirty, sixty and a hundredfold. Privately he explains it, identifying the seed as the word and the thorns as cares and riches. He adds sayings about a lamp not hidden under a basket and the measure you use being measured back, then two more parables: seed growing while the farmer sleeps, and the mustard seed becoming the largest plant. That evening a storm nearly swamps the boat while he sleeps in the stern; he rebukes the wind and the disciples ask who he is.
MRK 5:1-43	Across the lake a man living among the tombs, uncontainable by chains and cutting himself with stones, meets Jesus. The spirits name themselves Legion and ask to enter a herd of about two thousand pigs, which stampede into the sea and drown. The locals ask Jesus to leave; the healed man is sent to tell Decapolis instead. Back across the water Jairus begs him to come to his dying daughter. On the way a woman with twelve years of bleeding touches his clothes and is healed, and he stops to find her. Word comes that the girl has died; he takes three disciples inside and tells her to get up.
MRK 6:1-27	Teaching in his home town, Jesus is dismissed as the carpenter whose family everyone knows, and does little there because of their unbelief. He sends the twelve out two by two with a staff and nothing else, telling them to shake the dust off unwelcoming towns. Herod hears the reports and concludes John the Baptist has risen. The narrative doubles back: Herod had imprisoned John for condemning his marriage to Herodias, and at his birthday feast Herodias's daughter danced, was promised anything, and asked on her mother's advice for John's head on a platter. Herod sends a soldier to the prison.
MRK 6:28-56	John's head is delivered on a platter and his disciples bury the body. The apostles return and report, and Jesus takes them away to rest, but crowds run ahead on foot and arrive first. Seeing them as sheep without a shepherd, he teaches, then feeds five thousand men from five loaves and two fish, with twelve baskets of scraps left. He sends the disciples ahead and prays alone on the mountain, then walks out on the water in the fourth watch. They think he is a ghost. At Gennesaret the sick are laid in the marketplaces to touch his clothes.
MRK 7:1-37	Pharisees from Jerusalem object that his disciples eat with unwashed hands. Jesus quotes Isaiah against them and gives an example: a man who declares his property Corban can withhold support from his parents, which sets aside a command of God for a tradition. He tells the crowd that nothing entering a person defiles him, and privately lists what comes out of the heart instead. In the region of Tyre a Syrophoenician woman argues back about dogs eating crumbs and her daughter is freed. In Decapolis he takes a deaf man aside, touches his ears and tongue and says Ephphatha.
MRK 8:1-38	A crowd of four thousand has been with him three days without food, and seven loaves and a few fish feed them all, leaving seven baskets. Pharisees demand a sign from heaven and are refused. In the boat he warns about the yeast of the Pharisees and Herod, and when the disciples worry about bread he asks them to count the leftover baskets and whether they still do not understand. At Bethsaida a blind man first sees men like walking trees, then clearly. Peter calls him the Christ; when Jesus predicts his death Peter rebukes him and is called Satan.
MRK 9:1-26	Six days later Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain and is transfigured, his clothes whiter than any launderer could make them, with Moses and Elijah talking to him. Peter offers to build three tents because he does not know what to say. A cloud covers them and a voice names Jesus as beloved Son. Coming down, he tells them to say nothing until after the resurrection, and says Elijah has already come. At the bottom a father explains his son's convulsions and that the disciples failed. He says he believes and asks help for his unbelief, and the spirit is driven out, leaving the boy apparently dead.
MRK 9:27-50	Jesus lifts the boy up by the hand, and privately tells the disciples that this kind comes out only by prayer and fasting. Travelling through Galilee he predicts again that he will be handed over and killed and rise, which they neither understand nor dare question. Caught arguing about who is greatest, they are told the first must be last and servant of all, and he sets a child among them. Told about an outsider casting out demons, he says whoever is not against them is for them. He then warns about causing little ones to stumble, using the millstone, the severed hand, foot and eye, and ends on salt and peace.
MRK 10:1-29	Asked whether divorce is lawful, Jesus points past Moses's certificate to creation, saying the two become one flesh and no one should separate what God joined, then tells the disciples that remarriage after divorce is adultery either way. When the disciples turn children away he is indignant, saying the kingdom belongs to such as these. A man asks what he must do to inherit eternal life, claims to have kept the commandments, and is told to sell everything and follow; he leaves grieving because he is rich. Jesus says a camel through a needle's eye is easier, and Peter points out that they left everything.
MRK 10:30-52	Jesus finishes the promise of a hundredfold return with persecutions, and adds that the first will be last. On the road up to Jerusalem, with the followers afraid, he spells out that he will be handed over, mocked, spat on, flogged and killed, and rise on the third day. James and John immediately ask for the seats at his right and left; asked whether they can drink his cup, they say they can. The other ten are angry, and he tells them greatness among them means being a servant. Leaving Jericho, blind Bartimaeus shouts him down, is called over, and receives his sight.
MRK 11:1-33	Near Bethany two disciples fetch an unridden colt as instructed, and Jesus rides into Jerusalem over cloaks and branches while crowds shout Hosanna. He looks around the temple and leaves. Next morning, hungry, he finds a fig tree with leaves but no fruit and curses it, then clears the temple of sellers and money changers, quoting house of prayer against den of robbers, which sets the chief priests looking for a way to kill him. The tree is withered by morning, prompting teaching on faith, prayer and forgiveness. Asked by what authority he acts, he asks about John's baptism and they refuse to answer.
MRK 12:1-23	Jesus tells a parable about a vineyard let out to tenants who beat, stone and kill each servant sent for the owner's share, then kill his beloved son to take the inheritance. The owner will destroy them and give the vineyard to others. His hearers understand it is aimed at them but fear the crowd. Pharisees and Herodians try to trap him over the tax, and he asks whose image is on the denarius and says to render to Caesar what is Caesar's. Sadducees then pose a woman married in turn to seven brothers and ask whose wife she is at the resurrection.
MRK 12:24-44	Jesus tells the Sadducees they know neither the scriptures nor God's power: the risen do not marry, and God told Moses at the bush that he is God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, so he is God of the living. A scribe asks which commandment is greatest and hears the Shema plus love of neighbour; his agreement earns the reply that he is not far from the kingdom. Jesus then queries how the Christ can be David's son, warns against scribes who take the best seats and devour widows' houses, and points out a widow putting in two small coins, all she had.
MRK 13:1-37	A disciple admires the temple stones and Jesus says not one will be left standing. On the Mount of Olives four of them ask when. He answers with warnings: impostors claiming his name, wars, earthquakes and famines as birth pains, arrests and beatings, families betraying each other. When the abomination of desolation appears, Judea should flee to the mountains without stopping for a cloak. False christs will do signs. Then the sun and moon go dark, stars fall, and the Son of Man comes in clouds to gather the chosen. The fig tree shows summer is near, but no one knows the hour, so keep watch.
MRK 14:1-34	Two days before Passover the chief priests look for a quiet way to arrest him. At Bethany a woman breaks an alabaster jar of costly nard over his head; the grumbling about waste is answered by saying she has anointed him for burial. Judas goes to the priests for money. Two disciples follow a man with a water pitcher to the upper room and prepare the meal. At table Jesus says one of those dipping with him will betray him, then gives bread and cup as his body and blood. On the Mount of Olives he predicts they will all scatter and that Peter will deny him three times before the rooster crows twice.
MRK 14:35-72	In Gethsemane Jesus asks that the cup be taken from him, adding not what he wants but what God wants, and comes back three times to find the three asleep. Judas arrives with an armed crowd and identifies him with a kiss; a bystander cuts off a servant's ear, everyone runs, and one young man escapes naked, leaving his cloth. Before the council the witnesses contradict each other, so the high priest asks directly whether he is the Christ; his answer is taken as blasphemy and he is condemned, spat on and struck. In the courtyard Peter denies him three times, hears the rooster, and weeps.
MRK 15:1-47	Handed to Pilate in the morning, Jesus answers the question about being king of the Jews and then stops answering, which surprises Pilate. Offered the festival release, the crowd is steered by the priests to choose Barabbas and to demand crucifixion. Soldiers dress him in purple with a crown of thorns and mock him. Simon of Cyrene is made to carry the cross to Golgotha. He is crucified at the third hour between two robbers, his clothes divided by lot, mocked by passers by and priests. Darkness covers the land from noon; he cries out and dies, the temple veil tears, and the centurion calls him Son of God. Joseph of Arimathaea buries him.
MRK 16:1-20	After the Sabbath the three women bring spices and worry about the stone, which they find already rolled back. Inside, a young man in white tells them Jesus has risen and that the disciples and Peter should go to Galilee. They flee and say nothing out of fear. The rest of the chapter reports appearances: first to Mary Magdalene, who is not believed, then to two walking into the country, also disbelieved, then to the eleven at table, whom he rebukes. He commissions them to preach everywhere, lists signs that will follow, and is taken up to heaven.
NAM 1:1-15	The book opens with a vision about Nineveh, and its first move is to describe Yahweh as jealous and avenging, slow to anger but certain not to leave the guilty unpunished. He travels in whirlwind and storm with clouds as the dust of his feet, dries up sea and rivers, withers Bashan, Carmel and Lebanon, and makes the mountains quake. He is also called good, a stronghold for those who take refuge in him. Nineveh gets a flood, cut off idols and a grave; Judah is told to keep its feasts because the yoke is broken.
PHM 1:1-25	Paul writes from prison to Philemon, along with Apphia, Archippus and the church meeting in his house, praising his love and the way he has refreshed the saints. He then makes his request: although he could command, he asks instead, on behalf of Onesimus, Philemon's slave, whom Paul has come to regard as his own child and is sending back. He asks that Onesimus be received as Paul himself would be, no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother, and offers to pay whatever he owes, writing that promise in his own hand. He asks for a guest room to be prepared.
PHP 1:1-30	Paul thanks God for the Philippians' partnership from the first day and prays their love will grow in knowledge and discernment. He reports that his imprisonment has actually advanced the gospel, becoming known throughout the palace guard and emboldening others to speak. Some preach Christ out of rivalry to add to his troubles, but he says he is glad either way as long as Christ is proclaimed. He is torn between dying to be with Christ and staying for their sake, expects to remain, and tells them to stand firm and expect to suffer as he does.
PHP 2:1-30	Paul asks them to be of one mind, doing nothing from rivalry or conceit but counting others better than themselves, and points to Christ, who did not grasp at equality with God but emptied himself, took the form of a servant and obeyed to the point of death on a cross, and was therefore given the name at which every knee bows. They should work out their salvation without grumbling, shining as lights in a crooked generation. He plans to send Timothy, whom he calls uniquely trustworthy, and is sending Epaphroditus back, who nearly died and whom they should honour.
PHP 3:1-21	Paul warns against the dogs and the false circumcision, then lists what he could boast about if he wanted to: circumcised on the eighth day, of Benjamin, a Pharisee, blameless under the law, a persecutor out of zeal. All of it he now counts as loss and refuse next to knowing Christ and sharing his sufferings. He denies having arrived, describing himself as forgetting what is behind and straining toward the prize. He weeps over enemies of the cross whose god is the belly, and says their own citizenship is in heaven, where a Saviour will transform their bodies.
PHP 4:1-23	Paul urges Euodia and Syntyche to agree, and asks a colleague to help these women who laboured with him. He tells the Philippians to rejoice always, to be anxious about nothing but pray about everything, and promises the peace of God will guard their hearts. They should fix their minds on whatever is true, honourable, pure and lovely. He thanks them for their gift, noting they alone supported him after he left Macedonia, and says he has learned to be content whether full or hungry. Greetings come from the saints, including some of Caesar's household.
PS2 1:1-7	Seven verses spoken by David, telling his own story in miniature. He was the smallest of his brothers and the youngest in his father's house, keeping the sheep, and he made himself an instrument and tuned a lute. Asking who could report him to God, he answers that the Lord hears for himself. God sent an angel to take him from the flock and anoint him, passing over his taller and better looking brothers. The psalm ends with the Philistine, who cursed him by his idols, and with David drawing the man's own sword to behead him.
PSA 9:1-20	Thanksgiving for victory. The singer promises to praise Yahweh wholeheartedly because his enemies have stumbled and perished and their cities are forgotten. Yahweh reigns forever on a throne set up for judgment, and he is a stronghold for the oppressed and does not forget the cry of the afflicted. The psalm then turns to petition: have mercy, lift me from the gates of death. The nations have fallen into pits they dug themselves. It closes asking God to remind the nations they are only men.
PSA 10:1-18	A complaint that God seems far away while the wicked prosper. The wicked man boasts, has no room for God in his thoughts, and tells himself he will never be shaken and will never be called to account. He is described as a lion in ambush, murdering the innocent from hiding and dragging the helpless into his net. The psalmist calls on God to arise, break the arm of the wicked, and judge for the fatherless and the oppressed, insisting Yahweh does see and is king forever.
PSA 11:1-7	A short psalm of confidence answering advice to run. Others tell the singer to flee to the mountains like a bird because the wicked have their arrows on the string to shoot at the upright in the dark. He refuses, saying Yahweh is in his holy temple and on his throne, watching and testing everyone. The wicked will get blazing coals, fire, sulfur and scorching wind as their cup, while the upright will see God's face.
PSA 12:1-8	A plea for help in a society of liars. The faithful have disappeared, and everyone flatters his neighbor with a double heart while boasting that their own tongues will win and no one is lord over them. God answers directly, promising to arise because of the groaning of the needy and to set the oppressed in safety. Yahweh's words are contrasted with theirs: silver refined seven times. It ends noting the wicked strut about while worthless things are honored.
PSA 13:1-6	Six verses of impatience. The psalmist asks how long four times over: how long will God forget him, hide his face, leave him carrying sorrow every day and his enemy on top. He asks for an answer and for light in his eyes so he does not sleep in death, and so his enemy cannot claim victory. The last two verses turn without explanation to trust in God's loving kindness and a promise to sing, because God has been good to him.
PSA 14:1-7	The fool says in his heart there is no God. God looks down from heaven for anyone who understands or seeks him and finds no one: all have turned aside and become corrupt, not one does good. The wrongdoers who eat up God's people like bread are said to be seized with great fear, because God is with the righteous. It closes wishing salvation for Israel would come out of Zion, so that Jacob might rejoice.
PSA 15:1-5	A short entrance psalm in question and answer form. Who may live on God's holy hill? The one who walks blamelessly and speaks truth, who does not slander, harm a friend or insult a neighbor, who despises the vile and honors those who fear Yahweh, who keeps an oath even when it costs him, and who neither lends at interest nor takes a bribe against the innocent. Such a person will never be shaken.
PSA 16:1-11	A psalm of contentment and trust. The singer takes refuge in God, says he has no good apart from him, and refuses to pour out drink offerings or even name other gods. Using the language of land allotment, he says his portion and cup are assigned by Yahweh and the boundary lines fell in pleasant places. He blesses God for counsel given in the night, and ends confident he will not be abandoned to Sheol but shown the path of life.
PSA 17:1-15	A prayer for vindication from someone who insists he has nothing to hide. He asks God to hear a plea that comes from honest lips, and points out that God has already tested him in the night and found nothing. He asks to be kept as the apple of God's eye and hidden under the shadow of his wings from enemies who surround him like a lion crouched for prey. Their reward is in this life; his hope is to wake and see God's face.
PSA 18:1-50	A long royal thanksgiving for rescue. The singer piles up titles for God as rock, fortress, shield and high tower, then describes being caught in the cords of death and crying out. The answer is a storm theophany: the earth shakes, smoke and fire come from God's nostrils and mouth, he rides a cherub through thick darkness and shoots lightning until the sea floor is bare, then reaches down and pulls the singer out of deep waters. The rest credits God with his military success: trained hands, feet like a deer's, enemies beaten to dust and foreign nations submitting.
PSA 19:1-14	Two halves joined by a comparison. First the heavens: they speak without words in a voice that carries over the whole earth, and the sun runs its circuit like a bridegroom or an athlete, missing nothing with its heat. Then the law, called perfect, sure, right, pure and true, and worth more than fine gold and sweeter than honey. The psalm ends personally, asking forgiveness for hidden faults, protection from deliberate sins, and that his words and thoughts be acceptable.
PSA 20:1-9	A blessing sung over the king before battle. The congregation asks that Yahweh answer him in trouble, send help from the sanctuary in Zion, accept his sacrifices and grant what he has asked, and promises to raise banners when he wins. The speaker then declares confidence that God saves his anointed. The famous line follows: some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust the name of Yahweh. It closes with a plea for the king to be answered.
PSA 21:1-13	A companion to the previous psalm, sung after the request was granted. The king rejoices because God gave him his heart's desire, met him with blessings, set a crown of fine gold on his head and granted the long life he asked for. The second half turns on his enemies: God's hand will find them, they will burn like a furnace, their descendants will be cut off, and their plots against him cannot succeed. It ends calling on Yahweh to be exalted.
PSA 22:1-31	The psalm opens with the cry asking why God has forsaken him and does not answer day or night. The sufferer calls himself a worm, mocked and taunted by onlookers who tell him to let God rescue him. He describes being encircled by bulls, lions and dogs, poured out like water with bones out of joint, hands and feet pierced, his clothing divided by lot. Then it turns: God did hear, and the singer vows praise in the assembly, ending with all the nations and generations still unborn worshipping.
PSA 23:1-6	Six verses built on one image and then a second. Yahweh is the shepherd, so the singer lacks nothing: he is made to lie down in green pastures, led beside still waters, restored, and guided along right paths. Walking through the valley of the shadow of death, he fears nothing, because the shepherd's rod and staff are there. The image shifts to a host who sets a table in front of his enemies, anoints his head with oil and fills his cup past the brim.
PSA 24:1-10	The psalm opens by claiming the whole earth and everyone in it for Yahweh, who founded it on the seas. It then asks who may climb his hill and stand in his holy place, and answers: the one with clean hands and a pure heart who has not sworn deceitfully. The last section is a call and response at the city gates, telling the everlasting doors to lift up their heads for the King of glory, identified as Yahweh of Armies.
PSA 25:1-22	A prayer alternating between requests for teaching and requests for forgiveness. The singer lifts up his soul, asks not to be shamed, and repeatedly asks to be shown God's ways and guided in his truth. He asks God to forget the sins of his youth and to pardon an iniquity he admits is great. He describes God as instructing sinners and guiding the humble, then returns to his own state: lonely, afflicted, hated by many enemies. It ends asking redemption for all Israel.
PSA 26:1-12	A protest of innocence. The psalmist invites God to examine, test and try his heart, arguing he has walked in integrity, avoided the company of deceitful men and hypocrites, and refused to sit with evildoers. He speaks of washing his hands in innocence and walking around the altar to give thanks, and says he loves the house where God's glory dwells. He asks not to be swept away with the bloodthirsty and the bribe takers, and ends promising to bless Yahweh publicly.
PSA 27:1-14	Confidence first, then petition. With Yahweh as his light and salvation, the singer says he fears no army encamped against him, and names his one request: to live in Yahweh's house all his days and see his beauty. In trouble God will hide him and set him on a rock. The tone then shifts to pleading not to be abandoned, since false witnesses breathing cruelty have risen against him. He ends telling himself to wait for Yahweh and take courage.
PSA 28:1-9	The psalmist calls out to his rock and begs not to be met with silence, which would leave him among those going down to the pit. He asks not to be dragged off with the wicked, men who speak peace to their neighbors while planning mischief, and asks that they be paid back exactly according to their deeds. Midway the mood changes: God has heard, and the singer calls him his strength and shield. It closes asking God to shepherd his people.
PSA 29:1-11	A short hymn about a thunderstorm. It begins by calling on the heavenly beings to give Yahweh glory, then repeats the phrase Yahweh's voice seven times, describing thunder over the waters, cedars of Lebanon splintering, mountains skipping like calves, lightning, the wilderness of Kadesh shaking, and forests stripped bare. In his temple everything answers Glory. The psalm ends with Yahweh enthroned as king forever, giving strength to his people and blessing them with peace.
PSA 30:1-12	Thanksgiving after recovery from illness. The singer says he cried out and was healed, brought up from Sheol and kept from the pit. He admits that in his prosperity he had told himself he would never be shaken, and that when God hid his face he was thrown into confusion. He records the argument he used in prayer: dust cannot praise you. The psalm's summary lines are that weeping may last the night but joy comes in the morning, and that his mourning was turned into dancing.
PSA 31:1-24	A long prayer for rescue that keeps circling back to trust. The singer asks God to be a strong rock and pull him out of a hidden net, and commits his spirit into God's hand. He describes wasting away with grief, becoming contemptible to his neighbors, avoided in the street, forgotten like a dead man and like broken pottery, while enemies conspire to take his life. He insists his times are in God's hand, admits he panicked and said he was cut off, then praises the goodness stored up for those who take refuge, and tells the faithful to take courage.
PSA 32:1-11	A psalm about confession. It opens by calling blessed the person whose sin is forgiven and not counted against him. The singer describes what silence cost him: bones wasting away, groaning all day, God's hand heavy on him day and night, his strength dried up as in summer heat. When he acknowledged his sin instead of hiding it, it was forgiven. He then advises others to pray while God may be found, and not to be like a horse or mule that has to be steered by bit and bridle.
PSA 33:1-22	A hymn calling the righteous to sing a new song with lyre and ten stringed harp. It praises God's word, by which the heavens were made and the seas gathered and stored, and notes that he spoke and it stood firm. God frustrates the plans of nations while his own counsel lasts forever, and from heaven he watches everyone he has made. No king is saved by the size of his army and no horse can deliver anyone. The psalm ends waiting on Yahweh as help and shield.
PSA 34:1-22	A psalm of thanksgiving that turns into instruction. The singer blesses Yahweh at all times, invites others to magnify him together, and reports that he sought God and was delivered from all his fears; this poor man cried and was heard. He tells listeners to taste and see that Yahweh is good, then teaches the fear of Yahweh: keep your tongue from lies, turn from evil, seek peace and pursue it. God is near the broken hearted, watches over the righteous, and sets his face against evildoers.
PSA 35:1-28	A prayer asking God to take up arms in a lawsuit and a fight. The singer wants God to seize shield and spear, and asks that his pursuers be chaff before the wind on a dark and slippery road with the angel of Yahweh behind them, caught in the net they hid. He complains of false witnesses who repay good with evil: when they were sick he fasted and mourned for them as for a brother, and they gloated and gnashed their teeth at his misfortune. He asks for vindication and promises public thanks.
PSA 36:1-12	A contrast in two halves. The first describes the wicked man, who has no fear of God before his eyes, flatters himself too much to recognize his own sin, and lies awake on his bed plotting. The second turns to God's loving kindness, which reaches to the heavens, righteousness like mountains and judgments like the great deep, with people sheltering under the shadow of his wings and drinking from the river of his pleasures. The psalm ends asking not to be trampled by pride.
PSA 37:1-40	An extended answer to the complaint that the wicked prosper. Its advice is repeated in many forms: do not fret, do not envy, trust and do good, delight in Yahweh, commit your way to him, rest and wait patiently. The reason given each time is that the wicked wither like grass and vanish like smoke, while the humble inherit the land. Better a little that the righteous has than the wealth of many wicked. The speaker adds his own observation: he has grown old and never seen the righteous forsaken.
PSA 38:1-22	A prayer from someone who reads his illness as God's discipline. He asks not to be rebuked in wrath, describing God's arrows in him and a hand pressing hard, and links his rotting wounds and aching bones directly to his own sin, which he calls a burden too heavy to carry. His friends and relatives keep their distance while his enemies lay snares and spread rumours. He answers nothing, like a deaf and mute man, and confesses his sin, ending with a plea for God to hurry.
PSA 39:1-13	A meditation on how short life is. The singer resolves to keep his mouth bridled in front of the wicked, but the silence makes his heart burn until he finally speaks. What comes out is a request to be shown how few his days are: a lifetime measured in hand widths, every man a breath, walking like a shadow and hoarding what someone else will collect. He asks for relief from God's blow and, since he is only a passing stranger, to be spared long enough to recover.
PSA 40:1-17	Thanksgiving first, then a fresh emergency. The singer waited patiently and was lifted out of a pit of miry clay, set on a rock and given a new song. He says God did not want sacrifice and offering but an open ear, and declares that he delights to do God's will and has proclaimed it publicly rather than sealing his lips. Then the tone turns: countless troubles surround him and his own sins outnumber the hairs on his head. He asks God to hurry, calling himself poor and needy.
PSA 41:1-13	A psalm from a sickbed. It opens by blessing whoever considers the poor, promising God will sustain such a person through illness. The singer asks for healing and admits he has sinned. His enemies are asking when he will die, and visitors come to his bedside speaking falsely and then spread what they saw, saying an evil disease has him and he will not get up again. The sharpest line is that his own trusted friend, who shared his bread, has turned on him.
PSA 61:1-8	A short prayer from a man calling out from the end of the earth with an overwhelmed heart. He asks to be led to a rock higher than himself, recalls that God has been a strong tower against the enemy, and says he will shelter under God's wings and live in his tent. He notes that God has heard his vows and given him the heritage of those who fear him, prays for the king's life to be prolonged for generations, and promises daily praise.
PSA 62:1-12	The psalmist declares that his soul waits in silence for God alone, his rock and fortress, and says twice that he will not be shaken. He complains that his attackers mean to push him down like a leaning wall, blessing him aloud while cursing inwardly. He urges the people to trust God at all times and pour out their hearts to him, warns that people of low and high rank alike weigh less than a breath, and says not to trust in extortion or set the heart on increasing riches. Power belongs to God, who repays each person according to their work.
PSA 63:1-11	Written from a dry and waterless land, the psalm describes a soul thirsting for God as the body thirsts for water. The psalmist recalls seeing God's power and glory in the sanctuary, says God's loving kindness is better than life itself, and expects to be satisfied as if by rich food. He remembers God on his bed through the night watches and rejoices in the shadow of his wings. Those trying to kill him, he says, will go down into the earth, fall to the sword and become food for jackals, while the king rejoices and liars are silenced.
PSA 64:1-10	The psalmist asks God to hide him from a conspiracy of the wicked, who sharpen their tongues like swords and aim their words like arrows to shoot at innocent men from ambush. They encourage one another, lay snares in secret and congratulate themselves on a perfect plan, assuming nobody will see. God will shoot back, striking them suddenly with an arrow, and their own tongues will be their ruin. Onlookers will shake their heads, and everyone will consider what God has done, while the upright take refuge in him.
PSA 65:1-13	A psalm of praise and harvest. Praise waits for God in Zion, where vows are kept and prayer is heard; he atones for transgressions and blesses those he brings near to live in his courts. He forms the mountains, stills the roaring seas and the turmoil of the nations, and calls out morning and evening. The second half describes rain and crops: God visits the earth and waters it, drenches its furrows, softens it with showers and crowns the year with bounty, until the pastures fill with flocks and the valleys with grain.
PSA 42:1-11	A psalm of homesickness for the temple. The singer compares his thirst for God to a deer panting for water, asks when he can appear before God, and says his tears have been his food while people keep asking him where his God is. He remembers leading the festival crowd to God's house, which makes the present worse. From the far north, near the Jordan and Hermon, he says deep calls to deep and God's waves have gone over him. Twice he asks his own soul why it is in despair and tells it to hope.
PSA 43:1-5	Five verses continuing the previous psalm's mood. The singer asks God to plead his case against a godless nation and rescue him from deceitful men, then asks why he has been rejected and left mourning under enemy oppression. He requests that God send out his light and truth to lead him back to the holy hill and the altar, where he will praise God on the harp. It ends with the same refrain, asking his soul why it despairs and telling it to hope in God.
PSA 44:1-26	A national complaint after a military defeat. It begins with what the fathers reported: God drove out nations and planted Israel, and the land was won by his right hand rather than by anyone's sword. Then it turns on the present. God no longer marches with the armies, and the people are routed, plundered, scattered among the nations, sold for nothing and mocked by their neighbors. They insist they have not forgotten him or turned to a strange god, and demand to know why he is asleep and hiding his face.
PSA 45:1-17	A wedding song for the king. The poet says his tongue is like a skilled writer's pen, then addresses the king directly: strap on your sword, ride out for truth and righteousness, your arrows are sharp and the nations fall. His throne is called everlasting and his robes smell of myrrh, aloes and cassia. The second half addresses the bride, telling her to forget her father's house and honor her lord, and describes her led in gold and embroidery with her companions into the palace.
PSA 46:1-11	A short psalm of confidence in God as refuge. The singer says he will not fear even if the earth gives way and the mountains fall into a roaring sea. A river makes the city of God glad, and because God is inside her she will not be moved: nations raged, but he raised his voice and the earth melted. He is then shown making wars cease everywhere, breaking bows and spears and burning chariots. God speaks once: be still and know that I am God.
PSA 47:1-9	A brief enthronement hymn calling all the nations to clap and shout. Yahweh Most High is named great king over all the earth, the one who subdues peoples and chooses Israel's inheritance. God is described going up with a shout and the sound of a trumpet, which sets off a run of commands to sing praises. He reigns over the nations from his holy throne, and the psalm closes with the princes of the peoples gathered and the shields of the earth belonging to him.
PSA 48:1-14	A hymn about Jerusalem. Mount Zion is called beautiful in elevation and the joy of the whole earth, the city of the great King, with God himself proving to be a refuge in her citadels. A group of kings assembled and marched past, then took one look, panicked and fled in pains like a woman in labour, and ships of Tarshish are broken by the east wind. The psalm ends inviting the hearer to walk around Zion, count her towers and inspect her ramparts so the next generation can be told.
PSA 49:1-20	A wisdom psalm addressed to everyone, rich and poor alike, offering a riddle set to the harp. Its point is that money cannot buy anyone out of death: no payment is ever enough to ransom a life. Wise men die and so do fools, and both leave their wealth to someone else, however many estates they have named after themselves. Death is called the shepherd of that flock. Twice the psalm compares a rich man without understanding to animals that perish, and says his glory will not follow him down.
PSA 50:1-23	God arrives in fire and storm to hold court over his own people. His first complaint is about sacrifice: he does not need a bull from anyone's stall, since every animal in the forest and the cattle on a thousand hills are already his, and he would not mention it if he were hungry. What he wants is thanksgiving, kept vows and being called on in trouble. He then turns on the wicked, who recite his covenant while keeping company with thieves and adulterers and slandering their own brothers.
PSA 66:1-20	The psalm calls the whole earth to shout to God and to come and see his deeds, recalling the sea turned into dry land. It then describes the testing: God refined them like silver, brought them into prison, laid burdens on their backs, let men ride over their heads, and brought them through fire and water to a place of abundance. The psalmist promises burnt offerings of fat animals, rams, bulls and goats, and tells those who fear God that he prayed and was heard.
PSA 67:1-7	A short blessing psalm. The psalmist asks God to be merciful, to bless them and make his face shine on them, so that his way and his salvation may be known among all nations. Twice it repeats the call for all the peoples to praise God, and it asks the nations to be glad because God judges the peoples with equity. It closes by noting that the earth has yielded its increase and that God will bless them.
PSA 68:1-35	A long processional psalm. It opens asking God to arise and scatter his enemies like smoke and melting wax, and names him father of the fatherless, defender of widows, and the one who sets the lonely in families and brings prisoners out singing. It recalls the march through the wilderness with Sinai trembling, rain falling, kings fleeing and plunder divided, and God's chariots numbering tens of thousands. A temple procession follows with singers, musicians and tambourines, and princes of Benjamin, Judah, Zebulun and Naphtali. Kings bring gifts, Egypt and Ethiopia turn to God, and the psalm ends in praise.
PSA 69:1-36	The psalmist is drowning: the waters are at his neck and he sinks in deep mire with no foothold, weary with crying. He is hated without cause, has become a stranger to his own brothers, is talked about by those who sit in the gate and sung about by drunkards, and is given gall for food and vinegar for thirst. He asks not to be swallowed by the flood or the pit, then asks that his enemies' eyes be darkened, their homes left desolate and their names blotted out of the book of life. He ends promising praise and saying God will save Zion.
PSA 70:1-5	Five verses of urgent request. The psalmist asks God to hurry and deliver him, and to come quickly to help. He asks that those who seek his life be turned back in disgrace, especially those who say "Aha! Aha!", and that those who seek God rejoice and keep saying "Let God be exalted." He ends by calling himself poor and needy, naming God as his help and deliverer, and asking him again not to delay.
PSA 71:1-24	The prayer of an old man. He says he has relied on God since the womb and asks not to be rejected in his old age when his strength fails. His enemies are saying God has forsaken him and that nobody will rescue him, so he asks for their disgrace and for God to stay near. He wants to live long enough to declare God's strength to the next generation, recalls the bitter troubles God has shown him, and ends praising God with harp and lyre.
PSA 72:1-20	A prayer for the king. It asks God to give him justice and righteousness so he judges the poor fairly and breaks the oppressor, and describes his rule coming down like rain on mown grass. His dominion runs from sea to sea and from the River to the ends of the earth, with the kings of Tarshish, Sheba and Seba bringing tribute and all nations serving him. He rescues the needy who have no helper. The psalm ends with a blessing of God's glorious name and a note that the prayers of David, son of Jesse, end here.
PSA 73:1-28	The psalmist admits his feet nearly slipped because he envied the prosperity of the wicked, who die without struggle, wear pride like a chain and violence like clothing, and ask how God could possibly know anything. He felt he had kept his heart clean for nothing, since he was punished every morning. Trying to understand it was too painful until he entered God's sanctuary and considered their end: they stand in slippery places and are swept away like a dream on waking. He admits he had been a brute beast, and ends saying God holds his right hand and is his portion forever.
PSA 74:1-23	A lament after the sanctuary has been destroyed. The psalmist asks why God has rejected his own flock, and describes enemies roaring in the assembly, setting up their standards, hacking the carved work with axes and hammers, and burning the sanctuary to the ground. There are no signs and no prophet left, and nobody knows how long it will last. He recalls God dividing the sea, breaking the heads of Leviathan and setting the boundaries of the earth and the seasons, then asks God to remember the mockery, honour his covenant, and rise to plead his own cause.
PSA 75:1-10	The psalm gives thanks that God's name is near, then switches to God's own voice: he chooses the appointed time to judge, and he holds the pillars of the quaking earth. He tells the arrogant not to boast and the wicked not to lift up their horn or speak with a stiff neck. Exaltation comes from no direction on the compass, only from God, who puts one down and lifts another. In his hand is a cup of foaming spiced wine that the wicked drink to the dregs. The horns of the wicked are cut off and the horns of the righteous lifted up.
PSA 76:1-12	A short psalm about God as warrior. He is known in Judah, with his dwelling in Salem and Zion, and it was there he broke the flaming arrows, the shield, the sword and the weapons of war. Valiant men lie plundered and asleep, and at his rebuke both chariot and horse fall into a dead sleep. Nobody can stand before him when he is angry; the earth fell silent when he pronounced judgment from heaven to save the afflicted. The psalm ends telling people to make and keep vows and bring presents to the one feared by kings.
PSA 77:1-20	The psalmist cries out in trouble and refuses to be comforted, groaning when he remembers God, kept awake with his eyelids held open and too troubled to speak. He asks whether God has rejected them forever, whether his loving kindness has vanished and whether he has forgotten to be gracious. He then decides to appeal to the years of God's right hand and to remember his older deeds. The rest recalls the exodus: the waters writhing at the sight of God, thunder, lightning and arrows, God's path through the sea with footsteps nobody saw, and the people led like a flock by Moses and Aaron.
PSA 78:1-35	The psalmist announces a parable of old sayings that must be told to the next generation so they do not become stubborn like their fathers. Ephraim turned back on the day of battle and forgot God's deeds in Egypt: the sea split, the waters standing in a heap, the cloud by day and the fire by night, water brought out of rock. Even so they tested God by demanding food, asking whether he could set a table in the wilderness. God, angry, still sent manna, the bread of angels, and then meat carried by the east wind, birds as thick as sand, falling in the camp. While the food was still in their mouths his anger struck down their strongest young men, and only when he killed them did they seek him again.
PSA 78:36-72	The people flatter God with their mouths while their hearts are elsewhere, and he forgives repeatedly, remembering they are only flesh. The psalm recounts the plagues of Egypt: rivers turned to blood, flies and frogs, locusts and caterpillars, hail and frost on the vines, livestock struck, and the firstborn killed. God then led his people like sheep, drove out the nations and settled the tribes, but they provoked him with high places and carved images. He abandoned Shiloh, let his glory go into captivity, and gave the people to the sword until priests fell and widows could not weep. Then he woke like a man roused by wine, drove back his enemies, rejected Ephraim, chose Judah and Mount Zion, and took David from the sheepfolds to shepherd Israel.
PSA 79:1-13	A lament over a sacked Jerusalem. The nations have defiled the temple and left the city in heaps, the bodies of God's servants have been left for birds and animals, and their blood was spilled with nobody to bury them. The people have become a joke to their neighbours. The psalmist asks how long God will be angry, asks him to pour his wrath on the nations that do not know him, and asks that the sins of their forefathers not be counted against them. He asks that the sighing of prisoners be heard, that the neighbours be repaid sevenfold, and promises endless thanks.
PSA 80:1-19	A prayer addressed to the Shepherd of Israel, three times repeating the refrain asking God to turn them again and make his face shine so they may be saved. The people have been fed with the bread of tears and made a source of contention for their neighbours. The central image is a vine brought out of Egypt and planted after the nations were driven out: it took deep root, covered the mountains with its shadow and reached the sea and the River. The psalmist asks why its walls have been broken so passers by pluck it and a boar out of the wood ravages it, and asks God to look down and visit the vine again.
PSA 81:1-16	The psalm opens by calling for tambourine, lyre, harp and trumpet at the new moon and full moon, since the festival is a statute of God. God then speaks: he lifted the burden from their shoulders, freed their hands from the basket, answered them in the secret place of thunder and tested them at Meribah. He tells them to have no foreign god and to open their mouths wide so he can fill them, but says his people did not listen and wanted none of him, so he let them follow their own stubborn hearts. He wishes they would listen, since he would then subdue their enemies and feed them the finest wheat and honey out of the rock.
PSA 82:1-8	A short courtroom psalm. God stands in the great assembly and judges among the gods, asking how long they will judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked. He orders them to defend the weak, the poor and the fatherless, to maintain the rights of the oppressed and to rescue the needy from the hand of the wicked. They neither know nor understand and walk about in darkness while the foundations of the earth shake. God tells them that although they are gods and sons of the Most High, they will die like men. The psalm closes asking God to arise and judge the earth.
PSA 83:1-18	The psalmist asks God not to stay silent, because his enemies have conspired with one mind to wipe out Israel so its name is remembered no more. Ten allies are named: Edom, the Ishmaelites, Moab, the Hagrites, Gebal, Ammon, Amalek, Philistia with Tyre, and Assyria. He asks God to treat them as he treated Midian, Sisera and Jabin at the river Kishon, and to make their nobles like Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah and Zalmunna. He asks that they be made like tumbleweed and chaff, pursued with tempest and storm, so that they know Yahweh alone is Most High over all the earth.
PSA 84:1-12	A pilgrim psalm. The psalmist's soul faints for the courts of Yahweh, and he notes that the sparrow and the swallow have found nests near God's altars. He calls blessed those who live in God's house and those who set their hearts on pilgrimage, who turn the valley of Weeping into a place of springs and go from strength to strength until they appear before God in Zion. He says a day in God's courts is better than a thousand elsewhere and that he would rather be a doorkeeper there than live in the tents of wickedness, since God is sun and shield and withholds nothing good from the blameless.
PSA 85:1-13	The psalm begins by recalling that God restored the fortunes of Jacob, forgave the people's iniquity and turned from his anger. It then asks him to do it again: to stop his indignation, to stop being angry forever and to revive them so they can rejoice. The psalmist says he will listen for God to speak peace to his people, provided they do not return to folly, and that salvation is near those who fear him. It ends with mercy and truth meeting, righteousness and peace kissing, truth springing out of the earth and the land yielding its increase.
PSA 86:1-17	A prayer from someone calling himself poor and needy. He asks to be heard and preserved, says he calls on God all day long, and describes God as good, ready to forgive and abundant in loving kindness. He says no god compares to God and that all nations will come and worship him. He asks to be taught God's way and to be given an undivided heart, and thanks God for delivering his soul from the lowest Sheol. Proud and violent men have risen against him, so he asks for strength and for a visible sign of God's goodness that would shame those who hate him.
PSA 87:1-7	A seven-verse psalm about Zion. God's foundation is in the holy mountains, and he loves the gates of Zion more than all the other dwellings of Jacob. The psalm imagines a register of peoples in which Rahab, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Ethiopia are recorded as acknowledging God, each entry reading that this one was born there. Of Zion it will be said that this one and that one were born in her, and the Most High himself will establish her. It ends with singers and dancers saying that all their springs are in her.
PSA 88:1-18	The bleakest psalm in the collection, and it does not resolve. The psalmist has cried day and night; his life draws near to Sheol and he counts himself among those going down into the pit, set apart among the dead whom God remembers no more. He says God has laid him in the lowest pit, afflicted him with all his waves, taken his friends away and made him an abomination to them. He asks whether the dead can praise God or his faithfulness be declared in the grave, then asks why God rejects him and hides his face. It ends with lover and friend put far from him and his companions in darkness.
PSA 89:1-52	The long psalm of the broken covenant. It opens praising God's faithfulness and quoting his oath to David: his offspring established forever and his throne built up to all generations. God's power is described in the heavenly council, over the pride of the sea and in the breaking of Rahab. Then God's speech promises David victory, sonship and an enduring throne, with punishment for disobedient descendants but no withdrawal of loving kindness. At verse thirty-eight the psalm turns: God has renounced the covenant, thrown the crown in the dust, broken the strongholds and let passers by rob the king. The psalmist asks how long, notes how short life is, and asks where the former loving kindness went.
PSA 90:1-17	A psalm about how brief human life is. God has been their dwelling place for all generations, and existed before the mountains were born. A thousand years in his sight are like yesterday or a watch in the night, while people are swept away in their sleep and sprout like grass that withers by evening. Their days pass in his wrath and their secret sins are set in the light of his presence. Life runs seventy years, or eighty with strength, and even that is labour and sorrow. The psalmist asks to be taught to count his days, and asks God to satisfy them in the morning and establish the work of their hands.
PSA 91:1-16	A psalm of protection. Whoever lives in the secret place of the Most High rests in his shadow and is delivered from the fowler's snare and from deadly pestilence, covered with God's feathers and sheltered under his wings. The reader is told not to fear the terror by night, the arrow by day, the pestilence that walks in darkness or the destruction at noon: a thousand may fall alongside him and ten thousand at his right hand without touching him. God puts his angels in charge of him so he does not strike his foot on a stone, and he treads on lion and cobra. God speaks at the end, promising to answer, deliver, honour and satisfy him with long life.
PSA 92:1-15	A psalm for giving thanks, calling for God's loving kindness to be proclaimed in the morning and his faithfulness at night, with lute, harp and lyre. The psalmist says God's works have made him glad and his thoughts are very deep, something a senseless man does not grasp: the wicked spring up like grass and flourish, but will be destroyed forever. His own horn has been raised like a wild ox's and he is anointed with fresh oil, having seen and heard of his enemies. The righteous flourish like a palm and grow like a cedar in Lebanon, planted in God's house and still bearing fruit in old age.
PSA 93:1-5	Five verses declaring that Yahweh reigns. He is clothed with majesty and armed with strength, and the world he established cannot be moved. His throne was established long ago and he himself is from everlasting. The floods lift up their voice and their waves, but Yahweh on high is mightier than the many waters and the breakers of the sea. The psalm closes saying his statutes stand firm and that holiness adorns his house forever.
PSA 94:1-23	The psalmist calls on God as the one to whom vengeance belongs and asks how long the wicked will triumph. They boast, break God's people in pieces, kill the widow, the alien and the fatherless, and say God will not see. He answers with a question: the one who made the ear and the eye surely hears and sees. He calls blessed the man God disciplines and teaches, promises God will not forsake his people, and recalls that when his foot was slipping God's loving kindness held him up. God has turned the wicked's own iniquity back on them and will cut them off.
PSA 95:1-11	An invitation to worship that turns into a warning. It calls people to sing and shout to the rock of their salvation, since Yahweh is a great King above all gods, holding the deep places of the earth and the mountain heights, and having made the sea and the dry land. They are told to kneel before their Maker, because they are the sheep in his care. Then God speaks: do not harden your heart as at Meribah and Massah, where the fathers tested him. He was grieved with that generation for forty years and swore in his wrath that they would not enter his rest.
PSA 96:1-13	A call for the whole earth to sing a new song to Yahweh, proclaim his salvation daily and declare his glory among the nations. The gods of the peoples are only idols, while Yahweh made the heavens, with honour and majesty before him and strength and beauty in his sanctuary. The families of nations are told to bring an offering into his courts and to worship him in holy array. The nations are to be told that Yahweh reigns and that he will judge with equity, and the heavens, earth, sea, fields and the trees of the woods are all called to rejoice because he comes to judge.
PSA 97:1-12	Another psalm announcing that Yahweh reigns, calling the earth and the many islands to be glad. Clouds and darkness surround him, righteousness and justice are the foundation of his throne, fire goes before him and burns up his adversaries, his lightning lights up the world and the mountains melt like wax at his presence. Those who serve carved images are shamed, and even the gods are told to worship him. Zion and the daughters of Judah are glad because of his judgments. The psalm ends telling those who love God to hate evil, since light is sown for the righteous.
PSA 98:1-9	A short psalm calling for a new song because God has done marvellous things, working salvation with his right hand and his holy arm. He has shown his righteousness in the sight of the nations and remembered his loving kindness to the house of Israel, so that all the ends of the earth have seen it. The whole earth is told to make a joyful noise with harp, trumpets and the ram's horn. The sea, the rivers and the mountains are called to join in, because God comes to judge the world with righteousness and equity.
PSA 99:1-9	The psalm declares that Yahweh reigns, enthroned among the cherubim, and calls the peoples to tremble. He is great in Zion and high above all peoples, and three times the psalm says he is holy. His strength loves justice, and he executes justice and righteousness in Jacob. The people are told to worship at his footstool. It recalls Moses and Aaron among his priests and Samuel among those who called on him: they called and he answered from the pillar of cloud, and he forgave them while still taking vengeance for what they did.
PSA 100:1-5	Five verses of straightforward praise. All lands are told to shout for joy to Yahweh, serve him with gladness and come before him singing. They are to know that Yahweh is God, that he made them and that they are his people and the sheep of his pasture. They are told to enter his gates with thanksgiving and his courts with praise, giving thanks and blessing his name, because Yahweh is good and his loving kindness endures forever, his faithfulness to all generations.
PSA 101:1-8	A ruler's declaration of policy. The psalmist promises to sing of loving kindness and justice and to live a blameless life, walking with a blameless heart inside his own house. He will set no vile thing before his eyes and will have nothing to do with faithless men, perverse hearts or evil. He will silence anyone who secretly slanders a neighbour and refuse to tolerate the haughty and conceited, while keeping his eyes on the faithful, who may live with him and serve him. No deceiver or liar will stay in his house, and morning by morning he will cut off the wicked from Yahweh's city.
PSA 102:1-28	A prayer of the afflicted. His days vanish like smoke, his bones burn like a torch, he forgets to eat and his bones stick to his skin. He compares himself to a pelican of the wilderness, an owl of the waste places and a lone sparrow on a housetop, mocked all day by enemies who use his name as a curse, eating ashes and mixing tears with his drink. The psalm then turns to Zion: God will arise and pity her at the set time, hear the groans of prisoners and free the condemned, and the nations will fear his name. He asks not to be taken away in the middle of his days, noting that the heavens will wear out like a garment while God stays the same.
PSA 103:1-22	The psalmist tells his own soul to praise God and not forget his benefits: forgiveness of sins, healing of diseases, redemption from destruction, a crown of loving kindness, and a youth renewed like the eagle's. God executes justice for the oppressed and made his ways known to Moses. He is merciful and slow to anger, does not stay angry forever, and has not repaid them according to their sins. His loving kindness is as high as the heavens above the earth, and he has removed their transgressions as far as east is from west. He remembers people are dust and their days are grass. The psalm ends calling angels, armies and all his works to praise him.
PSA 104:1-35	A psalm of creation. God is clothed in light, stretches the heavens like a curtain, lays the beams of his rooms in the waters, makes the clouds his chariot and walks on the wings of the wind. He set the earth's foundations and set a boundary the waters may not cross. Springs water the animals, birds nest by them, grass grows for livestock and plants for people, giving wine, oil and bread. The cedars, storks, wild goats and rock badgers all have their places, and the moon and sun mark the seasons. Lions hunt by night and people work by day. The sea holds innumerable creatures and leviathan, formed to play there. All of them wait for God to feed them, and die when he takes their breath away.
PSA 105:1-45	A retelling of Israel's history as thanksgiving. God remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, promising Canaan when they were few and foreigners, and warned kings not to touch his anointed ones. He called a famine and sent Joseph ahead, sold as a slave with his feet in shackles and his neck in irons, until the king freed him and made him lord of his house. Israel came into Egypt and grew strong, so God sent Moses and Aaron, and the plagues followed: darkness, blood, frogs, flies, lice, hail, ruined vines and locusts, and finally the firstborn. He brought the people out with silver and gold, none of them feeble, gave them cloud and fire, quails and bread from the sky and water from the rock, and gave them the lands of the nations.
PSA 106:1-48	The same history told as confession. The psalmist admits that they and their fathers have sinned: rebelling at the Red Sea, forgetting God's works, craving food in the desert, envying Moses and Aaron, and making the calf at Horeb, exchanging their glory for the image of a grass-eating bull. Moses stood in the breach to stop their destruction.
