The earth swallowed Dathan and Abiram's company, they despised the pleasant land, joined themselves to Baal Peor until Phinehas stopped the plague, and angered God at Meribah. They failed to destroy the nations, mixed with them, served their idols and sacrificed their own sons and daughters. God gave them to their enemies, rescued them many times, and remembered his covenant. The psalm ends asking to be gathered from among the nations.
PSA 107:1-43	A thanksgiving psalm built on four stories of rescue, each ending with the same call to praise. Wanderers in the desert, hungry and thirsty with no city, cried out and were led by a straight way to one. Prisoners sitting in darkness and iron because they rebelled cried out, and God broke their chains and the gates of brass. Fools made ill by their own disobedience, unable to eat and near the gates of death, cried out and were healed. Sailors caught in a storm that lifted them to the sky and dropped them to the depths cried out, and God stilled the waves and brought them to harbour. The psalm ends noting that God turns rivers into deserts and deserts into pools, pours contempt on princes and lifts the needy.
PSA 108:1-13	The psalmist declares his heart is steadfast, wakes harp and lyre and says he will wake up the dawn, promising to thank God among the nations because his loving kindness is great above the heavens. He asks God to be exalted and to save with his right hand. God speaks from his sanctuary, claiming Shechem, the valley of Succoth, Gilead and Manasseh, with Ephraim as his helmet and Judah his scepter, Moab his wash pot and Edom the target of his sandal. The psalm then asks who will bring them into the fortified city, notes that God has not gone out with their armies, and says the help of man is worthless.
PSA 109:1-31	The psalmist asks God not to stay silent while lying and hateful people surround him and repay his love with hostility. He then curses one particular enemy at length: let a wicked adversary stand at his right hand, let him be judged guilty, let his days be few and another take his office, let his children be fatherless and his wife a widow, let his children beg, let creditors seize everything, let his name be blotted out and his parents' sins remembered. The reason given is that the man never showed kindness and persecuted the poor. The psalmist describes himself as poor and needy, fading like an evening shadow, shaken off like a locust, thin from fasting and mocked by those who see him. He asks for help so people know it was God's hand, and ends promising thanks.
PSA 110:1-7	A short royal psalm. Yahweh tells the psalmist's Lord to sit at his right hand until his enemies are made his footstool, and says he will send out the rod of his strength from Zion to rule among his enemies. His people offer themselves willingly in holy array, and he has the dew of his youth out of the womb of the morning. Yahweh swears, without changing his mind, that he is a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek. The Lord at his right hand will crush kings, judge among the nations, heap up dead bodies and crush the ruler of the whole earth, drinking from a brook along the way.
PSA 111:1-10	A short psalm of thanks in the congregation. God's works are great and worth pondering, his righteousness endures forever, and he has made his wonderful works remembered. He is gracious and merciful, has given food to those who fear him, and always remembers his covenant, showing his people his power by giving them the heritage of the nations. The works of his hands are truth and justice, his precepts sure and established forever. He has sent redemption to his people and ordained his covenant forever. The psalm ends with the line that the fear of Yahweh is the beginning of wisdom.
PSA 112:1-10	A companion psalm describing the man who fears God and delights in his commandments. His offspring will be mighty and his household will hold wealth and riches, while his righteousness endures forever. Light dawns in darkness for the upright, and it goes well with the man who deals graciously and lends. He will never be shaken and will be remembered forever, unafraid of bad news because his heart is steadfast. He has given freely to the poor, and his horn will be exalted with honour. The wicked will see it, gnash their teeth and melt away.
PSA 113:1-9	A short call to praise. The servants of Yahweh are told to praise his name from now on and forever, and from the rising of the sun to its setting. He is high above all nations with his glory above the heavens, seated on high yet stooping down to see what happens in heaven and on earth. He raises the poor out of the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap to seat them with princes, and he settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother of children.
PSA 114:1-8	An eight-verse psalm about the exodus. When Israel went out of Egypt from a people of foreign language, Judah became God's sanctuary and Israel his dominion. The sea saw it and fled, the Jordan was driven back, and the mountains skipped like rams and the little hills like lambs. The psalm then turns and questions them directly, asking the sea why it fled, the Jordan why it turned back, and the hills why they skipped. It calls the earth to tremble before the God of Jacob, who turned rock into a pool and flint into a spring.
PSA 115:1-18	The psalm asks that glory go to God's name rather than to them, and answers the nations who ask where their God is by saying he is in the heavens and does whatever he pleases. It then mocks idols of silver and gold made by human hands, listing what they cannot do: mouths that do not speak, eyes that do not see, ears that do not hear, noses that do not smell, hands that do not feel and feet that do not walk. Those who make them become like them. Israel, the house of Aaron and all who fear God are each told to trust in him as help and shield, and promised blessing. The dead do not praise God, but the living will bless him forever.
PSA 116:1-19	The psalmist says he loves Yahweh because God listened to him. The cords of death had surrounded him and the pains of Sheol had taken hold, so he called out and was saved when he had been brought low. He tells his soul to return to its rest, since God has delivered him from death, his eyes from tears and his feet from falling. He recalls saying in haste that all men are liars. Asking what he can give in return, he says he will take the cup of salvation, pay his vows in front of all the people, and offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving in the courts of God's house in Jerusalem.
PSA 117:1-2	The shortest psalm, only two verses. It calls all the nations to praise Yahweh and all the peoples to extol him. The reason given is that his loving kindness toward them is great and his faithfulness endures forever. It closes with a call to praise.
PSA 118:1-29	A processional thanksgiving. It opens with Israel, the house of Aaron and all who fear God each repeating that his loving kindness endures forever. The psalmist called out in distress and was answered, and says it is better to take refuge in God than to trust in man or princes. Nations surrounded him like bees and were quenched like burning thorns. He says God punished him severely but did not hand him over to death, and asks for the gates of righteousness to be opened so he can enter and give thanks. The rejected stone has become the cornerstone, this is the day God has made, and blessed is the one who comes in his name. It ends with the sacrifice bound to the altar horns and the opening line repeated.
PSA 119:1-60	The first third of the longest psalm, an extended meditation on God's law using a rotating set of words for it: law, statutes, precepts, ordinances, testimonies, commandments, word. It opens by calling blameless those who walk in God's law, then asks how a young man can keep his way pure and answers that he does it by living according to God's word. The psalmist says he has hidden that word in his heart so as not to sin, calls himself a stranger on the earth, and describes his soul laid low in the dust and weary with sorrow. He asks for understanding, for his eyes to be turned from worthless things, and for his heart to be turned from selfish gain. Though princes slander him, he keeps meditating, and says he will speak of God's statutes before kings.
PSA 119:61-116	The middle third. The psalmist is bound by the ropes of the wicked but rises at midnight to give thanks, and twice admits that his suffering did him good: before he was afflicted he went astray, and it was good for him to be afflicted so he could learn. He says the law is worth more to him than thousands of pieces of gold and silver, and compares himself to a wineskin shrivelled in the smoke. He claims to understand more than his teachers and more than the aged, calls God's promises sweeter than honey, and says God's word is a lamp to his feet and a light to his path. Enemies dig pits and lay snares, and he says he nearly was wiped from the earth.
PSA 119:117-176	The final third. God rejects those who stray and puts the wicked away like dross, and the psalmist's flesh trembles at his judgments. He says his eyes fail looking for salvation, streams of tears run down his face because people do not keep the law, and his zeal wears him out. He calls himself small and despised. He rises before dawn to cry for help and keeps his eyes open through the night watches to meditate, rejoices at God's word like someone finding great plunder, and praises seven times a day. He asks for his cry to come before God and for help, and closes by saying he has gone astray like a lost sheep and asking God to come and seek his servant.
PSA 120:1-7	A short psalm of complaint. The psalmist cried out in distress and was answered, and asks to be delivered from lying lips and a deceitful tongue. He asks what will be done to that tongue and answers himself: sharp arrows of the mighty and coals of juniper. He then complains about where he lives, in Meshech and among the tents of Kedar, saying his soul has dwelt too long with someone who hates peace. He ends by saying he is for peace, but that when he speaks, they are for war.
PSA 121:1-8	Eight verses about being kept safe. The psalmist lifts his eyes to the hills and asks where his help comes from, then answers that it comes from Yahweh, who made heaven and earth. God will not let his foot be moved, and the one who keeps Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps. Yahweh is his keeper and his shade at his right hand, so the sun will not harm him by day nor the moon by night. God will keep him from all evil and keep his going out and his coming in, from now on and forever.
PSA 122:1-9	A pilgrim's psalm about Jerusalem. The psalmist was glad when people said they should go to Yahweh's house, and now their feet are standing inside the city's gates. He describes Jerusalem as a city built compactly together, where the tribes go up to give thanks as an ordinance requires and where the thrones of David's house are set for judgment. He calls for prayer for the peace of Jerusalem, saying those who love her will prosper, and asks for peace within her walls. For the sake of his brothers and of God's house, he will seek the city's good.
PSA 123:1-4	A four-verse plea for mercy. The psalmist lifts his eyes to the one who sits in the heavens and compares his waiting to servants watching their master's hand and a maid watching her mistress's hand: their eyes stay on God until he shows mercy. He then asks twice for mercy, saying they have endured much contempt, and describes their souls as filled with the scoffing of those who are at ease and the contempt of the proud.
PSA 124:1-8	A psalm of narrow escape, built around a repeated condition: if Yahweh had not been on their side when people rose up against them, they would have been swallowed alive, and the waters and the proud waters would have gone over them. The psalmist blesses God for not handing them over as prey to their teeth, and says their soul escaped like a bird out of a fowler's snare, with the snare broken. He ends saying their help is in the name of Yahweh, who made heaven and earth.
PSA 125:1-5	Five verses about security. Those who trust in Yahweh are like Mount Zion, unmovable and lasting forever, and as the mountains surround Jerusalem, so God surrounds his people from now on. The psalmist says the scepter of wickedness will not remain over the land allotted to the righteous, so that the righteous will not put their own hands to evil. He asks God to do good to the good and upright in heart, while those who turn to crooked ways will be led away with the workers of iniquity. It ends with peace on Israel.
PSA 126:1-6	A short psalm about return. When God brought back those who returned to Zion, they felt like people dreaming; their mouths filled with laughter and their tongues with singing, and the nations said God had done great things for them. The psalmist agrees, then asks God to restore their fortunes again, like streams in the Negev. He ends with the promise that those who sow in tears will reap in joy, and that the one who goes out weeping carrying seed will come back with joy, carrying his sheaves.
PSA 127:1-5	Five verses on effort and its limits. Unless Yahweh builds the house, the builders labour in vain, and unless he watches the city, the watchman guards it in vain. Rising early and staying up late eating the bread of toil is pointless, since God gives sleep to those he loves. The psalm then turns to children, calling them a heritage from Yahweh and the fruit of the womb his reward. They are like arrows in a warrior's hand, and the man with a full quiver of them will not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate.
PSA 128:1-6	A short blessing on the person who fears God and walks in his ways. He will eat the produce of his own labour and it will go well with him. His wife will be like a fruitful vine in the inner parts of his house, and his children like olive plants around his table. The psalm says this is how the man who fears God is blessed, then asks that Yahweh bless him out of Zion so he sees the good of Jerusalem all his life and lives to see his children's children. It closes with peace on Israel.
PSA 129:1-8	Eight verses looking back on long affliction. Israel is called to say that it has been afflicted many times from its youth, yet the attackers have not prevailed. The psalmist describes his back as ground that plowers plowed, making long furrows, and says Yahweh is righteous and has cut apart the cords of the wicked. He asks that all who hate Zion be turned back and be like grass on a housetop, which withers before it grows: the reaper cannot fill his hand with it, nobody binds it into sheaves, and no passer by pronounces a blessing over it.
PSA 130:1-8	A short psalm crying out from the depths. The psalmist asks God to hear him, then observes that if God kept a record of sins nobody could stand, but that there is forgiveness with him, which is why he is feared. He waits for Yahweh and hopes in his word, saying his soul longs for the Lord more than watchmen long for the morning, a phrase he repeats. He tells Israel to hope in Yahweh, because with him there is loving kindness and abundant redemption, and he will redeem Israel from all their sins.
PSA 131:1-3	The shortest psalm after 117, only three verses. The psalmist says his heart is not haughty and his eyes are not lofty, and that he does not concern himself with great matters or things too wonderful for him. He says he has stilled and quieted his soul, comparing it twice to a weaned child with its mother. The last verse turns outward and tells Israel to hope in Yahweh from now on and forever.
PSA 132:1-18	A psalm about David and the ark. It asks God to remember David's affliction and the vow he swore not to enter his house or sleep until he found a dwelling place for the Mighty One of Jacob. The people recall hearing of it in Ephrathah and finding it in the field of Jaar, and call on God to arise into his resting place along with the ark of his strength, with priests clothed in righteousness. God then swears to David that his descendants will sit on his throne if they keep the covenant, and declares that he has chosen Zion as his resting place forever, where he will bless her provision, satisfy her poor with bread, clothe her priests with salvation, make David's horn bud and shame his enemies.
PSA 133:1-3	Three verses on unity. The psalmist says how good and pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity, then gives two comparisons. The first is precious oil poured on the head, running down onto the beard, specifically Aaron's beard, and down to the edge of his robes. The second is the dew of Hermon coming down on the hills of Zion. It is there, he says, that Yahweh gives his blessing, even life forever.
PSA 134:1-3	The last of the pilgrim psalms, and only three verses long. It calls on all the servants of Yahweh who stand by night in his house to praise him and to lift up their hands in the sanctuary. The final verse turns the blessing back on them, asking that Yahweh, who made heaven and earth, bless them out of Zion.
PSA 135:1-21	A call for the servants who stand in God's house to praise him, because he is good and has chosen Jacob as his own possession. He is above all gods and does whatever he pleases in heaven, earth and the seas, raising clouds from the ends of the earth, making lightning with the rain and bringing wind out of his storehouses. The psalm recalls the striking of Egypt's firstborn, the signs done to Pharaoh, and the defeat of Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, whose land became Israel's heritage. It then mocks idols of silver and gold that cannot speak, see or hear, and calls the houses of Israel, Aaron and Levi to praise.
PSA 136:1-26	A responsive psalm in which every one of the twenty-six verses ends with the same line, that his loving kindness endures forever. The first half gives thanks for creation: the God of gods who made the heavens by understanding, spread the earth above the waters, and made the sun to rule by day and the moon and stars by night. The second half runs through the exodus and conquest: the Egyptian firstborn struck, Israel brought out with a strong hand, the Red Sea divided, Pharaoh's army overthrown, the wilderness crossed, Sihon and Og killed and their land given as an inheritance. It ends with God remembering them in their low estate and giving food to every creature.
PSA 137:1-9	An exile's psalm. The people sat down and wept by the rivers of Babylon when they remembered Zion, hanging their harps on the willows, because their captors demanded that they sing songs of Zion for entertainment. They ask how they can sing God's song in a foreign land. The psalmist swears that if he forgets Jerusalem his right hand should forget its skill and his tongue stick to the roof of his mouth. He asks God to remember what Edom said, calling for the city to be razed to its foundation, and ends with a curse on Babylon, calling happy whoever repays her and dashes her little ones against the rock.
PSA 138:1-8	The psalmist gives thanks with his whole heart and sings before the gods, bowing toward the holy temple and thanking God for his loving kindness and truth, since he has exalted his name and his word above all. He recalls that on the day he called, God answered and strengthened his soul. He says all the kings of the earth will give thanks and sing of God's ways, because although God is high he looks after the lowly and knows the proud from a distance. Though he walks in the middle of trouble, God will revive him and save him with his right hand.
PSA 139:1-24	A psalm about being fully known. God has searched him and knows his sitting down and rising up, perceives his thoughts from far off and knows every word before he says it. The psalmist asks where he could go to escape God's presence and answers himself: heaven, Sheol, the wings of the dawn, the far parts of the sea, and even darkness, which shines like day to God. He says God knit him together in his mother's womb and wrote his days in a book before any of them existed, and that God's thoughts outnumber the sand. He then asks God to kill the wicked, says he hates those who hate God with perfect hatred, and closes by asking God to search him and lead him in the everlasting way.
PSA 140:1-13	A prayer for deliverance from violent men who plot mischief and gather for war, with tongues sharpened like a serpent's and viper's poison under their lips. They have hidden a snare, spread nets by the path and set traps to trip his feet. The psalmist calls God the strength of his salvation who covered his head in the day of battle, and asks that the desires of the wicked not be granted. He asks that the mischief of their own lips cover them, that burning coals fall on them and that they be thrown into fire and miry pits. He says God will maintain the cause of the afflicted.
PSA 141:1-10	A short evening prayer. The psalmist asks God to come quickly and to receive his prayer like incense and his lifted hands like the evening sacrifice. He asks God to set a watch before his mouth and keep the door of his lips, and not to let his heart turn to evil or share in the delicacies of wicked men. He says a rebuke from a righteous man is a kindness, like oil on the head, and should not be refused. He speaks of bones scattered at the mouth of Sheol as when the plow breaks up the earth, keeps his eyes on God, and asks that the wicked fall into their own nets while he passes by.
PSA 142:1-7	A short cry for help. The psalmist says he pours out his complaint before God and tells him his troubles, and that when his spirit was overwhelmed God knew the route he was taking, on which a snare had been hidden. He looks to his right and finds nobody concerned for him, no refuge and nobody who cares for his soul. He tells God he is his refuge and his portion in the land of the living, asks to be delivered from persecutors stronger than himself, and asks to be brought out of prison so he can give thanks, saying the righteous will gather round him.
PSA 143:1-12	The psalmist asks God to hear him and not to enter into judgment with him, since no living person is righteous in his sight. The enemy has struck him to the ground and made him live in dark places like those long dead, so his spirit is overwhelmed and his heart desolate. He remembers the days of old and meditates on God's works, spreading out his hands with a soul thirsty as a parched land. He asks to hear God's loving kindness in the morning and to be taught the way he should walk and the will of God, and asks that his enemies be cut off, since he is God's servant.
PSA 144:1-15	The psalmist blesses God as his rock, who teaches his hands to war and is his fortress, high tower, deliverer and shield. He then asks what man is, that God cares for him, since man is like a breath and his days like a passing shadow. He asks God to part the heavens and come down, touch the mountains so they smoke, throw out lightning and send arrows to scatter the enemy, and to rescue him from great waters and from foreigners whose mouths speak deceit. He promises a new song on a ten-stringed lyre. The psalm ends describing prosperity: sons like well-nurtured plants, daughters like carved pillars, full barns, thousands of sheep, strong oxen and no outcry in the streets.
PSA 145:1-21	A psalm of praise arranged as steady declaration. The psalmist says he will exalt God as King and praise him every day forever, since God's greatness is unsearchable and one generation will commend his works to another. God is gracious, merciful, slow to anger and of great loving kindness, good to all, with tender mercies over all his works. His kingdom is everlasting and he is faithful in all his words. He upholds all who fall and raises those who are bowed down, and the eyes of all wait for him as he opens his hand and satisfies every living thing. He is near to all who call on him in truth, saves those who fear him, and destroys the wicked.
ROM 9:1-33	Paul says he grieves for his own people and would accept being cut off himself if it helped them. He argues that descent from Abraham never guaranteed inclusion: Isaac was chosen over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau before either was born. God told Moses he shows mercy as he chooses, and hardened Pharaoh to display his power. To the objection that this is unfair, Paul answers that a potter may shape one lump into different vessels. He quotes Hosea and Isaiah on a remnant, and concludes Israel pursued righteousness by works and tripped over the stumbling stone, while Gentiles reached it by faith.
ROM 10:1-21	Paul says Israel has real zeal but lacks knowledge, seeking a righteousness of its own instead of God's. Christ, he says, is the fulfillment of the law for everyone who believes. Righteousness by faith requires no journey to heaven or the abyss: the word is near, in the mouth and the heart. Confessing Jesus as Lord and believing in the resurrection saves, with no distinction between Jew and Greek. He then traces the chain backward from calling to believing to hearing to preaching to being sent, and closes with Isaiah's picture of God stretching out his hands all day to a people who will not listen.
ROM 11:1-36	Paul denies that God has rejected Israel, citing himself as an Israelite and Elijah's seven thousand who never bowed to Baal. A remnant remains by grace; the rest were hardened. Their stumbling brought salvation to the Gentiles, meant to provoke jealousy. He compares Israel to an olive tree with branches broken off and wild branches grafted in, and warns the Gentiles not to boast, since the same God who cut off natural branches can cut them off too, and can graft the old ones back. The hardening is partial and temporary. He ends praising God's unsearchable judgments.
ROM 12:1-21	The argument turns to practice. Paul asks his readers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice and to be transformed by renewed minds rather than shaped by the world. Nobody should overrate himself, since the church is one body with different functions, and he lists the gifts: prophecy, service, teaching, exhortation, giving, leading, showing mercy. A rapid run of instructions follows: sincere love, hospitality, blessing persecutors, weeping with those who weep, refusing revenge because vengeance belongs to God, and feeding a hungry enemy. Overcome evil with good.
ROM 13:1-14	Paul tells his readers to submit to governing authorities, arguing that all authority comes from God and that rulers punish wrongdoing rather than good work. Taxes, customs, respect and honour should all be paid. The only lasting debt is love, which fulfils the whole law: the commandments against adultery, murder, theft and coveting all reduce to loving your neighbour as yourself. He then invokes the hour, saying the night is nearly over. They should wake up, drop the deeds of darkness, put on the armour of light, and make no provision for the flesh.
ROM 14:1-26	Paul addresses a dispute over food and holy days. One believer eats anything, another only vegetables; one keeps a special day, another treats all days alike. Neither should despise or judge the other, since each answers to God, not to fellow believers, and all will stand before Christ's judgment seat. Nothing is unclean in itself, but it is wrong to eat in a way that trips up someone else, because the kingdom is righteousness, peace and joy rather than eating and drinking. He closes with a doxology to the God who can establish them.
ROM 15:1-33	Paul tells the strong to carry the weak rather than please themselves, since Christ did not please himself either, and stacks up quotations showing Gentiles praising God alongside Israel. He then explains his own work: a priestly ministry to the Gentiles, preached from Jerusalem to Illyricum, deliberately in places where nobody had preached before. He plans to visit Rome on his way to Spain, but first must take a collection from Macedonia and Achaia to the poor believers in Jerusalem. He asks them to pray that he survives the hostility waiting in Judea.
ROM 16:1-25	Paul commends Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae, and greets by name more than two dozen people in Rome, among them Prisca and Aquila, who risked their lives for him, and Andronicus and Junia, fellow prisoners noted among the apostles. Several are women he credits with hard work. He warns them to avoid people who cause divisions by smooth flattery, promises God will soon crush Satan under their feet, and passes on greetings from Timothy, Gaius, Erastus the city treasurer, and Tertius, who wrote the letter down.
S3Y 1:1-29	The three men walk about in the furnace praising God, and Azarias prays aloud. His prayer concedes that everything that has happened to them and to Jerusalem was just, because the people sinned and disobeyed, and that they have been handed to a lawless king. With no temple, prince, prophet or sacrifice left, he offers a contrite heart in place of rams and bullocks, and asks that their enemies be shamed. Meanwhile the king's men keep stoking the fire with naphtha, pitch and brushwood until the flame shoots forty-nine cubits and kills the Chaldeans standing nearby. An angel comes down and turns the furnace into a cool damp wind.
S3Y 1:30-68	Unharmed, the three sing a long litany of blessing. It begins with God himself, in his holy temple, on the cherubim, on his throne and in the firmament, then calls on the whole of creation in turn to bless the Lord: heavens and angels, sun, moon and stars, showers and dew, winds, fire and heat, nights and days, frost and snow, lightning and clouds, mountains, growing things, seas, springs, whales, birds and animals. It then turns to people: Israel, the priests, the servants, the humble of heart, and finally the three men themselves, who thank God for pulling them out of the fire.
SUS 1:1-33	In Babylon, Susanna, the beautiful and devout wife of the wealthy Joakim, walks daily in her husband's garden. Two elders appointed as judges watch her, admit their lust to each other, and arrange to catch her alone. When she sends her maids away to fetch oil and shuts the garden doors so she can wash, they emerge and demand she sleep with them, threatening otherwise to testify that they found her with a young man. She reasons that either way is ruin, and chooses not to sin, and screams. They shout too, and their story shames the household. Next day she is summoned before the assembly and unveiled.
SUS 1:34-64	The two elders lay hands on her head and testify that a young man lay with her in the garden and escaped because he was too strong for them. The assembly believes them because they are judges, and condemns her to death. Susanna prays aloud to the God who knows secrets, and as she is led out God stirs up a young man named Daniel, who declares he will have no part in her blood and demands the case be reopened. He separates the two witnesses and asks each which tree it happened under; one says a mastic, the other a holm. Convicted from their own mouths, they are executed instead.
TIT 1:1-16	Paul reminds Titus that he was left in Crete to put things in order and appoint elders in every city. He lists the requirements: blameless, married once, with believing children, not arrogant or quick tempered, not a drinker or violent or greedy, hospitable, self-controlled, and able to hold to sound teaching and refute those who contradict it. He warns about deceivers, especially from the circumcision party, who upset whole households for money and must be silenced, quotes a Cretan prophet calling Cretans liars and gluttons, and says such people profess to know God while denying him by their deeds.
TIT 2:1-15	Paul gives Titus instructions by group. Older men should be temperate and sound in faith; older women reverent, not slanderers or heavy drinkers, and teachers of good who train the young wives to love their husbands and children and manage their homes; younger men sober minded, with Titus himself an example of integrity in teaching so opponents have nothing to accuse. Slaves should be trustworthy and not steal, so the teaching is adorned. He grounds all of it in the appearing of God's grace, which trains people to renounce worldly desires while awaiting the blessed hope.
TIT 3:1-15	Titus should remind them to obey rulers, to be ready for good work, to slander nobody and to be gentle, since they too were once foolish and enslaved to their desires. God saved them not by their own righteous works but through mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal in the Holy Spirit, making them heirs of eternal life. Titus should insist on good works but avoid foolish controversies, genealogies and legal disputes, and drop a divisive person after two warnings. Paul asks Titus to come to Nicopolis, and to help Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way.
TOB 1:1-22	Tobit introduces himself in the first person: a man of the tribe of Naphtali deported to Nineveh, who alone in his family kept going to Jerusalem with his tithes while the rest sacrificed to Baal. In exile he refused Gentile food and became purveyor to King Enemessar, leaving ten talents of silver in trust with Gabael in Media. Under Sennacherib he secretly buried Israelites the king had killed, was denounced, went into hiding and lost everything but his wife Anna and son Tobias. After Sennacherib's murder, his nephew Achiacharus, now a senior official, brings him back.
TOB 2:1-14	Home again for Pentecost, Tobit sends Tobias to find a poor relative to share the meal. Tobias returns saying a fellow Israelite has been strangled and dumped in the marketplace. Tobit leaves his food untouched, hides the body until sunset, then buries it, weeping and remembering Amos on feasts turned to mourning. The neighbors mock him for burying the dead again after fleeing for it. Sleeping by the courtyard wall with his face uncovered, he is blinded by sparrow droppings, and the physicians cannot help. He then accuses Anna of stealing a kid she was given, and she asks what his charity has come to.
TOB 3:1-17	Tobit prays in grief, admitting the sins of his fathers, and asks God to let him die rather than keep hearing false reproach. On the same day in Ecbatana, Sarah, daughter of Raguel, is taunted by her father's maids: she has been given to seven husbands and the demon Asmodaeus killed each one before the marriage was consummated. She considers hanging herself, decides it would disgrace her father, and prays instead to be released or at least spared the insults. Both prayers are heard, and Raphael is sent to heal Tobit's eyes, bind Asmodaeus, and give Sarah to Tobias.
TOB 4:1-21	Remembering the silver left with Gabael, Tobit calls Tobias in for what amounts to a deathbed lecture. He tells him to bury him, honor his mother and bury her beside him, keep God's commandments, and give alms in proportion to whatever he has, since almsgiving delivers from death. He insists on marrying within the family, citing Noah, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and adds practical rules: pay a worker the same day, avoid drunkenness, do to no one what you hate, take advice from the wise. Only at the end does he mention the ten talents at Rages.
TOB 5:1-22	Tobias points out that he does not know Gabael, so Tobit gives him the receipt and tells him to hire a guide. He finds Raphael, an angel, without knowing it, and the stranger says he knows the road and has lodged with Gabael. Tobit interviews him; he gives his name as Azarias son of Ananias, a kinsman, and Tobit welcomes him warmly and settles on a drachma a day. They set off, with the dog following. Anna weeps that her son has been sent away for money and says what they have is enough, and Tobit assures her a good angel will travel with him.
TOB 6:1-17	Camping by the Tigris, Tobias goes to wash and a fish tries to swallow him. On the angel's instruction he hauls it out and keeps the heart, liver and gall, and they eat the rest. Asked what the parts are for, Raphael explains that burning the heart and liver drives off a demon and the gall cures white films on the eyes. Nearing Ecbatana he proposes that Tobias marry Sarah, whose inheritance is rightfully his. Tobias objects that seven husbands have died in her bride chamber. Raphael tells him to burn the fish parts and pray, and Tobias falls in love with her.
TOB 7:1-18	At Raguel's house in Ecbatana, Sarah meets them at the door and Raguel remarks how much the young man resembles his cousin Tobit. On learning Tobias is Tobit's son he embraces him and weeps, and weeps again at the news of the blindness. A ram is killed for the meal, but Tobias asks Raphael to raise the marriage at once. Raguel agrees, admitting frankly that seven husbands died in the night, and Tobias refuses to eat until the covenant is made. Sarah is given to him under the law of Moses, a contract is written and sealed, and Edna comforts her weeping daughter.
TOB 8:1-21	Brought in to Sarah after supper, Tobias burns the fish's heart and liver on the incense ashes; the demon flees to upper Egypt and Raphael binds him. Tobias gets up from the bed and asks Sarah to pray with him, blessing God for making Eve as a helper for Adam and saying he takes her in truth rather than lust. She answers amen and they sleep. Meanwhile Raguel digs a grave in the dark in case there is another death, then sends a maid at dawn, who finds them both alive. He fills in the grave, blesses God, and holds a fourteen-day wedding feast.
TOB 9:1-6	A short chapter of errands. Because Raguel has made him swear to stay for the full wedding feast, Tobias sends Raphael on to Rages with a servant and two camels to collect the money from Gabael and bring him back for the celebration, explaining that his father is counting the days and will grieve if he is late. Raphael lodges with Gabael, hands over the receipt, and receives the sealed bags of silver. The two of them set out early and reach the feast, and Tobias blesses his wife.
TOB 10:1-12	Tobit counts the days past the expected return and wonders whether Gabael has died. Anna concludes their son is dead and starts mourning, going out every day to watch the road, refusing food by day and weeping all night for the whole fourteen days. Tobias asks Raguel to release him; Raguel offers to send word instead, but gives in. He hands over Sarah and half his property in servants, cattle and money, and blesses them. He tells Sarah to honor her new parents, and Edna asks Tobias not to grieve her daughter and hopes to see grandchildren.
TOB 11:1-19	Nearing Nineveh, Raphael suggests they run ahead of Sarah to prepare the house, and tells Tobias to bring the fish gall. Anna, watching the road, sees them coming, runs out and says she is ready to die now that she has seen her son. Tobit stumbles toward the door and Tobias catches him, rubs the gall on his eyes, and after they sting and he rubs them the white films peel away. He sees his son, blesses God, and goes out to the gate to welcome Sarah, to the amazement of onlookers. The wedding feast is kept another seven days.
TOB 12:1-22	Tobit tells Tobias to pay his guide well, and Tobias offers half of everything they brought back. Taking them aside, the stranger urges them to praise God publicly, saying it is right to keep a king's secret but to proclaim God's works, and that almsgiving delivers from death. Then he reveals himself: he is Raphael, one of the seven angels who present the prayers of the saints, sent because of their prayers and Tobit's burials of the dead. He explains he never really ate or drank, tells them to write everything in a book, and vanishes. They fall on their faces in fear.
TOB 13:1-18	A psalm of praise written by Tobit. He blesses the God who scourges and shows mercy, leads down to the grave and brings up again, and tells the scattered Israelites to give thanks to him among the Gentiles, because their exile is discipline and he will gather them again if they turn to him wholeheartedly. The second half addresses Jerusalem directly, promising that the tabernacle will be rebuilt, that nations will come from far off with gifts, and that her walls and towers will be built with sapphires, emeralds and gold, her streets paved with precious stones and shouting Hallelujah.
TOB 14:1-15	The book closes with dates and a deathbed speech. Tobit went blind at fifty-eight and was healed eight years later. Grown very old, he tells Tobias to leave Nineveh with his six sons, because Jonah's prophecy against the city will come true, and predicts the desolation of Jerusalem, its rebuilding, and the nations turning to God and burying their idols. He asks to be buried decently with Anna, cites Achiacharus and Aman as proof that almsgiving delivers, and dies at a hundred and fifty-eight. Tobias moves to Ecbatana, inherits from both households, and hears of Nineveh's fall before his own death.
PSA 146:1-10	The psalmist vows to praise Yahweh as long as he lives, and warns against trusting princes, whose thoughts perish on the day their breath departs. Happy instead is the one whose help is the God of Jacob, maker of heaven, earth and sea, who keeps justice for the oppressed, feeds the hungry, frees prisoners, opens the eyes of the blind, and upholds foreigners, the fatherless and widows. Yahweh reigns forever.
PSA 147:1-20	Praise is called good, pleasant and fitting. Yahweh rebuilds Jerusalem and gathers Israel's outcasts, heals the brokenhearted, and counts the stars and calls them all by name. He takes no pleasure in the strength of a horse, but in those who hope in his loving kindness. He sends rain and grass, feeds livestock and young ravens, gives snow like wool and hail like pebbles, then melts them with a word. His statutes were shown to Israel alone.
PSA 148:1-14	A call for the whole creation to praise Yahweh, working downward from heaven to earth. Angels, sun, moon, stars and the waters above the heavens praise him because he commanded and they were created. Then sea creatures, lightning, hail, snow, wind, mountains, fruit trees, cedars, wild animals, livestock, birds, kings, princes, young men, maidens, old men and children. His name alone is exalted, and he has lifted up the horn of his people.
PSA 149:1-9	Israel is called to sing Yahweh a new song in the assembly of the saints, to rejoice in its maker and King, and to praise him with dance, tambourine and harp. Yahweh takes pleasure in his people and crowns the humble with salvation. The saints sing for joy on their beds, with the high praises of God in their mouths and a two-edged sword in their hand, to bind kings with chains and carry out the written judgment.
PSA 150:1-6	The last psalm is six verses of praise and nothing else. Praise God in his sanctuary and in his heavens, for his acts of power and his excellent greatness, with the sounding of the trumpet, harp and lyre, tambourine and dancing, stringed instruments and flute, loud cymbals and resounding cymbals. The closing line widens the summons past Israel and past instruments: let everything that has breath praise Yah.
HEB 5:1-14	A high priest is chosen from among men to offer gifts and sacrifices, and can deal gently with the ignorant because he shares their weakness. Nobody takes the office himself: Aaron was called, and so was Christ, named a priest after the order of Melchizedek. Christ prayed with strong crying and tears, learned obedience through suffering, and became the author of eternal salvation. The writer then breaks off to say his readers have grown dull, need milk rather than solid food, and ought to be teachers by now.
HEB 6:1-20	The writer urges his readers past elementary teaching: repentance, faith, baptisms, laying on of hands, resurrection, judgment. He warns that those once enlightened who then fall away cannot be renewed to repentance; land that drinks rain and grows thorns is burned. Still, he expects better of them, since God will not forget the service they showed the saints. God's promise to Abraham was sworn by himself, there being no one greater, so hope is an anchor of the soul reaching behind the veil, where Jesus has already gone.
HEB 7:1-28	Melchizedek met Abraham returning from battle, blessed him and received a tenth of the plunder. His name means king of righteousness, his city means peace, and he appears with no genealogy and no recorded beginning or end. Since the greater blesses the lesser, and Levi was still unborn in Abraham, the writer argues this priesthood outranks Aaron's. A change of priesthood requires a change of law. Jesus comes from Judah, holds his office by oath and endless life, and offered himself once for all.
HEB 8:1-13	The main point, the writer says, is this high priest, seated at the right hand of the throne in heaven, serving a tabernacle the Lord pitched rather than men. Earthly priests serve a copy and shadow; Moses was told to build to the pattern shown him on the mountain. He then quotes Jeremiah's new covenant at length: laws written on the heart, everyone knowing God, sins remembered no more. Calling a covenant new, he notes, makes the first one old and near vanishing.
HEB 9:1-28	The furniture of the first sanctuary is listed: lamp stand, table and show bread in the Holy Place, and behind the second veil the ark holding the manna, Aaron's rod and the tablets. Priests served the outer room continually; the high priest entered the inner one once a year with blood. Christ, the argument runs, entered heaven itself once with his own blood. A will takes effect only at a death, and under the law almost nothing is cleansed without blood. He will appear a second time.
HOS 1:1-11	Hosea is told to marry a prostitute, because the land itself has been unfaithful. He marries Gomer, and their three children are named as sentences against Israel: Jezreel, for the blood Yahweh will avenge on the house of Jehu; Lo-Ruhamah, meaning no more mercy for Israel, though Judah will be spared; and Lo-Ammi, meaning "not my people." The chapter then reverses itself, promising Israel will be as countless as sand and called sons of the living God, reunited with Judah under one head.
HOS 2:1-23	The marriage becomes the accusation. Israel is the wife who chased lovers for bread, wool, oil and wine, never realising Yahweh supplied all of it. He threatens to strip her bare, end her feasts and new moons, and lay waste the vines she called her wages. Then the tone turns: he will lead her into the wilderness and speak tenderly, give her the valley of Achor as a door of hope, and betroth her forever in righteousness and faithfulness. Lo-Ammi is undone: "You are my people."
HOS 3:1-5	Hosea is told to go and love an adulterous woman again, as a picture of how Yahweh loves Israel while it turns to other gods and raisin cakes. He buys her for fifteen pieces of silver and a homer and a half of barley, and requires that she stay with him and be with no one else, promising the same in return. Israel likewise will live a long stretch with no king, sacrifice or idol, then return and seek Yahweh and David their king.
HOS 4:1-19	Yahweh brings a formal charge against the land: no truth, no goodness, no knowledge of God, only cursing, lying, murder, theft and adultery, until the land mourns and even the fish die. The priests get the worst of it, since they feed on the people's sin, and the verdict is "like people, like priest." Idols consulted, sacrifices on every hilltop, drinking and prostitution that take away understanding. Israel is a stubborn heifer, and Ephraim is so joined to idols that the order is simply to leave him alone.
HOS 5:1-15	Priests, people and palace are all summoned to hear judgement. Ephraim is known to Yahweh and cannot hide; their deeds themselves prevent them turning back, and when they bring flocks and herds to seek him they will not find him, because he has withdrawn. Trumpets sound at Gibeah and Ramah. Yahweh calls himself a moth to Ephraim and rot to Judah, then a lion who tears and carries off. Ephraim turns to Assyria for a cure it cannot give.
1CH 18:1-17	David defeats the Philistines and takes Gath, subdues Moab, and beats Hadadezer of Zobah as far as the Euphrates, hamstringing the chariot horses. Twenty-two thousand Syrians of Damascus fall, and Syria pays tribute. The brass taken from Hadadezer's cities is noted as the metal Solomon later used for the bronze sea and pillars. Tou of Hamath sends gifts by his son Hadoram, and David dedicates all the plunder to Yahweh. Abishai defeats Edom. A list of David's officials closes the chapter.
1CH 19:1-19	Nahash of Ammon dies and David sends envoys to console his son Hanun. Hanun's advisers call them spies, so he shaves the men and cuts their clothes off at the buttocks; David tells them to wait at Jericho until their beards grow. Ammon hires thirty-two thousand chariots from Mesopotamia and Syria. Facing enemies front and behind, Joab splits the army with Abishai and both forces rout their opponents. David later crosses the Jordan and defeats the Syrian reinforcements, killing their commander Shophach.
1CH 20:1-8	In the spring Joab takes the army out, ravages Ammon and besieges Rabbah while David remains in Jerusalem. David comes for the end, takes the Ammonite king's crown of a talent of gold, plunders the city and puts its people to forced labour with saws and axes. Three later fights with the Philistines follow: Sibbecai kills Sippai, Elhanan kills Lahmi the brother of Goliath, and Jonathan the son of David's brother kills a giant with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot.
1CH 21:1-30	Satan incites David to number Israel. Joab objects, obeys under protest, and leaves out Levi and Benjamin; the total is over a million and a half swordsmen. God is displeased, and Gad offers David three punishments. David chooses to fall into God's hand, and seventy thousand die of plague. Seeing the angel with a drawn sword over Jerusalem, David buys the threshing floor of Ornan for six hundred shekels of gold, refusing a gift, and builds an altar. Fire answers from heaven and the plague stops.
1CH 22:1-19	David declares Ornan's threshing floor the site of God's house and begins stockpiling for it: dressed stone cut by resident foreigners, iron, brass beyond weighing, and cedar from Tyre and Sidon. He tells Solomon that he was forbidden to build because he had shed much blood, and that a son of peace would build instead. He hands over a hundred thousand talents of gold and a million of silver, urges Solomon to keep the law, and orders the princes of Israel to help him.
1CH 23:1-32	Old and near death, David makes Solomon king and organises the Levites. Thirty-eight thousand are counted from age thirty: twenty-four thousand for temple work, six thousand officers and judges, four thousand gatekeepers, four thousand musicians. The clans of Gershon, Kohath and Merari are listed, including Eleazar son of Mahli, who left only daughters, married by their cousins. Because the tabernacle no longer has to be carried, the age of service is lowered to twenty. Their duties are set: assist the priests, prepare offerings, and praise morning and evening.
1CH 24:1-31	The priests are organised into twenty-four courses. Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu died childless, so the line runs through Eleazar and Ithamar, with sixteen chief houses from Eleazar and eight from Ithamar. Zadok and Ahimelech help David divide them, and the order is settled by lot so that no house has precedence, the scribe Shemaiah recording the results before the king. The twenty-four names are listed in order, from Jehoiarib first to Maaziah last. The remaining Levites cast lots the same way.
1CH 25:1-31	David and the army captains set apart the sons of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun to prophesy with harps, lyres and cymbals. Heman, the king's seer, had fourteen sons and three daughters. Two hundred and eighty-eight trained musicians are counted in all. They cast lots for their turns of duty, small and great alike, teacher along with student, and the result is twenty-four groups of twelve, listed in order from Joseph to Romamti-Ezer.
1CH 26:1-32	The gatekeepers are divided by family and assigned gates by lot: east, north, south, west and the storehouse, with watchman set opposite watchman. Obed-Edom's line numbers sixty-two, the text noting that God blessed him. Hosah made a son who was not the firstborn his chief. Shebuel, descended from Moses, oversees the treasuries, and Shelomoth keeps the dedicated spoil given by Samuel, Saul, Abner and Joab for repairing the house. Other Levites serve as officers and judges outside Jerusalem.
1CH 27:1-34	Israel's militia is arranged in twelve divisions of twenty-four thousand men, each serving one month of the year, with its commander named. Then the tribal chiefs are listed. A note records that David did not count those under twenty, and that Joab began a census but never finished it, wrath having fallen on Israel, so the figure was left out of the royal records. Finally the stewards of the king's estates, herds, vineyards and camels, and his counsellors, including Ahithophel and Hushai the king's friend.
1CH 28:1-21	David assembles the officials of Israel and explains that he wanted to build the temple but was refused because he was a man of war who had shed blood. God chose Solomon to build it, and his kingdom will stand if he keeps the commandments. David charges his son to serve God with a whole heart, then hands over the plans: the porch, rooms, treasuries, courts, the weights of gold and silver for every vessel and lampstand, and the golden cherubim over the ark. He says the pattern came in writing from God's hand.
1CH 29:1-14	David tells the assembly that Solomon is young and the work is huge, and that beyond the materials already stockpiled he is giving his own treasure: three thousand talents of gold from Ophir and seven thousand of refined silver. He asks who else will give. The leaders respond with gold, silver, brass, iron and precious stones handed to Jehiel. The people rejoice at their own willingness, and David blesses God before them all, saying that greatness, power and riches are God's and that everything given came from God's hand first.
1CH 29:15-30	David's prayer continues, calling the people strangers whose days on earth are a shadow, and asking God to keep this willing spirit in them and to give Solomon a whole heart to build the house. The assembly blesses God and bows. The next day they sacrifice a thousand bulls, a thousand rams and a thousand lambs, and make Solomon king a second time, anointing Zadok as priest. Solomon prospers and all Israel obeys him. David dies old and rich after forty years, seven in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem.
1ES 1:1-29	The book opens with Josiah's Passover. He sets the priests in their courses, tells the Levites they need no longer carry the ark and should stand by their divisions, and gives thirty thousand lambs and kids and three thousand calves from his own property, with officials adding thousands more. The Levites roast and boil the offerings, serve the people first, then the priests who worked until night, while the singers and gatekeepers stay at their posts. No such Passover since Samuel. Josiah then rides out against Pharaoh at Carchemish, ignoring Jeremiah's word, and meets him at Megiddo.
1ES 1:30-58	Wounded, Josiah asks to be carried out, is taken to Jerusalem in a second chariot and dies. Jeremiah laments him and the mourning becomes a permanent ordinance. Joachaz reigns three months before Egypt deposes him and taxes the land, installing Joakim, who is later chained and taken to Babylon with the holy vessels. His son lasts three months and ten days. Zedekiah breaks his sworn oath and ignores Jeremiah, the leaders defile the temple, the messengers are mocked, and Babylon burns the house, breaks the walls and deports the survivors for seventy Sabbath years.
1ES 2:1-30	Cyrus, stirred by God in his first year, proclaims that the Lord of Israel has made him king of the world and charged him to build a house at Jerusalem, and that anyone of that people may go, helped by their neighbours with gold, silver, horses and cattle. He brings out the vessels Nebuchadnezzar had set among his idols and has his treasurer deliver them to Sanabassar, five thousand four hundred and sixty-nine in all. Later, officials in Samaria write to Artaxerxes calling Jerusalem a rebellious city; the archives agree, and the work is halted by force.
1ES 3:1-24	Darius holds a great feast for his whole empire, then goes to bed and wakes again. Three young bodyguards propose a contest: each will write down what he thinks is strongest, and the king will judge, the winner to wear purple, drink from gold, ride with golden bridles and be called the king's cousin. They seal their answers under his pillow. The first writes that wine is strongest, the second the king, the third women, but above all truth. Called to argue, the first says wine levels king and orphan, erases debt and memory, and turns friends to swords.
1ES 4:1-34	The second argues for the king: one man commands armies to kill and be killed, farmers to hand over their harvest, and cities to be built or levelled, and he sleeps while others keep watch. The third, Zerubbabel, argues for women: they bear the kings and the men who plant the vineyards, men leave father and country for a wife, and thieves bring their plunder home to her. He describes seeing the concubine Apame take the crown off the king's head and strike him, while he flattered her to be reconciled. Then he turns to truth.
1ES 4:35-63	Zerubbabel argues that the earth is great, heaven high and the sun swift, but greater is the one who made them, and truth is stronger than all. Wine, kings, women and all people are unrighteous and perish, but truth lives and conquers. The assembly shouts that truth is great. Offered anything, Zerubbabel asks only that Darius keep his vow to rebuild Jerusalem and return the vessels. The king kisses him and writes letters for safe passage, cedar from Lebanon, freedom from tribute, and yearly grants for the temple and its offerings.
1ES 5:1-29	The heads of families are chosen to go up by tribe, with wives, children, servants and cattle, and Darius sends a thousand horsemen to escort them safely to Jerusalem, with tabrets and flutes playing them out. The leaders are named, Zerubbabel and Jeshua at their head, and the returning families are listed by ancestor and then by town, from the sons of Phoros at two thousand one hundred and seventy-two down through Bethlehem, Netophah and Anathoth. Four priestly houses follow, numbering over four thousand, then seventy-four Levites, a hundred and twenty-eight singers and a hundred and thirty-nine gatekeepers.
1ES 5:30-50	The temple servants and the sons of Solomon's servants are listed, three hundred and seventy-two in all. Some who came up could not show their families or descent, and priests whose names were not found in the register, including one who married Augia and took her father's name, were barred from office until a high priest with Urim and Thummim should arise. Israel from twelve years old upward numbers 42,360, with servants, singers and livestock counted. In the seventh month they gather and set up the altar, hostile though the surrounding nations are.
1ES 5:51-73	They keep the feast of tabernacles and the regular offerings although no temple is yet standing, paying masons and carpenters and sending goods to Sidon and Tyre for cedar floated to Joppa. In the second month of the second year the foundation is laid, Levites of twenty and upward overseeing the work, priests in vestments with trumpets and the sons of Asaph with cymbals. The elders who had seen the former house weep so loudly the trumpets cannot be heard. Neighbours who offer to help are refused, and they obstruct the work for two years.
1ES 6:1-19	In Darius' second year Haggai and Zechariah prophesy, and Zerubbabel and Jeshua restart the building with the prophets helping them. Sisinnes, governor of Syria and Phoenicia, arrives with Sathrabuzanes to ask by whose order they build and who the builders are, but they are not stopped while the question goes to the king. Their letter reports great new stonework going up fast, and quotes the elders' answer: they are servants of the God who made heaven and earth, rebuilding what Nebuchadnezzar burned, under an order of Cyrus who returned the vessels.
1ES 6:20-34	The letter notes that Sanabassarus laid the foundation and the work has dragged on unfinished ever since, and asks that the royal archives at Babylon be searched. The scroll is found instead at Ekbatana in Media, recording Cyrus' order with the temple's dimensions and the charge on the royal treasury. Darius orders the governors not to meddle, tells them to fund the work and the daily sacrifices from provincial tribute so prayers may be made for the king, and rules that anyone breaking the order shall be hanged on a beam from his own house.
1ES 7:1-15	Sisinnes and Sathrabuzanes carry out the order carefully, assisting the elders, and the work prospers while Haggai and Zechariah prophesy. The house is finished on the twenty-third of Adar in Darius' sixth year, by the commandment of God and the consent of Cyrus, Darius and Artaxerxes. At the dedication they offer a hundred bulls, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs and twelve goats for the twelve tribes. Passover follows on the fourteenth of the first month, kept by all who had separated themselves from the surrounding peoples, with seven days of unleavened bread.
1ES 8:1-29	Under Artaxerxes, Ezra, traced through sixteen generations to Aaron, goes up from Babylon as a scribe skilled in the law of Moses, taking priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants with him, leaving at the new moon of the first month and arriving in the fifth. The king's written commission lets any willing Jew go, sends gifts vowed by the king and his seven counsellors, orders the treasurers of Syria and Phoenicia to supply up to a hundred talents of silver, exempts all temple staff from tax, and tells Ezra to appoint judges and teach those who do not know the law.
1ES 8:30-65	Ezra lists the family heads who came up with him, each with his number of men. Camped three days at the river Theras, he finds no priests or Levites in the company, and sends eleven leading men to Iddo at Casiphia to ask for ministers; they return with eighteen of Mahli's line, twenty more, and two hundred and twenty temple servants. He vows a fast rather than ask the king for an escort, having said God protects those who seek him. He weighs out silver, gold and vessels to twelve priests, and it is weighed again in Jerusalem.
1ES 8:66-96	The offerings made and the king's orders delivered, the leading men tell Ezra that Israel, priests and Levites have not separated from the surrounding peoples, and that the rulers and nobles led the way. He tears his clothes and his holy garment, pulls out his hair, and sits until the evening sacrifice, then prays that sins have reached to heaven since their fathers' time, that mercy left them a root, and that they cannot stand before God. A great crowd gathers weeping, and Jechonias proposes an oath to put away the foreign wives and their children.
1ES 9:1-28	Ezra withdraws to a chamber and neither eats nor drinks, mourning. A proclamation orders everyone of the captivity to Jerusalem within two or three days, on pain of losing their cattle to the temple and being expelled from the assembly. They gather on the twentieth of the ninth month, trembling in foul weather, and agree to Ezra's charge, but ask that commissioners handle the matter over time since the crowd is large and the rain heavy. Four men take it on, the inquiry runs three months, and the priests involved are named, beginning with four of Jeshua's line.
1ES 9:29-55	The register of those with foreign wives continues through the families of Bebai, Mani, Addi, Annas, Asom, Baani and others, and the text states that they put them away with their children. On the new moon of the seventh month the whole assembly gathers before the temple porch and asks Ezra to bring the law. He reads from a wooden platform, with seven men on his right and six on his left, from morning until midday, and the Levites explain it. Told the day is holy, the people stop weeping and go to eat, drink and send portions to those who have nothing.
1MA 6:1-32	Antiochus tries to plunder a rich temple at Elymais in Persia and is driven off. Retreating toward Babylon he hears his armies in Judah are routed, Lysias shamed and the abomination pulled down. He falls sick with grief, tells his Friends he is dying for what he did at Jerusalem, hands Philip his diadem, robe and signet to raise his son, and dies. Lysias crowns the boy as Eupator instead. Petitioned by the citadel garrison, the new king marches with a hundred thousand foot, twenty thousand horse and thirty-two elephants against Bethsura.
1MA 6:33-63	The elephants are shown the blood of grapes and mulberries to stir them, each given a thousand armoured men, five hundred horsemen and a wooden tower of fighters. Six hundred of the king's men fall. Eleazar Avaran, believing the king rides the tallest beast, stabs it from below and dies beneath it. The Jews withdraw. Bethsura surrenders for want of food in the sabbath year, and the besieged sanctuary starves. Hearing Philip is seizing the government, Lysias makes peace granting the Jews their own laws. The king swears to it, then pulls the wall down anyway.
1MA 7:1-24	Demetrius, son of Seleucus, leaves Rome and takes a city by the sea; the army seizes Antiochus and Lysias, and he has them killed without looking at them. Alcimus, wanting the high priesthood, accuses Judas before him. Demetrius sends Bacchides with Alcimus and an army, offering peace deceitfully; Judas will not listen. The Hasidaeans trust Alcimus because he is a priest of Aaron's line, and sixty of them are killed in one day. Bacchides kills more and throws them into the great pit, leaves troops with Alcimus, and goes home.
1MA 7:25-50	Alcimus goes back to the king with fresh accusations, and Demetrius sends Nicanor to destroy the people. Nicanor's peaceful approach conceals a plan to seize Judas, which Judas discovers. They fight at Capharsalama, where five hundred of Nicanor's men fall. Nicanor mocks the priests and swears to burn the house unless Judas is handed over. On the thirteenth of Adar the armies meet at Adasa. Nicanor falls first, his army throws down its arms, and the villages close in until none are left. His head and right hand are hung up beside Jerusalem.
1MA 8:1-15	Judas hears reports of the Romans: their conquest of the Gauls, their seizure of the silver and gold mines of Spain, their defeat of Philip and Perseus, and their capture of Antiochus the Great, who came with a hundred and twenty elephants, was taken alive, and had to pay tribute, give hostages and surrender India, Media and Lydia. They crushed the Greeks, they make and depose kings, and none of them wears a crown or purple. Three hundred and twenty men sit in their senate house daily.
1MA 8:16-32	The report adds that the Romans entrust government to one man each year, with no envy among them. Judas sends Eupolemus son of John and Jason son of Eleazar on the long journey to Rome to make a treaty. The senate agrees and writes it on tablets of brass: each side will help the other in war and supply no food, arms, money or ships to the other's enemies, and either party may amend the terms. Rome also writes to Demetrius, asking why he oppresses their friends the Jews, and threatening war.
1MA 9:1-24	Demetrius sends Bacchides and Alcimus into Judah again. Judas camps at Elasa with three thousand chosen men against twenty thousand foot and two thousand horse; most slip away, leaving eight hundred. He refuses to flee, saying he will not leave a reproach against his glory. The battle runs from morning to evening; Judas breaks the right wing and pursues it to Mount Azotus, but the left wing closes behind him and he falls. Jonathan and Simon bury him at Modin, and Israel mourns. Lawless men rise up, and a great famine follows.
1MA 9:25-50	Bacchides puts the ungodly in charge of the country and hunts down Judas's friends. They choose Jonathan as their leader in his brother's place, and Bacchides seeks to kill him, so Jonathan withdraws to the wilderness of Tekoah. The children of Jambri seize his brother John and his baggage, so Jonathan and Simon ambush a Jambri wedding party coming from Nadabath and turn the marriage into mourning. Cornered at the Jordan, Jonathan strikes at Bacchides, who turns away, and the company swims the river. About a thousand of Bacchides' men fall.
1MA 9:51-73	Bacchides garrisons the fortresses and holds the sons of the chief men hostage in the citadel. Alcimus orders the wall of the inner court pulled down, undoing the work of the prophets, and while the demolition begins he is struck with a palsy, loses his speech, and dies in great torment. Bacchides goes home and the land rests two years. The lawless call him back; Jonathan raids the countryside while Simon burns the siege engines at Bethbasi. Beaten, Bacchides kills his advisers, makes peace, returns the captives, and never comes back.
1MA 10:1-32	Alexander Epiphanes takes Ptolemais and claims the throne, so Demetrius writes to Jonathan first, authorising him to raise an army and releasing the hostages in the citadel. Jonathan rebuilds the walls of Jerusalem, and the foreigners abandon Bacchides' strongholds. Alexander then appoints Jonathan high priest and King's Friend, sending a purple robe and a crown of gold; Jonathan puts on the holy garments at the feast of tabernacles. Demetrius answers with a longer offer still, cancelling tributes, salt duties and crown taxes, freeing Jerusalem, and yielding the citadel.
1MA 10:33-58	Demetrius's offer continues: captives freed, feasts and sabbaths exempt from exaction, thirty thousand Jews enrolled and paid as royal troops under their own officers and laws, three Samaritan districts annexed to Judea, Ptolemais given to the sanctuary, and building costs met from royal revenue. Jonathan and the people give it no credence, remembering the harm he had done, and stay with Alexander. The two kings join battle; Alexander's army flees, but Demetrius falls that day. Alexander then marries Ptolemy's daughter Cleopatra at Ptolemais with great pomp.
1MA 10:59-89	Alexander summons Jonathan to Ptolemais, has him clothed in purple, seats him beside himself, and proclaims that no man may complain against him; his accusers flee, and he is made a Chief Friend and governor of a province. Demetrius's son comes from Crete, and his general Apollonius taunts Jonathan to come down from the mountains into the plain. Jonathan takes Joppa, then meets Apollonius at Azotus, where hidden horsemen surround him and throw darts all day until they tire. Simon breaks the phalanx; about eight thousand die, and Jonathan is given Ekron.
1MA 11:1-26	Ptolemy of Egypt enters Syria with peaceful words and garrisons every city he passes. At Azotus he is shown the burned temple of Dagon and the heaps of dead as a complaint against Jonathan, and says nothing. He then takes his daughter back from Alexander, gives her to Demetrius, and wears the diadems of both Egypt and Asia. Alexander is routed, flees to Arabia, and Zabdiel the Arabian sends his head to Ptolemy, who dies three days later. Demetrius reigns. Jonathan besieges the citadel, is summoned to Ptolemais, goes with gifts, and is honoured.
1MA 11:27-48	Demetrius confirms Jonathan's high priesthood and, for three hundred talents, frees Judea and the three Samaritan districts from tribute, tenths, tolls, saltpits and crown taxes, in a letter to be posted on the holy mount. Feeling secure, he dismisses his own forces, who hate him for it. Tryphon begins working to put Alexander's young son Antiochus on the throne. Jonathan asks Demetrius to clear the citadel; Demetrius asks for troops instead, and Jonathan's three thousand men save him when a hundred and twenty thousand citizens of Antioch rise to kill him.
1MA 11:49-74	The city surrenders, and the Jews return to Jerusalem with spoil and honour. Demetrius, secure again, breaks every promise he made to Jonathan. Tryphon returns with the young Antiochus, wins over the troops Demetrius dismissed, routs him, and takes Antioch and the elephants. The boy king confirms Jonathan's high priesthood and makes Simon captain from the Ladder of Tyre to the borders of Egypt. Jonathan burns the suburbs of Gaza until it yields. At Hazor his army is ambushed and flees but for two captains; Jonathan prays, rallies, and three thousand of the enemy fall.
1MA 12:1-28	Jonathan sends envoys to Rome to renew the friendship, and writes to the Spartans as well, citing an old letter from king Arius to the high priest Onias claiming the Spartans and the Jews are kindred, both of the stock of Abraham. His letter says the Jews need nothing, having the holy books, but do not wish to become estranged, and that they remember the Spartans in their sacrifices. Demetrius's princes return with a larger army; Jonathan meets them at Hamath, learns from spies of a planned night attack, and keeps his men armed and watching.
1MA 12:29-53	The enemy slip away in the night leaving their fires burning, and Jonathan does not know until morning; he pursues, fails to catch them, and raids the Zabadaean Arabs instead. Simon takes Joppa before Demetrius's men can. They raise the walls of Jerusalem and build a mound to cut the citadel off from the city so no one can buy or sell there. Tryphon, wanting the crown, greets Jonathan warmly at Bethshan, persuades him to send his army home and come to Ptolemais with a thousand men, then shuts the gates and seizes him. Israel mourns.
1MA 13:1-29	Simon calls Jerusalem together, says his whole family has died for Israel and he is left alone, and promises to avenge the nation; the people make him leader in place of Judas and Jonathan. He finishes the walls and takes Joppa. Tryphon demands a hundred talents and two of Jonathan's sons as the price of release; Simon knows it is deceit but pays, so that no one can blame him. Tryphon keeps Jonathan anyway, is turned back by a great snowfall, and kills him at Bascama. Simon buries him at Modin under a monument of seven pyramids with carved arms and ships.
1MA 13:30-53	Tryphon murders the young king Antiochus and takes the crown himself. Simon fortifies Judea and sends Demetrius a golden crown and a palm branch; Demetrius grants immunity, forgives what is owed and confirms the strongholds. In the 170th year the Gentile yoke is lifted and contracts are dated to the first year of Simon. He takes Gazara by siege engine, expels the inhabitants and cleanses the houses of idols. The starving citadel surrenders, and Simon enters it with palm branches, harps and hymns, making the day an annual feast. His son John is made commander.
1MA 14:1-27	Demetrius goes into Media for reinforcements and is taken alive by Arsaces and imprisoned. Under Simon the land has rest: Joppa becomes a harbour, the borders are enlarged, the fields yield, old men sit talking in the streets, and every man sits under his vine and fig tree with none to make him afraid. Rome and Sparta, hearing Jonathan is dead and Simon has succeeded him, write on tablets of brass to renew the alliance, and the Spartan letter is read at Jerusalem. Simon sends Numenius to Rome with a gold shield of a thousand pound weight.
1MA 14:28-49	The decree is read at a great assembly at Asaramel. It recites what Mattathias's sons did, how Simon armed the nation at his own expense and fortified Bethsura, Joppa and Gazara, and how Demetrius confirmed him. The people make Simon leader and high priest forever, until a faithful prophet arises, with charge of the sanctuary, the country, the arms and the strongholds. No one may contradict him, convene an assembly without him, or wear purple or a gold buckle. It is engraved on brass in the sanctuary, with copies in the treasury.
1MA 15:1-22	Antiochus, son of Demetrius, writes from the isles to Simon, confirming every remission earlier kings granted, releasing all debts, leaving Jerusalem and the sanctuary free, letting him keep his arms and strongholds, and allowing him to coin his own money. He lands in the 174th year, the armies desert to him, and he besieges Tryphon at Dor by land and sea with a hundred and twenty thousand men. Numenius returns from Rome with a letter from the consul Lucius telling the kings and countries not to harm the Jews and to hand fugitives over to Simon.
1MA 15:23-41	The Roman letter is copied to Sparta, Delos, Rhodes, Cyprus, Cyrene and a long list of other places. Simon sends Antiochus two thousand picked men with silver and gold; Antiochus refuses them and repudiates every agreement, sending Athenobius to demand Joppa, Gazara and the citadel, or a thousand talents. Athenobius sees Simon's gold and silver plate and is amazed. Simon answers that they hold only their fathers' inheritance, and offers a hundred talents for the two towns. Athenobius leaves in a rage. Cendebaeus is made coastal commander and raids Judea from Kidron.
1MA 16:1-24	John brings word from Gazara of Cendebaeus's raids, and Simon, now old, hands the war to his sons Judas and John with twenty thousand men. At the brook the troops hesitate, so John crosses first and they follow; Cendebaeus is routed, Judas is wounded, Kidron is burned and about two thousand fall. Ptolemy son of Abubus, Simon's son in law and captain of the plain of Jericho, invites Simon and his sons Mattathias and Judas to a banquet at the stronghold of Dok and kills them there. He sends men to kill John at Gazara, but John is warned and kills them first.
2CH 1:1-17	Solomon, established as king, leads the assembly to the high place at Gibeon, where the Tent of Meeting and the bronze altar Bezalel made still stand, and offers a thousand burnt offerings. That night God tells him to ask for anything. Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge to govern so large a people. Because he did not ask for wealth, honour or long life, God grants wisdom and adds riches beyond any king before or after. Solomon returns to Jerusalem and accumulates chariots, horses and silver.
2CH 2:1-18	Solomon determines to build a house for God and a palace for himself, and musters a workforce of seventy thousand carriers, eighty thousand quarrymen and three thousand six hundred overseers. He writes to Huram of Tyre asking for timber and a master craftsman, admitting that heaven itself cannot contain God and the house can only be a place to burn incense. Huram replies in writing, blesses Israel's God, and sends Huram-abi, whose mother was of Dan, promising timber floated by sea to Joppa. The labourers are the resident foreigners, counted at 153,600.
2CH 3:1-17	Solomon begins building on Mount Moriah, where God appeared to David, on Ornan's threshing floor, in the fourth year of his reign. The house measures sixty cubits by twenty, with a porch as wide as the house. Cypress ceilings and walls are overlaid with gold from Parvaim and engraved with cherubim, the most holy place alone taking six hundred talents; even the nails weigh fifty shekels of gold. Two carved cherubim stand with wings spanning twenty cubits. A veil of blue, purple and crimson hangs, and two pillars are named Jachin and Boaz.
2CH 4:1-22	The furnishings are made: a bronze altar twenty cubits square, and a cast metal sea ten cubits across resting on twelve oxen facing outward in four directions, holding three thousand baths.
